representations.normalized:
Let n be a positive integer and let C[z] = C[z_1, ..., z_n] denote the polynomial ring in n variables over the complex numbers. For a polynomial P(z) ∈ C[z], define its Hessian matrix by Hes(P) = (∂²P/∂z_i ∂z_j)_{1 ≤ i,j ≤ n}, and call P Hessian nilpotent if Hes(P) is a nilpotent matrix (equivalently, all eigenvalues of Hes(P) are zero, viewed as a matrix with entries in C[z]). Let Δ = Σ_{i=1}^n ∂²/∂z_i² denote the Laplace operator on C[z].

Prove or disprove: for every homogeneous polynomial P(z) ∈ C[z] of degree 4 that is Hessian nilpotent, there exists a positive integer M (depending on P) such that Δ^m(P(z)^{m+1}) = 0 for all integers m ≥ M.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The statement is the degree-4 Vanishing Conjecture introduced by Wenhua Zhao, shown to be equivalent to the classical Jacobian Conjecture. The Jacobian Conjecture remains open in general, and the degree-4 Vanishing Conjecture is likewise reported as an open problem in subsequent literature (e.g., surveys of Hessian nilpotent polynomials and Vanishing Conjecture work through the 2010s and 2020s). Only partial results in low dimensions or under additional hypotheses are known.

Determine all pairs of integers $(x,y)$ satisfying the equation
$$\binom{x}{2}=\binom{y}{5},$$
equivalently
$$\frac{x(x-1)}{2}=\frac{y(y-1)(y-2)(y-3)(y-4)}{120},$$
where $\binom{a}{b}$ denotes the usual binomial coefficient extended to integers $a$ by the polynomial $a(a-1)\cdots(a-b+1)/b!$.

$$\binom{x}{2}=\binom{y}{5},$$
equivalently
$$\frac{x(x-1)}{2}=\frac{y(y-1)(y-2)(y-3)(y-4)}{120},$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The equation $\binom{x}{2}=\binom{y}{5}$ defines a curve of genus 2, which falls outside the elliptic cases (k,l)∈{(2,3),(2,4),(2,6),(2,8),(3,4),(3,6),(4,6),(4,8)} settled by Stroeker and de Weger (1999). The case (k,l)=(2,5) was subsequently resolved by Bugeaud, Mignotte, Siksek, Stoll and Tengely via Chabauty-type and Mordell–Weil sieve methods on the associated hyperelliptic curve, yielding a finite explicit list of integral solutions.

representations.normalized:
Work over the formal power series ring $\mathbb{C}[[z]] = \mathbb{C}[[z_1,\ldots,z_n]]$. For $P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]]$, let $\nabla P = (\partial P/\partial z_1,\ldots,\partial P/\partial z_n)$ and let $\mathrm{Hes}\,P = \big(\partial^2 P/\partial z_i\partial z_j\big)_{1\le i,j\le n}$ denote its Hessian matrix. Write $o(P)$ for the order (lowest total degree of a nonzero monomial) of $P$. Call $P$ \emph{Hessian nilpotent (HN)} if $\mathrm{Hes}\,P$ is a nilpotent matrix over $\mathbb{C}[[z]]$.

Assume $P\in\mathbb{C}[[z]]$ satisfies $o(P)\ge 2$ and that $(\mathrm{Hes}\,P)(0)$ is nilpotent. Define the symmetric formal map
$$F(z) = z - \nabla P(z),$$
and let $G(z) = z + H(z)$ be its formal compositional inverse, so $F(G(z)) = G(F(z)) = z$. It is known that the higher-order part $H(z)$ is itself a gradient, i.e.\ there exists a unique formal power series $Q(z)\in\mathbb{C}[[z]]$ with $o(Q)\ge 2$ and $Q(0)=0$ such that $H(z) = \nabla Q(z)$; the series $Q$ is called the \emph{inversion pair} of $P$.

The series $P$ is called \emph{self-inverting} if $Q(z) = P(z)$.

Question: must every self-inverting polynomial, or more generally every self-inverting formal power series, be Hessian nilpotent?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

A web search did not surface a published resolution of this specific question (whether all self-inverting polynomials/formal power series are Hessian nilpotent). Related work by Wenhua Zhao and others on Hessian nilpotent polynomials and the reduction of the Jacobian conjecture to a vanishing conjecture remains active, and only partial results on self-inverting maps (e.g., for sums of fourth powers under linear independence or small numbers of vectors) appear. No source found confirming a complete solution; status is unknown but apparently still open.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The equation x^2 - 2 = y^p has received substantial attention. It has been resolved for small primes (p ≤ 13) and for sufficiently large primes (p > 911, with bounds extended further via linear forms in logarithms, showing any non-trivial solution would satisfy y > 10^1000). A 2025 arXiv preprint by Katz and Pratt continues the program, but a complete proof covering all primes p ≥ 3 has not yet been published; the problem remains only partially solved.

representations.normalized:
Let $\mathbb{C}[[z]] = \mathbb{C}[[z_1,\dots,z_n]]$ denote the ring of formal power series in $n$ variables over $\mathbb{C}$, and let $\Delta = \sum_{i=1}^n \partial^2/\partial z_i^2$ be the standard Laplacian. A formal power series $P(z) \in \mathbb{C}[[z]]$ is called Hessian nilpotent (HN) if its Hessian matrix $\mathrm{Hess}(P) = \big(\partial^2 P/\partial z_i \partial z_j\big)_{1\le i,j\le n}$ is nilpotent as a matrix over $\mathbb{C}[[z]]$. The Vanishing Conjecture (VC) for $P(z)$ asserts that
$$\Delta^m\!\big(P(z)^{m+1}\big) = 0 \quad \text{for all sufficiently large } m \ge 1.$$

Question: Does there exist a Hessian nilpotent formal power series $P(z) \in \mathbb{C}[[z]] \setminus \mathbb{C}[z]$ (i.e., not a polynomial) for which the Vanishing Conjecture fails, meaning $\Delta^m(P(z)^{m+1}) \ne 0$ for infinitely many $m$? Either exhibit such a $P(z)$ or prove that no such example exists.
representations.original:
Let $\mathbb{C}[[z]] = \mathbb{C}[[z_1,\dots,z_n]]$ denote the ring of formal power series in $n$ variables over $\mathbb{C}$, and let $\Delta = \sum_{i=1}^n \partial^2/\partial z_i^2$ be the standard Laplacian. A formal power series $P(z) \in \mathbb{C}[[z]]$ is called Hessian nilpotent (HN) if its Hessian matrix $\mathrm{Hess}(P) = \big(\partial^2 P/\partial z_i \partial z_j\big)_{1\le i,j\le n}$ is nilpotent as a matrix over $\mathbb{C}[[z]]$. The Vanishing Conjecture (VC) for $P(z)$ asserts that
$$\Delta^m\!\big(P(z)^{m+1}\big) = 0 \quad \text{for all sufficiently large } m \ge 1.$$

Question: Does there exist a Hessian nilpotent formal power series $P(z) \in \mathbb{C}[[z]] \setminus \mathbb{C}[z]$ (i.e., not a polynomial) for which the Vanishing Conjecture fails, meaning $\Delta^m(P(z)^{m+1}) \ne 0$ for infinitely many $m$? Either exhibit such a $P(z)$ or prove that no such example exists.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

No counterexample of a non-polynomial Hessian nilpotent formal power series violating the Vanishing Conjecture appears to be known. Related work (e.g., Zhao's 2008 survey on HN polynomials, and de Bondt's counterexamples in the differential-operator setting with non-constant coefficients, plus failure of the VC for Laurent formal power series) addresses neighboring formulations but does not resolve the formal-power-series case in $\mathbb{C}[[z]]$. The problem appears to remain open.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is a conjecture posed by Wenhua Zhao in the context of the Vanishing Conjecture, which is known to be equivalent to the Jacobian Conjecture. representations.normalized:
Setup. Let $z=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ and let $P(z)\in\mathbb{C}[z_1,\dots,z_n]$ be a homogeneous polynomial. Let $\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\partial^{2}/\partial z_{i}^{2}$ be the standard Laplacian. The polynomial $P$ is called Hessian nilpotent (HN) if its Hessian matrix $\big(\partial^{2}P/\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}\big)_{i,j=1}^{n}$ is nilpotent; equivalently, $\Delta^{m}(P^{m})=0$ for every integer $m\ge 1$.

The Vanishing Conjecture (VC) for $P$ asserts: if $\Delta^{m}(P^{m})=0$ for all $m\ge 1$, then there exists $N\ge 1$ such that $\Delta^{m}(P^{m+1})=0$ for all $m\ge N$.

To a homogeneous HN polynomial $P(z)$ one associates a labeled graph $G(P)$ as follows. Write $P(z)=\sum_{\alpha} c_{\alpha} z^{\alpha}$ in multi-index notation. The vertex set of $G(P)$ is $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$ (one vertex per variable). For each monomial $z^{\alpha}=z_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\cdots z_{n}^{\alpha_{n}}$ appearing in $P$ with nonzero coefficient $c_{\alpha}$, one places a (hyper)edge labeled by $c_{\alpha}$ that records the multiset of variables (with multiplicity given by $\alpha$) occurring in that monomial; equivalently, $G(P)$ encodes the support of $P$ together with the coefficient labels.

Problem. Find necessary or sufficient conditions on the labeled graph $G(P)$ that guarantee the Vanishing Conjecture holds for the homogeneous Hessian nilpotent polynomial $P(z)$. That is, identify combinatorial properties of $G(P)$ (structure, symmetries, edge labels, connectivity, etc.) under which one can prove, or which must hold whenever, $\Delta^{m}(P^{m+1})=0$ for all sufficiently large $m$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is equivalent to asking for a power-saving lower bound on how close integers can be to powers of e, i.e., on $|n - e^m|$ for integers $n, m$. The problem is listed among open Diophantine problems and no resolution has been found.

This is the set-theoretic version of the Salmon Conjecture. It has been solved: a computational proof using numerical algebraic geometry and representation theory was given by Bates–Oeding ("Toward a Salmon Conjecture", Experimental Mathematics, 2011), and a fully theoretical proof without numerical computation was given by Friedland and Gross (arXiv:1104.1776, J. Algebra 2012), establishing that the variety of 4×4×4 tensors of border rank at most 4 is cut out set-theoretically by polynomials of degrees 5, 6, and 9.

Let G be a directed acyclic graph whose vertices are partitioned into observed and hidden random variables, each taking finitely many states. The associated graphical statistical model is the image of the parametrization map sending the conditional probability tables at the vertices of G to the joint probability distribution on the observed variables, viewed as a tensor in a tensor product of finite-dimensional vector spaces. Let V_G denote the Zariski closure of this image inside the corresponding projective space of tensors.

Develop a systematic theory for the geometry and commutative algebra of the varieties V_G, in the following sense:

(a) Express V_G as a variety constructed by "gluing" classical secant varieties of Segre, Veronese, and Segre–Veronese varieties along combinatorial data dictated by the graph G and by the marginalization over hidden vertices. Make this gluing construction precise as an iterated geometric operation on secant varieties indexed by the structure of G.

(b) Using the natural action of the product of general linear groups on the ambient tensor space, give a representation-theoretic description of the homogeneous ideal I(V_G): identify the GL-isotypic components in each graded piece I(V_G)_d, and describe explicit highest-weight generators of these components in terms of Schur functors and the combinatorics of G.

In particular, determine the minimal generators and dimensions of V_G, and characterize for which graphs G with hidden variables the variety V_G is defined set-theoretically (respectively, ideal-theoretically) by equations coming from secant varieties of Segre products of projective spaces associated to subsets of vertices of G.

Let $\mathbb{P}^n$ denote complex projective $n$-space with homogeneous coordinates $(p_0:p_1:\cdots:p_n)$, and let $M \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ be an irreducible projective variety. For a data vector $u = (u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_n) \in \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$, define the likelihood function
$$L(p_0, p_1, \ldots, p_n) = \frac{p_0^{u_0}\, p_1^{u_1}\, \cdots\, p_n^{u_n}}{(p_0 + p_1 + \cdots + p_n)^{u_0 + u_1 + \cdots + u_n}},$$
viewed as a rational function on $\mathbb{P}^n$. The maximum likelihood degree (ML degree) of $M$ is defined as the number of complex critical points of the restriction $L|_M$, where one counts only critical points lying in the smooth locus of $M$ and avoiding the divisor where $L$ has a pole or zero, and where $u$ is assumed generic.

Provide a geometric characterization of all irreducible projective varieties $M \subset \mathbb{P}^n$ whose ML degree equals $1$ (equivalently, those statistical models for which the maximum likelihood estimator is a single rational function of the data).

June Huh (arXiv:1301.2732, "Varieties with maximum likelihood degree one") proved that a projective variety has ML degree one if and only if it is the image of a reduced A-discriminantal variety under a monomial map with finite fibers, and the corresponding MLE is given by Kapranov's Horn uniformization. representations.normalized:
An algebraic statistical model for discrete data with n+1 states is, by definition, the intersection of an irreducible projective variety X ⊂ ℙ^n (defined over ℝ) with the open probability simplex Δ_n = {(p_0,…,p_n) ∈ ℝ^{n+1}_{>0} : Σ p_i = 1}. Given an observed data vector u = (u_0,…,u_n) ∈ ℤ^{n+1}_{≥0} of counts, the maximum likelihood estimation problem asks for the points of X ∩ Δ_n that maximize the log-likelihood function ℓ_u(p) = Σ_i u_i log p_i. Over ℂ, the number of complex critical points of ℓ_u on the smooth locus of X (for generic u) is a well-defined invariant, called the maximum likelihood degree of X.

Develop a general theory of the geometry of maximum likelihood estimation for such algebraic statistical models. Specifically:

(a) For a smooth (or suitably mild-singularity) projective variety X ⊂ ℙ^n defining a statistical model, give intrinsic geometric/topological formulas for the maximum likelihood degree of X in terms of invariants such as Chern classes, Euler characteristics of the very affine variety X° = X ∖ {p_0 ⋯ p_n (Σ p_i) = 0}, characteristic classes of associated sheaves, or polar/conormal varieties.

(b) Identify how qualitative statistical features of the model (e.g., identifiability, existence and uniqueness of the MLE, behavior on the boundary of the simplex, model dimension, presence of latent variables, conditional independence structure) correspond to geometric properties of X (e.g., singularities, degree, secant or join structure, toric structure, discriminant loci, dual variety).

(c) Provide criteria, in terms of the geometry of X, under which the MLE exists and is unique for generic data, and characterize the locus of data vectors u for which the likelihood equations have non-generic behavior (the ML data discriminant).

The goal is a dictionary translating between statistical properties of algebraic models and geometric/topological invariants of the corresponding projective varieties.

Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be pairwise coprime nonzero integers and let $p$ be a prime number. Consider the Diophantine equation
$$ a x^{p} + b y^{p} = c z^{2}. $$
Define $S_{p}(a,b,c)$ to be the set of triples $(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{Z}^{3}$ satisfying this equation with $xyz \neq 0$ (nontrivial) and $\gcd(x,y,z) = 1$ (proper). Prove the following two statements.

(i) If none of the integers $a+b$, $a-b$, $b-a$ belongs to the set $c\mathbb{Z}^{2} = \{c n^{2} : n \in \mathbb{Z}\}$, then there exists a constant $f(a,b,c)$ such that for every prime $p > f(a,b,c)$ the set $S_{p}(a,b,c)$ is empty.

(ii) If at least one of the integers $a+b$, $a-b$, $b-a$ belongs to $c\mathbb{Z}^{2}$, then there exists a constant $g(a,b,c)$ such that for every prime $p > g(a,b,c)$ and every $(x,y,z) \in S_{p}(a,b,c)$ one has $xy = \pm 1$.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ be an algebraic statistical model, i.e., a statistical model whose parameter space and probability distributions are described by polynomial equations. Given i.i.d. observed data, the maximum likelihood estimator is obtained by maximizing the likelihood function $L(\theta)$ over $\mathcal{M}$. The critical equations $\nabla \log L(\theta) = 0$ define an algebraic system, and the maximum likelihood degree (ML degree) of $\mathcal{M}$ is defined as the number of complex critical points of the log-likelihood function for generic data.

Two iterative numerical algorithms are commonly used to compute maximum likelihood estimates for such models:
(i) Iterative Proportional Scaling (IPS), which iteratively rescales marginals of a contingency table to match observed marginals in a hierarchical log-linear model;
(ii) The Expectation–Maximization (EM) algorithm, which alternates between computing expected sufficient statistics under the current parameter estimate (E-step) and maximizing the resulting expected log-likelihood (M-step).

Determine whether, and in what precise quantitative sense, the ML degree of an algebraic statistical model $\mathcal{M}$ governs the convergence properties (e.g., rate of convergence, number of iterations to a prescribed tolerance, existence and frequency of multiple stationary points and local maxima reached from random initializations) of IPS and of the EM algorithm applied to $\mathcal{M}$. Provide either a theorem relating the ML degree to such convergence quantities, or establish that no such general relationship exists.

Let $m, n, r$ be positive integers with $r \le \min(m,n)$, and let $\mathcal{V}_{m,n,r} \subset \mathbb{C}^{m \times n}$ denote the (complex) determinantal variety of $m \times n$ matrices of rank at most $r$, cut out by the vanishing of all $(r+1)\times(r+1)$ minors. Consider the open subset $U \subset \mathbb{C}^{m \times n}$ where all entries $p_{ij}$ as well as all row sums $p_{i+} = \sum_j p_{ij}$, all column sums $p_{+j} = \sum_i p_{ij}$, and the total sum $p_{++} = \sum_{i,j} p_{ij}$ are nonzero. For a generic data matrix $u = (u_{ij}) \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}^{m \times n}$ with $u_{++} = \sum_{i,j} u_{ij}$, define the log-likelihood function
$$\ell_u(P) = \sum_{i,j} u_{ij} \log p_{ij} \;-\; u_{++} \log p_{++}$$
on $U \cap \mathcal{V}_{m,n,r}^{\mathrm{sm}}$. The maximum likelihood degree $\mathrm{MLdeg}(m,n,r)$ is the number of complex critical points of $\ell_u$ on the smooth locus of $\mathcal{V}_{m,n,r}$ for generic $u$.

Problem: Find a closed-form formula, in terms of $m$, $n$, and $r$, for $\mathrm{MLdeg}(m,n,r)$. As a specific test case, determine $\mathrm{MLdeg}(4,4,2)$.

Let $\mathcal{M}$ denote the set of $4\times 4$ matrices $P=(p_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le 4}$ with strictly positive real entries and rank at most $2$. Define the likelihood function $L:\mathcal{M}\to\mathbb{R}_{>0}$ by
$$L(P)=\frac{\prod_{i=1}^{4} p_{ii}^{4}\cdot\prod_{i\ne j} p_{ij}^{2}}{\bigl(\sum_{i,j} p_{ij}\bigr)^{40}}.$$
Consider the matrix
$$\hat{P}=\frac{1}{40}\begin{pmatrix}3&3&2&2\\3&3&2&2\\2&2&3&3\\2&2&3&3\end{pmatrix}.$$
Note that $\hat{P}$ has positive entries, rank $2$, and entries summing to $1$. Determine whether $\hat{P}$ is a global maximum of $L$ over $\mathcal{M}$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The conjecture (Sturmfels' "100 Swiss Francs problem") was resolved affirmatively in 2008 by Mingfu Zhu (with collaborators Gao and Jiang), who proved that the proposed matrix is indeed the global maximum of the likelihood function on the rank-2 model. Let $A$, $B$, $C$ be fixed nonzero integers. Consider the Diophantine equation
$$A X^2 + B Y^3 = C Z^5$$
in unknowns $X, Y, Z \in \mathbb{Z}$ subject to the coprimality condition $\gcd(X, Y, Z) = 1$.

For each prime $p$, by a "coprime $p$-adic solution" we mean a triple $(X, Y, Z) \in \mathbb{Z}_p^3$ satisfying the equation such that at least one of $X, Y, Z$ is a unit in $\mathbb{Z}_p$ (equivalently, $X, Y, Z$ are not all divisible by $p$).

Question: Does a Hasse (local-global) principle hold for this equation? That is, is the existence of a coprime integer solution $(X, Y, Z) \in \mathbb{Z}^3$ equivalent to the existence of a coprime $p$-adic solution for every prime $p$ (together with a real solution)?

The equation $AX^2+BY^3=CZ^5$ has signature $(2,3,5)$, which is in the spherical (finite-solution) range of generalized Fermat equations. Work by Darmon–Granville and others shows there are no local or class-group obstructions when $A,B,C$ are pairwise coprime, and complete solutions are known only for specific small cases (e.g. $A=B=C=1$ via Edwards). No proof or disproof of a general Hasse principle for arbitrary nonzero $A,B,C$ appears in the literature; the problem appears to remain open.

For a covariance matrix $\Sigma\in\mathrm{PD}_n$, distinct indices $i,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, and a subset $K\subseteq\{1,\dots,n\}\setminus\{i,j\}$, write $[i\perp\!\!\!\perp j\mid K]$ for the partial covariance, equivalently the $(i,j)$-almost-principal minor $\det\Sigma_{i\cup K,\,j\cup K}$; this quantity vanishes precisely when the components $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given $X_K$ under the Gaussian distribution $\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)$.

Define a Gaussian conditional independence (GCI) model to be any semi-algebraic subset of $\mathrm{PD}_n$ that can be defined by a finite system of polynomial equations of the form

Let $\mathrm{PD}_n$ denote the cone of $n\times n$ real symmetric positive definite matrices. For a subset $I\subseteq[n]:=\{1,\dots,n\}$ and $\Sigma=(\sigma_{ij})\in\mathrm{PD}_n$, let $\Sigma_I$ denote the principal submatrix of $\Sigma$ indexed by $I$, with the convention $\det(\Sigma_\emptyset)=1$. A function $h:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb{R}$ is called submodular if $h(\emptyset)=0$ and
$$h(I\cup J)+h(I\cap J)\le h(I)+h(J)\qquad\text{for all }I,J\subseteq[n].$$
Let $\mathrm{SubMod}_n\subset\mathbb{R}^{2^{[n]}}$ denote the (closed convex polyhedral) cone of submodular functions on $[n]$. Define the entropy map
$$H:\mathrm{PD}_n\longrightarrow\mathrm{SubMod}_n,\qquad H(\Sigma)_I=-\log\det(\Sigma_I)\quad\text{for }I\subseteq[n].$$
(The fact that $H(\Sigma)$ is submodular reflects the strong subadditivity of Gaussian differential entropy.)

Solve the following:
\begin{enumerate}
\item Characterize the image $H(\mathrm{PD}_n)\subseteq\mathrm{SubMod}_n$, i.e.\ determine which submodular functions $h:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb{R}$ arise as $-\log\det(\Sigma_I)_{I\subseteq[n]}$ for some $\Sigma\in\mathrm{PD}_n$.
\item Describe how $H(\mathrm{PD}_n)$ intersects each face of the polyhedral cone $\mathrm{SubMod}_n$.
\item Describe the fibers $H^{-1}(h)$ for $h\in H(\mathrm{PD}_n)$, that is, the set of positive definite matrices having a prescribed tuple of log-principal-minors.
\end{enumerate}

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Recent work has made substantial progress on this question. The tropicalization of the image of the principal minor map on $\mathrm{PD}_n$ has been computed and shown to coincide with the intersection of the affine tropical flag variety with the submodular cone (El Maazouz; Tran–Sturmfels and collaborators, 2021–2024). Fibers of the principal minor map over symmetric/Hermitian matrices have been characterized, and new algebraic inequalities cutting out the image have been derived. However, an exact semi-algebraic description of the image $H(\mathrm{PD}_n)$ and a complete description of its intersection with all faces of $\mathrm{SubMod}_n$ in general $n$ remain open.

Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be discrete random variables with $X_i$ taking values in a finite set $[d_i] = \{1, \dots, d_i\}$. The joint distribution is encoded as a nonnegative tensor $p = (p_{i_1 \cdots i_n}) \in \mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{d_1 \times \cdots \times d_n}$ with $\sum p_{i_1\cdots i_n} = 1$. For disjoint subsets $I, J, K \subseteq \{1,\dots,n\}$, the conditional independence (CI) statement $X_I \perp\!\!\!\perp X_J \mid X_K$ is equivalent to a system of homogeneous quadratic polynomial equations in the entries of $p$ (the vanishing of certain $2\times 2$ minors of suitable flattenings of the tensor of marginals).

Fix a collection $\mathcal{C}$ of CI statements. Let $\mathcal{S}$ denote the full set of CI statements among the variables $X_1, \dots, X_n$. The strict CI variety associated to $\mathcal{C}$ is the constructible subset of $\mathbb{C}^{d_1 \times \cdots \times d_n}$ consisting of tensors for which every CI statement in $\mathcal{C}$ holds and every CI statement in $\mathcal{S} \setminus \mathcal{C}$ fails. The strict CI model is the intersection of the strict CI variety with the open positive orthant $\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d_1 \times \cdots \times d_n}$.

Question: Does every nonempty strict CI model contain a $\mathbb{Q}$-rational point, i.e., a point all of whose coordinates are rational numbers?

Let $M_d$ denote the algebra of $d\times d$ complex matrices. A linear map $\Phi : M_{d_1}\to M_{d_2}$ is called completely positive and trace preserving (CPT, a quantum channel) if $\mathrm{id}_{M_n}\otimes\Phi$ maps positive semidefinite matrices to positive semidefinite matrices for every $n\ge 1$, and $\mathrm{tr}(\Phi(A))=\mathrm{tr}(A)$ for all $A\in M_{d_1}$. Every such $\Phi$ admits a Kraus representation $\Phi(A)=\sum_{k=1}^{r} F_k A F_k^*$ with $F_k\in M_{d_2,d_1}$ and $\sum_k F_k^*F_k = I_{d_1}$; the minimal such $r$ equals the rank of the Choi matrix $C(\Phi)=\sum_{i,j} E_{ij}\otimes\Phi(E_{ij})\in M_{d_1}\otimes M_{d_2}$ (the Choi rank).

The set of CPT maps $\Phi:M_{d_1}\to M_{d_2}$ is convex and compact. Let $\mathcal{E}(d_1,d_2)$ denote its set of extreme points. It is known that a CPT map with Kraus operators $\{F_k\}_{k=1}^{r}$ is extreme if and only if the family $\{F_j^*F_k\}_{j,k=1}^{r}$ is linearly independent in $M_{d_1}$, and that the closure $\overline{\mathcal{E}(d_1,d_2)}$ coincides exactly with the set of CPT maps $\Phi:M_{d_1}\to M_{d_2}$ whose Choi rank is at most $d_1$.

Problem. For all input dimensions $d_1>2$ and arbitrary output dimensions $d_2$, give an explicit characterization, classification, or parameterization of the closure $\overline{\mathcal{E}(d_1,d_2)}$, equivalently, of the convex set of CPT maps $\Phi:M_{d_1}\to M_{d_2}$ whose Choi rank does not exceed $d_1$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ be a semi-algebraic set defined by a Boolean combination of polynomial equalities and inequalities involving $s$ polynomials in $\mathbb{R}[X_1,\dots,X_k]$, each of degree at most $d$. For $i \ge 0$, let $b_i(S) = \dim_{\mathbb{Q}} H_i(S;\mathbb{Q})$ denote the $i$-th Betti number of $S$ (with respect to singular homology with rational coefficients). An algorithm is said to run in single exponential time (in the ambient dimension $k$) if its arithmetic complexity, on inputs encoded by such polynomials with integer or rational coefficients of bounded bit-size, is bounded by $(s\,d)^{k^{O(1)}}$.

It is known that, for every fixed constant $\ell \ge 0$, there is an algorithm that, given such a description of $S$, computes the Betti numbers $b_0(S), b_1(S), \dots, b_\ell(S)$ in single exponential time in $k$. It is also known that all Betti numbers of $S$ can be computed in doubly exponential time (e.g.\ via cylindrical algebraic decomposition).

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given $S$ as above, computes the entire sequence of Betti numbers $b_0(S), b_1(S), \dots, b_k(S)$ in time single exponential in $k$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of computing all Betti numbers of a semi-algebraic set in single exponential time is widely described as a central open problem in algorithmic semi-algebraic geometry. As of 2023–2024, only partial results are known: single exponential time algorithms exist for the Euler–Poincaré characteristic, for $b_0$ and $b_1$, and (Basu and collaborators) for the first $\ell$ Betti numbers for any fixed $\ell$, as well as recent extensions to homology of semi-algebraic maps and diagrams. No single exponential algorithm computing the full Betti sequence is known.

Let $M_d$ denote the algebra of $d\times d$ complex matrices. A linear map $\Phi: M_{d_1}\to M_{d_2}$ is called completely positive and trace-preserving (CPT) if $\Phi\otimes \mathrm{id}_{M_n}$ maps positive semidefinite matrices to positive semidefinite matrices for every $n\geq 1$, and $\mathrm{tr}(\Phi(X)) = \mathrm{tr}(X)$ for all $X\in M_{d_1}$. The Choi matrix of $\Phi$ is $C_\Phi = \sum_{i,j=1}^{d_1} E_{ij}\otimes \Phi(E_{ij}) \in M_{d_1}\otimes M_{d_2}$, where $E_{ij}$ are the standard matrix units, and the Choi rank of $\Phi$ is the rank of $C_\Phi$ (equivalently, the minimum number of Kraus operators needed to express $\Phi$).

Prove or disprove: for every CPT map $\Phi: M_{d_1}\to M_{d_2}$ there exist CPT maps $\Phi_1,\dots,\Phi_{d_2}: M_{d_1}\to M_{d_2}$, each having Choi rank at most $d_2$, such that
$$\Phi = \frac{1}{d_2}\sum_{m=1}^{d_2}\Phi_m.$$

A semi-algebraic set S ⊂ R^k is a finite Boolean combination of sets of the form {x ∈ R^k : P(x) ⋈ 0}, where P ∈ R[X_1,...,X_k] and ⋈ ∈ {=, >, <, ≥, ≤}. For such a set, let b_i(S) denote its i-th Betti number (the rank of the i-th singular homology group with rational coefficients) and let χ(S) = Σ_i (-1)^i b_i(S) denote its Euler–Poincaré characteristic.

It is known algorithmically that, given a description of S by polynomials of bounded degree:
(a) the Euler–Poincaré characteristic χ(S) can be computed in single-exponential time in k;
(b) the lowest Betti numbers b_0(S), b_1(S), ..., b_ℓ(S) for any fixed ℓ, and (by Alexander-type duality in the basic semi-algebraic case) the highest Betti numbers, can also be computed in single-exponential time;
(c) however, no single-exponential time algorithm is currently known for computing the "middle" Betti numbers b_i(S) when i is allowed to grow with the dimension.

Question. Are the middle Betti numbers of semi-algebraic sets intrinsically harder to compute than the lowest Betti numbers, the highest Betti numbers, or the Euler–Poincaré characteristic? Specifically:

(1) Establish a complexity-theoretic hardness result (for example, in terms of #P-hardness, PSPACE-hardness, or another standard complexity class) for the problem of computing b_i(S) when i lies in the "middle" range, that provably separates this problem from the computation of b_0(S), the top Betti number, or χ(S).

(2) Provide a complexity-theoretic analogue, valid for semi-algebraic sets, of the geometric phenomenon for smooth projective complex varieties in which the middle Betti numbers carry essentially all the topological information, thereby explaining why the middle Betti numbers should be computationally the hardest among all b_i(S).

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^k$ be a semi-algebraic set defined by a system of $\ell$ quadratic inequalities
$$ P_1(x_1,\dots,x_k) \;\bowtie_1\; 0,\ \dots,\ P_\ell(x_1,\dots,x_k) \;\bowtie_\ell\; 0, $$
where each $P_i \in \mathbb{R}[x_1,\dots,x_k]$ has total degree at most $2$ and each $\bowtie_i \in \{<,\le,=,\ne,\ge,>\}$. The number of semi-algebraically connected components of $S$ is denoted $b_0(S)$.

It is known that:
- Emptiness of $S$ can be decided, and a set of sample points meeting every connected component of $S$ can be computed, by algorithms whose arithmetic complexity is bounded by $k^{O(\ell)}$.
- The Euler–Poincaré characteristic of $S$ can likewise be computed in time $k^{O(\ell)}$.
- The number $b_0(S)$ of connected components can be computed by algorithms whose complexity is bounded by $k^{2^{O(\ell)}}$ (as a special case of computing all Betti numbers).

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given the data $(P_1,\dots,P_\ell;\bowtie_1,\dots,\bowtie_\ell)$ as above, computes $b_0(S)$ with arithmetic complexity bounded by $k^{O(\ell)}$, or at least by $k^{O(\ell^2)}$? Equivalently, is there an algorithm for counting the connected components of semi-algebraic sets defined by $\ell$ quadratic inequalities in $\mathbb{R}^k$ that is substantially more efficient than the doubly-exponential-in-$\ell$ bound coming from general all-Betti-number methods?

Let $\mathrm{R}$ be a real closed field and let $S \subset \mathrm{R}^k$ be a semi-algebraic set defined by a quantifier-free formula involving $s$ polynomials of degree at most $d$ in $k$ variables. A roadmap of $S$ is a semi-algebraic subset $M \subset S$ of dimension at most one such that:
(i) every semi-algebraically connected component of $S$ has a non-empty and semi-algebraically connected intersection with $M$, and
(ii) for every $x \in \mathrm{R}$, every semi-algebraically connected component of $S \cap \{X_1 = x\}$ has a non-empty intersection with $M$.

The currently known general roadmap algorithms for arbitrary semi-algebraic sets have complexity of the form $(s\,d)^{k^{O(1)}}$, with the exponent of $k$ being quadratic, i.e., of order $O(k^2)$. By contrast, testing emptiness of such a semi-algebraic set can be done with complexity $s^{k+1} d^{O(k)}$, in which the exponent of $k$ is linear.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given a quantifier-free formula defining an arbitrary semi-algebraic set $S \subset \mathrm{R}^k$ with parameters $s,d,k$ as above, computes a roadmap of $S$ (and in particular decides semi-algebraic connectivity, and outputs connecting paths) in time $(s\,d)^{O(k)}$, that is, with the exponent of $k$ improved from $O(k^2)$ to $O(k)$? Equivalently, can the complexity of testing semi-algebraic connectivity be made asymptotically the same as that of testing emptiness, and does any such complexity improvement also yield correspondingly sharper effective bounds on the lengths (description complexity) of semi-algebraic connecting paths between two points lying in the same connected component of $S$?

For real algebraic sets (a special case), substantial progress has been made: Safey El Din–Schost obtained a probabilistic roadmap of complexity $(nD)^{O(n\log k)}$; Basu–Roy–Safey El Din–Schost (FoCM 2014) gave a baby-step/giant-step roadmap of complexity $d^{O(k\sqrt{k})}$; and Basu–Roy (2014) gave a divide-and-conquer roadmap of complexity $(kd)^{O(k)}$, achieving the linear exponent in $k$ for bounded smooth real algebraic sets. For arbitrary (general) semi-algebraic sets, however, no algorithm with $(sd)^{O(k)}$ complexity is known: existing algorithms still have exponent $O(k^2)$ (or comparable). Hence the problem is partially solved (resolved for algebraic sets, open in general).

Let $d_1, d_2$ be positive integers, and let $A$ be a positive semidefinite matrix on $\mathbb{C}^{d_1} \otimes \mathbb{C}^{d_2}$ (a $d_1 d_2 \times d_1 d_2$ matrix). Write $A$ in block form as a $d_2 \times d_2$ array of blocks $A_{jk}$, where each $A_{jk}$ is a $d_1 \times d_1$ complex matrix ($j,k = 1,\dots,d_2$). Let $M := \sum_{j=1}^{d_2} A_{jj}$ (a $d_1 \times d_1$ positive semidefinite matrix).

For each $m = 1,\dots,d_2$, a "block vector" $X_m$ is a column composed of $d_2$ blocks $X_{jm}$ ($j = 1,\dots,d_2$), each of size $d_1 \times d_1$. Identifying such a column with a $(d_1 d_2) \times d_1$ matrix, define $X_m X_m^\dagger$ as the $(d_1 d_2) \times (d_1 d_2)$ matrix whose $(j,k)$-block is $X_{jm} X_{km}^\dagger$.

Prove or disprove: there always exist block vectors $X_1,\dots,X_{d_2}$ such that
$$ A = \frac{1}{d_2} \sum_{m=1}^{d_2} X_m X_m^\dagger, $$
and, for every $m \in \{1,\dots,d_2\}$,
$$ \sum_{k=1}^{d_2} X_{km} X_{km}^\dagger = M. $$

(In the scalar case $d_1 = 1$, the statement reduces to a known lemma of Horn on diagonals of positive semidefinite matrices; the question is whether this generalizes to block matrices in the form above.)

$$k := \max_{\xi \in \Omega} \operatorname{rank} D\Gamma(\xi),$$
and assume $1 \le k \le n-1$. Let
$$\Omega^{(k)} := \{\xi \in \Omega : \operatorname{rank} D\Gamma(\xi) = k\},$$
which is open and dense in $\Omega$. Assume further that for every $\xi \in \Omega^{(k)}$ the level set
$$\Gamma^{-1}(\Gamma(\xi)) = \{\eta \in \Omega : \Gamma(\eta) = \Gamma(\xi)\}$$
is an affine $(n-k)$-dimensional subspace passing through $\xi$; equivalently,
$$\Gamma^{-1}(\Gamma(\xi)) \cap \Omega^{(k)} = (\xi + \kappa(\xi)) \cap \Omega^{(k)}, \qquad \kappa(\xi) := \ker D\Gamma(\xi).$$
Thus on $\Omega^{(k)}$ the assignment $\xi \mapsto \xi + \kappa(\xi)$ defines a holomorphic fibration of $\Omega^{(k)}$ by affine $(n-k)$-planes.

Question: Under what conditions (and in what sense) does this affine fibration extend analytically from $\Omega^{(k)}$ to all of $\Omega$? Specifically, characterize when there exists a holomorphic distribution of affine $(n-k)$-dimensional subspaces $\xi \mapsto \xi + \tilde\kappa(\xi)$ defined on all of $\Omega$ that agrees with $\xi + \kappa(\xi)$ for every $\xi \in \Omega^{(k)}$.

Let $d\ge 2$ and let $M_d(\mathbb{C})$ denote the algebra of $d\times d$ complex matrices. Define the Werner–Holevo channel $W:M_d(\mathbb{C})\to M_d(\mathbb{C})$ by
$$W(\rho)=\frac{(\operatorname{Tr}\rho)\,I-\rho^{T}}{d-1},$$
where $\rho^{T}$ denotes the transpose in a fixed basis. For $x\in[0,1]$, define the depolarized Werner–Holevo channel
$$\Phi_x(\rho)=x\rho+(1-x)\,W(\rho).$$
For a quantum channel $\Phi$ and $p\ge 1$, define the maximal output $p$-norm
$$\nu_p(\Phi)=\sup_{\rho}\;\bigl\|\Phi(\rho)\bigr\|_p,$$
where the supremum is over all density matrices $\rho$ in the input space and $\|A\|_p=(\operatorname{Tr}|A|^p)^{1/p}$.

Prove or disprove: for every $d\ge 2$, every $x\in[0,1]$, and every $1\le p\le 2$,
$$\nu_p(\Phi_x\otimes\Phi_x)=\bigl[\nu_p(\Phi_x)\bigr]^{2}.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The case p=2 was settled by S. Michalakis (arXiv:0707.1722, 2007), proving multiplicativity of the maximal output 2-norm for two copies of the depolarized Werner–Holevo channel. For the undepolarized Werner–Holevo channel W itself, multiplicativity in the range 1≤p≤2 was established by Datta and others (arXiv:quant-ph/0410063). However, the general counterexamples of Hastings and Winter/Werner concern p>1 for arbitrary channels, and the full range 1≤p≤2 for the depolarized family Φ_x does not appear to have been completely resolved in the literature located. Status of the general statement is therefore partially solved (p=2 only).

Let $(\mathcal{A}, A)$ be a maximal Banach operator ideal, i.e., a Banach ideal $\mathcal{A}$ on the class of all bounded linear operators between Banach spaces, equipped with an ideal norm $A$, satisfying the maximality property that for every operator $T\colon X\to Y$, $T\in\mathcal{A}$ with $A(T)\le c$ if and only if $A(Q_N T J_M)\le c$ for every finite-dimensional subspace $M\subseteq X$ and every closed finite-codimensional subspace $N\subseteq Y$ (where $J_M\colon M\hookrightarrow X$ is the inclusion and $Q_N\colon Y\twoheadrightarrow Y/N$ is the quotient map).

For a Banach space $Y$, let $j_Y\colon Y\hookrightarrow Y''$ denote the canonical embedding into its bidual.

We say that $(\mathcal{A}, A)$ satisfies the principle of $\mathcal{A}$-local reflexivity ($\mathcal{A}$-LRP) if for every finite-dimensional Banach space $E$, every Banach space $Y$, every finite-dimensional subspace $F\subseteq Y'$, every operator $T\in\mathcal{L}(E, Y'')$ with $T\in\mathcal{A}$, and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists an operator $S\in\mathcal{L}(E, Y)$ such that
(i) $A(S)\le (1+\varepsilon)\, A(T)$;
(ii) $\langle Sx, y'\rangle = \langle y', Tx\rangle$ for all $(x, y')\in E\times F$;
(iii) $j_Y\, Sx = Tx$ for all $x\in T^{-1}(j_Y(Y))$.

Question: Does every maximal Banach ideal $(\mathcal{A}, A)$ satisfy the $\mathcal{A}$-LRP?

Let $d\geq 2$ and let $M_\varepsilon$ be a quantum channel acting on $d\times d$ density matrices whose output is always close to the maximally mixed state in the sense that
$$\big\|M_\varepsilon(\rho)-\tfrac{1}{d}I\big\| < \varepsilon$$
for every input state $\rho$ (in some fixed unitarily invariant norm, e.g. the trace norm). For $x\in[0,1]$, define the polarized channel
$$\Phi_{x,\varepsilon}(\rho) \;=\; x\,\rho \;+\; (1-x)\,M_\varepsilon(\rho).$$
For a channel $\Phi$ and $p\geq 1$, define the maximal output $p$-norm
$$\nu_p(\Phi) \;=\; \sup_{\rho}\big\|\Phi(\rho)\big\|_p,$$
where $\|A\|_p=(\operatorname{Tr}|A|^p)^{1/p}$ and the supremum is over input density matrices.

Question: Does $\Phi_{x,\varepsilon}$ satisfy the multiplicativity identity
$$\nu_p\big(\Phi_{x,\varepsilon}\otimes \Omega\big) \;=\; \nu_p(\Phi_{x,\varepsilon})\,\nu_p(\Omega)$$
for every quantum channel $\Omega$, in the range $1\leq p\leq 2$, at least when $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small? If not, for which pairs $(x,p)$ does multiplicativity hold, and how does the admissible region depend on $\varepsilon$?

The general maximal output p-norm multiplicativity conjecture was disproved for all p>1 by Hayden–Winter (2008), and Hastings (2009) disproved additivity at p=1. Setup. Let $\mathfrak{L}$ denote the class of all bounded linear operators between Banach spaces. A Banach ideal $(\mathcal{A},A)$ is an assignment, to every pair $(X,Y)$ of Banach spaces, of a linear subspace $\mathcal{A}(X,Y)\subseteq \mathfrak{L}(X,Y)$ together with a complete norm $A$ on $\mathcal{A}(X,Y)$ such that:
(a) $A(\,\cdot\,)\geq \|\cdot\|$ and $\mathcal{A}$ contains all finite-rank operators with $A(y^*\otimes x)=\|y^*\|\,\|x\|$;
(b) $\mathcal{A}$ is two-sided ideal: for $R\in\mathfrak{L}(X_0,X)$, $T\in\mathcal{A}(X,Y)$, $S\in\mathfrak{L}(Y,Y_0)$, $S T R\in\mathcal{A}(X_0,Y_0)$ with $A(STR)\leq \|S\|\,A(T)\,\|R\|$.

The Banach ideal $(\mathcal{A},A)$ is maximal if it equals its bidual ideal in the sense of Pietsch, i.e. if for every $T\in\mathfrak{L}(X,Y)$,
$$A(T)=\sup\{A(Q_F T J_E):\,E\subseteq X\text{ finite-dim}, F\subseteq Y\text{ finite-codim}\},$$
where $J_E:E\hookrightarrow X$ is the inclusion and $Q_F:Y\to Y/F$ is the quotient map.

Definition (right-accessibility). $(\mathcal{A},A)$ is right-accessible if for every finite-dimensional Banach space $E$, every Banach space $Y$, every operator $T\in\mathfrak{L}(E,Y)$, and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exist a finite-dimensional subspace $N\subseteq Y$ and an operator $S\in\mathfrak{L}(E,N)$ with $T=J^Y_N S$ (where $J^Y_N:N\hookrightarrow Y$) and $A(S)\leq (1+\varepsilon)A(T)$.

Definition (A-LRP). $(\mathcal{A},A)$ satisfies the $\mathcal{A}$-local reflexivity principle if for every Banach space $X$, every Banach space $Y$, every operator $T\in\mathcal{A}(X,Y^{**})$, every finite-dimensional subspace $E\subseteq X$, every finite-dimensional subspace $G\subseteq Y^*$, and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists $\widetilde{T}\in\mathcal{A}(X,Y)$ with $A(\widetilde{T})\leq (1+\varepsilon)A(T)$ such that $\langle y^*,\widetilde{T}x\rangle=\langle T x, y^*\rangle$ for all $x\in E$ and $y^*\in G$.

Problem. Let $(\mathcal{A},A)$ be a maximal Banach ideal. Are the following two statements equivalent?
(i) $(\mathcal{A},A)$ is right-accessible.
(ii) $(\mathcal{A},A)$ satisfies the $\mathcal{A}$-local reflexivity principle.

Let $d \geq 2$ be an integer and let $M_d$ denote the algebra of $d \times d$ complex matrices. Let $X$ be the cyclic shift operator on $\mathbb{C}^d$, defined by $X|j\rangle = |j+1 \bmod d\rangle$ for $j = 0, 1, \dots, d-1$. For each choice of unitaries $U_0, U_1, \dots, U_{d-1} \in M_{d-1}$, define operators $A_0, A_1, \dots, A_{d-1} \in M_d$ by
$$A_k = \frac{1}{\sqrt{d-1}}\, X^k \begin{pmatrix} U_k & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad k = 0, 1, \dots, d-1,$$
where the block decomposition is with respect to $\mathbb{C}^d = \mathbb{C}^{d-1} \oplus \mathbb{C}$. These operators satisfy $\sum_{k=0}^{d-1} A_k^\dagger A_k = I_d$, and they define a completely positive trace-preserving map (a "sub-unitary channel")
$$\Phi : M_d \to M_d, \qquad \Phi(\rho) = \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} A_k \rho A_k^\dagger.$$
For a density matrix $\sigma$ on $\mathbb{C}^d \otimes \mathbb{C}^d$ and $p \in [1, \infty]$, consider the Schatten $p$-norm $\|(\Phi \otimes \Phi)(\sigma)\|_p$, viewed as a function of the input state $\sigma$.

A pure state $|\psi\rangle \in \mathbb{C}^d \otimes \mathbb{C}^d$ is called maximally entangled if its reduced density matrices on each factor are $I_d/d$.

Question: For every choice of unitaries $U_0, \dots, U_{d-1} \in M_{d-1}$ and every $p \in [1, \infty]$, does the set of local (relative) maxima of $\sigma \mapsto \|(\Phi \otimes \Phi)(\sigma)\|_p$ over the set of density matrices on $\mathbb{C}^d \otimes \mathbb{C}^d$ always contain at least one state of the form $|\psi\rangle\langle\psi|$ with $|\psi\rangle$ maximally entangled? If not, characterize the values of $p$ and the conditions on the unitaries $U_k$ under which a maximally entangled input yields a relative maximum.

Setup. Let $d\ge 2$ and let $\{X^k\}_{k=0}^{d-1}$ denote the cyclic shift operators on $\mathbb{C}^d$, defined by $X|j\rangle = |j+1 \bmod d\rangle$. For an arbitrary family of unitaries $U_0,U_1,\dots,U_{d-1}\in M_{d-1}(\mathbb{C})$, define operators on $\mathbb{C}^d$ by
$$A_k \;=\; \frac{1}{\sqrt{d-1}}\, X^{k}\begin{pmatrix} U_k & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},\qquad k=0,1,\dots,d-1,$$
where the block decomposition is with respect to $\mathbb{C}^{d-1}\oplus\mathbb{C}$. One checks that $\sum_{k=0}^{d-1} A_k^*A_k \le I$, so the map
$$\Phi(\rho) \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{d-1} A_k\,\rho\,A_k^{*}$$
is a sub-unitary (completely positive, trace non-increasing) quantum channel on $M_d(\mathbb{C})$.

For a quantum channel $\Psi$ on $M_n(\mathbb{C})$ and $p>1$, the maximal output $p$-norm is
$$\nu_p(\Psi) \;=\; \sup_{\rho}\; \|\Psi(\rho)\|_p,$$
where the supremum runs over density matrices $\rho$ on $\mathbb{C}^n$ and $\|\cdot\|_p$ denotes the Schatten $p$-norm.

Problem. Exhibit, for some $p>1$, a choice of dimension $d$, unitaries $U_0,\dots,U_{d-1}\in M_{d-1}(\mathbb{C})$, and an auxiliary quantum channel $\Omega$, for which the channel $\Phi$ defined above violates multiplicativity of the maximal output $p$-norm:
$$\nu_p(\Phi\otimes\Omega) \;>\; \nu_p(\Phi)\,\nu_p(\Omega).$$
Equivalently, produce new counterexamples to maximal output $p$-norm multiplicativity within this family of sub-unitary channels with Kraus operators of the above form.

Work in the category of bounded linear operators between Banach spaces. A Banach operator ideal is a pair (A, ‖·‖_A) where A is an operator ideal in the sense of Pietsch (a class A of operators stable under sums and under composition with arbitrary bounded operators on the left and right, containing all finite-rank operators) and ‖·‖_A is an ideal norm: a norm on each component A(X,Y) that satisfies ‖x*⊗y‖_A = ‖x*‖·‖y‖, ‖S+T‖_A ≤ ‖S‖_A+‖T‖_A, and ‖BTA‖_A ≤ ‖B‖·‖T‖_A·‖A‖ whenever the composition is defined. A quasi-Banach ideal is defined analogously with a quasi-norm in place of a norm.

Given two (quasi-)Banach operator ideals A and B, their product A∘B is the operator ideal consisting of all bounded operators T : X → Z that admit a factorization T = US with S ∈ B(X,Y) and U ∈ A(Y,Z) for some Banach space Y, equipped with the natural quasi-norm ‖T‖_{A∘B} = inf ‖U‖_A·‖S‖_B. The ideal A∘B is called normed if there exists an ideal norm on A∘B that is equivalent to the quotient quasi-norm above, i.e. if (A∘B, ‖·‖_{A∘B}) admits an ideal norm.

For a Banach operator ideal A, let A** denote its biconjugate (maximal hull) Banach ideal in the sense of Pietsch.

Let L_p (1 ≤ p ≤ ∞) denote the maximal Banach operator ideal of operators that factor through an L_p(μ)-space (equivalently, the maximal Banach ideal naturally associated with that factorization), with its standard factorization norm; in particular L_1 corresponds to operators factoring through an L_1-space, L_2 to those factoring through a Hilbert space, and L_∞ to operators factoring through an L_∞-space.

Problem. Is the product Banach operator ideal (L_1 ∘ L_∞)** ∘ L_2 normed? Equivalently, does this product of operator ideals admit an ideal norm (rather than only a natural quasi-norm)?

representations.normalized:
Setup. A quantum channel is a completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) linear map $\mathcal{N}: \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_A) \to \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_B)$ between matrix algebras on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. Every channel admits a Stinespring/Kraus representation $\mathcal{N}(\rho) = \sum_{k=1}^{r} K_k \rho K_k^\dagger$ with $\sum_k K_k^\dagger K_k = I_A$, and a complementary channel $\mathcal{N}^c: \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_A) \to \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_E)$ obtained by tracing over the system instead of the environment in a Stinespring dilation.

Call $\mathcal{N}$ a sub-unitary channel if there exist $d \in \mathbb{N}$, an integer $r \le d$, and Kraus operators of the form $K_k = \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{r}} U_k$ for $k=1,\dots,r$, where each $U_k$ is a $d\times d$ unitary matrix; equivalently $\mathcal{N}(\rho) = \tfrac{1}{r}\sum_{k=1}^r U_k \rho U_k^\dagger$ with $\dim \mathcal{H}_A = \dim \mathcal{H}_B = d$. A random sub-unitary channel is obtained by sampling $U_1,\dots,U_r$ independently from the Haar measure on the unitary group $\mathrm{U}(d)$.

The coherent information of $\mathcal{N}$ at input state $\rho$ is
$$I_c(\rho,\mathcal{N}) = S(\mathcal{N}(\rho)) - S(\mathcal{N}^c(\rho)),$$
where $S(\sigma) = -\mathrm{Tr}(\sigma \log \sigma)$ is the von Neumann entropy. Its single-letter coherent information is $Q^{(1)}(\mathcal{N}) = \max_\rho I_c(\rho,\mathcal{N})$, and its quantum capacity is
$$Q(\mathcal{N}) = \lim_{n\to\infty} \tfrac{1}{n} Q^{(1)}(\mathcal{N}^{\otimes n}).$$
The channel $\mathcal{N}$ is called degradable if there exists a CPTP map $\mathcal{D}$ with $\mathcal{D}\circ\mathcal{N} = \mathcal{N}^c$, and its coherent information is called additive if $Q^{(1)}(\mathcal{N}^{\otimes n}) = n\, Q^{(1)}(\mathcal{N})$ for all $n\ge 1$.

Problems. For a random sub-unitary channel with parameters $(d,r)$ as above:

(a) Determine the typical (almost-sure or high-probability, as $d\to\infty$ with $r$ fixed or scaling appropriately) value and concentration behavior of the single-letter coherent information $Q^{(1)}(\mathcal{N})$ and the quantum capacity $Q(\mathcal{N})$.

(b) Characterize the values of $(d,r)$ and the events on the underlying Haar product measure for which the realized channel $\mathcal{N}$ is degradable.

(c) Characterize the values of $(d,r)$ and the events for which the coherent information of $\mathcal{N}$ is additive.

Background. A Banach operator ideal (A, A) assigns to every pair of Banach spaces X, Y a linear subspace A(X,Y) of the bounded operators B(X,Y) together with a complete norm A(·) which dominates the operator norm and satisfies the usual ideal property A(SAT) ≤ ‖S‖·A(A)·‖T‖. The ideal is called maximal if A(X,Y) consists of all T ∈ B(X,Y) for which sup{A(QTI) : I : E → X finite-dimensional inclusion, Q : Y → F/N finite-codimensional quotient} is finite, with A(·) equal to this supremum, and injective if for every isometric embedding J : Y → Z one has A(JT) = A(T).

Let C2 denote the maximal injective Banach operator ideal of cotype 2 operators (operators T : X → Y such that Y has cotype 2 with respect to T in the usual sense, equipped with its natural cotype-2 constant). Let C2* denote its adjoint (dual) ideal in the sense of operator ideals. Let L_∞ denote the maximal Banach ideal of operators factoring through an L_∞-space, with its associated factorization norm.

For two Banach ideals (A, A) and (B, B), the product ideal A ∘ B is defined by T ∈ (A ∘ B)(X,Y) iff there exist a Banach space Z and operators B ∈ B(X,Z), A ∈ A(Z,Y) with T = AB, normed by (A ∘ B)(T) = inf A(A)·B(B) over all such factorizations.

A product ideal A ∘ B is said to have property (I) if for every ε > 0 and every finite-rank operator L ∈ (A ∘ B)(X,Y) there exists a factorization L = AB with A ∈ A, B ∈ B such that A(A)·B(B) ≤ (1+ε)·(A ∘ B)(L) and A has finite-dimensional range.

Problem. Does the product ideal C2* ∘ L_∞ have property (I)?

For a quantum channel Φ (a completely positive trace-preserving linear map between matrix algebras) and a real number p ≥ 1, define the maximal output p-norm by
   ν_p(Φ) := sup_ρ ‖Φ(ρ)‖_p,
where the supremum is taken over all density matrices ρ on the input space and ‖A‖_p = (Tr |A|^p)^{1/p}.

The maximal output p-norm multiplicativity conjecture asserts that for every pair of quantum channels Φ and Ω,
   ν_p(Φ ⊗ Ω) = ν_p(Φ) · ν_p(Ω).

Two questions are posed:
(a) Exhibit pairs of quantum channels (Φ, Ω) for which ν_p(Φ ⊗ Ω) > ν_p(Φ) · ν_p(Ω), beyond the Werner–Holevo channel example and small perturbations of it.
(b) Determine whether such counterexamples can occur in the regime 1 ≤ p ≤ 2, or whether multiplicativity in fact holds throughout 1 ≤ p ≤ 2.

Recall that an operator ideal A is called right-accessible if for every finite-dimensional Banach space E, every Banach space F, every operator T ∈ L(E,F), and every ε>0, there exist a finite-dimensional Banach space E_0, an operator S ∈ L(E,E_0), and an operator T_0 ∈ A(E_0,F) such that T = T_0 ∘ S and ‖T_0‖_A · ‖S‖ ≤ (1+ε)·‖T‖_A. The composition ideal B ∘ L_∞ is the ideal of operators that factor through an L_∞-space followed by an operator from B. The ideal B ∘ L_∞ is said to have property (I) if its component on every pair of Banach spaces is closed in the operator norm topology. The B-local reformulation property (B-LRP) for a pair of Banach spaces (X_0, Y_0) is the statement that B(X_0, Y_0) coincides isometrically with the local hull obtained by testing on finite-dimensional subspaces.

Known fact. If (B, ‖·‖_B) is a maximal Banach ideal, X_0 and Y_0 are Banach spaces such that the dual X_0' and Y_0 are both of cotype 2, B*(X_0, Y_0) is not contained in the ideal L_2(X_0, Y_0) of 2-summing operators, and the composition ideal B ∘ L_∞ is right-accessible and has property (I), then the pair (X_0, Y_0) does not satisfy the B-LRP.

Question. Can the hypothesis that B ∘ L_∞ is right-accessible be removed while preserving the same conclusion? That is: assuming (B, ‖·‖_B) is a maximal Banach ideal, X_0' and Y_0 are of cotype 2, B*(X_0, Y_0) ⊄ L_2(X_0, Y_0), and B ∘ L_∞ has property (I), does it still follow that the B-LRP fails for (X_0, Y_0)?

Let $\Phi:\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_A)\to\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{K}_A)$ and $\Omega:\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_B)\to\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{K}_B)$ be quantum channels (completely positive trace-preserving linear maps between matrix algebras on finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces). For a real number $p\ge 1$, define the maximal output $p$-norm of a channel $\Phi$ by
\[
\nu_p(\Phi) \;=\; \sup_{\rho}\, \|\Phi(\rho)\|_p \;=\; \sup_{\rho}\,\bigl(\mathrm{Tr}\,|\Phi(\rho)|^p\bigr)^{1/p},
\]
where the supremum is over all density operators $\rho$ on the input space, and $\|X\|_p=(\mathrm{Tr}|X|^p)^{1/p}$ is the Schatten $p$-norm. The channel $\Phi\otimes\Omega$ acts on density operators of the bipartite system $\mathcal{H}_A\otimes\mathcal{H}_B$.

The maximal output $p$-norm multiplicativity property at the value $p=2$ asserts
\[
\nu_2(\Phi\otimes\Omega) \;=\; \nu_2(\Phi)\,\nu_2(\Omega). \tag{$\ast$}
\]

Identify and characterize broad classes of pairs of quantum channels $(\Phi,\Omega)$ for which the equality $(\ast)$ can be rigorously established, and provide proofs of multiplicativity at $p=2$ for as wide a class of channels as possible.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Multiplicativity at p=2 is known for several classes (e.g., entanglement-breaking channels, unital qubit channels, depolarizing channels, Hadamard channels, and Gaussian channels in appropriate settings), proved by King, Shor, and others. However, Hayden–Winter (arXiv:0707.3291) showed that the general maximal p-norm multiplicativity conjecture is false for all p>1, including p=2 in a neighborhood interpretation, and Hastings later disproved additivity. Thus multiplicativity at p=2 cannot hold for all channels, and the program of identifying the largest natural classes where it does hold is ongoing and partially resolved.

Let $G$ be an infinite-dimensional Lie group (a group equipped with a smooth manifold structure modeled on a locally convex topological vector space, such that multiplication and inversion are smooth), and write $L(G) = T_1 G$ for its Lie algebra. For $k \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, a subset $H \subseteq G$ endowed with a smooth manifold structure is called $C^k$-initial in $G$ if the inclusion $\lambda \colon H \to G$ is $C^k$ and, for every $C^k$-manifold $X$ and every map $f \colon X \to H$, the composition $\lambda \circ f$ being $C^k$ implies that $f$ itself is $C^k$. A subgroup $H \subseteq G$ is called an initial Lie subgroup of $G$ if it admits a smooth manifold structure making it a Lie group, making it $C^k$-initial in $G$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$, and making the induced tangent map $L(\lambda) \colon L(H) \to L(G)$ injective.

Question: Does every subgroup $H$ of every infinite-dimensional Lie group $G$ admit such a smooth manifold structure making it an initial Lie subgroup of $G$?

Equivalently, decide whether the additive subgroup $\ell^\infty$ of bounded real sequences, viewed as a subgroup of the infinite-dimensional Lie group $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{N}}$ (with the product topology and the obvious smooth structure), can be given the structure of an initial Lie subgroup.

Setup. A qubit channel is a completely positive trace-preserving linear map Φ : M₂(ℂ) → M₂(ℂ). For ρ ∈ M₂(ℂ), the maximal output p-norm of Φ (for p ≥ 1) is

  ν_p(Φ) := sup_{ρ ≥ 0, Tr ρ = 1} ‖Φ(ρ)‖_p,

where ‖A‖_p = (Tr |A|^p)^{1/p}. The channel Φ is said to be multiplicative for p-norms if for every channel Ψ (acting on any finite-dimensional matrix algebra),

  ν_p(Φ ⊗ Ψ) = ν_p(Φ) · ν_p(Ψ).

The two-Pauli qubit channel is the channel

  Φ_{2P}(ρ) = (1 − x) ρ + (x/2) (σ_x ρ σ_x + σ_z ρ σ_z),  x ∈ [0,1],

where σ_x, σ_z are the Pauli matrices. In the Bloch representation it acts as a diagonal map (r_x, r_y, r_z) ↦ (λ_x r_x, λ_y r_y, λ_z r_z) with multipliers (λ_x, λ_y, λ_z) = (1 − x, 1 − 2x, 1 − x); for x > 1/2 the middle multiplier is negative. By a unitary rotation one can conjugate Φ_{2P} into a channel with all multipliers non-negative, and known proofs of p-norm multiplicativity for Φ_{2P} pass through such conjugation.

Problem. Produce a proof, valid for all p ∈ [1, ∞] (in particular for the relevant range establishing additivity-type results), that the two-Pauli qubit channel Φ_{2P} satisfies

  ν_p(Φ_{2P} ⊗ Ψ) = ν_p(Φ_{2P}) · ν_p(Ψ)

for every channel Ψ, without using unitary equivalence to a Pauli-diagonal channel whose Bloch multipliers are all non-negative.

The general maximal p-norm multiplicativity conjecture for quantum channels was disproved (Hastings; Hayden–Winter) for sufficiently large p, but multiplicativity for the two-Pauli qubit channel is established via known King-style proofs that do invoke unitary equivalence to a channel with non-negative multipliers. Let $G_1 \subseteq G_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be an ascending sequence of finite-dimensional real Lie groups such that each inclusion map $G_n \hookrightarrow G_{n+1}$ is a smooth homomorphism, and let $G = \varinjlim G_n$ denote the corresponding direct limit Lie group (in the category of Lie groups modeled on locally convex spaces, with its natural direct-limit smooth structure).

Recall that a subgroup $H \subseteq G$ endowed with a Lie group structure is called an initial Lie subgroup of $G$ if the inclusion $\iota: H \to G$ is smooth and, for every smooth manifold $M$ and every map $f: M \to H$, $f$ is smooth whenever $\iota \circ f: M \to G$ is smooth. More strongly, the inclusion is called strongly $C^k$-initial (for $k \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$) if for every $C^k$-manifold $M$ and every map $f: M \to H$, $f$ is $C^k$ whenever $\iota \circ f: M \to G$ is $C^k$.

For an arbitrary subgroup $H \subseteq G$, set $H_n := G_n \cap H$ and equip $H_n$ with a finite-dimensional Lie group structure induced from $G_n$ and $H$, then equip $H$ with the direct-limit Lie group structure $H = \varinjlim H_n$.

Prove or disprove: with these structures, the inclusion $H \to G$ is strongly $C^k$-initial for every $k \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{\infty\}$; in particular, every subgroup of $G$ is an initial Lie subgroup of $G$.

Let $\Phi:\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_A)\to\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_B)$ be a completely positive trace-preserving (CPT) linear map between finite-dimensional matrix algebras. Recall that $\Phi$ is called extreme if it is an extreme point of the convex set of CPT maps from $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_A)$ to $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_B)$; equivalently, by Choi's theorem, $\Phi$ has a Kraus representation $\Phi(\rho)=\sum_{k=1}^{r} A_k\rho A_k^*$ such that the operators $\{A_j^*A_k\}_{j,k=1}^{r}$ are linearly independent.

Define the minimal output von Neumann entropy of $\Phi$ by
$$S_{\min}(\Phi)=\inf_{\rho}\, S(\Phi(\rho)),\qquad S(\sigma)=-\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma\log\sigma),$$
the infimum being over density matrices on $\mathcal{H}_A$. For $1\le p\le\infty$ define the maximal output $p$-norm
$$\nu_p(\Phi)=\sup_{\rho}\,\|\Phi(\rho)\|_p,\qquad \|\sigma\|_p=(\operatorname{Tr}|\sigma|^p)^{1/p}.$$

Identify new classes of extreme CPT maps $\Phi$ such that, for every CPT map $\Omega$ (in some natural class, e.g. all CPT maps, or all maps in the same class), one can prove either the additivity relation
$$S_{\min}(\Phi\otimes\Omega)=S_{\min}(\Phi)+S_{\min}(\Omega),$$
or the multiplicativity relation
$$\nu_p(\Phi\otimes\Omega)=\nu_p(\Phi)\,\nu_p(\Omega)$$
for some $p>1$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The general additivity conjecture for minimal output von Neumann entropy was disproved by Hastings (2009) via random channel constructions, with later analyses by Fukuda–King–Moser and Aubrun–Szarek. Multiplicativity of maximal output $p$-norms for $p>1$ was also disproved (Hayden–Winter). However, additivity/multiplicativity is still proved for specific classes of channels (entanglement-breaking, unital qubit, depolarizing, Hadamard, etc.), and the broader task of identifying new classes of extreme CPT maps for which these relations hold remains an active research direction with only partial results.

Let $G_1 \subseteq G_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be an ascending sequence of finite-dimensional real Lie groups such that each inclusion $G_n \hookrightarrow G_{n+1}$ is a smooth homomorphism, and let $G = \varinjlim G_n$ be the direct limit, equipped with the finest topology making all inclusions $G_n \to G$ continuous (so that $G$ is a topological group). Let $\mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$ denote the set of continuous one-parameter subgroups of $G$, equipped with the compact-open topology, and let scalar multiplication be defined by $(s\cdot \gamma)(t) := \gamma(st)$.

The topological group $G$ is said to be a topological group with Lie algebra (in the sense of Hofmann–Morris) if:
(a) for all $\gamma, \eta \in \mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$, the limit
$$(\gamma + \eta)(t) := \lim_{n \to \infty} \big(\gamma(t/n)\,\eta(t/n)\big)^n$$
exists for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and defines a continuous homomorphism $\mathbb{R} \to G$;
(b) with this addition and the scalar multiplication above, $\mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$ is a topological vector space;
(c) there exists a continuous bilinear map $[\cdot,\cdot] : \mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G) \times \mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G) \to \mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$ given by a commutator limit, making $\mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$ into a topological Lie algebra.

Question: Is every such direct limit $G = \varinjlim G_n$ a topological group with Lie algebra in this sense, with $\mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$ naturally identified as a topological Lie algebra with the Lie algebra $L(G) = \varinjlim L(G_n)$ of $G$?

Let $G_1 \subseteq G_2 \subseteq \cdots$ be an ascending sequence of finite-dimensional real Lie groups such that each inclusion $G_n \hookrightarrow G_{n+1}$ is a smooth homomorphism, and let $G = \varinjlim G_n$ be the direct limit, equipped with the finest topology making all inclusions $G_n \to G$ continuous (so that $G$ is a topological group). Let $\mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$ denote the set of continuous one-parameter subgroups of $G$, equipped with the compact-open topology, and let scalar multiplication be defined by $(s\cdot \gamma)(t) := \gamma(st)$.

The topological group $G$ is said to be a topological group with Lie algebra (in the sense of Hofmann–Morris) if:
(a) for all $\gamma, \eta \in \mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$, the limit
$$(\gamma + \eta)(t) := \lim_{n \to \infty} \big(\gamma(t/n)\,\eta(t/n)\big)^n$$
exists for every $t \in \mathbb{R}$ and defines a continuous homomorphism $\mathbb{R} \to G$;
(b) with this addition and the scalar multiplication above, $\mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$ is a topological vector space;
(c) there exists a continuous bilinear map $[\cdot,\cdot] : \mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G) \times \mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G) \to \mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$ given by a commutator limit, making $\mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$ into a topological Lie algebra.

Question: Is every such direct limit $G = \varinjlim G_n$ a topological group with Lie algebra in this sense, with $\mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$ naturally identified as a topological Lie algebra with the Lie algebra $L(G) = \varinjlim L(G_n)$ of $G$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question is answered affirmatively: every direct limit of finite-dimensional Lie groups along smooth inclusions is a topological group with Lie algebra in the Hofmann–Morris sense, and the natural map $L(G) \to \mathrm{Hom}_c(\mathbb{R}, G)$ is a homeomorphism of topological Lie algebras.

Let $\Phi:\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_A)\to\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{K}_A)$ and $\Omega:\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_B)\to\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{K}_B)$ be quantum channels (completely positive trace-preserving linear maps between matrix algebras). For $p>0$, $p\neq 1$, the Rényi entropy of order $p$ of a density operator $\rho$ is
$$S^p(\rho)=\frac{1}{1-p}\log\operatorname{Tr}(\rho^p),$$
and for $p=1$ it is the von Neumann entropy $S(\rho)=-\operatorname{Tr}(\rho\log\rho)$. The minimal output Rényi $p$-entropy of a channel $\Phi$ is
$$S^p_{\min}(\Phi)=\inf_{\rho}S^p(\Phi(\rho)),$$
where the infimum is over input density operators (equivalently, pure states).

Decide the following statement: for every pair of quantum channels $\Phi$ and $\Omega$, there exists $p^*>0$ such that either
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] $p^*<1$ and $S^p_{\min}(\Phi\otimes\Omega)=S^p_{\min}(\Phi)+S^p_{\min}(\Omega)$ holds for every $p\in(p^*,1)$, or
\item[(ii)] $p^*>1$ and $S^p_{\min}(\Phi\otimes\Omega)=S^p_{\min}(\Phi)+S^p_{\min}(\Omega)$ holds for every $p\in(1,p^*)$.
\end{enumerate}
That is, prove this dichotomy holds for all channel pairs, or exhibit a counterexample.

The conjecture appears to be refuted. Hastings (2009) produced channels for which additivity of minimum output von Neumann entropy fails at $p=1$; subsequent analyses (Aubrun–Szarek–Werner; Cubitt–Harrow–Leung–Montanaro–Winter; Collins–Fukuda–Nechita and others) show that the same random-subspace constructions yield violations of additivity of the minimum output Rényi $p$-entropy on intervals adjacent to $p=1$ (in particular for $p\in(1-p_0,1)$ with $p_0\approx 0.2855$). Combined with Hayden–Winter / Grudka–Horodecki / recent constructive results showing violations for all $p>1$, there exist fixed pairs $(\Phi,\Omega)$ for which additivity fails on every one-sided neighborhood of $p=1$, contradicting the conjectured dichotomy.

Let $A$ be a Banach algebra with Jacobson radical $\operatorname{rad}(A)$, and let $Z(A/\operatorname{rad}(A))$ denote the centre of the quotient Banach algebra $A/\operatorname{rad}(A)$. Define
$$Z(A) := \pi^{-1}\bigl(Z(A/\operatorname{rad}(A))\bigr),$$
where $\pi: A \to A/\operatorname{rad}(A)$ is the canonical quotient map (so $Z(A)$ is the centre modulo the radical).

Let $\delta: A \to A$ be a (not necessarily continuous) derivation, i.e. a linear map satisfying $\delta(xy) = \delta(x)y + x\delta(y)$ for all $x, y \in A$. Suppose that
$$[x, \delta x] := x\,\delta x - \delta x \cdot x \in Z(A) \qquad \text{for every } x \in A.$$

Question: Does it follow that $\delta(A) \subseteq \operatorname{rad}(A)$? Equivalently, under the same hypothesis, must $\delta$ be spectrally bounded (i.e. must there exist a constant $M \geq 0$ such that the spectral radius satisfies $r(\delta x) \leq M\, r(x)$ for all $x \in A$)?

The noncommutative Singer–Wermer conjecture, asking whether every (possibly discontinuous) derivation on a noncommutative Banach algebra maps into the Jacobson radical (under the centre-modulo-radical commutator hypothesis), remains open. Recall that for a unital C*-algebra A, the Glimm ideals of A are the closed two-sided ideals of A generated by the maximal ideals of the center Z(A); equivalently, they are the intersections of the primitive ideals of A lying over a single point of the maximal ideal space of Z(A). The set of Glimm ideals of A is in natural bijection with the maximal ideal space of Z(A).

Question: Suppose T : A → B is a surjective unital spectral isometry between unital C*-algebras. Must T leave every Glimm ideal of A invariant, in the sense that for each Glimm ideal G of A there is a Glimm ideal G' of B with T(G) = G' (equivalently, T induces a bijection between the Glimm ideals of A and those of B compatible with T)?

$$ S^p_{\min}(\Phi^{\otimes n}) \;=\; n\,S^p_{\min}(\Phi) \quad \text{for every } 1\le n<m,$$

$$ S^p_{\min}(\Phi^{\otimes m}) \;<\; m\,S^p_{\min}(\Phi).$$

Let $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ denote the bounded operators on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, and let a quantum channel be a completely positive trace-preserving linear map $\Phi:\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_A)\to\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_B)$. For $p\ge 1$, define the maximal output $p$-norm
$$\nu_p(\Phi)=\sup_{\rho}\,\|\Phi(\rho)\|_p,$$
where the supremum runs over density operators $\rho$ on $\mathcal{H}_A$ and $\|X\|_p=(\mathrm{Tr}|X|^p)^{1/p}$. A pair $(\Phi,\Omega)$ of channels is said to be a counterexample to maximal output $p$-norm multiplicativity if
$$\nu_p(\Phi\otimes\Omega)>\nu_p(\Phi)\,\nu_p(\Omega).$$

For a channel $\Phi$ with Stinespring isometry $V:\mathcal{H}_A\to\mathcal{H}_B\otimes\mathcal{H}_E$ and complementary channel $\Phi^c(\rho)=\mathrm{Tr}_B(V\rho V^\dagger)$, define:
- the coherent information $I_c(\rho,\Phi)=S(\Phi(\rho))-S(\Phi^c(\rho))$, where $S(\sigma)=-\mathrm{Tr}(\sigma\log\sigma)$ is the von Neumann entropy;
- the completely bounded (CB) entropy $S_{\mathrm{CB}}(\Phi)$, defined as the regularized minimum, over all input states $\rho_{RA}$ on an arbitrary reference system $R$ tensored with the input, of $S(\Phi^c(\rho_A))-S(\Phi(\rho_A))$ optimized in the CB sense (equivalently, $-\inf_\rho I_c(\rho,\Phi)$ in the appropriate completely bounded regularization).

Question: For every $p>1$ and every pair of channels $(\Phi,\Omega)$ that violates maximal output $p$-norm multiplicativity, must at least one of the following hold for the channels involved?
(a) The CB entropy is non-negative;
(b) The maximum coherent information $\max_\rho I_c(\rho,\Phi)$ equals zero.

$$T(x) \;=\; \gamma\,S(x) + (1-\gamma)\,\tau(x) \qquad \text{for every } x\in A?$$

Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and let $\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H})$ denote the set of density matrices on $\mathcal{H}$, i.e. positive semidefinite operators $\gamma$ on $\mathcal{H}$ with $\operatorname{Tr}\gamma = 1$. A quantum channel $\Phi : \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_A) \to \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_B)$ is a completely positive trace-preserving linear map. The von Neumann entropy of a density matrix $\rho$ is $S(\rho) = -\operatorname{Tr}(\rho \log \rho)$, and the minimal output entropy of a channel $\Phi$ is
$$S_{\min}(\Phi) \;=\; \inf_{\gamma \in \mathcal{D}(\mathcal{H}_A)} S\bigl(\Phi(\gamma)\bigr).$$
Given two quantum channels $\Phi$ and $\Omega$, the tensor product $\Phi \otimes \Omega$ is again a quantum channel acting on density matrices of the joint system.

Determine whether the additivity identity
$$S_{\min}(\Phi \otimes \Omega) \;=\; S_{\min}(\Phi) + S_{\min}(\Omega)$$
holds for all pairs of quantum channels $\Phi, \Omega$. Either prove that the equality always holds, or exhibit a pair of channels for which it fails.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The additivity conjecture for minimal output entropy was disproved by M. B. Hastings in 2009 ("Superadditivity of communication capacity using entangled inputs", Nature Physics 5, 255–257), who gave a non-constructive counterexample using random unitary channels in high dimension. Subsequent work has refined and simplified the counterexample. Thus the problem is solved in the negative: additivity does not hold in general.

Let $\mathcal{H}_A$, $\mathcal{H}_B$, $\mathcal{H}_E$ be finite-dimensional complex Hilbert spaces. Recall that a quantum channel is a completely positive trace-preserving (CPTP) linear map between spaces of trace-class operators. Every channel $M : B(\mathcal{H}_A) \to B(\mathcal{H}_B)$ admits a Stinespring isometry $V_M : \mathcal{H}_A \to \mathcal{H}_B \otimes \mathcal{H}_E$ such that $M(\rho) = \mathrm{Tr}_E(V_M \rho V_M^*)$; the complementary channel is defined by $M^C(\rho) = \mathrm{Tr}_B(V_M \rho V_M^*)$. The Choi rank of $M$ is the minimum dimension of $\mathcal{H}_E$ in any Stinespring dilation, equivalently the rank of the Choi matrix of $M$. A channel $M$ is called degradable if there exists a channel $D$ with $D \circ M = M^C$.

Two channels $M$ and $N$ (with appropriately compatible input/output spaces) are said to be mutually degradable if there exist channels $X$ and $Y$ such that
$$ X \circ M = N^C \quad \text{and} \quad Y \circ N = M^C. $$

Note that if $M = I$ is the identity channel, then $M^C$ is (up to isometry) the trace, so the conditions reduce trivially and any channel $N$ pairs with $I$. Exhibit nontrivial pairs $(M, N)$ of mutually degradable channels in which neither channel is the identity. In particular, construct a pair $(M, N)$ such that both $M$ and $N$ act on a $d$-dimensional input system, both have Choi rank equal to $d$, and neither $M$ nor $N$ is individually degradable; or prove that no such pair exists.

representations.normalized:
Setup. Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a finite-dimensional complex Hilbert space and let $U(\mathcal{H})$ denote its unitary group. For an integer $N\ge 2$, consider the $N$-fold tensor power $\mathcal{H}^{\otimes N}$, and let $\mathcal{H}^{\wedge N}\subset \mathcal{H}^{\otimes N}$ (resp. $\mathcal{H}^{\vee N}$) denote its totally antisymmetric (resp. totally symmetric) subspace. An $N$-fermion (resp. $N$-boson) density matrix is a positive semidefinite trace-one operator $\rho_{1,\dots,N}$ supported on $\mathcal{H}^{\wedge N}$ (resp. $\mathcal{H}^{\vee N}$). For $1\le p\le N$, the $p$-particle reduced density matrix is
$$\rho_{1,\dots,p}\;=\;\mathrm{Tr}_{p+1,\dots,N}\,\rho_{1,\dots,N},$$
which acts on $\mathcal{H}^{\wedge p}$ (resp. $\mathcal{H}^{\vee p}$).

Local unitary action. The unitary group $U(\mathcal{H})$ acts on operators on $\mathcal{H}^{\otimes p}$ via the diagonal representation $U^{\otimes p}$, i.e. by
$$\rho \;\longmapsto\; U^{\otimes p}\,\rho\,(U^{\otimes p})^\dagger,\qquad U\in U(\mathcal{H}).$$
A local invariant of a $p$-particle density matrix is a function of $\rho_{1,\dots,p}$ that is constant on each orbit of this action. A set $\{I_\alpha\}$ of local invariants is called complete if it separates orbits, i.e. two $p$-particle density matrices have the same values of all $I_\alpha$ if and only if they lie in the same $U^{\otimes p}$-orbit. The set is called minimal if no proper subset is complete.

Problem. Take $p=2$. Exhibit, for both the antisymmetric case (operators on $\mathcal{H}^{\wedge 2}$) and the symmetric case (operators on $\mathcal{H}^{\vee 2}$), a minimal complete set of local invariants of a two-particle density matrix under the action $\rho \mapsto (U\otimes U)\rho(U\otimes U)^\dagger$, $U\in U(\mathcal{H})$. The set should be expressive enough that the two-particle $N$-representability conditions (necessary and sufficient conditions on $\rho_{1,2}$ for the existence of an $N$-particle antisymmetric/symmetric density matrix $\rho_{1,\dots,N}$ with $\mathrm{Tr}_{3,\dots,N}\rho_{1,\dots,N}=\rho_{1,2}$) can be formulated in terms of these invariants.

Setup. For positive integers $n,k$ and $0<r<1$, let $\Delta^m\subset\mathbb{C}^m$ denote the open unit polydisc, $\Delta^m(s)$ the polydisc of polyradius $s$, and $A^k(r,1)=\Delta^k\setminus\overline{\Delta^k(r)}$ the spherical shell. Define the Hartogs figure
$$H^k_n(r)=\bigl(\Delta^n(1-r)\times\Delta^k\bigr)\;\cup\;\bigl(\Delta^n\times A^k(r,1)\bigr)\subset\Delta^{n+k}.$$

Classes of target spaces. A complex manifold (or complex space) $X$ is said to belong to the class $\mathcal{P}^-_k$ if every meromorphic map from $H^k_n(r)$ into $X$ extends meromorphically to $\Delta^{n+k}$ minus a (possibly empty) analytic-type singular set; and to the (stronger) class $\mathcal{G}_k$ if, in addition, the existence of a non-removable singularity forces strong topological/complex-structural constraints on $X$ (e.g. existence of rational curves, non-Kähler structure, etc., as in known results for $k=1$). Assume $X$ is compact, or more generally disk-convex.

Problem. Prove or disprove the following:

(a) (General extension.) For every $n,k\ge 1$ and every compact or disk-convex complex manifold/space $X\in\mathcal{P}^-_k$, every meromorphic map $f:H^k_n(r)\dashrightarrow X$ extends to a meromorphic map on $\Delta^{n+k}\setminus A$, where $A$ is a closed subset of Hausdorff $(2n-1)$-dimensional measure zero.

(b) (Topological rigidity in $\mathcal{G}_k$.) If furthermore $X\in\mathcal{G}_k$ and the singular set $A$ in (a) is nonempty, then $X$ must satisfy very restrictive conditions on its topology and complex structure (to be made precise, paralleling the case $k=1$).

(c) (Equidimensional case.) In particular, the three-dimensional Hartogs-type extension theorem for equidimensional meromorphic maps holds in every dimension: every meromorphic map between equidimensional complex manifolds from $H^k_n(r)$ into a compact manifold of class $\mathcal{P}^-_k$ extends as in (a).

Let $n\ge 2$. Let $V$ be a compact complex affine $n$-fold, i.e. a compact complex manifold of complex dimension $n$ equipped with a holomorphic affine structure (a maximal atlas of holomorphic charts into $\mathbb{C}^n$ whose transition maps are restrictions of complex affine transformations of $\mathbb{C}^n$). The developing map of this structure realizes the universal cover $\widetilde V$ as a Riemann domain $(\widetilde V,\widetilde\pi)$ over $\mathbb{C}^n$ with locally biholomorphic projection $\widetilde\pi:\widetilde V\to\mathbb{C}^n$.

Recall that $(\widetilde V,\widetilde\pi)$ is said to be pseudoconcave at a boundary point $p\in\partial\widetilde V$ if there is an open neighborhood $U$ of $p$ in the natural completion such that, for every plurisubharmonic function $\varphi$ defined on $U\cap\widetilde V$ and continuous up to $p$, one has $\varphi(p)\le\sup_{U\cap\widetilde V}\varphi$ (equivalently, the boundary is pseudoconcave in the sense of Andreotti). A compact complex manifold $V$ of dimension $n$ is said to contain a spherical shell (of dimension $n$) if there exists a holomorphic embedding of a neighborhood of the unit sphere $S^{2n-1}\subset\mathbb{C}^n$ into $V$ which is not homologous to zero (equivalently, whose image does not bound in $V$).

Question: Suppose that $(\widetilde V,\widetilde\pi)$ is pseudoconcave at some boundary point. Does it follow that $V$ contains a spherical shell of dimension $n$?

Let $\Delta \subset \mathbb{C}$ denote the unit disk, and let $\pi : \mathcal{X} \to \Delta$ be a proper holomorphic submersion whose fibers $X_t = \pi^{-1}(t)$ are compact complex manifolds (a complex deformation of compact complex manifolds). Suppose that for every $t \in \Delta$ with $t \neq 0$, the fiber $X_t$ possesses the meromorphic extension property.

Must the central fiber $X_0$ also possess the meromorphic extension property?
