representations.normalized:
Type Ia supernovae are stellar explosions whose ejecta spectra show no hydrogen and no helium lines, a feature commonly interpreted as evidence that the exploding object is a highly evolved star such as a carbon–oxygen white dwarf. The widely held hypothesis is that the progenitor of every Type Ia supernova is a moderate-mass binary system in which a white dwarf accretes from, or merges with, a companion star. However, both white dwarfs and the plausible companions (main-sequence, subgiant, helium-star, or second white-dwarf companions) are intrinsically faint, so direct identification of a Type Ia progenitor in pre-explosion imaging or of a surviving companion in post-explosion imaging is not generically feasible.

Problem: Identify and justify a set of direct or circumstantial observational signatures that can collectively establish whether the progenitors of Type Ia supernovae are indeed moderate-mass binary systems. In particular, specify observational tests (for example, searches for circumstellar matter, narrow time-variable absorption features, early-time light-curve excesses from companion interaction, surviving companions in supernova remnants, delay-time distributions, host-galaxy stellar-population dependences, radio/X-ray limits on accretion winds, or progenitor-system constraints from gravitational-wave or astrometric surveys) and explain how each signature would discriminate between the binary-progenitor hypothesis and alternatives, given the faintness constraints that preclude routine pre- or post-explosion identification.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question of which binary configurations produce Type Ia supernovae remains an active and partially resolved problem in astrophysics. Recent reviews (2024–2025) describe a "contemporary view of a long-standing puzzle" in which multiple progenitor channels are now favored, with mounting circumstantial evidence: non-detections of accretion winds rule out many symbiotic and strongly accreting single-degenerate systems; a super-Chandrasekhar double white dwarf candidate at 49 pc has been characterized; and gravitational-wave-detectable double white dwarf progenitor candidates have been identified. However, a definitive, universal demonstration that all SNe Ia originate from moderate-mass binaries, and an unambiguous identification of the dominant channel, is still lacking.

Consider an incompressible viscoelastic fluid in a bounded domain Ω ⊂ ℝ^d (d = 2 or 3) with smooth boundary, on a time interval (0, T). The motion is governed by the incompressibility condition div v = 0, the momentum balance

  ρ(∂_t v + (v·∇)v) = div σ_total − ∇p + f,   σ_total = 2μ E + τ,

and a Jeffreys-type constitutive relation for the extra (non-Newtonian) stress τ (or equivalently for the total deviatoric stress σ):

  σ + λ_1 (Dσ/Dt) = 2η ( E + λ_2 (DE/Dt) ),

where E = (∇v + (∇v)^T)/2 is the symmetric strain-rate tensor, W = (∇v − (∇v)^T)/2 is the vorticity tensor, λ_1 > λ_2 > 0 are relaxation/retardation times, η > 0 is a viscosity parameter, and the objective time derivative is taken to be the Jaumann (corotational) derivative

  D_0 T / Dt := ∂_t T + (v·∇)T + T W − W T,

acting on a symmetric tensor field T. The system is supplemented with the no-slip boundary condition v|_{∂Ω} = 0 and initial data v(0,·) = v_0, σ(0,·) = σ_0 with appropriate regularity (e.g. v_0 ∈ L^2, σ_0 ∈ L^2).

Question. Does this initial-boundary value problem admit a global-in-time weak solution (v, σ) for arbitrary finite-energy initial data and right-hand side f? In particular, in any approximation/limit-passage scheme that constructs such a weak solution, can one rigorously justify the identity

  η|_{t=0} = 0

(where η here denotes the defect/concentration measure or weak-limit residual associated with the non-Newtonian stress in the passage to the limit), which is required to close the argument and identify the limit of the nonlinear stress terms?

Existence of global weak solutions for Jeffreys-type viscoelastic models has been established in several works (e.g. Vorotnikov 2004, and subsequent results on attractors and regularized models). However, the specific concern about whether the corotational/Jaumann-derivative case is fully justified — in particular whether the identity η|_{t=0} = 0 used in the limit-passage step for the non-Newtonian stress can be rigorously verified — does not appear to be conclusively settled in the literature accessible by search. The status is therefore reported as unknown.

Consider the initial-boundary value problem for the evolutionary motion of an incompressible viscoelastic fluid of Jeffreys type in a bounded domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n=2,3$) with smooth boundary. The velocity field $v(t,x)$ and pressure $p(t,x)$ satisfy the system
$$\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} + (v\cdot\nabla)v - \mathrm{Div}\,\sigma + \nabla p = f, \qquad \mathrm{div}\, v = 0,$$
where the deviatoric stress tensor $\sigma$ obeys the Jeffreys constitutive relation
$$\sigma + \lambda_1 \frac{\mathcal{D}\sigma}{\mathcal{D}t} = 2\mu\!\left(\mathcal{E}(v) + \lambda_2 \frac{\mathcal{D}\mathcal{E}(v)}{\mathcal{D}t}\right),$$
with relaxation time $\lambda_1>0$, retardation time $\lambda_2\in(0,\lambda_1)$, viscosity $\mu>0$, rate-of-strain tensor $\mathcal{E}(v)=\tfrac{1}{2}(\nabla v + \nabla v^\top)$, and an objective (e.g. Jaumann or upper-convected) time derivative $\mathcal{D}/\mathcal{D}t$. The system is supplemented with no-slip boundary condition $v|_{\partial\Omega}=0$ and initial data $v(0,\cdot)=v_0$.

Assume that, for suitable classes of initial data and external force $f$, global-in-time (possibly weak or generalized) solutions of this problem have been constructed, giving rise to a (multivalued) dynamical system or a trajectory space on the phase space of divergence-free vector fields.

Question: Can one construct, for this dynamical system, a generalized global attractor (e.g. a trajectory attractor or a minimal attracting set in an appropriate weak topology) and/or an inertial manifold (a finite-dimensional, positively invariant Lipschitz manifold attracting all trajectories at an exponential rate)?

Stars with main-sequence masses in the range 3–8 solar masses are known to evolve into Cepheid variables after leaving the main sequence and later to terminate their regular evolution by passing through a planetary-nebula phase. Type Ia supernovae are believed to arise from binary systems containing at least one white dwarf, but the detailed statistical properties of the progenitor binaries (e.g. mass ratios, separations, orbital period distributions, occurrence rates of white-dwarf companions) and the parameters that determine whether such a binary will eventually produce a Type Ia explosion remain uncertain.

Question: Can a systematic observational survey of white-dwarf companions to Cepheid variables determine the statistical properties of binary systems capable of producing Type Ia supernovae, and identify the crucial physical parameters (such as component masses, separations, and mass-transfer history) that lead to a Type Ia supernova explosion?

Let $p$ be an odd prime, and let $\left(\frac{\cdot}{7}\right)$ denote the Legendre symbol modulo $7$. Prove or disprove the following congruences modulo $p^2$:

(a) If $\left(\frac{p}{7}\right) = 1$ (equivalently $p \equiv 1, 2, 4 \pmod{7}$), then $p$ can be written as $p = x^2 + 7y^2$ with $x, y \in \mathbb{Z}$, and
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \binom{2k}{k}^{3} \equiv 4x^2 - 2p \pmod{p^2}.$$

(b) If $\left(\frac{p}{7}\right) = -1$ (equivalently $p \equiv 3, 5, 6 \pmod{7}$), then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \binom{2k}{k}^{3} \equiv 0 \pmod{p^2}.$$

Here $\binom{2k}{k} = \frac{(2k)!}{(k!)^2}$ denotes the central binomial coefficient.

Type Ia supernovae (SNe Ia) are used as cosmological distance indicators by means of the empirical "brighter-slower" standardization relation: SNe Ia with intrinsically brighter peak luminosities exhibit broader (more slowly declining) optical light curves than fainter ones, allowing peak luminosities to be inferred from light-curve shape. SNe Ia are believed to arise from two broad progenitor channels: a "prompt" (fast) component, with characteristic delay times from star formation to explosion of less than about 100 Myr, and a "tardy" (delayed) component, with delay times typically exceeding 1 Gyr.

Address the following two coupled questions:

(a) Identify a physical mechanism (e.g., progenitor mass, metallicity, central density of the white dwarf, ^56Ni yield, opacity, explosion energetics, or progenitor channel) that explains, from first principles, why brighter SNe Ia have broader light curves than fainter ones, and derive (within an explicit model) the functional form of the resulting peak-luminosity / light-curve-width relation.

(b) Let f_prompt(z) and f_tardy(z) = 1 − f_prompt(z) denote the fraction of SNe Ia at redshift z drawn from the prompt and tardy progenitor channels, respectively, and suppose the two channels have intrinsic mean post-standardization residuals ΔM_prompt and ΔM_tardy in absolute magnitude. Quantify the resulting bias in the inferred distance modulus μ(z), and propagate this bias to estimate the maximum systematic shift in the inferred dark-energy equation-of-state parameter w (and its time derivative w_a) over the redshift range 0 ≤ z ≲ 1.5, given that f_prompt(z) increases with z because of the cosmic star-formation history.

The physical origin of the brighter-slower relation remains incompletely understood, though candidate explanations (progenitor white-dwarf central density, metallicity, ^56Ni mass, opacity) have been advanced. Recent observational work establishes a robust, redshift-evolving dependence of standardized SN Ia luminosity on host-galaxy stellar age (progenitor age), with claims that this bias is significant enough to alter inferred dark-energy parameters and is not absorbed by the usual mass-step correction. The cosmological-bias question is therefore actively studied with quantitative estimates available, but a full first-principles theory of the standardization relation and a definitive correction prescription are not yet established.

Let $p$ denote a prime, $a$ a positive integer, and $\binom{2k}{k}$ the central binomial coefficient. Decide whether both of the following statements hold.

(i) For every prime $p$ and every positive integer $a$ such that $p^a \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor 2 p^a/3 \rfloor} (21k+8)\binom{2k}{k}^{3} \equiv 8\,p^{a} \pmod{p^{\,a+5+(-1)^{p}}},$$
where the exponent of the modulus is $a+6$ when $p=2$ and $a+4$ when $p$ is odd.

(ii) Conversely, every integer $n>1$ that satisfies
$$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} (21k+8)\binom{2k}{k}^{3} \equiv 8\,n \pmod{n^{4}}$$
is necessarily prime.

Prove both assertions or provide a counterexample.

Core-collapse supernovae are believed to arise from the gravitational collapse of the iron core of massive stars (initial mass M > 8 M_sun) at the end of nuclear burning. Among the spectroscopic subtypes, Type Ib and Type Ic supernovae (collectively Type Ib/c) are distinguished by the absence of hydrogen lines (Ib) and the additional absence of helium lines (Ic) in their spectra, indicating progenitors that have lost their outer envelopes (so-called stripped-envelope events). Possible progenitor channels include single massive Wolf–Rayet stars and lower-mass stars stripped via interaction in close binary systems.

Direct identification has been hampered by: (i) the rarity of Type Ib/c events relative to Type II, leading to typically larger host-galaxy distances; (ii) the diffraction-limited resolution of pre-explosion imaging (e.g., HST), insufficient to resolve candidate stars in crowded fields at such distances; and (iii) the very high effective temperatures of stripped-envelope progenitors, for which a few optical photometric bands constrain the bolometric luminosity (and hence the inferred stellar mass) only as a weak lower limit, leaving a large allowed parameter space.

Problem. Determine the true progenitor types and the distribution of zero-age main-sequence (or pre-explosion) stellar masses of Type Ib/c core-collapse supernovae, and devise an observational/inferential strategy that yields unambiguous (rather than merely lower-limit) identifications of individual progenitors despite the rarity of such events, the typically large distances of their host galaxies, the resolution limits of available pre-explosion imaging, and the weak constraints provided by optical photometry on bolometric luminosity and progenitor mass.

Core-collapse supernovae are commonly subdivided into several observational subclasses based on their spectra and light curves: Type IIP (plateau hydrogen-rich), Type IIL (linearly declining hydrogen-rich), Type IIn (narrow hydrogen emission lines indicating dense circumstellar material), Type IIb (hydrogen-poor, transitioning to a helium-dominated spectrum), and Type Ib/c (hydrogen-deficient, with Type Ic also helium-deficient). Direct identification of progenitors in pre-explosion imaging gives zero-age main-sequence (ZAMS) mass estimates of approximately 8–16 M☉ for about a dozen Type IIP progenitors (red supergiants), while indirect lower limits for Type Ib/c progenitors lie above approximately 20 M☉, leaving an apparent gap in the inferred progenitor mass distribution between roughly 16 M☉ and 20 M☉.

Question: Determine whether the progenitors of Type IIb, Type IIn, and Type IIL core-collapse supernovae have ZAMS masses lying in this 16–20 M☉ gap, or whether membership in these subclasses is instead governed predominantly by parameters other than initial mass — in particular by binary companion interaction (mass transfer, common envelope) or by stellar rotation — which strip or modify the hydrogen envelope and thereby determine the explosion appearance. Equivalently, identify the dominant physical parameter (initial mass vs. binarity/rotation) that distinguishes the IIb, IIn, and IIL channels.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent observational and theoretical work has accumulated substantial evidence that binarity (and to a lesser degree rotation and metallicity-dependent mass loss) plays the dominant role in producing Type IIb and IIL supernovae, rather than the progenitors simply filling the 16–20 M☉ gap. Hα-association studies indicate IIL progenitors have masses similar to IIP, with envelope stripping by a binary companion shaping the light curve; IIb progenitors are widely modeled as binary-stripped stars. Type IIn remains less well understood: host-galaxy studies suggest many IIn arise from moderate-mass progenitors rather than the most massive stars, again pointing to circumstellar/binary effects, but no consensus mass range or single mechanism is established. Thus the question is partially resolved in favor of binarity/envelope-stripping as a key parameter, but precise progenitor mass distributions for all three subclasses remain open.

Establish or refute the following three statements:

(i) For every integer $n\ge 2$,
$$\frac{n(2n+1)}{\binom{2n}{n}}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(11k+3)\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\binom{3k}{k}\,64^{\,n-1-k}\in\mathbb{Z}.$$

$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\binom{3k}{k}}{64^{k}}\equiv\begin{cases} x^{2}-2p\pmod{p^{2}} & \text{if }\left(\tfrac{p}{11}\right)=1\text{ and }4p=x^{2}+11y^{2}\text{ with }x,y\in\mathbb{Z},\\ 0\pmod{p^{2}} & \text{if }\left(\tfrac{p}{11}\right)=-1,\text{ i.e., }p\equiv 2,6,7,8,10\pmod{11}.\end{cases}$$
Moreover, for every odd prime $p$ and every positive integer $a$,

$$p\sum_{k=1}^{(p-1)/2}\frac{(11k-3)\,64^{k}}{k^{3}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\binom{3k}{k}}\equiv 32\,q_p(2)-\tfrac{64}{3}p^{2}B_{p-3}\pmod{p^{3}}.$$

In observational and theoretical astrophysics of stellar explosions, consider the population of faint core-collapse supernovae (CC-SNe), i.e. transient events arising from the gravitational collapse of a massive star whose peak absolute B-band magnitude M_B is much fainter than that of typical Type II supernovae (which peak around M_B ≈ −17 to −18). Existing observations have established Type II events as faint as M_B ≈ −14, and possibly fainter. Address the following quantitative questions about this population:

1. Faintness limit: Determine the minimum peak luminosity (equivalently, the maximum/least negative peak absolute magnitude M_B) attainable by a genuine core-collapse supernova explosion, as a function of progenitor mass, explosion energy, and ejected ^{56}Ni mass.
2. Nova–supernova boundary: Identify the observational and physical criteria (e.g. peak luminosity, light-curve shape, ejecta mass, kinetic energy, spectral signatures) that sharply distinguish nova outbursts from genuine supernova explosions in the regime where their peak luminosities overlap.
3. Volumetric rate: Estimate the local volumetric rate (per unit volume per unit time) and the fraction, relative to all core-collapse supernovae, of faint CC-SNe (say with M_B ≳ −15), correcting for observational selection effects against low-luminosity transients.
4. Explosion channels: Enumerate the distinct physical explosion channels (e.g. low-energy neutrino-driven explosions of high-mass progenitors with substantial fallback, electron-capture supernovae from super-AGB stars, failed/partial explosions, mass-loss–powered transients, etc.) capable of producing such faint core-collapse events, and assess how many additional, currently unrecognized channels may contribute.

Provide quantitative answers with associated uncertainties.

The questions concern the luminosity floor, rate, and explosion channels of faint core-collapse supernovae. While progress has been made (e.g. recognition of electron-capture SNe, identification of intermediate-luminosity red transients, and surveys like ZTF/ATLAS expanding the faint-SN sample), no consensus quantitative answers exist for the faintness limit, the nova–SN boundary, the total faint-SN rate, or a complete enumeration of explosion channels. The problem remains open.

The integrality assertion (part (i)) of this Z.-W. Sun conjecture was proved by V. J. W. Guo (arXiv:1601.04250, "Proof of Sun's conjectures on integer-valued polynomials," published in J. Math. Anal. Appl. 2016), as part of his confirmation of two of Sun's integer-valued conjectures. The supercongruence mod $p^4$ in (ii) involving $(10k+3)$ and $B_{p-3}$ has been addressed in subsequent work by Guo and Zudilin via $q$-analogues for primes $p>2$. The mod-$p^2$ supercongruence in (ii) involving the representation $p=x^2+2y^2$ and the closed-form Ramanujan-type series identity in (iii) do not appear to have a fully verified proof in the literature found, so those parts are best treated as not confirmed.

Exceptionally luminous Type II supernovae have been observed whose peak absolute B-band magnitudes rival or exceed those of typical Type Ia supernovae (M_B < -19.5), with notable examples reaching even brighter peak luminosities. Address the following questions about such "ultra-bright" Type II supernovae:

(a) What is the maximum possible peak luminosity (or absolute magnitude) attainable by ultra-bright Type II supernovae?

(b) What is the underlying physical class or explosion mechanism responsible for these events?

(c) Why do such ultra-bright Type II supernovae occur?

In particular, evaluate the hypothesis that these events are pair-instability (pair-annihilation) explosions of ultramassive progenitor stars with zero-age main-sequence mass M > 140 M_sun and extremely low metallicity Z < 10^{-3} Z_sun. Specifically, determine whether such ultramassive, extremely metal-poor progenitors can plausibly exist in the local Universe after more than 13 billion years of cosmic chemical evolution, and hence whether the pair-instability mechanism can account for the observed ultra-bright Type II supernovae in the local Universe.

Subsequent work has identified a class of "superluminous supernovae" (SLSNe) reaching M < -21, with multiple proposed mechanisms (pair-instability, magnetar spin-down, circumstellar interaction). A few candidates (e.g., SN 2007bi) have been argued to be pair-instability events, but most local SLSNe are now generally attributed to magnetar-powered or interaction-powered models rather than classical pair-instability in extremely metal-poor ultramassive stars. The questions of the absolute maximum luminosity and the dominant mechanism are not fully settled, so the problem is partially solved.

Let $p>3$ be a prime, and let $B_n$ and $E_n$ denote the Bernoulli and Euler numbers, respectively. Let $\left(\tfrac{\cdot}{p}\right)$ denote the Legendre symbol. Establish (or refute) all of the following congruences and integrality statement.

(i) If $p\equiv 1\pmod 6$, write $p=x^2+3y^2$ with $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}^3}{16^k}\equiv 4x^2-2p\pmod{p^2},\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{k\binom{2k}{k}^3}{16^k}\equiv \frac{p-4x^2}{3}\pmod{p^2}.$$

(ii) If $p\equiv 5\pmod 6$, then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}^3}{16^k}\equiv 0\pmod{p^2},\qquad \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{k\binom{2k}{k}^3}{16^k}\equiv \frac{p}{3}\pmod{p^2}.$$

(iii) For every positive integer $a$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p^a-1}\frac{(3k+1)\binom{2k}{k}^3}{16^k}\equiv p^a\Bigl(1+\tfrac{7}{6}\,p^3\,B_{p-3}\Bigr)\pmod{p^{a+3}}$$
(equivalently, $p^a\sum_{k=0}^{p^a-1}(3k+1)\binom{2k}{k}^3/16^k\equiv 1+\tfrac{7}{6}p^3 B_{p-3}\pmod{p^4}$ in the appropriate normalization).

(iv)
$$\sum_{k=0}^{(p-1)/2}\frac{(3k+1)\binom{2k}{k}^3}{16^k}\equiv p+2\Bigl(\tfrac{-1}{p}\Bigr)p^3 E_{p-3}\pmod{p^4}.$$

(v) For every integer $n\geq 2$,
$$2n\binom{2n}{n}\,\Bigl|\;\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(3k+1)\binom{2k}{k}^3\,16^{n-1-k},$$
i.e. the quotient $\dfrac{1}{2n\binom{2n}{n}}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(3k+1)\binom{2k}{k}^3 16^{n-1-k}$ is an integer.

Several pieces of this multi-part conjecture have been settled. The integrality statement (v) and related divisibility properties were proved by Guo and Zeng (arXiv:1511.05553) and by J.-C. Liu / Guo. The mod-$p^2$ congruences in case $p\equiv 1\pmod 6$ (with $p=x^2+3y^2$) have been established (in part by G.-S. Mao and collaborators), and the mod-$p^4$ congruence (iv) involving $E_{p-3}$ has been treated by WZ-type proofs (e.g., the Ramanujan Journal paper by Guillera and others). The full mod-$p^{a+3}$ statement (iii) for all $a\geq 1$ does not appear to be uniformly verified in the literature; thus the conjecture as a whole is partially solved but not fully closed.

representations.normalized: Consider stars with zero-age main-sequence masses in the approximate range 30–40 to 100 solar masses. Determine the final outcome of their stellar evolution: specifically, do such stars terminate their lives in observable but very faint explosive transients, or do they undergo direct collapse into black holes with no luminous explosion ("disappearance")? Furthermore, devise an observational strategy — such as repeated, regular monitoring of a sufficiently large sample of nearby galaxies to identify bright stars that vanish without a conventional supernova signature — that can detect such failed-explosion / direct-collapse events, and quantify the rate at which such disappearances occur relative to ordinary core-collapse supernovae.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Dedicated surveys (notably the Large Binocular Telescope failed-supernova search) have implemented the proposed monitoring strategy and identified candidate "disappearing" massive stars, most prominently N6946-BH1, a ~25 M☉ supergiant that vanished after a modest 2009 outburst and is consistent with direct collapse to a black hole. Subsequent JWST observations (2024) reveal the source is a blend of multiple objects and a stellar-merger interpretation cannot be ruled out, so the failed-supernova interpretation is suggestive but not definitive. The broader question of the typical fate of 30–100 M☉ stars remains under active investigation.

(a) Prove or disprove that for every odd prime $p$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{(3k+1)\binom{2k}{k}^{3}}{(-8)^{k}} \;\equiv\; p\left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)+p^{3}E_{p-3}\pmod{p^{4}}.$$

(b) Define
$$a_n \;=\; \frac{1}{2n\binom{2n}{n}}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(3k+1)\binom{2k}{k}^{3}(-8)^{n-1-k}.$$

A long-duration gamma-ray burst (GRB) is a brief, intense flash of gamma rays from a cosmological source, frequently associated with the core-collapse death of a massive star. A Type Ic supernova (SNIc) is a core-collapse supernova whose spectrum lacks hydrogen and helium lines, indicating a progenitor stripped of its outer envelopes. Observationally, several long GRBs have been firmly associated with SNIc counterparts, and both populations preferentially occur in active star-forming regions. Yet only a small fraction of detected GRBs show an accompanying SNIc, and only a small fraction of observed SNIc show any conspicuous prompt gamma-ray emission. Some GRBs are observationally inconsistent with any associated supernova down to deep optical limits, while many SNIc show no evidence of a relativistic jet or high-energy transient.

Determine the physical conditions and progenitor/explosion parameters (such as progenitor mass, rotation rate, metallicity, magnetic-field configuration, jet launching efficiency, jet opening angle and viewing geometry, envelope structure and jet break-out conditions, central-engine type — black hole versus magnetar — and binary versus single-star evolution) that govern the GRB–supernova connection. Specifically:

(a) Identify necessary and sufficient physical conditions under which a core-collapse event of a stripped-envelope massive star (in particular, a Type Ic supernova) does or does not produce an observable gamma-ray burst.

(b) Identify the physical conditions under which a long-duration gamma-ray burst occurs without producing a detectable associated supernova.

A complete solution should provide a predictive framework explaining the observed ratios of SNIc with and without GRBs, and of GRBs with and without supernovae, consistent with the full set of multi-wavelength observations.

Recent literature (2024–2025) continues to investigate the GRB–supernova connection. Recent JWST observations have both detected supernovae following GRBs at high redshift and revealed GRBs without classical r-process or supernova signatures, supporting the hypothesis that most collapsing massive stars fail to launch a successful relativistic jet through the stellar envelope, and that some long GRBs may have compact-object-merger progenitors. A complete predictive theory of the necessary and sufficient progenitor/engine conditions remains unresolved.

Develop a quantitative stellar-evolution modeling framework for the progenitors of core-collapse supernovae — namely single and binary stars whose zero-age main-sequence mass exceeds 3 solar masses (B-type and O-type stars) — that explicitly and self-consistently incorporates both rotation and magnetic fields throughout the entire evolution leading up to the supernova explosion. Specifically, formulate and justify:

1. The set of magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) evolution equations (including angular-momentum transport, magnetic-field generation/amplification mechanisms such as the Tayler–Spruit dynamo or analogous instabilities, and dissipation) to be coupled with the standard stellar-structure equations (mass conservation, hydrostatic equilibrium, energy conservation, energy transport, and nuclear burning).

2. The treatment of rotationally induced mixing (meridional circulation, shear instabilities, GSF and ABCD instabilities) and its interaction with magnetic torques.

3. Boundary and initial conditions for rotation profiles and magnetic-field topology consistent with observed B- and O-type star populations, together with prescriptions for mass loss that depend on rotation and magnetic field.

4. Predictions, derivable from this framework, for the pre-supernova rotation rate, magnetic-field strength and geometry, core angular momentum, and final compact remnant properties (neutron-star spin, magnetar formation, black-hole spin), and for the resulting explosion morphology and energetics.

Demonstrate that the resulting models reproduce known observational constraints on rotating massive stars and on supernova progenitors, and identify which physical ingredients are indispensable for a physically complete description of the progenitor evolution.

This is an active, unresolved modeling problem in stellar astrophysics. Significant progress has been made via codes such as MESA, GENEC, and KEPLER incorporating rotation and (in some cases) magnetic torques via the Tayler–Spruit dynamo, but a fully self-consistent MHD treatment of rotating massive-star evolution to core collapse remains open, with continuing disagreements about angular-momentum transport, magnetic-field amplification, and predicted remnant spins.

representations.normalized:
Consider the population of supernovae (SNe) — the explosive endpoints of stellar evolution, occurring in various spectroscopic and photometric subclasses (e.g., thermonuclear Type Ia and core-collapse Types II, Ib, Ic, and their subtypes) — viewed as a phenomenon distributed across cosmic history. Let the SN phenomenon be characterized by observables such as event rates per unit comoving volume, luminosity functions, light-curve shapes, spectral properties, ejecta masses, kinetic energies, nucleosynthetic yields, and progenitor channels. Let these observables depend on the following parameters: (i) metallicity Z of the progenitor and its environment; (ii) the stellar population from which the progenitor is drawn (including age distribution, initial mass function, and binarity); (iii) cosmic age (equivalently redshift z); and (iv) host environment (host galaxy morphology, mass, star-formation rate, local interstellar medium properties).

Problem: Determine, quantitatively, how each class of supernova phenomenon evolves as a function of (Z, stellar population, cosmic age z, environment, and any further relevant parameters) across cosmic time. In particular:

1. Establish the functional dependences of SN rates, luminosities, spectra, and explosion parameters on (Z, population age, z, host environment).
2. Identify which intrinsic properties of SNe are universal versus which evolve with cosmic time.
3. Specify how to incorporate these dependences as systematic corrections or priors when SNe are used as cosmological tools (e.g., Type Ia SNe as standardizable candles for measuring distances, the expansion history, and dark energy parameters; core-collapse SNe as tracers of star formation and chemical enrichment).
4. Provide a framework that accounts for these evolutionary effects in a way that allows SNe to be used reliably to probe the workings and evolution of the Universe.

Let $p>5$ be a prime. For an integer $a$ and odd prime $q$, let $\left(\frac{a}{q}\right)$ denote the Legendre symbol. Recall the multinomial coefficient $\binom{3k}{k,k,k} = \frac{(3k)!}{(k!)^3}$.

Prove or disprove the following two assertions.

(1) For every prime $p>5$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \frac{\binom{6k}{3k}\binom{3k}{k,k,k}}{(-960)^{3k}} \equiv \begin{cases} \left(\dfrac{p}{15}\right)(x^2 - 2p) \pmod{p^2}, & \text{if } \left(\dfrac{p}{43}\right)=1 \text{ and } 4p = x^2 + 43y^2 \text{ with } x,y\in\mathbb{Z},\\[4pt] 0 \pmod{p^2}, & \text{if } \left(\dfrac{p}{43}\right)=-1. \end{cases}$$

(2) For every integer $n\ge 2$, define
$$a_n := \frac{1}{2n(2n+1)}\binom{2n}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(5418k+263)(-9603)^{n-1-k}\binom{6k}{3k}\binom{3k}{k,k,k}.$$
Then $a_n \in \mathbb{Z}$ unless $2n+1$ is a power of $3$, in which case $3a_n \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus 3\mathbb{Z}$.

representations.normalized: Devise a physically grounded classification scheme for supernovae that can replace or supplement existing purely morphological (spectral/light-curve based) subclass definitions. Concretely: propose a taxonomy whose primary categories are defined by intrinsic physical parameters of the explosion — such as the nature of the progenitor system (single massive star, interacting binary, white dwarf in a binary, etc.), the explosion mechanism (thermonuclear runaway, iron-core collapse, electron-capture collapse, pair instability, magnetar-driven, etc.), the energy source powering the light curve (radioactive decay, shock interaction with circumstellar medium, central engine), the ejecta mass and composition, and the circumstellar environment — rather than by observational morphology alone. The scheme should (i) be unambiguously assignable from currently obtainable observations and physical modeling, (ii) accommodate newly discovered diversity without requiring proliferation of ad hoc named subclasses, and (iii) avoid creating the impression that an explosion mechanism is understood merely because a new morphological label has been introduced. Specify the categories, the criteria that place an event in each category, and demonstrate how known supernova types (Ia, Ib, Ic, IIP, IIL, IIn, IIb, superluminous, Ca-rich, .Ia, etc.) map into the proposed scheme.

where C(6k,3k) is the binomial coefficient and M(3k;k,k,k) = (3k)!/(k!)^3 is the multinomial coefficient. Let (·/·) denote the Legendre symbol. Prove or disprove the following three assertions.

(i) Modulo p^2,
  S(p) ≡ (-330/p)(x^2 - 2p) (mod p^2)  if (p/67) = 1 and 4p = x^2 + 67 y^2 with x, y ∈ ℤ,
  S(p) ≡ 0 (mod p^2)  if (p/67) = -1.

(ii) The supercongruence
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} (261702 k + 10177) · C(6k,3k) · M(3k;k,k,k) / (-5280)^{3k} ≡ 10177 p · (-330/p) (mod p^3).

(iii) For every integer n ≥ 2, the number
  a_n := (1 / (2n(2n+1))) · C(2n,n) · Σ_{k=0}^{n-1} (261702 k + 10177) · (-5280^3)^{n-1-k} · C(6k,3k) · M(3k;k,k,k)
is an integer, except when 2n+1 is a power of 3, in which case 3 a_n is an integer but a_n is not (equivalently, 3 a_n ∈ ℤ \ 3ℤ).

Let $B_n(x)$ denote the Bernoulli polynomials and let $\left(\frac{\cdot}{\cdot}\right)$ denote the Legendre/Jacobi symbol. Define the constant
$$K := L\!\left(2,\left(\tfrac{-3}{\cdot}\right)\right) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{\left(\tfrac{k}{3}\right)}{k^2} = 0.781302412896486296867187429624\ldots .$$
Prove or disprove the following three assertions.

(i) For every prime $p>3$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \frac{\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\binom{3k}{k}}{(-27)^{k}} \equiv \begin{cases} 4x^{2}-2p \pmod{p^{2}}, & \text{if } p\equiv 1,4\pmod{15}\text{ and } p=x^{2}+15y^{2}\ (x,y\in\mathbb{Z}),\\ 20x^{2}-2p \pmod{p^{2}}, & \text{if } p\equiv 2,8\pmod{15}\text{ and } p=5x^{2}+3y^{2}\ (x,y\in\mathbb{Z}),\\ 0 \pmod{p^{2}}, & \text{if } \left(\tfrac{p}{15}\right)=-1. \end{cases}$$
Moreover, for $n\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$ define
$$a_n := 2n(2n+1)\binom{2n}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(15k+4)\,\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\binom{3k}{k}(-27)^{n-1-k}.$$
Then $a_n\in\mathbb{Z}$ unless $2n+1$ is a power of $3$, in which case $3a_n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus 3\mathbb{Z}$.

(ii) For every prime $p>3$ and every $a\in\mathbb{Z}^{+}$,
$$p^{a}\sum_{k=0}^{p^{a}-1} \frac{15k+4}{(-27)^{k}}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\binom{3k}{k} \equiv 4(p^{a})+(p^{a-1})\cdot \frac{4}{3}\,p^{2}\,B_{p-2}(1/3) \pmod{p^{3}},$$
and
$$p^{a}\sum_{k=0}^{p^{a}-1} \frac{5k+1}{(-144)^{k}}\binom{4k}{k,k,k,k} \equiv (p^{a})+(p^{a-1})\cdot \frac{5}{12}\,p^{2}\,B_{p-2}(1/4) \pmod{p^{3}}.$$

(iii) The identity
$$\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{(5k-1)(-144)^{k}}{k^{3}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\binom{4k}{2k}} = -\frac{45}{2}\,K$$
holds.

Within the framework of semi-analytic models of galaxy formation, dark matter halo merger trees (the hierarchical record of progenitor halos that merge to form a given halo as a function of cosmic time) can be constructed in two principal ways:

(a) Analytically, via Monte Carlo realizations based on the extended Press–Schechter (EPS) formalism, which uses the spherical-collapse, excursion-set conditional mass function
P(M_1, z_1 | M_2, z_2) for a progenitor of mass M_1 at redshift z_1 of a descendant halo of mass M_2 at redshift z_2 < z_1, derived from a Gaussian random field of linear density perturbations with a specified power spectrum.

(b) Numerically, by identifying bound dark matter halos in cosmological N-body simulations at successive redshifts and linking progenitors to descendants on the basis of shared particle membership.

Recent work indicates that the conditional mass functions, progenitor mass distributions, and assembly-time statistics produced by the EPS formalism do not, in general, reproduce those measured directly from N-body simulations.

Quantify, as a function of halo mass M and redshift z, the resulting differences in the predictions of a fixed semi-analytic galaxy formation model — including the galaxy stellar mass function, luminosity function, color and metallicity distributions, star-formation-rate density, and satellite galaxy abundance — when its merger trees are supplied by the classical EPS Monte Carlo algorithm versus when they are extracted from a cosmological N-body simulation with identical cosmological parameters and initial power spectrum, with all other ingredients of the model held fixed. In particular, determine for which observable statistics, halo mass ranges, and redshift intervals the discrepancies are statistically significant, and characterize the systematic biases introduced by using EPS-based trees.

The question of how intermittent radio-mode AGN feedback can globally and stably suppress cooling flows in massive clusters remains an active open problem. Consider the galaxy stellar mass function Φ(M⋆, z), defined as the comoving number density of galaxies per unit logarithmic stellar mass M⋆ at redshift z. Standard hierarchical semi-analytic models of galaxy formation, built on the ΛCDM cosmological framework with prescriptions for gas cooling, star formation, supernova and AGN feedback, and galaxy mergers within dark-matter halo merger trees, predict that galaxies with present-day stellar mass M⋆ ≳ 10^11 M_⊙ should have grown in stellar mass by a factor of approximately 2 to 4 between redshift z ≈ 1 and z = 0, primarily through dry mergers. In contrast, observational determinations of Φ(M⋆, z) at the high-mass end (M⋆ ≳ 10^11 M_⊙) over the same redshift interval indicate little to no significant evolution in the comoving abundance of such massive galaxies.

Provide a physically motivated and quantitatively consistent explanation that reconciles this discrepancy. Specifically, identify modifications to the assembly history of massive galaxies — whether in the merger rate, the efficiency or fraction of stellar mass lost during mergers (e.g., to intracluster light), the satellite-disruption prescription, AGN feedback at late times, or in observational systematics affecting M⋆ determinations (initial mass function, photometric stellar-mass estimates, progenitor effect) — that would simultaneously satisfy:
(i) the predicted factor 2–4 mass growth of individual massive galaxies since z ∼ 1, and
(ii) the observed near-constancy of the massive end of Φ(M⋆, z) over 0 ≤ z ≲ 1.

Subsequent work has narrowed but not fully closed the tension. Improvements include accounting for stellar mass loss to intracluster light during mergers, revised satellite-disruption and AGN-feedback prescriptions, and reassessments of observational stellar-mass systematics (IMF variations, progenitor bias). (a) For every prime $p>5$ with $p\equiv 1\pmod 4$ and every positive integer $a$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p^{a}-1} k^{3}\,\frac{\binom{2k}{k}^{3}}{64^{k}} \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{2a}}.$$

$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} (-1)^{n k}\,\binom{-1/m}{k}^{n} \equiv 0 \pmod{p^{2}},$$
where $\binom{-1/m}{k}=\frac{(-1/m)(-1/m-1)\cdots(-1/m-k+1)}{k!}\in\mathbb{Z}_p$.

(c) Let $p>2$ be a prime and $n\ge 2$ an integer. Suppose $x\in\mathbb{Z}_p$ satisfies $x\equiv -2k\pmod p$ for some integer $k\in\{1,2,\ldots,\lfloor(p+1)/(2n+1)\rfloor\}$. Then

representations.normalized:
In hierarchical structure formation, the brightest cluster galaxy (BCG) of a galaxy cluster is the most luminous member, typically located near the cluster center. Observational studies of BCGs in the redshift range 0 ≤ z ≤ 1 commonly report photometry within fixed metric apertures that capture only 25–50% of the total light belonging to the combined BCG plus intracluster light (ICL) component, and find results consistent with no significant stellar mass growth of the BCG since z ∼ 1. In contrast, semi-analytic models of galaxy formation built on top of cosmological dark-matter merger trees, in which the BCG's stellar mass is computed as the total stellar mass formed in or accreted onto the central galaxy of the most massive cluster halo, predict that the BCG stellar mass grows by roughly a factor of four between z ∼ 1 and z = 0.

Determine whether this discrepancy reflects a genuine failure of the underlying physical model of BCG mass assembly, or whether it can be fully reconciled by:
(i) consistently comparing model predictions and observations using the same fixed metric aperture, accounting for the fraction of total BCG+ICL light enclosed; and
(ii) incorporating into the semi-analytic models the spatial distribution of stellar light in cluster galaxies together with the tidal stripping and harassment of stars from satellite galaxies into a diffuse intracluster light component, so that mass accreted onto the central halo is partitioned between the BCG and the ICL.

Specifically, decide whether implementing (i) and (ii) suffices to bring the predicted BCG mass-growth history since z ∼ 1 into quantitative agreement with the observed mass-growth history.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent work on semi-analytic models and high-resolution cosmological simulations has shown that consistently comparing model predictions to observations within fixed metric apertures, and including tidal stripping of stars from satellites into an intracluster-light component, substantially reduces the discrepancy between predicted and observed BCG mass growth since z ∼ 1. The question is therefore considered partially resolved rather than a fundamental failure of hierarchical models.

In semi-analytic models of galaxy formation, when a galaxy becomes a satellite of a larger halo it is conventionally assumed that its hot gas reservoir is stripped instantaneously and completely, so that gas cooling onto the satellite is shut off; combined with efficient supernova feedback, this rapidly exhausts the satellite's cold gas and drives it onto the red sequence on short time-scales. This prescription is known to overproduce faint red satellite galaxies and to underpopulate the intermediate "green valley" of the galaxy colour distribution relative to observations.

Formulate and justify a physically motivated modification of the treatment of (i) hot-gas stripping from satellite galaxies after infall and (ii) the resulting shutdown of star formation, to be incorporated into a semi-analytic model of galaxy formation, such that the predicted satellite colour distribution simultaneously:

1. reduces the excess population of faint red satellites,
2. produces a green-valley population whose number density and colour distribution is consistent with observed values, and
3. preserves agreement with the observed overall satellite colour distribution and with other observational constraints (luminosity function, central-galaxy colours, etc.).

Specify the prescription explicitly (for example, the timescale and radial dependence of hot-gas removal, any retention of gas after infall, ram-pressure or tidal stripping criteria, and the coupling to supernova feedback), and demonstrate quantitatively that the resulting model satisfies the above three requirements.

The "satellite overquenching" / strangulation problem in semi-analytic models remains an active and unresolved issue. Numerous works since 2009 (e.g., Font et al. 2008, Weinmann et al., Kang & van den Bosch, Henriques et al. 2015, 2020, Cora et al., Xie et al. 2020) have replaced instantaneous hot-gas stripping with gradual ram-pressure/tidal stripping prescriptions and have improved—but not fully resolved—the satellite colour distribution and green-valley population. No single prescription is yet accepted as a complete solution.

representations.normalized:
Consider hierarchical galaxy formation in the cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm, in which galaxy disks form within dark-matter halos that grow by mergers. Two key observational benchmarks must be simultaneously reproduced by such a model:

(i) the galaxy luminosity function Φ(L), giving the comoving number density of galaxies as a function of luminosity L;

(ii) the Tully–Fisher relation, the empirical correlation L ∝ V^α between the luminosity L of a spiral disk and its rotation (circular) velocity V, including the absolute zero-point (normalization) of this relation.

Within a semi-analytic framework, model each galaxy as a centrifugally supported exponential disk embedded in an NFW dark-matter halo, with disk scale length and half-mass radius R_{1/2} computed from angular-momentum conservation and adiabatic contraction (i.e., a "realistic" size calculation rather than identifying the disk velocity with the halo virial velocity). Define the model Tully–Fisher velocity as the total circular velocity V_c(R_{1/2}) of the disk+halo system evaluated at the stellar half-mass radius.

Question: Can a hierarchical CDM-based galaxy-formation model simultaneously fit Φ(L) and the zero-point of the L–V_c(R_{1/2}) Tully–Fisher relation? If matching both is impossible, determine whether the obstruction stems from approximations in the disk-size/rotation-curve calculation (e.g., adiabatic contraction prescription, angular-momentum assignment, baryonic feedback on the inner halo profile) or from a more fundamental shortcoming of the CDM paradigm itself (e.g., halo concentration–mass relation or inner density profile).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The simultaneous reproduction of the galaxy luminosity function and the Tully–Fisher zero-point with a realistic disk-size calculation has been a long-standing tension in semi-analytic CDM models. Subsequent work (e.g., Dutton et al. 2007/2011 "The Tully-Fisher Zero Point Problem", Trujillo-Gomez et al., and the MNRAS paper "The hierarchical build-up of the Tully–Fisher relation") has proposed partial reconciliations involving low stellar mass-to-light ratios, reduced halo concentrations, suppressed adiabatic contraction or expansion of inner halos by baryonic feedback, but no consensus solution has fully resolved whether the residual tension is a modelling artifact or a fundamental CDM issue. The status is therefore best described as partially solved.

For a positive integer n, let $H_n=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\frac{1}{j}$ denote the n-th harmonic number (with $H_0=0$), and let $B_n$ denote the n-th Bernoulli number. Prove or disprove the following three congruences.

(i) For every odd prime $p$,
$$\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{1}{k\,2^k}\binom{2k}{k}\;\equiv\;-\,H_{(p-1)/2}^{\,2}\;+\;\frac{7}{16}\,p^{2}\,B_{p-3}\pmod{p^{3}}.$$

(ii) For every prime $p>3$,
$$\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{1}{k\,3^k}\binom{2k}{k}\;\equiv\;-\,2\!\!\sum_{\substack{k=1\\ k\not\equiv 0\,(\bmod 3)}}^{p-1}\frac{1}{k}\pmod{p^{3}}.$$

(iii) For every prime $p>5$,
$$\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{1}{k^{2}\,4^k}\binom{2k}{k}\;\equiv\;-\,H_{(p-1)/2}^{\,2}\;-\;\frac{7}{4}\cdot\frac{H_{p-1}}{p}\pmod{p^{3}}.$$

(Each congruence is to be interpreted in the p-adic integers, where the rational denominators involved are coprime to $p$.)

Denote by $H_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}1/k$ the $n$-th harmonic number, by $B_n$ the $n$-th Bernoulli number, by $\left(\frac{\cdot}{p}\right)$ the Legendre symbol, and define $\overline{H}_k^{(2)}=\sum_{0<j\le k}1/(2j-1)^2$. Prove or disprove the following congruences (modulo the indicated prime powers, with all rational numbers regarded as $p$-adic integers):

(i) $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{(p-3)/2}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}}{(2k+1)\,16^k}\equiv (-1)^{(p-1)/2}\!\left(H_{p-1}+\tfrac{3}{160}p^4 B_{p-5}\right)\pmod{p^5};$

(ii) $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{(p-3)/2}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}}{(2k+1)^3 16^k}\equiv (-1)^{(p-1)/2}\!\left(H_{p-1}+\tfrac{1}{36}p^2 B_{p-5}\right)\pmod{p^3};$

(iii) $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{(p-3)/2}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}}{(2k+1)^2(-16)^k}\equiv \tfrac{1}{5}H_{p-1}\pmod{p^3};$

(iv) $\displaystyle\sum_{p/2<k<p}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}}{(2k+1)^2(-16)^k}\equiv -\tfrac{1}{4}B_{p-3}\pmod{p^2};$

$$T_n \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{n} \binom{n}{k}^{2}\binom{2k}{k}\binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}.$$

Prove or disprove the following two statements.

(i) For every prime $p > 3$,
$$\sum_{n=0}^{p-1} \frac{3n^{2}+n}{16^{n}}\, T_n \;\equiv\; -4\,p^{4}\,q_p(2) \;+\; 6\,p^{5}\,q_p(2)^{2} \pmod{p^{6}}.$$

(ii) For every integer $m > 1$, the rational number
$$a_m \;=\; \frac{1}{2\,m^{3}(m-1)} \sum_{n=0}^{m-1} (3n^{2}+n)\,16^{\,m-1-n}\, T_n$$
is an integer; moreover, $a_m$ is odd if and only if $m$ is a power of $2$.

Let $p > 3$ be a prime, and let $\left(\frac{\cdot}{p}\right)$ denote the Legendre symbol.

(a) Suppose $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$ and write $p = x^2 + y^2$ with integers $x, y$ satisfying $x \equiv 1 \pmod 4$ and $y \equiv 0 \pmod 2$. Prove or disprove that
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \frac{\binom{2k}{k}\binom{4k}{2k}}{72^k} \equiv \left(\frac{6}{p}\right)\!\left(2x - \frac{p}{2x}\right) \pmod{p^2},$$
and
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \frac{1 - k}{72^k}\binom{2k}{k}\binom{4k}{2k} \equiv \left(\frac{6}{p}\right) x \pmod{p^2}.$$

(b) Suppose $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$. Prove or disprove that
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1} \frac{\binom{2k}{k}\binom{4k}{2k}}{72^k} \equiv \left(\frac{6}{p}\right)\frac{2p}{\binom{(p+1)/2}{(p+1)/4}} \pmod{p^2}.$$

Here in (b), $(p+1)/4$ is interpreted in the natural way when $p \equiv 3 \pmod 4$ so that $(p+1)/2$ is even, and $\binom{(p+1)/2}{(p+1)/4}$ is the corresponding central-type binomial coefficient; the rational expression $2p/\binom{(p+1)/2}{(p+1)/4}$ is to be understood modulo $p^2$ via the inverse of the binomial coefficient (which is a $p$-adic unit times $p$ as needed).

A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a lattice order ≤ such that the group operation is order-preserving in both arguments; equivalently, the operations ∧ (meet) and ∨ (join) are defined and translation-invariant. An ℓ-group G is called archimedean if, for all a, b ∈ G with a, b ≥ e (the identity), the condition a^n ≤ b for every positive integer n implies a = e. An ℓ-homomorphism between ℓ-groups is a group homomorphism that also preserves the lattice operations ∧ and ∨.

It is known that the class of archimedean ℓ-groups is closed under subobjects and (Cartesian) products but is not closed under ℓ-homomorphic images: there exist ℓ-homomorphisms φ : G → H with G archimedean but φ(G) not archimedean.

Problem. Determine necessary and/or sufficient conditions on an ℓ-homomorphism φ : G → H between ℓ-groups (or on its kernel, or on the source G and target H) under which the archimedean property is preserved, i.e., conditions guaranteeing that the image φ(G) (equivalently, the quotient G/ker φ as an ℓ-group) is archimedean whenever G is archimedean.

Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $a$ be a positive integer. Throughout, $\left(\frac{\cdot}{\cdot}\right)$ denotes the Jacobi symbol, and $\lfloor x\rfloor$ is the floor function. Decide whether all of the following statements are true.

(i) If $p^a\equiv 1,2\pmod 5$, or if $a>1$ and $p\not\equiv 3\pmod 5$, then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor 4p^a/5\rfloor}(-1)^k\binom{2k}{k}\equiv\left(\frac{5}{p^a}\right)\pmod{p^2}.$$
If $p^a\equiv 1,3\pmod 5$, or if $a>1$ and $p\not\equiv 2\pmod 5$, then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor 3p^a/5\rfloor}(-1)^k\binom{2k}{k}\equiv\left(\frac{5}{p^a}\right)\pmod{p^2}.$$
Consequently, if $p^a\equiv 1\pmod 5$, then
$$\sum_{p^a/5<k<4p^a/5}(-1)^k\binom{2k}{k}\equiv 0\pmod{p^2}.$$

(ii) If $p\equiv 1,7\pmod{10}$, or if $a>2$, then

A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group $H$ equipped with a lattice order $\le$ that is translation-invariant on both sides: for all $a,b,x,y \in H$, $a \le b$ implies $xay \le xby$. Question: Let $H$ be a countable ℓ-group. Does there exist an abelian ℓ-group $G$ such that $G$ is isomorphic to $H$ as a lattice?

Let $\{P_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ denote the Catalan–Larcombe–French numbers, defined by
$$P_n=\sum_{k=0}^{n}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\binom{2(n-k)}{n-k}^{2}\Big/\binom{n}{k},$$
so that $P_0=1,\ P_1=8,\ P_2=80,\ P_3=896,\dots$

Prove or disprove the following supercongruences for primes $p$.

(i) Suppose $p$ is a prime with $p\equiv 1$ or $3\pmod 8$. Then $p$ can be written uniquely (up to signs) as $p=x^{2}+2y^{2}$ with $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$; choose the sign of $x$ so that $x\equiv 1$ or $3\pmod 8$. Then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{P_{k}}{(-8)^{k}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}\equiv\begin{cases}0\pmod{p^{2}}, & p\equiv 1\pmod 8,\\[2pt](-1)^{(p-3)/8}\!\left(\dfrac{p}{2x}-2x\right)\pmod{p^{2}}, & p\equiv 3\pmod 8,\end{cases}$$
and
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{k\,P_{k}}{(-8)^{k}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}\equiv(-1)^{(x+1)/2}\!\left(x+\frac{p}{2x}\right)\pmod{p^{2}}.$$

(ii) For every prime $p\equiv 7\pmod 8$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\binom{p-1}{k}\,\frac{P_{k}}{8^{k}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}\equiv 0\pmod{p^{2}}.$$

Here all rational numbers appearing on the left-hand sides are interpreted modulo $p^{2}$ via their representatives in the localization $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$, which makes sense because $\binom{2k}{k}$ is not divisible by $p$ for $0\le k\le p-1$.

A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a partial order ≤ that is translation-invariant (i.e., a ≤ b implies xay ≤ xby for all x,y ∈ G) and such that (G, ≤) is a lattice (every pair of elements has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound). A lattice order on G is called archimedean if for all a, b ∈ G with a > e (the identity) and b > e, there exists a positive integer n such that nb is not ≤ a (equivalently, in the abelian additive setting: whenever 0 < a, b in G and na ≤ b for all positive integers n, then a = 0). An abelian group G is torsion-free if no nonzero element has finite order.

Question: Does every torsion-free abelian group admit an archimedean lattice order? That is, for every torsion-free abelian group G, does there exist a partial order on G making G into an archimedean lattice-ordered group?

Let $\{u_k(4,1)\}_{k\geq 0}$ be the Lucas sequence defined by $u_0=0$, $u_1=1$, and $u_{k+1}=4u_k-u_{k-1}$ for $k\geq 1$. For an odd prime $p>3$, prove or disprove the following.

(i) If $p\equiv 7\pmod{12}$ and $p=x^2+3y^2$ with integers $x,y$ chosen so that $y\equiv 1\pmod 4$, then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{u_k(4,1)}{4^k}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\;\equiv\;(-1)^{(p+1)/4}\Bigl(4y-\frac{p}{3y}\Bigr)\pmod{p^2},$$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{k\,u_k(4,1)}{4^k}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\;\equiv\;(-1)^{(p-3)/4}\Bigl(6y-\frac{7p}{3y}\Bigr)\pmod{p^2}.$$

(ii) If $p\equiv 1\pmod{12}$, then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{u_k(4,1)}{4^k}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\;\equiv\;0\pmod{p^2}.$$

Here $\frac{p}{3y}$ and $\frac{7p}{3y}$ denote the products $p\cdot(3y)^{-1}$ and $7p\cdot(3y)^{-1}$ modulo $p^2$, where $(3y)^{-1}$ is the multiplicative inverse of $3y$ modulo $p^2$.

A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is an algebraic structure (G, ·, ⁻¹, e, ∧, ∨) such that (G, ·, ⁻¹, e) is a group, (G, ∧, ∨) is a lattice, and the group multiplication distributes over both lattice operations on either side, i.e. a(b ∧ c)d = abd ∧ acd and a(b ∨ c)d = abd ∨ acd for all a, b, c, d ∈ G.

A quasi-variety of ℓ-groups is a class of ℓ-groups defined by a set of quasi-identities (universally quantified implications whose premises are finite conjunctions of equations and whose conclusion is a single equation), or equivalently a class closed under isomorphisms, substructures, direct products, and ultraproducts. The collection Lq of all quasi-varieties of ℓ-groups carries a natural binary operation: for quasi-varieties U and V, define U · V to be the quasi-variety generated by all ℓ-groups G that possess a convex normal ℓ-subgroup H ∈ U with G/H ∈ V. Under this product, Lq becomes a semigroup.

(a) Describe explicitly the idempotents of (Lq, ·), i.e. the quasi-varieties Q satisfying Q · Q = Q.

(b) Determine the cardinality of the set of such idempotents.

Let $\mathcal{L}_\ell = \{\cdot, {}^{-1}, e, \vee, \wedge\}$ be the signature of lattice-ordered groups (ℓ-groups), where $(G,\cdot,{}^{-1},e)$ is a group and $(G,\vee,\wedge)$ is a lattice such that the group operation distributes over the lattice operations. A quasi-identity is a universally quantified first-order formula of the form
$$\bigl(\,\bigwedge_{i=1}^n s_i(\bar{x}) = t_i(\bar{x})\,\bigr) \;\Rightarrow\; s(\bar{x}) = t(\bar{x}),$$
where $s_i,t_i,s,t$ are terms in the given signature. A class of algebras is a quasi-variety if it is axiomatized by a set of quasi-identities (equivalently, it is closed under isomorphisms, substructures, direct products, and ultraproducts). For a class $\mathcal{X}$ of ℓ-groups, let $\ell\text{-var}(\mathcal{X})$ denote the variety of ℓ-groups generated by $\mathcal{X}$, that is, the smallest equationally axiomatized class of ℓ-groups containing $\mathcal{X}$. A variety is said to be finitely based if it can be axiomatized (relative to the variety of all ℓ-groups) by a finite set of identities.

Question: If $\mathcal{X}$ is a quasi-variety of ℓ-groups defined by a finite set of quasi-identities, must the variety $\ell\text{-var}(\mathcal{X})$ be finitely based?

For an odd prime $p$ and integer $a$ with $\gcd(a,p)=1$, $a^{-1}$ denotes the inverse of $a$ modulo $p^2$, and $\binom{2k}{k}^{-2}$ is interpreted accordingly when defined. Decide whether all of the following congruences hold.

(i) If $p\equiv 1\pmod{12}$ and $p=x^2+3y^2$ with $x\equiv 1\pmod 3$, then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{v_k(4,1)}{4^k\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}\equiv (-1)^{(p-1)/4+(x-1)/2}\Bigl(4x-\frac{p}{x}\Bigr)\pmod{p^2},$$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{v_k(4,1)}{64^k\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}\equiv (-1)^{(x-1)/2}\Bigl(4x-\frac{p}{x}\Bigr)\pmod{p^2},$$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{k\,v_k(4,1)}{4^k\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}\equiv (-1)^{(p-1)/4+(x+1)/2}\Bigl(4x-\frac{2p}{x}\Bigr)\pmod{p^2},$$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{k\,v_k(4,1)}{64^k\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}\equiv (-1)^{(x-1)/2}\Bigl(2x-\frac{p}{x}\Bigr)\pmod{p^2}.$$

(ii) If $p\equiv 7\pmod{12}$ and $p=x^2+3y^2$ with $y\equiv 1\pmod 4$, then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{v_k(4,1)}{4^k\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}\equiv (-1)^{(p-3)/4}\Bigl(12y-\frac{p}{y}\Bigr)\pmod{p^2},$$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{k\,v_k(4,1)}{4^k\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}\equiv (-1)^{(p+1)/4}\Bigl(20y-\frac{8p}{y}\Bigr)\pmod{p^2},$$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{k\,v_k(4,1)}{64^k\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}\equiv 4y\pmod{p^2}.$$

(iii) If $p\equiv 11\pmod{12}$, then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\binom{p-1}{k}\frac{v_k(4,1)}{(-4)^k\binom{2k}{k}^{2}}\equiv 0\pmod{p^2}.$$

Define the Almkvist–Zudilin numbers $\{A_k\}_{k\geq 0}$ by
$$A_k=\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor k/3\rfloor}(-1)^{k-3j}3^{k-3j}\binom{k}{3j}\binom{k+j}{j}\frac{(3j)!}{j!^3},$$
and for an indeterminate (or rational/integer parameter) $x$, set
$$A_k(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{k}\binom{k}{j}^{2}\binom{2j}{j}\binom{2k-2j}{k-j}x^j.$$
Let $p$ denote a prime, and let $\bigl(\tfrac{\cdot}{p}\bigr)$ be the Legendre symbol. Prove or disprove the following three assertions.

(i) For every odd prime $p$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}A_k\equiv\begin{cases}4x^{2}-2p\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 1,3\pmod 8\text{ and }p=x^{2}+2y^{2},\ x,y\in\mathbb Z,\\ 0\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 5,7\pmod 8;\end{cases}$$
and
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}A_k\equiv\begin{cases}4x^{2}-2p\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 1\pmod 3\text{ and }p=x^{2}+3y^{2},\ x,y\in\mathbb Z,\\ 0\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 2\pmod 3.\end{cases}$$

(ii) For every prime $p>3$:
- if $p\equiv 1\pmod 3$, then $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}A_k\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}^{3}}{16^{k}}\pmod{p^{3}};$
- if $p\equiv 1,3\pmod 8$, then $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}A_k\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{4k}{k,k,k,k}}{256^{k}}\pmod{p^{3}}.$

(iii) For every prime $p>3$, and every
$$x\in\{1,-4,9,-48,81,-324,2401,9801,-25920,-777924,96059601\}\cup\{\tfrac{81}{256},-\tfrac{9}{16},\tfrac{81}{32},-3969\}$$
with $x\not\equiv 0\pmod p$,

$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}A_k\equiv\begin{cases}4x^{2}-2p\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 1,3\pmod 8\text{ and }p=x^{2}+2y^{2},\ x,y\in\mathbb Z,\\ 0\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 5,7\pmod 8;\end{cases}$$
and
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}A_k\equiv\begin{cases}4x^{2}-2p\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 1\pmod 3\text{ and }p=x^{2}+3y^{2},\ x,y\in\mathbb Z,\\ 0\pmod{p^{2}},&\text{if }p\equiv 2\pmod 3.\end{cases}$$

(ii) For every prime $p>3$:
- if $p\equiv 1\pmod 3$, then $\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}A_k\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}^{3}}{16^{k}}\pmod{p^{3}};$

$$x\in\{1,-4,9,-48,81,-324,2401,9801,-25920,-777924,96059601\}\cup\{\tfrac{81}{256},-\tfrac{9}{16},\tfrac{81}{32},-3969\}$$
with $x\not\equiv 0\pmod p$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}A_k(x)\equiv\Bigl(\tfrac{x}{p}\Bigr)\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{4k}{k,k,k,k}}{(256x)^{k}}\pmod{p^{2}}.$$

For an odd prime $p$ and an integer $a$ coprime to $p$, let $q_p(a) = (a^{p-1} - 1)/p$ denote the Fermat quotient, let $H_m = \sum_{j=1}^{m} 1/j$ denote the $m$-th harmonic number, and let $B_n$ denote the $n$-th Bernoulli number.

Prove or disprove the following statements for every prime $p > 3$:

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem appears to remain open. Known results show the amalgamation property fails for several natural non-abelian varieties — e.g., the variety of representable ℓ-groups (Powell–Tsinakis and later proofs), and ℓ-metabelian ℓ-groups exhibit non-amalgamation phenomena. Only o-approximable varieties can have amalgamation, and the abelian variety is the principal known positive example. No published result exhibits a non-abelian variety of ℓ-groups with the amalgamation property.

Background. A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a lattice order ≤ such that the group multiplication is order-preserving in both arguments; equivalently, G is a group with binary operations ∧ and ∨ making (G, ∧, ∨) a lattice and satisfying a(x ∧ y)b = axb ∧ ayb and a(x ∨ y)b = axb ∨ ayb for all a, b, x, y ∈ G. The class of ℓ-groups, viewed in the signature (·, ⁻¹, e, ∧, ∨), forms a variety.

A quasi-variety of ℓ-groups is a class of ℓ-groups defined by quasi-identities, i.e. universally quantified implications of the form
  (s₁ = t₁ ∧ … ∧ sₙ = tₙ) ⟹ s = t,
where the sᵢ, tᵢ, s, t are ℓ-group terms. The quasi-variety generated by a class K, denoted Q(K), is the smallest quasi-variety containing K; equivalently, it is the closure of K under isomorphisms, subalgebras, direct products, and ultraproducts.

For a totally ordered set (Ω, ≤), let Aut(Ω, ≤) denote the group of order-preserving bijections of Ω onto itself. Equipped with the pointwise lattice operations
  (f ∨ g)(x) = max(f(x), g(x)),  (f ∧ g)(x) = min(f(x), g(x)),
Aut(Ω, ≤) is an ℓ-group.

Problem. Determine, in terms of explicit quasi-identities (or by an explicit description), the quasi-variety of ℓ-groups generated by the class { Aut(Ω, ≤) : (Ω, ≤) is a totally ordered set }.

Let the Domb numbers be defined by
  D_k = sum_{j=0}^{k} C(k,j)^2 · C(2j,j) · C(2(k-j), k-j),
and for integers A, B let the Lucas-type sequences {u_k(A,B)} and {v_k(A,B)} be defined by
  u_0=0, u_1=1, u_{k+1} = A·u_k − B·u_{k-1};
  v_0=2, v_1=A, v_{k+1} = A·v_k − B·v_{k-1}.
For an odd prime p and integer a, let (a/p) denote the Legendre symbol. For nonzero integer m, the falling-factorial-like coefficient D_k(m) is taken in the standard sense used for Domb-related sums (so that D_k(m)^3 means the cube of D_k(m)).

Decide whether the following congruences hold for every prime p > 3.

(i)
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} D_k(−3)^3  ≡  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} (−1)^k D_k(2)^3
  ≡  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} (−1)^k D_k(−1)^3
  ≡  (−2/p) · Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} (−1)^k D_k(1)^3
  ≡  { (−1/p)(4x^2 − 2p)  (mod p^2),  if p ≡ 1 (mod 3) and p = x^2 + 3y^2 with x,y ∈ Z;
       0                  (mod p^2),  if p ≡ 2 (mod 3). }

Moreover,
  (−1/p) · Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} (−1)^k D_k(1)^3 ≡
   { 4x^2 − 2p  (mod p^2),  if p ≡ 1, 7 (mod 24) and p = x^2 + 6y^2;
     8x^2 − 2p  (mod p^2),  if p ≡ 5, 11 (mod 24) and p = 2x^2 + 3y^2;
     0          (mod p^2),  if (−6/p) = −1. }

And
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} D_k(3)^3  ≡  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} (−1)^k D_k(−4)^3
  ≡ (−5/p) · Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} (−1)^k D_k(−1)^3
  ≡ { 4x^2 − 2p   (mod p^2),  if p ≡ 1, 4 (mod 15) and p = x^2 + 15y^2;
      12x^2 − 2p  (mod p^2),  if p ≡ 2, 8 (mod 15) and p = 3x^2 + 5y^2;
      0           (mod p^2),  if (p/15) = −1. }

(ii) Set u_k = u_k(6,1) and v_k = v_k(6,1).
If (−6/p) = −1, then
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} D_k^3 · u_k ≡ Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} D_k^3 · v_k ≡ 0 (mod p^2).
If p ≡ 1, 7 (mod 24) and p = x^2 + 6y^2 with x,y ∈ Z, then
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} D_k^3 u_k ≡ 0 (mod p^2),
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} k · D_k^3 u_k ≡ −(11/96) x^2 (mod p^2),
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} D_k^3 v_k ≡ 8x^2 − 4p (mod p^2),
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} (2k+1) D_k^3 v_k ≡ −p/4 (mod p^2).
If p ≡ 5, 11 (mod 24) and p = 2x^2 + 3y^2 with x,y ∈ Z, then
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} D_k^3 u_k ≡ 8x^2 − 2p (mod p^2),
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} (128k + 53) D_k^3 u_k ≡ 30p (mod p^3),
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} D_k^3 v_k ≡ 12p − 48x^2 (mod p^2),
  Σ_{k=0}^{p-1} (144k + 61) D_k^3 v_k ≡ −186p (mod p^2).

Prove or disprove these congruences.

Let $p>3$ be a prime and let $\left(\frac{\cdot}{p}\right)$ denote the Legendre symbol. Define the Motzkin numbers
$$M_n=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\binom{n}{2k}\binom{2k}{k}\frac{1}{k+1}\qquad(n=0,1,2,\ldots),$$
the central trinomial coefficients $T_n$ as the coefficient of $x^n$ in $(1+x+x^2)^n$ (equivalently, the constant term of $(1+x+x^{-1})^n$), and the harmonic numbers $H_n=\sum_{k=1}^{n}1/k$ (with $H_0=0$). Prove or disprove the following four supercongruences:
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}M_k^{\,2}\equiv (2-6p)\!\left(\frac{p}{3}\right)\pmod{p^2},$$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}kM_k^{\,2}\equiv (9p-1)\!\left(\frac{p}{3}\right)\pmod{p^2},$$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}T_kM_k\equiv 4\!\left(\frac{p}{3}\right)+p\!\left(1-9\!\left(\frac{p}{3}\right)\right)\pmod{p^2},$$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{T_kH_k}{3^k}\equiv 3+\!\left(\frac{p}{3}\right)^{\!2}-p\!\left(1+\!\left(\frac{p}{3}\right)\right)\pmod{p^2}.$$

A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a partial order ≤ that is a lattice and is preserved by left and right multiplication; equivalently, G carries binary lattice operations ∨ and ∧ such that the group operations are order-preserving in each argument. For a positive integer n, the free ℓ-group F_n on n generators is the free object on n generators in the variety of lattice-ordered groups (signature: group operations together with ∨ and ∧).

The conjugacy problem for a finitely generated ℓ-group G (presented by ℓ-group words in fixed generators) asks for an algorithm that, given two ℓ-group words u and v in the generators, decides whether the elements of G they represent are conjugate in the underlying group, i.e., whether there exists g ∈ G with g⁻¹ u g = v.

Question: For every finite n ≥ 2, does the free lattice-ordered group F_n on n generators have a soluble (decidable) conjugacy problem?

For integers $b,c$ and a nonnegative integer $n$, define the generalized central trinomial coefficient
$$T_n(b,c) \;=\; [x^n]\,(x^2+bx+c)^n \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\binom{n}{2k}\binom{2k}{k} b^{n-2k} c^{k}.$$
Let $\left(\tfrac{\cdot}{p}\right)$ denote the Legendre symbol. Prove or disprove the following two statements.

(i) For every odd prime $p$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{T_k(2,2)^2}{4^k} \;-\; \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}^2}{8^k} \;\equiv\; \begin{cases} 0 \pmod{p^3}, & \text{if } p\equiv 1\pmod 4,\\[2pt] 0 \pmod{p^2}, & \text{if } p\equiv 3\pmod 4. \end{cases}$$

(ii) For every prime $p>3$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{T_k(4,1)^2}{4^k} \;\equiv\; \sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\frac{T_k(4,1)^2}{36^k} \;\equiv\; \left(\frac{-1}{p}\right)\pmod{p^2}.$$

A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a partial order ≤ such that (G, ≤) is a lattice and the group multiplication is order-preserving in both arguments (i.e., a ≤ b implies xay ≤ xby for all x, y ∈ G). For a partially ordered set (Ω, ≤), let Aut(Ω, ≤) denote the group of all order-automorphisms of (Ω, ≤) (bijections f: Ω → Ω such that x ≤ y ⇔ f(x) ≤ f(y)), endowed with the pointwise partial order f ≤ g ⇔ f(x) ≤ g(x) for all x ∈ Ω. Under this order, Aut(Ω, ≤) is a lattice-ordered group whenever the pointwise supremum and infimum of any two automorphisms are again automorphisms; in general, one considers those Aut(Ω, ≤) that form ℓ-groups.

An ℓ-isomorphism between two ℓ-groups is a group isomorphism that is also an order-isomorphism (equivalently, a lattice isomorphism).

Question: Is every ℓ-group ℓ-isomorphic to Aut(Ω, ≤) for some partially ordered set (Ω, ≤)?

A variety of ℓ-groups is a class of ℓ-groups closed under homomorphic images, subalgebras, and direct products, equivalently a class defined by a set of equations in the language of ℓ-groups. Given a variety V of ℓ-groups and a family {G_i}_{i ∈ I} of ℓ-groups in V, the free product (coproduct) ⨿_V G_i in V is the ℓ-group in V together with ℓ-group homomorphisms G_i → ⨿_V G_i that is universal among such cocones in V. The word problem for a finitely presented ℓ-group H in V is said to be solvable if there is an algorithm that, given any word w in the generators, decides whether w = e in H.

Characterize precisely those varieties V of ℓ-groups with the following property: whenever {G_i}_{i ∈ I} is a finite family of finitely presented ℓ-groups in V each having solvable word problem, the free product ⨿_V G_i (which is also finitely presented in V) has solvable word problem.

There are canonical embeddings of each factor G_i into the free product, and inside ∐_V G_i one may consider the ℓ-subgroup generated by the union of the images of the factors.

Characterize all varieties V of ℓ-groups with the following property: for every family {G_i}_{i ∈ I} of ℓ-groups in V, the ℓ-subgroup of ∐_V G_i generated by the images of the factors G_i is equal to the entire free product ∐_V G_i (equivalently, the canonical maps from the factors jointly generate, as an ℓ-subgroup, the whole V-free product).

Let $G$ be a lattice-ordered group (an $\ell$-group): a group equipped with a lattice order such that the group operation distributes over the lattice operations $\wedge$ and $\vee$ on both sides. A subgroup $H \le G$ is called an $\ell$-subgroup if it is closed under the lattice operations of $G$ (i.e., $a,b \in H$ implies $a \wedge b \in H$ and $a \vee b \in H$). An $\ell$-subgroup $H$ of $G$ is said to be closed if, whenever a subset $S \subseteq H$ has a supremum $\bigvee S$ in $G$, that supremum lies in $H$ (and dually for infima). The $\ell$-group $G$ is called discrete if every strictly positive element of $G$ dominates an atom, i.e., for every $g \in G$ with $g > e$ there exists $a \in G$ with $e < a \le g$ such that no element of $G$ lies strictly between $e$ and $a$.

Question: If every $\ell$-subgroup of an $\ell$-group $G$ is closed, must $G$ be discrete?

An element $0<a\in G$ is called compact if whenever $a\le \bigvee_{i\in I} a_i$ for some set $\{a_i:i\in I\}\subseteq G^+$ for which the join exists, there is a finite subset $F\subseteq I$ with $a\le \bigvee_{i\in F}a_i$. An $\ell$-subgroup $H$ of $G$ is called closed if whenever $S\subseteq H$ has a join $\bigvee S$ in $G$, that join lies in $H$ (and likewise for meets).

Prove or disprove: an $\ell$-group $G$ is generated (as an $\ell$-group) by its compact elements if and only if every $\ell$-subgroup of $G$ is closed.

Let $G$ be a partially ordered group (p.o. group), i.e., a group equipped with a partial order $\le$ that is translation-invariant on both sides: for all $a,b,x,y\in G$, $a\le b$ implies $xay\le xby$. A right order on $G$ is a total order $\preceq$ on $G$ that is right-invariant ($a\preceq b \Rightarrow ax\preceq bx$ for all $x\in G$); the positive cone of such an order is a subset $P\subseteq G$ with $P\cdot P\subseteq P$, $P\cap P^{-1}=\{e\}$, $P\cup P^{-1}=G$, and $g^{-1}Pg \subseteq P$ is not required (so $P$ is only a right-order cone). Say that the partial order on $G$ is the intersection of right orders if its positive cone $P_G=\{g\in G: g\ge e\}$ equals the intersection of the positive cones of some family of right orders on $G$.

An $\ell$-group is a group $L$ that is also a lattice with respect to a partial order which is translation-invariant on both sides (so all binary sups $a\vee b$ and infs $a\wedge b$ exist). An order-embedding of a p.o. group $G$ into an $\ell$-group $L$ is an injective group homomorphism $\varphi:G\to L$ such that for all $a,b\in G$, $a\le b$ in $G$ if and only if $\varphi(a)\le \varphi(b)$ in $L$. Such an embedding is said to preserve existing sups and infs if whenever a subset $S\subseteq G$ has a supremum (respectively, infimum) in $G$, then $\varphi(S)$ has a supremum (respectively, infimum) in $L$ and it equals $\varphi(\sup S)$ (respectively, $\varphi(\inf S)$).

Question: If $G$ is a p.o. group whose order is the intersection of right orders, can $G$ be order-embedded into an $\ell$-group via an embedding that preserves all existing suprema and infima of $G$?

A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group $G$ equipped with a lattice order $\le$ such that the group operation is order-preserving in both arguments, i.e. $a\le b$ implies $xay\le xby$ for all $x,y\in G$. Equivalently, $G$ carries binary lattice operations $\vee$ and $\wedge$ that are compatible with multiplication.

A topological lattice-ordered group (tℓ-group) is an ℓ-group $G$ together with a topology $\tau$ on $G$ such that the group operations $(x,y)\mapsto xy$ and $x\mapsto x^{-1}$ are continuous, and the lattice operations $(x,y)\mapsto x\vee y$ and $(x,y)\mapsto x\wedge y$ are also continuous (with $G\times G$ given the product topology).

A free tℓ-group on a topological space $X$ would be a tℓ-group $F(X)$ together with a continuous map $\iota:X\to F(X)$ such that for every tℓ-group $H$ and every continuous map $f:X\to H$ there exists a unique continuous ℓ-group homomorphism $\bar f:F(X)\to H$ with $\bar f\circ\iota=f$.

Question: Do free tℓ-groups exist? If they exist, give an explicit description of them.

representations.normalized:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group $G$ equipped with a partial order $\le$ such that $G$ is a lattice under $\le$ and the group multiplication is order-preserving on both sides, i.e. $a \le b$ implies $xay \le xby$ for all $x,y \in G$. A topological lattice-ordered group (tℓ-group) is an ℓ-group $G$ endowed with a topology making it a topological group and such that the lattice operations $\vee$ and $\wedge$ are continuous as maps $G \times G \to G$. The tℓ-group is called connected if its underlying topological space is connected. An ℓ-group $G$ is called Archimedean if for all $a, b \in G$ with $a, b > e$, the relation $a^n \le b$ for every positive integer $n$ implies $a = e$ (equivalently, no strictly positive element is infinitesimal with respect to another).

Question: Must every connected tℓ-group be Archimedean?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

Recent work on connected topological lattice-ordered groups (Algebra Universalis, 2022) reportedly resolves Pshenichnov's question in the negative: admitting a connected ℓ-group topology does not imply that the ℓ-group is Archimedean (nor even representable) in general. Under the additional hypothesis that the ℓ-group has a basis, admitting such a topology does force the ℓ-group to be a subdirect product of copies of ℝ (hence Archimedean).

[{"title": "Connected topological lattice-ordered groups", "url": "https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00012-022-00800-6", "snippet": "Two open problems about lattice-ordered groups that admit a connected lattice-ordered group topology are answered; in the general case, admitting such a topology does not imply Archimedean or representable.", "claim": "Pshenichnov's question is answered negatively: a connected tℓ-group need not be Archimedean."}]

representations.normalized:
A topological lattice-ordered group (tℓ-group) is a group G equipped simultaneously with:
(i) a Hausdorff topology making the group operations (multiplication and inversion) continuous, and
(ii) a partial order ≤ that is translation-invariant on both sides and turns (G, ≤) into a lattice (every pair of elements has a supremum and infimum), such that the lattice operations ∨ and ∧ are also continuous with respect to the topology.

The rank of a tℓ-group G is defined as the cardinality of a maximal set of pairwise disjoint strictly positive elements (equivalently, the cardinality of a maximal antichain of strictly positive elements in the lattice order). G is said to have finite rank if this cardinality is a finite integer n.

Question: Suppose G is a connected tℓ-group of finite rank n. Must G be isomorphic, as an abstract group, to the additive group ℝⁿ?

representations.normalized:
A topological lattice-ordered group (tℓ-group) is a group $G$ equipped simultaneously with a lattice order $\le$ compatible with the group operation (so that $G$ is an ℓ-group: translations are order-preserving and the lattice operations $\wedge,\vee$ are well-defined and group-equivariant) and a Hausdorff group topology with respect to which the lattice operations $\wedge,\vee:G\times G\to G$ are continuous. A tℓ-subgroup of $G$ is a subgroup that is also a sublattice; an ℓ-isomorphism between ℓ-groups is a group isomorphism that is also a lattice isomorphism. A topological isomorphism between tℓ-groups is an ℓ-isomorphism that is simultaneously a homeomorphism.

Suppose $G$ is a tℓ-group containing two closed normal tℓ-subgroups $H_1$ and $H_2$ such that, as an ℓ-group, $G$ is ℓ-isomorphic to the direct sum $H_1\oplus H_2$ (where each $H_i$ is regarded with the ℓ-group structure inherited from $G$).

Question: Must $G$ be topologically isomorphic to the direct sum $H_1\oplus H_2$ (equipped with the product topology)?

For integers $b$ and $c$, define the generalized central trinomial coefficient
$$T_n(b,c)=\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}\binom{n}{2k}\binom{2k}{k}b^{n-2k}c^k,$$
which is the coefficient of $x^n$ in $(x^2+bx+c)^n$ (equivalently, $T_n(b,c)$ is determined by $T_0=1$, $T_1=b$, and $(n+1)T_{n+1}=(2n+1)bT_n-n(b^2-4c)T_{n-1}$). For an odd prime $p$ and an integer $a$ coprime to $p$, let $\left(\tfrac{a}{p}\right)$ denote the Legendre symbol.

Prove or disprove the following statement.

Let $p$ be a prime distinct from $2$, $5$, and $19$. Then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\frac{T_{2k}(5778,1)}{1216^{2k}}\equiv\begin{cases}4x^{2}-2p\pmod{p^{2}}&\text{if }\left(\tfrac{2}{p}\right)=\left(\tfrac{p}{5}\right)=\left(\tfrac{p}{19}\right)=1,\ p=x^{2}+190y^{2},\\[2pt]
8x^{2}-2p\pmod{p^{2}}&\text{if }\left(\tfrac{2}{p}\right)=1,\ \left(\tfrac{p}{5}\right)=\left(\tfrac{p}{19}\right)=-1,\ p=2x^{2}+95y^{2},\\[2pt]
2p-20x^{2}\pmod{p^{2}}&\text{if }\left(\tfrac{2}{p}\right)=\left(\tfrac{p}{5}\right)=-1,\ \left(\tfrac{p}{19}\right)=1,\ p=5x^{2}+38y^{2},\\[2pt]
2p-40x^{2}\pmod{p^{2}}&\text{if }\left(\tfrac{2}{p}\right)=\left(\tfrac{p}{19}\right)=-1,\ \left(\tfrac{p}{5}\right)=1,\ p=10x^{2}+19y^{2},\\[2pt]
0\pmod{p^{2}}&\text{if }\left(\tfrac{-190}{p}\right)=-1,
\end{cases}$$
and
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(57720k+24893)\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\frac{T_{2k}(5778,1)}{1216^{2k}}\equiv p\!\left(11548+13345\!\left(\tfrac{-190}{p}\right)\right)\pmod{p^{2}}.$$
Moreover, provided $p\neq 17$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\frac{T_{2k}(5778,1)}{439280^{2k}}\equiv\left(\tfrac{-95}{p}\right)\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\frac{T_{2k}(5778,1)}{1216^{2k}}\pmod{p^{2}}$$
and
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(57720k+3967)\binom{2k}{k}^{2}\frac{T_{2k}(5778,1)}{439280^{2k}}\equiv p\!\left(\tfrac{-95}{p}\right)\!\left(3983-16\!\left(\tfrac{-190}{p}\right)\right)\pmod{p^{2}}.$$
