representations.normalized:
An ℓ-group (lattice-ordered group) is an algebraic structure $(G,\cdot,{}^{-1},e,\wedge,\vee)$ such that $(G,\cdot,{}^{-1},e)$ is a group, $(G,\wedge,\vee)$ is a lattice, and the group multiplication distributes over the lattice operations on both sides (equivalently, $a\le b$ implies $cad\le cbd$ for all $a,b,c,d\in G$). A variety of ℓ-groups is a class of ℓ-groups closed under taking subalgebras, homomorphic images, and direct products; equivalently, it is the class of ℓ-groups satisfying some set of identities in the language $\{\cdot,{}^{-1},e,\wedge,\vee\}$.

For a positive integer $n$, an ℓ-group $G$ is said to have rank at most $n$ if every set of $n+1$ pairwise disjoint strictly positive elements of $G$ contains two elements that are not disjoint (where $a,b>e$ are disjoint when $a\wedge b=e$). A variety $\mathcal V$ of ℓ-groups is said to have finite rank if there exists $n\in\mathbb N$ such that every member of $\mathcal V$ has rank at most $n$; otherwise $\mathcal V$ does not have finite rank.

Problem. Exhibit a variety $\mathcal V$ of ℓ-groups such that $\mathcal V$ does not have finite rank, but every proper subvariety of $\mathcal V$ has finite rank.

representations.normalized:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a partial order ≤ such that (G, ≤) is a lattice and the group operation is order-preserving in both arguments (equivalently, x ≤ y implies a x b ≤ a y b for all a, b ∈ G). An ℓ-ideal of an ℓ-group G is a normal convex ℓ-subgroup of G, i.e., a normal subgroup H ⊆ G that is closed under the lattice operations and satisfies the convexity condition: if h ∈ H, g ∈ G, and |g| ≤ |h| (where |x| = x ∨ x⁻¹), then g ∈ H. The set Id(G) of all ℓ-ideals of G, ordered by inclusion, forms a complete distributive lattice.

For each ℓ-group G, let L(G) = (Id(G); ∩, +) be the lattice of ℓ-ideals of G (where + denotes the join, i.e., the ℓ-ideal generated by the union). Consider the class 𝒦 = {L(G) : G is an ℓ-group} of all such lattices, viewed as structures in the language of lattices {∧, ∨}, and let Th(𝒦) denote the set of first-order sentences in this language that are true in every member of 𝒦.

Question: Is Th(𝒦) decidable? That is, does there exist an algorithm that, given a first-order sentence φ in the language of lattices, decides whether φ holds in the lattice of ℓ-ideals of every ℓ-group?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

For the restricted class of abelian ℓ-groups, the elementary theory of the ℓ-ideal lattices has been shown to be undecidable (Algebra and Logic, 2005, "Elementary Theory for l-Ideal Lattices of Abelian l-Groups", giving a negative answer to Problem 5.20 in the Kourovka Notebook). This builds on Gurevich's hereditary undecidability of the theory of lattice-ordered abelian groups. The general question for arbitrary (not necessarily abelian) ℓ-groups thus has a negative answer in the abelian sub-case, which already implies undecidability for the full class; however, we did not locate a single source explicitly attributing the resolution of the general question as posed.

[{"title": "Elementary Theory for l-Ideal Lattices of Abelian l-Groups", "url": "https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10469-005-0029-5", "snippet": "The elementary theory of l-ideal lattices of Abelian lattice-ordered groups is undecidable, giving a negative solution to Problem 5.20 in the Kourovka Notebook.", "claim": "The elementary theory of ℓ-ideal lattices of abelian ℓ-groups is undecidable."}, {"title": "Computing on Lattice-Ordered Abelian Groups", "url": "https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-48006-6_15", "snippet": "Starting from a classical theorem of Gurevich and Kokorin, we survey theories of lattice-ordered abelian groups; Gurevich proved the hereditary undecidability of the theory of lattice-ordered abelian groups.", "claim": "Foundational undecidability result by Gurevich for ℓ-groups underlies the negative answer."}]

representations.normalized:
A totally ordered group is a group $G$ equipped with a total order $\leq$ such that $a \leq b$ implies $xay \leq xby$ for all $x,y,a,b \in G$. A lattice-ordered group ($\ell$-group) is a group equipped with a lattice order that is invariant under left and right multiplication. A group is orderable if it admits a total order making it a totally ordered group, and lattice-orderable if it admits a lattice order making it an $\ell$-group.

Let $\{(G_i, \leq_i) : i \in I\}$ be a family of totally ordered groups, and let $H_i \leq G_i$ be subgroups together with order-preserving isomorphisms $\varphi_{ij}: H_i \to H_j$ that form a compatible system (so that all $H_i$ are identified via order-isomorphisms with a common ordered subgroup $H$). Form the group-theoretic free product with amalgamation $P = \ast_H \, G_i$ amalgamating the subgroups $H_i$ via the given order-isomorphisms.

Question: Does there exist such a family for which the amalgamated free product $P$ is not orderable (admits no total order making it a totally ordered group) yet is lattice-orderable (admits some lattice order making it an $\ell$-group)?

An ℓ-group (lattice-ordered group) is an algebraic structure (G, ·, ⁻¹, e, ∨, ∧) such that (G, ·, ⁻¹, e) is a group, (G, ∨, ∧) is a lattice, and the group multiplication distributes over both lattice operations on the left and the right. A class of ℓ-groups is a variety if it is closed under taking sub-ℓ-groups, homomorphic images, and arbitrary direct products; equivalently, by Birkhoff's theorem, it is the class of all ℓ-groups satisfying some set of equations in the language (·, ⁻¹, e, ∨, ∧). A variety is said to be finitely based if it can be axiomatized by finitely many such equations.

An ℓ-group G is called nilpotent if its underlying group is nilpotent. Let 𝒩 denote the variety of ℓ-groups generated by the class of all nilpotent ℓ-groups (i.e., the smallest variety of ℓ-groups containing every nilpotent ℓ-group).

Question: Is the variety 𝒩 finitely based?

representations.normalized:
A lattice-ordered group (ℓ-group) is a group G equipped with a lattice order ≤ such that the group operation is compatible with the lattice operations, i.e. for all a,b,c,d ∈ G, a ≤ b implies cad ≤ cbd. An element u ∈ G is called a strong (order) unit if for every g ∈ G there exists a positive integer n = n(g) such that u^{-n} ≤ g ≤ u^n. Note that the condition defining a strong unit is not expressible by a single first-order sentence in the language of ℓ-groups.

Develop a structure theory for the class of pairs (G, u) where G is an ℓ-group and u is a distinguished strong unit of G. In particular:
(a) Identify natural axiomatizations (possibly in infinitary logic or as a quasi-variety in an enriched language) for this class.
(b) Describe the relationship between (G, u) and the algebras arising from many-valued logics (such as MV-algebras and related structures), extending the Mundici-style categorical equivalence between abelian ℓ-groups with strong unit and MV-algebras to broader classes of (not necessarily abelian) ℓ-groups.
(c) Investigate representation theorems, free objects, and model-theoretic properties (e.g. amalgamation, decidability of the theory) of the class of ℓ-groups with strong unit.

Work on ℓ-groups with strong unit and their connection to many-valued logics (MV-algebras via Mundici's equivalence, GMV-algebras, pseudo-MV-algebras of Dvurečenskij, etc.) has progressed considerably, but the broader program of fully classifying (G, u) for non-abelian ℓ-groups remains active and is not regarded as solved.

For each nonnegative integer $n$, define
$$s_n \;=\; \frac{\binom{6n}{3n}\binom{3n}{n}}{2(2n+1)\binom{2n}{n}}.$$

(a) Prove or disprove: for every prime $p>3$,
$$\sum_{k=1}^{p-1} \frac{s_k}{108^{\,k}} \;\equiv\; \begin{cases} 0 \pmod{p}, & \text{if } p \equiv \pm 1 \pmod{12},\\[2pt] -1 \pmod{p}, & \text{if } p \equiv \pm 5 \pmod{12}.\end{cases}$$

(b) Prove or disprove: there exist positive integers $t_1, t_2, t_3, \dots$ such that for every real $x$ with $|x| \le 1/(6\sqrt{3})$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} s_k\, x^{2k+1} \;+\; \frac{1}{24} \;-\; \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} t_k\, x^{2k} \;=\; \cos\!\left(\tfrac{2}{3}\arccos\!\left(6\sqrt{3}\,x\right)\right),$$
and moreover $t_p \equiv -2 \pmod{p}$ for every prime $p$.

Let $\{F_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ and $\{L_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ denote the Fibonacci and Lucas sequences, defined by $F_0=0$, $F_1=1$, $L_0=2$, $L_1=1$, and $F_{n+1}=F_n+F_{n-1}$, $L_{n+1}=L_n+L_{n-1}$ for $n\ge 1$. For an odd prime $p\ne 5$, let $\left(\tfrac{\cdot}{5}\right)$ denote the Legendre symbol modulo $5$, and define the Fibonacci–Fermat quotient
$$q := \frac{F_{p-\left(\tfrac{p}{5}\right)}}{p}\in\mathbb{Z}.$$
Prove or disprove that for every prime $p\notin\{2,5\}$ the following four congruences hold simultaneously modulo $p^2$:
$$p\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{F_{2k}}{k^2\binom{2k}{k}} \equiv -\left(\tfrac{p}{5}\right)\!\left(\tfrac{3}{2}q + \tfrac{5}{4}p\,q^2\right)\pmod{p^2},$$
$$p\sum_{k=1}^{p-1}\frac{L_{2k}}{k^2\binom{2k}{k}} \equiv -\tfrac{5}{2}q - \tfrac{15}{4}p\,q^2\pmod{p^2},$$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{(p-3)/2}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}\,F_{2k+1}}{(2k+1)\,16^k} \equiv (-1)^{(p+1)/2}\left(\tfrac{p}{5}\right)\!\left(\tfrac{1}{2}q + \tfrac{5}{8}p\,q^2\right)\pmod{p^2},$$
$$\sum_{k=0}^{(p-3)/2}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}\,L_{2k+1}}{(2k+1)\,16^k} \equiv (-1)^{(p+1)/2}\!\left(\tfrac{5}{2}q + \tfrac{5}{8}p\,q^2\right)\pmod{p^2}.$$
Here all rational numbers appearing on either side are interpreted modulo $p^2$ via their unique representatives in $\mathbb{Z}/p^2\mathbb{Z}$ (the denominators $2,4,8$ are invertible modulo $p^2$).

An algebraic theory T is a first-order theory in a fixed signature whose axioms are universally quantified equations (so its models form a variety). Given such a theory T, a finitely generated model G of T is called quasi-finitely axiomatisable (QFA) within T if there exists a single first-order sentence σ in the language of T such that:

(i) G ⊨ σ, and
(ii) for every finitely generated model H of T with H ⊨ σ, one has H ≅ G.

Recall:
• An ℓ-group (lattice-ordered group) is a structure (G, ·, ⁻¹, e, ∧, ∨) such that (G, ·, ⁻¹, e) is a group, (G, ∧, ∨) is a lattice, and the group operation distributes over ∧ and ∨ (equivalently, x ≤ y implies axb ≤ ayb for all a, b).
• An abelian ℓ-group is an ℓ-group whose underlying group is abelian.
• A totally ordered group is a group equipped with a total order ≤ such that x ≤ y implies axb ≤ ayb for all a, b; equivalently, an ℓ-group whose lattice order is total.

Investigate the QFA finitely generated models in each of the three algebraic theories T = (ℓ-groups), T = (abelian ℓ-groups), and T = (totally ordered groups). Specifically:

1. Characterize, as completely as possible, which finitely generated ℓ-groups are QFA within the theory of ℓ-groups.
2. Characterize which finitely generated abelian ℓ-groups are QFA within the theory of abelian ℓ-groups.
3. Characterize which finitely generated totally ordered groups are QFA within the theory of totally ordered groups.

In particular, exhibit non-trivial classes of examples (and, where possible, non-examples) of QFA structures in each setting, and determine whether analogues of known group-theoretic criteria — such as "QFA iff prime model of its complete theory" — hold in the ordered/lattice-ordered context.

$$S(n)\;=\;\frac{(-1)^{n-1}}{n^2(n+1)\binom{2n}{n}}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{u_{k+1}(4,1)}{\binom{2k}{k}}.$$
(Here it is understood that, although $S(n)$ is a priori a rational number, it is conjectured to be a $3$-adic integer, so the congruences below make sense.)

(1) For every positive integer $n$,
$$S(n)\;\equiv\;\begin{cases}1\pmod 9 & \text{if } n\equiv 0,2\pmod 9,\\[2pt] 4\pmod 9 & \text{if } n\equiv 5,6\pmod 9,\\[2pt] -2\pmod 9 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

$$3^{2a}\sum_{k=0}^{3^a-1}\frac{u_{k+1}(4,1)}{\binom{2k}{k}}\pmod{3^b}$$
depends only on $b$ (and not on $a$).

A group $G$ is called right-orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is invariant under right multiplication: $a \le b$ implies $ac \le bc$ for all $a,b,c \in G$. A right order $\le$ on $G$ is called a Conrad order (or of Conrad type) if for every pair of elements $a,b \in G$ with $a,b > 1$, there exists a positive integer $N$ such that $ab^N > b$.

Define a group $G$ to be strictly bounded if there exists a positive integer $n$ (depending only on $G$) such that for every pair of elements $x, y \in G$, the subgroup $\langle x^{y^m} \mid m \in \mathbb{Z}\rangle$ generated by all conjugates of $x$ by integer powers of $y$ admits a generating set of cardinality at most $n$.

Question: Does every strictly bounded right-orderable group admit a Conrad right order?

(i) For every positive integer $n$,

(ii) For every integer $a>\nu_3(m-1)$,
$$\frac{1}{3^a}\sum_{k=0}^{3^a-1}\binom{3^a-1}{k}(-1)^k\binom{2k}{k}m^k\;\equiv\;-\frac{m-1}{3}\pmod{3^{\nu_3(m-1)}}.$$

(iii) For every integer $a\ge 2$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{3^a-1}\binom{3^a-1}{k}(-1)^k\binom{2k}{k}\;\equiv\;-3^{2a-1}\pmod{3^{2a}}.$$

Determine whether (i), (ii), and (iii) are all true.

Let $G$ be a group. Denote by $\mathcal{F}(G)$ the family of all finite non-empty subsets of $G$. Then $\mathcal{F}(G)$ is a monoid under the multiplication
$$A \cdot B = \{ab : a \in A,\, b \in B\}$$
induced by the group operation, with identity $\{e\}$. A monoid homomorphism $\sigma : \mathcal{F}(G) \to G$ satisfying $\sigma(\{g\}) = g$ for every $g \in G$ is called a retraction.

Recall that $G$ is called a unique product group (u.p. group) if for any two finite non-empty subsets $A, B \subseteq G$ there exists at least one element $g \in G$ that can be expressed in exactly one way as $g = ab$ with $a \in A$ and $b \in B$.

Question: Suppose $G$ admits at least one retraction $\sigma : \mathcal{F}(G) \to G$. Must $G$ be a unique product group?

(i) Let $m\ge 2$ be an integer with $m>2$, let $r$ be an integer with $r\ge -m/2$ such that $m\not\equiv r \pmod 2$, and let $p>r$ be an odd prime not dividing $m$ with $p\equiv r\pmod m$. Then
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{km}\binom{r/m}{k}^{m}\equiv 0\pmod{p^{3}}.$$

(ii) Let $m\ge 2$ be an integer, let $r$ be an integer with $r\ge -m$, and let $p>r$ be an odd prime not dividing $m$ with $p\equiv r\pmod{2m}$. Then for every $n=1,2,\dots,m-1$,
$$\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^{k}\binom{r/m}{k}^{2n+1}\equiv 0\pmod{p^{2}}.$$

(iii) For every prime $p$ and every positive integer $n$,
$$\nu_p\!\left(\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}(-1)^{k}\binom{-1/(p+1)}{k}^{p+1}\right)\ge c_p\,\bigl\lfloor \nu_p(n)+1\bigr\rfloor,$$
where $c_p=1$ if $p=2$, $c_p=3$ if $p=3$, and $c_p=5$ if $p\ge 5$.

A right-ordered group is a group $G$ together with a total order $\le$ such that $a\le b$ implies $ac\le bc$ for all $a,b,c\in G$. A group is right-orderable if it admits such an order. Following standard terminology, denote by $(\mathrm{OR})^{*}$ the class of groups whose every right-order can be extended in some prescribed manner (right-orderable groups with a fixed compatible structure). A group $G$ is metabelian if its commutator subgroup $[G,G]$ is abelian, and soluble if it has a finite derived series. A right-ordered group $H$ is divisible if for every $h\in H$ and every positive integer $n$ there exists $x\in H$ with $x^{n}=h$. Given right-ordered groups $(G,\le_G)$ and $(H,\le_H)$, an o-embedding of $G$ into $H$ is an injective group homomorphism $\varphi:G\to H$ that is order-preserving, i.e. $a\le_G b\iff \varphi(a)\le_H \varphi(b)$.

Question: Can every metabelian right-ordered group (respectively, right-orderable group, respectively $(\mathrm{OR})^{*}$-group) be o-embedded in a divisible metabelian right-ordered group (respectively, right-orderable, respectively $(\mathrm{OR})^{*}$-group)? Answer the analogous questions with "metabelian" replaced by "soluble".

Use the convention $\binom{x}{l}=\frac{x(x-1)\cdots(x-l+1)}{l!}$ for $x\in\mathbb{Q}$ and $l\in\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$, and $\lfloor\cdot\rfloor$ for the floor function.

Prove or disprove the following statement. Let $p$ be a prime, let $l,n\in\mathbb{N}$, and let $r\in\mathbb{Z}$. If $p\nmid n$ or $p\nmid r$, then
$$
\nu_p\!\left(\sum_{\substack{0\le k\le n\\ k\equiv r\,(\bmod\,p)}}\binom{n}{k}(-1)^k\binom{(k-r)/p}{l}\right)\;\ge\;\Big\lfloor\tfrac{n-lp-1}{p-1}\Big\rfloor+\nu_p\!\left(\binom{\lfloor(n-l-1)/(p-1)\rfloor}{l}\right),
$$
where the inner binomial coefficient $\binom{(k-r)/p}{l}$ is evaluated using the convention above (the sum runs only over $k$ with $k\equiv r\pmod p$, so $(k-r)/p\in\mathbb{Z}$).

$$\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \binom{2k}{k}\, 2^k \equiv (-1)^{(n-1)/2} \pmod{n^2},$$
must $n$ be prime?

$$a_1 + a_2 + \cdots + a_{n-1} \equiv 0 \pmod{n^2},$$
must $n$ be prime?

\[
\Gamma \;=\; (\rho,\; X_G,\; \{\rho_x\}_{x \in X_G}),
\]
where:
- $\rho : G \to \mathrm{Aut}(H^2(X;\mathbb{Z}),\cup)$ is the induced action on second cohomology, preserving the cup-product intersection form;
- $X_G = \{x \in X : G_x \neq \{1\}\}$ is the fixed-point (singular) set of the action, where $G_x$ denotes the isotropy subgroup of $x$;
- for each $x \in X_G$, the map $\rho_x : G_x \to GL(4,\mathbb{R})$ is the linear isotropy representation modeling the action on a $G_x$-invariant neighborhood of $x$.

Let $\mathcal{D}(X,p)$ denote the set of all such triples $\Gamma$ realized by some $\mathbb{Z}_p$-action on $X$, considered up to the natural equivalence (conjugation of $\rho$ by automorphisms of the intersection form, equivariant identification of singular sets, and equivalence of local representations).

Problem: Describe and bound the complexity of the set $\mathcal{D}(X,p)$ as $X$ ranges over closed simply connected $4$-manifolds. In particular, determine which triples $\Gamma$ are realizable, and find effective constraints (in terms of the intersection form of $X$, the prime $p$, and the topology of $X_G$) that classify $\mathcal{D}(X,p)$.

$$\mathcal{S}(X) = \{G : G \text{ is a finite group acting smoothly and effectively on } X\},$$

Investigate the following two-way relationship between the smooth structure on $X$ and the collection $\mathcal{S}(X)$:

(a) To what extent does the smooth structure of $X$ determine $\mathcal{S}(X)$? More precisely, can one exhibit pairs $(X_1, X_2)$ of closed 4-manifolds that are homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic for which $\mathcal{S}(X_1) \neq \mathcal{S}(X_2)$, either as sets of finite groups or as sets of smooth conjugacy classes of actions? Identify invariants of the smooth structure (e.g. Seiberg–Witten or gauge-theoretic invariants) that obstruct or constrain which finite groups can act smoothly.

(b) Conversely, to what extent does the collection $\mathcal{S}(X)$, together with the conjugacy classes of smooth actions, determine the smooth structure on $X$? In particular, do there exist closed 4-manifolds $X_1$ and $X_2$ that are homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic and for which the sets $\mathcal{S}(X_1)$ and $\mathcal{S}(X_2)$ (with their action data) coincide?

Question: Is it true that every smooth action of a finite group $G$ on $S^4$ which has at least one isolated fixed point is smoothly conjugate to a linear action?

A right order on a group $G$ is a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is right-invariant: $x\le y$ implies $xz\le yz$ for all $x,y,z\in G$. The positive cone of $\le$ is $P=\{g\in G:g>1\}$. A right order $\le$ on $G$ is called a Conrad right order if for every pair $a,b\in P$ there exists a positive integer $n$ with $a b^n > b$ (equivalently, the order has the Conrad property). A group is orderable if it admits a two-sided invariant total order. For a subset $S\subseteq G$, write $I(S)$ for the isolator of $S$ in $G$, namely $I(S)=\{g\in G: g^n\in S\text{ for some }n\ge 1\}$. A group $K$ is a central extension of $G$ if there is a short exact sequence $1\to Z\to K\to G\to 1$ with $Z$ contained in the center of $K$. A group is residually torsion-free nilpotent if for every non-identity element $g$ there is a normal subgroup $N$ with $g\notin N$ and $G/N$ torsion-free nilpotent.

Let $G$ be a soluble orderable group such that every right order on $G$ is a Conrad right order. Determine whether each of the following holds:

(i) Is every right order on every subgroup of $G$ a Conrad right order?

(ii) If $H\le G$ satisfies $G = I(H)$, is every right order on $H$ a Conrad right order?

(iii) If $H\le G$ has finite index in $G$, is every right order on $H$ a Conrad right order?

(iv) If $G$ is non-abelian, must $G$ contain a non-commutative free subsemigroup (a subsemigroup isomorphic to the free semigroup on two generators)?

(v) If $K$ is any central extension of $G$, is every right order on $K$ a Conrad right order?

(vi) If, in addition, $G$ is finitely generated, must $G$ be residually torsion-free nilpotent?

Let $G$ be a group. A (total) order $\le$ on $G$ is called a (two-sided) order if it is invariant under both left and right multiplication: $x \le y$ implies $axb \le ayb$ for all $a,b \in G$. A right order on $G$ is a total order $\le$ such that $x \le y$ implies $xa \le ya$ for all $a \in G$. A homotopy K3 surface is a smooth, closed, simply-connected 4-manifold that is homotopy equivalent to a K3 surface. A K3 group is a finite group that admits a faithful symplectic action (i.e., an action preserving a holomorphic symplectic form) on some complex K3 surface; by a theorem of Mukai, such groups are exactly the subgroups of the Mathieu group M23 having at least five orbits on a 24-element set, and they were classified explicitly by Mukai, Xiao, and Kondo.

Question: Does there exist a finite group G that is not a K3 group but nevertheless admits either
(a) a smooth, faithful action on some homotopy K3 surface, or
(b) a symplectic, faithful action (with respect to some symplectic structure) on some symplectic homotopy K3 surface?

Equivalently, is the class of finite groups admitting smooth (respectively symplectic) faithful actions on homotopy K3 surfaces strictly larger than the class of K3 groups?

A right order on a group $G$ is a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is invariant under right multiplication: $a\le b$ implies $ag\le bg$ for all $a,b,g\in G$. Equivalently, a right order is determined by its positive cone $P=\{g\in G:g>1\}$, which satisfies $P\cdot P\subseteq P$ and $G\setminus\{1\}=P\sqcup P^{-1}$. For any $g\in G$, the conjugate cone $P^g=g^{-1}Pg$ is again the positive cone of a right order on $G$.

A group $N$ is nilpotent if its lower central series terminates at $\{1\}$. A divisible completion of a torsion-free nilpotent group $N$ is an overgroup $N^{\#}\supseteq N$ that is nilpotent and divisible (every element has an $n$-th root for every positive integer $n$); a minimal such completion exists and is unique up to isomorphism over $N$.

Let $G$ be a right-orderable group and let $N$ be a nilpotent subgroup of $G$. Let $P$ be the positive cone of some right order on $G$, so that $P\cap N$ is the positive cone of an induced right order on $N$. Let $N^{\#}$ be a minimal divisible completion of $N$, and suppose $P^{\#}\subseteq N^{\#}$ is the positive cone of a right order on $N^{\#}$ extending the order on $N$ with positive cone $P\cap N$ (so $P^{\#}\cap N=P\cap N$). For $g\in N^{\#}$, let $\le_g$ denote the right order on $N$ whose positive cone is $(P^{\#})^g\cap N$.

Question: Must $\le_g$ extend to a right order on the whole group $G$?

Background. A homotopy K3 surface is a closed smooth (or topological) 4-manifold homotopy equivalent to a K3 surface; its second cohomology, equipped with the intersection form, is isometric to the K3 lattice $L_{K3}=3U\oplus 2E_8(-1)$, where $U$ is the hyperbolic plane. By a theorem of Nikulin, an order-$p$ symplectic automorphism of an algebraic K3 surface (which exists only for primes $p\in\{2,3,5,7\}$) has a fixed-point set consisting of a fixed finite number $n_p$ of isolated points, and at each such point $x$ the differential gives a local complex linear representation $\rho_x$ of $\mathbb Z/p$ on $T_xX\cong\mathbb C^2$ of a prescribed (Nikulin) type. The induced action on $L_{K3}$ is, up to lattice isomorphism, independent of the K3 surface and of the chosen automorphism.

Problem. Let $p$ be a prime and let $\mathbb Z/p$ act on a homotopy K3 surface $X$ in one of the following categories: locally linear topological, smooth, or (when $X$ carries a symplectic structure) symplectic. Assume that the fixed-point data $(X^{\mathbb Z/p},\{\rho_x\}_{x\in X^{\mathbb Z/p}})$, consisting of the set of fixed points together with the local linear representations at each fixed point, coincides with the fixed-point data of an order-$p$ symplectic automorphism of a (genuine) K3 surface as classified by Nikulin. Determine what can be concluded about the induced representation $\rho$ of $\mathbb Z/p$ on the K3 lattice $H^2(X;\mathbb Z)\cong L_{K3}$. In particular, must $\rho$ agree (as an isometric $\mathbb Z/p$-representation on $L_{K3}$) with the representation induced by an order-$p$ symplectic automorphism of a K3 surface?

A group $G$ is called **right-orderable** if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ such that for all $x, y, z \in G$, the inequality $x \le y$ implies $xz \le yz$. Equivalently, $G$ admits a subset $P \subseteq G$ (a positive cone) with $P \cdot P \subseteq P$, $P \cap P^{-1} = \emptyset$, and $P \cup P^{-1} \cup \{1\} = G$.

It is known that every right-orderable group is a unique product group.

**Question.** Is every unique product group right-orderable?

Let X be a smooth, closed, simply-connected 4-manifold homeomorphic to a K3 surface and equipped with a symplectic form ω; call (X,ω) a symplectic homotopy K3 surface. Define the exoticness r_X of X to be the largest integer r such that X admits r distinct Seiberg–Witten basic classes whose pairwise differences are nonzero (equivalently, a measure of how exotic the smooth structure is, taking values 0 ≤ r_X ≤ 3, with r_X = 3 being the maximally exotic case). A finite group G is said to act by symplectic symmetries on (X,ω) if it acts effectively on X by diffeomorphisms preserving ω. Call a finite group G "small" if there exists a symplectic homotopy K3 surface (X,ω) with r_X = 3 on which G acts faithfully by symplectic symmetries.

Determine, classify, or otherwise describe the collection of all such "small" finite groups: which finite groups can occur, what structural restrictions (order, abelian/solvable type, embedding into known K3 symplectic groups such as Mukai's list, etc.) must they satisfy, and is this collection strictly smaller than the class of finite groups acting symplectically on a generic (non-maximally-exotic) symplectic homotopy K3 surface?

Call a group $G$ an $R^*$-group if for every nonidentity element $g \in G$, no nonempty product of conjugates of $g$ in $G$ equals the identity; that is, for every $n \ge 1$, every $g \in G \setminus \{1\}$, and all $x_1, \dots, x_n \in G$, one has
$$x_1^{-1} g x_1 \cdot x_2^{-1} g x_2 \cdots x_n^{-1} g x_n \ne 1.$$
(Equivalently, $G$ is right-orderable iff such products never equal 1 for arbitrary choices; the $R^*$ condition isolates the property that no nontrivial element is a product of conjugates of itself.)

Question: If $\{G_i\}_{i \in I}$ is a family of $R^*$-groups, is the free product $\ast_{i \in I} G_i$ also an $R^*$-group?

Let $X$ be a closed smooth oriented $4$-manifold that does not admit any smooth (effective) action of the circle group $S^1$. It is conjectured (and known in special cases such as holomorphic or symplectic actions) that there exists a constant $C = C(X) > 0$ such that, for every prime $p > C$, the manifold $X$ admits no nontrivial smooth action of the cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}_p$ of order $p$.

Recall that for a closed oriented smooth $4$-manifold $X$ with $b_2^+(X) \ge 2$, the Seiberg–Witten invariant is a function
\[ \mathrm{SW}_X : \mathrm{Spin}^c(X) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Z}, \]
and a class $K \in H^2(X;\mathbb{Z})$ is called a Seiberg–Witten basic class if $K = c_1(\mathfrak{s})$ for some $\mathrm{Spin}^c$-structure $\mathfrak{s}$ on $X$ with $\mathrm{SW}_X(\mathfrak{s}) \ne 0$.

Question. For general smooth $\mathbb{Z}_p$-actions on $X$, can the constant $C(X)$ above be expressed in terms of invariants of the smooth $4$-manifold $X$? In particular, determine which invariants of the smooth structure of $X$ (such as the set of Seiberg–Witten basic classes, the values of the Seiberg–Witten invariants, or related refinements) enter into an admissible bound $C(X)$, and give an explicit formula or recipe describing the way in which these invariants control $C(X)$.

Setup. Consider a normal linear regression model with unknown variance:
  Y = X β + ε,    ε ~ N_n(0, σ² I_n),
where Y ∈ ℝ^n is the observed response, X is an n×k design matrix of full column rank k, β ∈ ℝ^k and σ² > 0 are unknown parameters. Let Ỹ ∈ ℝ^n be a future independent response satisfying Ỹ = X β + ε̃, ε̃ ~ N_n(0, σ² I_n), independently of Y.

Special design assumption (AS1). Assume m ≥ k ≥ 3 and that there exists a positive integer N and an m×k matrix X̃ of full column rank such that n = mN and
  X = 1_N ⊗ X̃,
so that X consists of N vertically stacked copies of X̃.

α-divergence loss. For −1 < α < 1, the α-divergence between a true predictive density p(ỹ | β, σ²) for Ỹ and a candidate predictive density q(ỹ) is
  D_α(p, q) = (4 / (1 − α²)) ∫ [ (1 − α)/2 · p(ỹ) + (1 + α)/2 · q(ỹ) − p(ỹ)^{(1−α)/2} q(ỹ)^{(1+α)/2} ] dỹ,
and the corresponding risk of a predictive density q(· | Y) is R_α(β, σ²; q) = E[ D_α(p(· | β, σ²), q(· | Y)) ].

Priors and predictive densities. Define
  π_{I,1}(β, σ²) = (σ²)^{−1}        (right-invariant prior),
  π_{S,1}(β, σ²) = (β' X̃' X̃ β)^{1 − k/2} · (σ²)^{−2}    (shrinkage prior).
Let q_{I,1}(ỹ | Y) and q_{S,1}(ỹ | Y) denote the (generalized) Bayes predictive densities of Ỹ given Y under the priors π_{I,1} and π_{S,1}, respectively. The predictive density q_{I,1} is the best invariant predictive density.

Question. Under assumption (AS1) and for every α with −1 < α < 1, does q_{S,1} dominate q_{I,1} under D_α-loss in the sense that
  R_α(β, σ²; q_{S,1}) ≤ R_α(β, σ²; q_{I,1})    for all (β, σ²) with β ≠ 0,
with strict inequality for at least one (β, σ²)?

Consider the normal linear regression model with unknown variance. Let Y = Xβ + σε, where X is a known n×k design matrix of full column rank, β ∈ ℝ^k is an unknown regression coefficient vector, σ² > 0 is an unknown variance, and ε ~ N_n(0, I_n). One wishes to predict a future observation Ỹ = X̃β + σε̃, where X̃ is a known ñ×k design matrix and ε̃ ~ N_ñ(0, I_ñ) is independent of ε, by means of a predictive density p̂(ỹ | y) for Ỹ given Y = y.

The performance of a predictive density p̂(· | y) is measured under the D₁ loss
  D₁(β, σ²; p̂(· | y)) = ∫ {p(ỹ | β, σ²) − p̂(ỹ | y)} log{p(ỹ | β, σ²)/p̂(ỹ | y)} dỹ,
the symmetrized Kullback–Leibler divergence between the true density p(ỹ | β, σ²) and the predictive density p̂(· | y); the risk is the expectation of this loss over Y. The best invariant predictive density is the predictive density that minimizes the risk among all predictive densities equivariant under the natural group of location–scale transformations associated with (β, σ²).

A predictive density is called Bayesian if it is the posterior predictive density obtained from some (possibly improper) prior π(β, σ²): namely p̂_π(ỹ | y) = ∫ p(ỹ | β, σ²) π(β, σ² | y) dβ dσ².

Question: In the low-dimensional regimes k = 1 and k = 2, does there exist a (generalized) Bayesian predictive density p̂_π that strictly dominates the best invariant predictive density under D₁ risk, uniformly in (β, σ²)?

Definitions and setup. A group $G$ is called an o-group (orderable group) if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is two-sided invariant, i.e. $a \le b$ implies $xay \le xby$ for all $x,y \in G$. Given a normal subgroup $H \trianglelefteq G$, a total order $\le$ on $H$ is called $G$-invariant if it is preserved under conjugation by every element of $G$: $a \le b$ implies $g^{-1}ag \le g^{-1}bg$ for every $g \in G$ and $a,b \in H$. A group is periodic if every element has finite order. representations.normalized:
Setup. Consider the normal linear regression prediction problem with unknown variance. Observe Y = Xβ + σε_Y ∈ R^n, where X is a known n×k design matrix of full column rank k, β ∈ R^k and σ^2 > 0 are unknown, and ε_Y ~ N_n(0, I_n). One wishes to predict a future independent observation Ỹ = X̃β + σε_{Ỹ} ∈ R^m, where X̃ is a known m×k design matrix of full column rank k and ε_{Ỹ} ~ N_m(0, I_m), independent of ε_Y.

A predictive density p̂(ỹ ; y) for Ỹ given Y is evaluated by the α-divergence loss
   D_α(p, p̂) = (4/(1−α^2)) ∫ [ 1 − (p̂(ỹ)/p(ỹ))^{(1−α)/2} ] p(ỹ) dỹ,    α ∈ (−1, 1),
with D_{−1} interpreted as the reverse Kullback–Leibler divergence (limit α → −1).

The model is invariant under the group of location–scale transformations (β, σ) ↦ (β + Xc/… , cσ) appropriate to this regression setting, and there is a unique best invariant predictive density p̂_I (the formal Bayes rule with respect to the right-invariant prior π(β, σ) ∝ 1/σ); p̂_I has constant frequentist risk under D_α.

Question. Suppose k ∈ {1, 2} and −1 ≤ α < 1.

(a) Is the best invariant predictive density p̂_I inadmissible under D_α loss; that is, does there exist a predictive density p̂ such that the risk R(β, σ; p̂) ≤ R(β, σ; p̂_I) for all (β, σ), with strict inequality for some (β, σ)?

(b) If so, exhibit a Bayesian predictive density (or a class of Bayesian predictive densities, e.g. arising from a hierarchical / shrinkage prior on β) that dominates p̂_I under D_α.

A compact hyperkähler manifold is a compact, simply connected Kähler manifold $X$ of complex dimension $2n$ admitting a nowhere-degenerate holomorphic symplectic 2-form $\sigma \in H^0(X, \Omega^2_X)$ such that $H^0(X,\Omega^2_X) = \mathbb{C}\cdot\sigma$. Two hyperkähler manifolds are considered equivalent if they are deformation equivalent (i.e., they appear as fibers of a smooth proper holomorphic family with connected base in the category of complex manifolds). The currently known deformation classes of compact hyperkähler manifolds are: the Hilbert scheme $\mathrm{Hilb}^n(S)$ of $n$ points on a K3 surface $S$ (for each $n\geq 1$); the generalized Kummer variety $K_n(A)$ associated to an abelian surface $A$ (for each $n\geq 1$); and the two sporadic examples $\mathrm{OG}_6$ and $\mathrm{OG}_{10}$ constructed by O'Grady in dimensions $6$ and $10$.

Problem: Construct a compact hyperkähler manifold that is not deformation equivalent to any of the four known families above, or prove that no other deformation classes exist.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The classification of compact hyperkähler manifolds remains a major open problem. As of 2026, only the four known deformation types are known: K3^[n], generalized Kummer K_n, OG6, and OG10. No new deformation classes have been constructed since O'Grady's examples (1999, 2003), and no classification result excluding new examples has been established. Recent surveys (e.g., by Debarre, Sawon, Beauville, Huybrechts) continue to list this as a central open question.

A hyperkähler manifold is a simply connected compact Kähler manifold $X$ such that $H^0(X, \Omega_X^2)$ is generated by a nowhere-degenerate holomorphic 2-form. The second integral cohomology $H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})$ carries a pure weight-2 Hodge structure together with the integral Beauville–Bogomolov–Fujiki quadratic form, making it a lattice; an isomorphism of abelian groups $\lambda: H^2(X,\mathbb{Z}) \to H^2(X',\mathbb{Z})$ is called a Hodge isometry if it preserves both the Hodge decomposition and the Beauville–Bogomolov–Fujiki form.

Let $X$ and $X'$ be hyperkähler manifolds of the same complex dimension and suppose there exists a Hodge isometry $\lambda: H^2(X,\mathbb{Z}) \to H^2(X',\mathbb{Z})$.

(a) Determine what geometric relationship between $X$ and $X'$ must follow from the existence of such a $\lambda$ (e.g., deformation equivalence, bimeromorphic equivalence, or isomorphism).

(b) Identify additional structural conditions one may impose on $\lambda$ (beyond preservation of the Hodge structure and the Beauville–Bogomolov–Fujiki form) that force $X$ and $X'$ to be biholomorphic, and determine whether such conditions suffice in general.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Verbitsky's global Torelli theorem (2009, published in Duke Math. J. 2013, with an erratum) establishes that for hyperkähler manifolds of the same deformation type, the existence of a Hodge isometry $H^2(X,\mathbb{Z}) \to H^2(X',\mathbb{Z})$ that is a parallel transport operator is equivalent to $X$ and $X'$ being bimeromorphic, and that requiring the isometry to send a Kähler class to a Kähler class yields an isomorphism. However, in general a Hodge isometry alone need not even imply that $X$ and $X'$ are deformation equivalent: counterexamples to a naive Hodge-theoretic Torelli statement are known beyond the K3$^{[n]}$ case (e.g., for some OG-type or non-prime-power $n-1$ cases). So the question is partially solved: definitive in the deformation-equivalent / parallel-transport setting, but open/negative in full generality.

Let X be a compact, simply connected, irreducible hyperkähler (holomorphic symplectic) manifold of complex dimension 2r, that is, X is Kähler, simply connected, and H^0(X, Ω_X^2) is generated by an everywhere non-degenerate holomorphic 2-form. There exists a canonical primitive integral quadratic form

   q : H^2(X, Z) → Z,

of signature (3, b_2(X) − 3), called the Beauville–Bogomolov form, together with a positive rational number f_X (the Fujiki constant) satisfying the Fujiki relation

   ∫_X α^{2r} = f_X · q(α)^r   for every α ∈ H^2(X, Z).

Both q and f_X depend only on the oriented topological type of X.

Address the following three questions.

(a) Is the integral quadratic form q necessarily even, i.e. does q(α) ∈ 2Z hold for every α ∈ H^2(X, Z)?

(b) More generally, classify which integral quadratic lattices of signature (3, b_2 − 3) can be realized as (H^2(X, Z), q) for some irreducible hyperkähler manifold X.

(c) Determine the set of possible values of the Fujiki constant f_X as X ranges over all irreducible hyperkähler manifolds.

Prove or disprove: for every positive integer $n$, the set of deformation equivalence classes of irreducible holomorphic symplectic manifolds of complex dimension $2n$ is finite.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The conjecture remains open in general. Only four deformation types are currently known in each even complex dimension ≥ 4 (the Hilbert schemes of K3 surfaces, generalized Kummer varieties, and the two O'Grady examples). Partial finiteness results are known under additional hypotheses: Huybrechts proved finiteness within each fixed Beauville–Bogomolov lattice type, and further finiteness theorems (due to Charles, Sawon, and others) hold for polarized families or under topological/lattice constraints, but unconditional finiteness in each dimension is unproven.

A partial order on $G$ is a reflexive, antisymmetric, transitive relation that is preserved on both sides by group multiplication. Call $G$ an $O^*$-group if every partial order on $G$ that is two-sided invariant under multiplication can be extended to a total order making $G$ a totally ordered group.

Working in the first-order language of group theory, let $\mathcal{O}$ denote the class of all orderable groups and let $\mathcal{O}^*$ denote the class of all $O^*$-groups. The axiomatic closure of $\mathcal{O}^*$ is the smallest elementary class (i.e., class axiomatizable by a set of first-order sentences) containing $\mathcal{O}^*$.

Question: Is $\mathcal{O}$ equal to the axiomatic closure of $\mathcal{O}^*$?

Guan's bounds (b_2 ∈ {3,...,8} ∪ {23}) remain the state of the art for irreducible compact hyperkähler fourfolds. No example with b_2 = 3, 4, 5, 6, or 7 is known, but no further values have been excluded in general; the only known examples have b_2 = 7 (generalized Kummer K_2) or b_2 = 23 (Hilbert square of K3, OG6 in dim 4 doesn't apply). An ordered group is a pair (G, ≤) where G is a group and ≤ is a total order on G that is bi-invariant: x ≤ y implies axb ≤ ayb for all a, b ∈ G. A group G is called orderable if there exists at least one such total order on G. A partial order on G is a partial order ≼ that is also bi-invariant under left and right multiplication. An orderable group G is called an O*-group if every bi-invariant partial order on G can be extended to a bi-invariant total order on G.

For an integer n ≥ 1, define the iterated commutator [x, n y] recursively by [x, 1 y] = [x, y] = x⁻¹y⁻¹xy and [x, k+1 y] = [[x, k y], y]. A group G is called n-Engel if [x, n y] = 1 for all x, y ∈ G, and G is called an Engel group if for every pair x, y ∈ G there exists n = n(x, y) ≥ 1 with [x, n y] = 1. An orderable group that is Engel is called an Engel orderable group.

Question: Is every Engel orderable group an O*-group?

A Lagrangian fibration on X is a surjective holomorphic map with connected fibers f: X → B onto a normal projective base B of dimension r, whose general fiber is a Lagrangian subvariety with respect to the holomorphic symplectic form; in this hyperkähler setting the base B is necessarily isomorphic to P^r whenever it is smooth.

Prove or disprove the following two statements:

(a) If L is a nontrivial nef line bundle on X with q(L) = 0, then there exists a Lagrangian fibration f: X → P^r and an integer k ≥ 1 such that L ≅ f^* O_{P^r}(k).

(b) There exists a hyperkähler manifold X' bimeromorphic to X admitting a Lagrangian fibration X' → P^r if and only if X carries a line bundle L ≇ O_X with q(L) = 0.

Definitions and setup. A group $G$ is called orderable if there exists a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is two-sided invariant, i.e. $a\le b$ implies $xay\le xby$ for all $a,b,x,y\in G$. An invariant (partial or total) order $\le$ on $G$ is called weakly abelian if for all $a,b\in G$ with $a>e$ (the identity), one has $b^{-1}ab < a^{2}$; equivalently, no positive element is conjugate to an element exceeding its square.

Define two classes of orderable groups:
- $O^{*}$: the class of orderable groups $G$ such that every $G$-invariant partial order on $G$ can be extended to a $G$-invariant total order on $G$.
- $W^{*}$: the class of orderable groups $G$ such that every $G$-invariant weakly abelian partial order on $G$ can be extended to a $G$-invariant weakly abelian total order on $G$.

Question. Does there exist a group in $W^{*}$ that does not belong to $O^{*}$? Equivalently, is the set difference $W^{*}\setminus O^{*}$ non-empty?

Let $S$ be a smooth complex projective K3 surface, polarized by an ample line bundle $H$ with $H^2 = 2g-2$ (so $S$ has genus $g$). For an integer $r \geq 2$, let $S^{[r]}$ denote the Hilbert scheme of length-$r$ zero-dimensional subschemes of $S$; this is a smooth projective irreducible holomorphic symplectic variety of dimension $2r$ deforming as a hyperkähler manifold of $K3^{[r]}$-type. The polarization $H$ on $S$ together with a choice of additional class induces polarizations on $S^{[r]}$; deforming the pair $(S^{[r]}, L)$ in the moduli space of polarized hyperkähler varieties of $K3^{[r]}$-type yields a $20$-dimensional family inside the $21$-dimensional deformation space, and a "locally complete projective family" is a family of polarized hyperkähler varieties of $K3^{[r]}$-type whose image in moduli has full dimension $21$.

(a) For each genus $g \in \{2, 3, 4, \dots\}$ and for some choice of polarization on $S^{[2]}$, give an explicit projective-geometric description of the general projective deformation of $S^{[2]}$, or at least exhibit new examples of locally complete projective families of polarized hyperkähler fourfolds of $K3^{[2]}$-type beyond the previously known cases (Beauville–Donagi cubic fourfolds, varieties of sums of powers, Debarre–Voisin, and Iliev–Ranestad).

(b) Solve the analogous problem for $S^{[r]}$ with $r \geq 3$: produce locally complete projective families of polarized hyperkähler $2r$-folds of $K3^{[r]}$-type and describe the general projective deformation.

The problem remains a guiding open question in hyperkähler geometry, but new examples and partial descriptions have appeared. Recent work on projective models for Hilbert squares of K3 surfaces (e.g., a 2025 preprint and earlier results on ⟨2⟩-polarized Hilbert squares of generic K3 surfaces, and Debarre–Voisin / Iliev–Ranestad type constructions) provides projective descriptions and additional locally complete families for $S^{[2]}$, particularly in low genus and for genera 7 and 8 via Mukai models. A (two-sided) order on a group $G$ is a total order $\le$ on $G$ that is invariant under both left and right multiplication: for all $a,b,c\in G$, if $a\le b$ then $ca\le cb$ and $ac\le bc$. Equivalently, an order is determined by its positive cone $P=\{g\in G:g>1\}$, which is a subset of $G$ satisfying $P\cdot P\subseteq P$, $P\sqcup\{1\}\sqcup P^{-1}=G$, and $gPg^{-1}\subseteq P$ for every $g\in G$. Two orders are considered distinct when their positive cones differ. Note that orders come in pairs: if $P$ is a positive cone, so is $P^{-1}$, so the number of orders on a nontrivially orderable group is always even.

Problem. For each positive integer $k$, exhibit an orderable group $G_k$ that admits exactly $2k$ orders.

Let $X$ be a projective hyperkähler manifold; that is, a simply connected smooth projective complex variety such that $H^0(X,\Omega_X^2)$ is spanned by a nowhere-degenerate holomorphic 2-form. Let $\mathrm{CH}(X)$ denote the Chow ring of $X$ with rational (or integral) coefficients, and let $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$ denote its Picard group. Let $c_i(X)\in\mathrm{CH}(X)$ denote the Chern classes of the tangent bundle of $X$, and let $\mathrm{cl}\colon \mathrm{CH}(X)\to H^*(X,\mathbb{Z})$ be the cycle class map.

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every choice of divisor classes $D_1,\dots,D_k\in\mathrm{Pic}(X)$ and every class $z\in\mathrm{CH}(X)$ that can be written as a polynomial in $D_1,\dots,D_k$ and in the Chern classes $c_1(X),\dots,c_{\dim X}(X)$, the implication
$$\mathrm{cl}(z)=0\ \text{in}\ H^*(X,\mathbb{Z})\quad\Longrightarrow\quad z=0\ \text{in}\ \mathrm{CH}(X)$$
holds. Equivalently, show that the subring of $\mathrm{CH}(X)$ generated by $\mathrm{Pic}(X)$ and the Chern classes of $X$ injects into the cohomology ring of $X$.

Let $X$ be a Fano complex manifold (i.e., a compact complex manifold whose anticanonical bundle $-K_X$ is ample) endowed with a holomorphic Poisson structure $\tau \in H^0(X, \wedge^2 T_X)$. The Poisson bivector induces a skew-symmetric bundle map $\tau^\sharp : \Omega^1_X \to T_X$, and at every point $x \in X$ the rank of $\tau$ at $x$ is defined as the rank of $\tau^\sharp(x)$ (which is necessarily an even integer). For each even integer $k \ge 0$, define
\[ X_k := \{ x \in X : \mathrm{rk}\, \tau(x) = k \}, \qquad X_{\le s} := \bigsqcup_{\substack{k \le s \\ k \text{ even}}} X_k. \]
Prove or disprove: for every even integer $s$ with $s < \dim_{\mathbb{C}} X$, the closed subset $X_{\le s}$ contains an irreducible component of dimension strictly greater than $s$.

The conjecture (Bondal's rank conjecture on degeneracy loci of holomorphic Poisson structures on Fano manifolds) appears to remain open in general. Polishchuk established a weaker bound, implying the conjecture for Poisson structures of generic rank ≤ 2 and for Fano varieties of dimension ≤ 3. Gualtieri–Pym and subsequent works (including a 2026 note by Aza) provide further partial evidence, including for Fano fourfolds, but the full conjecture is still cited as a conjecture in recent literature.

A compact complex manifold $Z$ of complex dimension $2n+1$ is called a holomorphic contact manifold if there exists a holomorphic line bundle $L \to Z$ together with a holomorphic 1-form $\theta \in H^0(Z, \Omega^1_Z \otimes L)$ such that $\theta \wedge (d\theta)^n$ is a nowhere-vanishing section of $K_Z \otimes L^{n+1}$; equivalently, the kernel $F \subset TZ$ of $\theta$ is a corank-one holomorphic distribution that is maximally non-integrable. A projective contact manifold is a holomorphic contact manifold whose underlying complex manifold is projective.

Two known families of projective contact manifolds are:

(a) For any compact complex manifold $M$, the projectivized cotangent bundle $\mathbb{P}(T^*M)$, equipped with its canonical contact structure coming from the Liouville form on $T^*M$.

(b) For any simple complex Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$, let $G$ be the adjoint group of $\mathfrak{g}$ acting on the projective space $\mathbb{P}(\mathfrak{g})$. Then this action admits a unique closed orbit $X_{\mathfrak{g}} \subset \mathbb{P}(\mathfrak{g})$ (every other orbit contains $X_{\mathfrak{g}}$ in its closure), and $X_{\mathfrak{g}}$ is a Fano manifold carrying a natural homogeneous holomorphic contact structure.

Question: Prove or disprove that every projective contact manifold is biholomorphic, as a contact manifold, to one of type (a) or type (b).

The classification (known as the LeBrun–Salamon conjecture) remains open in full generality as of 2024. Significant partial results exist: it is known in low dimensions (contact Fano manifolds of dimension ≤ 9 with a Kähler–Einstein metric, equivalently positive quaternion-Kähler manifolds of real dimension ≤ 16), for contact Fano manifolds with sufficiently large reductive automorphism group (rank ≥ max(2,(n-3)/2) on a (2n+1)-dimensional contact Fano), and in cases where the contact line bundle does not generate $H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})$.

A Riemannian manifold $(M^{4n}, g)$ of real dimension $4n \geq 4$ is called quaternion-Kähler if its holonomy group is contained in $\mathrm{Sp}(n)\cdot\mathrm{Sp}(1) \subset \mathrm{SO}(4n)$. Every such manifold is automatically Einstein, so its scalar curvature is constant. The known compact examples with positive scalar curvature are the so-called Wolf spaces, which are symmetric spaces of compact type associated to compact simple Lie groups (e.g. $\mathbb{HP}^n$, $\mathrm{Gr}_2(\mathbb{C}^{n+2})$, $\widetilde{\mathrm{Gr}}_4(\mathbb{R}^{n+4})$, and five exceptional examples), and these are homogeneous.

Prove or disprove: every compact quaternion-Kähler manifold of positive scalar curvature is homogeneous (equivalently, isometric to a Wolf space).

An ordered group is a group $G$ equipped with a total order $\leq$ that is invariant under both left and right multiplication. The group $G$ is called divisible if for every $g \in G$ and every positive integer $n$ there exists $x \in G$ with $x^n = g$. Suppose $G$ is an ordered group that admits an order-embedding into some divisible ordered group $D$ (i.e., there is an injective group homomorphism $G \hookrightarrow D$ that preserves the order). For such $G$, define the isolator $I(G)$ inside a divisible ordered extension $G^*$ to be the smallest subgroup of $G^*$ containing $G$ that is closed under taking $n$-th roots whenever those roots exist; an extension $G^*$ of $G$ is called a minimal divisible completion of $G$ if $G^*$ is itself a divisible ordered group containing $G$ as an ordered subgroup and $G^* = I(G)$. Let $\mathcal{D}_G$ denote the class of all minimal divisible completions of $G$ (up to isomorphism over $G$).

(i) Does there exist a group $K \in \mathcal{D}_G$ such that for every $H \in \mathcal{D}_G$ there is a group homomorphism $K \twoheadrightarrow H$ that is the identity on $G$?

(ii) Answer the same question under the additional assumption that $G$ is metabelian.

Let $P = A_1 A_2 \cdots A_n$ be a convex polygon with $n \ge 4$ sides that is circumscribed to a circle $\omega$ (i.e., every side of $P$ is tangent to $\omega$). For each side $A_i A_{i+1}$ let $T_i$ denote its point of tangency with $\omega$. Define the family of lines
$$\mathcal{D} = \{A_i A_j : 1 \le i < j \le n,\ j - i 
ot\equiv \pm 1 \pmod{n}\} \;\cup\; \{T_i T_j : 1 \le i < j \le n,\ j - i 
ot\equiv \pm 1 \pmod{n}\},$$
that is, the set consisting of all diagonals of $P$ together with all lines joining the tangency points of pairs of non-adjacent sides.

It is known that $\mathcal{D}$ always contains at least three concurrent lines. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on $P$ (and on $n$) under which more than three lines of $\mathcal{D}$ pass through a single point, and describe explicitly the families of circumscribed polygons for which such higher-order concurrences occur.

Let q be a prime power and let X be a smooth, projective, geometrically irreducible curve of genus g defined over the finite field F_{q^2}. The curve X is called F_{q^2}-maximal if its number of F_{q^2}-rational points attains the Hasse–Weil upper bound:
   #X(F_{q^2}) = q^2 + 1 + 2gq.
Fix an F_{q^2}-rational point P_0 of X and consider the complete linear series
   D = |(q+1)P_0|,
called the Frobenius linear series of X. Let r = dim D denote its projective dimension, and let
   (ε_0, ε_1, …, ε_r),  with 0 = ε_0 < ε_1 < … < ε_r,
be the generic (D, P)-order sequence at a general point P (the sequence of Hasse derivative orders associated to a morphism corresponding to D).

It is known that for an F_{q^2}-maximal curve one always has ε_r = q, and that for r = 3 the order sequence has the form (0, 1, ε_2, q) with ε_2 ∈ {2, 3, …}.

Question: Does there exist an F_{q^2}-maximal curve X (for some prime power q) whose Frobenius linear series D = |(q+1)P_0| has projective dimension r = 3 and whose generic D-order sequence is exactly
   (0, 1, 3, q),
i.e. with ε_2 = 3?

$$\frac{|PA|}{|PA_1|}\cdot\frac{|PB|}{|PB_1|}\cdot\frac{|PC|}{|PC_1|} \;=\; \frac{|AB|\cdot|BC|\cdot|CA|}{|A_1B|\cdot|B_1C|\cdot|C_1A|}.$$

Formulate and prove the analogous statement for an arbitrary (convex) polygon. More precisely: let $A_1A_2\cdots A_n$ be a convex polygon ($n\ge 3$) in the Euclidean plane, and for each vertex $A_i$ let $B_i$ be a point on a designated side (or diagonal) of the polygon such that the $n$ cevian-like segments $A_iB_i$ are all concurrent at a common point $P$. Determine an identity, generalizing the triangle identity above, that relates the ratios $|PA_i|/|PB_i|$ to ratios of side lengths (or diagonal lengths) of the polygon, and give a complete proof of this identity.

A two-way k-head finite automaton operates on an input string w bounded by left and right endmarkers. It has k read-only heads, each of which may move left, right, or stay in place at every step, subject to the endmarker boundaries. The machine is deterministic (a 2DFA(k)) if its transition function is single-valued, and nondeterministic (a 2NFA(k)) if it is multi-valued; in either case the machine accepts w iff there exists a computation starting in the initial state with all heads at the left endmarker that reaches an accepting configuration. Let L(2DFA(k)) and L(2NFA(k)) denote the classes of languages over a finite alphabet accepted by 2DFA(k) and 2NFA(k), respectively.

It is known that L(2DFA(k)) ⊆ L(2NFA(k)) for every k ≥ 1. The question is:

For every fixed integer k ≥ 2, is the inclusion L(2DFA(k)) ⊆ L(2NFA(k)) strict, i.e., does there exist a language accepted by some nondeterministic two-way k-head finite automaton that cannot be accepted by any deterministic two-way k-head finite automaton (with the same number of heads k)? Equivalently, determine whether L(2DFA(k)) ⊊ L(2NFA(k)) holds for each fixed k ≥ 2, or whether the two classes coincide for some such k.

A two-way one-head finite automaton over a finite alphabet Σ is a finite-state machine with a read-only input tape (containing the input bracketed by left and right end-markers) and a single read/write-free head that may move left, right, or stay. Formally, a 2NFA(1) is a tuple M=(Q,Σ,δ,q_0,F) where Q is a finite set of states, q_0∈Q is the initial state, F⊆Q is the set of accepting states, and δ:Q×(Σ∪{⊢,⊣}) → 2^{Q×{−1,0,+1}} is a nondeterministic transition relation (subject to the standard convention that the head never falls off the end-markers). The automaton accepts an input w∈Σ* iff some computation starting at the left end-marker in state q_0 eventually enters a state of F. A 2DFA(1) is the same model with δ a (partial) function into Q×{−1,0,+1}.

Define f:ℕ→ℕ by
  f(n) = min { m : every n-state 2NFA(1) over any finite alphabet has an equivalent 2DFA(1) with at most m states }.

Determine f(n) exactly, or, equivalently, determine matching upper and lower bounds on the number of states sufficient and necessary in the worst case to simulate an arbitrary n-state 2NFA(1) by an equivalent 2DFA(1). In particular, decide whether f(n) is bounded by a polynomial in n.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is the classical Sakoda–Sipser question (1978) on the cost of removing nondeterminism from two-way finite automata. The general problem remains open: it is unknown whether every n-state 2NFA can be converted to a 2DFA with polynomially many states, and no exact bound on f(n) is known. A one-way k-head finite automaton (1DFA(k)) is a finite automaton equipped with k read-only input heads, all of which scan an input word w (with end markers) from left to right; in each step the automaton reads the symbols under its heads, then, depending on its current state and the symbols read, updates its state and decides for each head independently whether to advance one cell or stay. Such an automaton is called data-independent (oblivious) if the movement of every head depends only on the length |w| of the input, and not on the actual symbols of w; equivalently, each head's trajectory (the sequence of positions it occupies over time) is a function of |w| alone. Let 1DiDFA(k) denote the class of languages accepted by deterministic one-way data-independent k-head finite automata.

Question: Is the head hierarchy for one-way data-independent finite automata strict at every level? That is, prove or disprove that for every integer k ≥ 1,
   1DiDFA(k) ⊊ 1DiDFA(k+1),
i.e., there exists a language recognizable by some one-way data-independent (k+1)-head finite automaton that is not recognizable by any one-way data-independent k-head finite automaton.

Let $X = \mathbb{R}^n$ and let $f : X \to [-\infty, +\infty]$ be a convex Legendre function in the sense of Bauschke–Borwein–Combettes; that is, $f$ is proper, lower semicontinuous, convex, essentially smooth, and essentially strictly convex. Set $U = \operatorname{int}\,\operatorname{dom} f$, which is a nonempty open convex set on which $f$ is differentiable. The Bregman distance induced by $f$ is
$$D(x,y) = f(x) - f(y) - \langle \nabla f(y), x - y\rangle, \qquad y \in U,\ x \in X,$$
with the convention $D(x,y) = +\infty$ when $f(x) = +\infty$. Recall that $f$ is called supercoercive if $\lim_{\|x\|\to\infty} f(x)/\|x\| = +\infty$.

Let $C$ be a nonempty closed subset of $U$. For $y \in U$ define the left Bregman nearest-point map
$$\overleftarrow{P}_C(y) = \{x \in C : D(x,y) = \inf_{z \in C} D(z,y)\}.$$
The set $C$ is called left $D$-Chebyshev if $\overleftarrow{P}_C(y)$ is a singleton for every $y \in U$.

It is known that if $f$ is supercoercive and $C \subseteq U$ is closed and left $D$-Chebyshev, then $C$ is convex.

Question: Is the supercoercivity hypothesis on $f$ essential? Equivalently, does there exist a convex Legendre function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ that is not supercoercive together with a nonempty closed left $D$-Chebyshev subset $C \subseteq U$ that fails to be convex? Or, can the implication "left $D$-Chebyshev $\Rightarrow$ convex" be proved without assuming supercoercivity?

\[ D_f = \{ p(S)f : p \in \mathbb{C}[Z] \}, \qquad H_f = \overline{D_f} \subseteq H, \qquad S_f = S\!\restriction_{D_f}, \]
viewed as a densely defined operator in the Hilbert space $H_f$ with domain $D_f$. Call $S_f$ the cyclic portion of $S$ at $f$.

Recall that a densely defined operator $T$ in a Hilbert space $K$ is called subnormal if there exist a Hilbert space $\mathcal{K} \supseteq K$ and a densely defined normal operator $N$ in $\mathcal{K}$ with $D(T) \subseteq D(N)$ and $Tg = Ng$ for every $g \in D(T)$.

Consider the following infinite-horizon optimal stopping problem (the Chow–Robbins game). A player repeatedly tosses a fair coin, generating an infinite sequence of independent Bernoulli(1/2) outcomes. At any finite stage, let h denote the number of heads and t the number of tails observed so far. The player may stop at any (a.s. finite) stopping time τ with respect to the natural filtration; if at the moment of stopping there have been h heads and t tails, the payoff is h/(h+t) (with the convention that the player must take at least one toss). The value function is

  V(h,t) = sup_{τ ≥ 0} E[(h + H_τ)/(h + t + τ)],

where H_τ is the number of heads in the next τ tosses. A state (h,t) is called a STOP state if h/(h+t) ≥ V(h,t), i.e. immediate stopping is optimal, and a CONTINUE state otherwise.

Problem: Determine, rigorously and explicitly, the optimal stopping rule for every state (h,t) with h,t ≥ 0 and h+t ≥ 1. Equivalently, give a complete and rigorous characterization of the set of STOP states. The principal difficulty is that for a given state (h,t) one must establish a rigorous non-trivial upper bound (strictly less than 1) for the finite-horizon values f_N(h,t) that holds uniformly in N, in order to certify that (h,t) is genuinely a STOP state rather than a CONTINUE state.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The Chow–Robbins game (1965) remains unsolved in full generality: no closed-form description of the complete optimal stopping rule is known. However, substantial progress has been made. Häggström and Wästlund (2013) introduced rigorous backward-induction bounds settling many states. Christensen and Fischer (Adv. Appl. Probab., 2022, "Exact solution to the Chow–Robbins game for almost all n, using a Catalan triangle") gave the exact optimal rule for all n up to roughly a third of a billion (all d from 2 to 15363). Asymptotic boundaries are known (≈ 1/2 + 0.41996.../√n). The general problem of certifying every STOP state remains open.

Let f: R^n -> (-infinity, +infinity] be a Legendre function in the sense of Rockafellar; that is, f is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, the interior U = int(dom f) is nonempty, f is essentially smooth (differentiable on U with ||grad f(x_k)|| -> infinity whenever x_k -> x in the boundary of U) and essentially strictly convex (strictly convex on every convex subset of dom(∂f)). Suppose further that f has full domain, i.e. dom f = U = R^n, and write grad f for its gradient.

For x, y in R^n, define the Bregman distance induced by f by
   D(x, y) = f(x) - f(y) - <grad f(y), x - y>.
A nonempty closed set C ⊂ R^n is called right D-Chebyshev if for every x in R^n there exists a unique point c ∈ C minimizing the map c ↦ D(x, c) over C.

Question: Does there exist a Legendre function f: R^n -> (-infinity, +infinity] with dom f = R^n such that f is not a quadratic function (i.e., f is not of the form x ↦ (1/2)<Ax,x> + <b,x> + c with A symmetric positive definite), yet every nonempty closed convex subset of R^n is right D-Chebyshev with respect to D? Equivalently, can the gradient grad f of such a Legendre function be nonaffine while still mapping every closed convex set to a closed convex set (i.e., be a nonaffine convexity-preserving homeomorphism of R^n)?

Consider an infinite sequence of independent fair coin tosses $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ with $P(X_i = +1) = P(X_i = -1) = 1/2$. Let $S_n = X_1 + \cdots + X_n$ (so $S_n$ equals the number of heads minus the number of tails after $n$ tosses). A player observes the tosses sequentially and may stop at any (possibly randomized) stopping time $\tau \geq 1$, receiving the payoff $S_\tau / \tau$. The Chow–Robbins game asks for stopping rules that maximize $E[S_\tau/\tau]$.

It is known that the optimal rule is determined by integers $\beta_n$ such that it is optimal to stop at time $n$ if and only if $S_n \geq \beta_n$. Concretely, define $V(n,k)$ to be the supremum, over all stopping times $\tau \geq n$ adapted to the natural filtration, of $E[S_\tau/\tau \mid S_n = k]$, and let $\beta_n$ be the smallest integer $k$ such that $k/n \geq V(n,k)$.

Determine whether $\beta_8 = 2$. Equivalently, after 8 tosses with 5 heads and 3 tails (so $S_8 = 2$ and the immediate payoff is $5/8 = 0.625$), decide whether stopping immediately is optimal in the infinite-horizon game, i.e., whether $V(8,2) = 5/8$.

Let $X = \mathbb{R}^n_{++} = \{x\in\mathbb{R}^n : x_i > 0 \text{ for all } i\}$ denote the strictly positive orthant. Let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be the negative (Boltzmann–Shannon) entropy
\[
f(x) = \sum_{i=1}^n \big(x_i \ln x_i - x_i\big),
\]
which is a Legendre function on $X$. The associated Bregman distance is
\[
D(x,y) = f(x) - f(y) - \langle \nabla f(y), x - y\rangle = \sum_{i=1}^n \Big(x_i \ln\tfrac{x_i}{y_i} - x_i + y_i\Big), \qquad x,y \in X.
\]
For a nonempty subset $C \subseteq X$ and a point $y \in X$, define the right Bregman projection of $y$ onto $C$ as the set
\[
\overrightarrow{P}_C(y) = \operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in C} D(c, y).
\]
The set $C$ is called right $D$-Chebyshev if $\overrightarrow{P}_C(y)$ is a singleton for every $y \in X$.

It is known that every closed convex subset of $X$ is right $D$-Chebyshev, and also that there exist nonconvex subsets of $X$ that are right $D$-Chebyshev.

Problem. Give an exact characterization of the class of right $D$-Chebyshev subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n_{++}$ for the negative-entropy Bregman distance $D$ defined above.

representations.normalized:
Consider the following Bayesian setup for confirming a universal generalization such as "every object in a given (potentially infinite) population has property B" (e.g., "all ravens are black"). Model the population as an i.i.d. sequence of Bernoulli trials with unknown parameter θ ∈ [0,1], where θ is the limiting fraction of objects having property B. Place a prior probability measure μ on [0,1] that is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure (for example, the uniform density, giving the Bayes–Laplace model). Let H denote the universal hypothesis "θ = 1," and let X_1, X_2, … ∈ {0,1} denote successive observations, with X_i = 1 meaning the i-th object has property B.

Because μ({1}) = 0 under any continuous prior, one has P(H) = 0, and consequently
P(H ∣ X_1 = 1, …, X_n = 1) = 0 for every finite n,
so no finite amount of confirmatory evidence ever raises the posterior probability of H above 0.

Problem: Devise a principled Bayesian (or Solomonoff-style algorithmic-probability) framework — specifying an admissible class of prior distributions, or a modified hypothesis space, or an alternative notion of confirmation — under which:
(i) the universal hypothesis H = "all objects have property B" receives strictly positive prior probability, or is otherwise rendered confirmable;
(ii) after observing n consecutive successes X_1 = … = X_n = 1, the posterior probability (or analogous degree of confirmation) of H is strictly positive and tends to 1 as n → ∞;
(iii) the framework remains coherent with standard Bayesian updating, is invariant under natural reparametrizations of θ, and reduces to reasonable predictive behavior in the non-universal regime.

Characterize such frameworks and justify their philosophical and mathematical adequacy as a resolution of the zero-prior obstruction to confirming universal hypotheses.

Solomonoff's universal prior assigns positive probability to every computable hypothesis, including universal generalizations, and Hutter (2007, "On Universal Prediction and Bayesian Confirmation") shows that within this algorithmic framework the zero-prior problem is avoided: the universal hypothesis receives positive prior weight and its posterior tends to 1 under all-positive evidence. Thus the issue is partially solved (resolved in the Solomonoff/algorithmic setting) but not closed in the broader foundational sense.

Setting. Let $X=\mathbb{R}^n$ and let $f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ be a Legendre function, i.e. a proper, lower semicontinuous, convex function that is both essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex. Set $U:=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom} f)$ and assume:
(i) $f$ is twice continuously differentiable on $U$;
(ii) the Hessian $\nabla^{2}f(y)$ is positive definite for every $y\in U$.

For a nonempty closed subset $C\subseteq U$, the left Bregman nearest-point map (associated with $f$) is
$$\overleftarrow{P}_{C}(y):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in C}\, D_{f}(c,y),\qquad y\in U,$$
where $D_{f}(c,y):=f(c)-f(y)-\langle\nabla f(y),c-y\rangle$ is the Bregman distance. The function $f$ is called supercoercive if $f(x)/\|x\|\to+\infty$ as $\|x\|\to\infty$.

Known fact. If, in addition to (i)–(ii), $f$ is supercoercive, then for every nonempty closed $C\subseteq U$ the map $\overleftarrow{P}_{C}$ is single-valued almost everywhere on $U$ and on a generic (i.e. residual) subset of $U$.

Question. Is the supercoercivity hypothesis essential for this conclusion? Equivalently: does there exist a Legendre function $f$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying (i) and (ii) but not supercoercive, together with a nonempty closed subset $C\subseteq U$, such that $\overleftarrow{P}_{C}$ fails to be single-valued either almost everywhere or generically on $U$? Or, on the contrary, can the supercoercivity assumption be removed while preserving the almost-everywhere and generic single-valuedness conclusion?

Hempel's "black raven" paradox in confirmation theory is the following puzzle. Consider a universe of objects, each of which may or may not have the property R (being a raven) and may or may not have the property B (being black). Consider the universal hypothesis

  H : ∀x (R(x) → B(x))   ("all ravens are black").

Confirmation theory adopts the following two principles:

(i) Nicod's criterion: a universal hypothesis of the form ∀x (P(x) → Q(x)) is confirmed (its credibility is increased) by the observation of any individual a satisfying both P(a) and Q(a).

(ii) Equivalence condition: if two hypotheses H₁ and H₂ are logically equivalent, then any observation that confirms H₁ also confirms H₂ (and vice versa).

Now H is logically equivalent to its contrapositive

  H' : ∀x (¬B(x) → ¬R(x))   ("all non-black things are non-ravens").

By Nicod's criterion applied to H', the observation of an object that is both non-black and a non-raven (e.g., a white sock) confirms H'. By the equivalence condition, this observation must therefore also confirm H. This conclusion — that observing a white sock confirms the hypothesis that all ravens are black — appears absurd.

Problem. Provide a precise, principled formal account of confirmation (specifying what relation "evidence E confirms hypothesis H" means, e.g., via a probabilistic, Bayesian, algorithmic-information-theoretic, or other rigorously defined framework) under which:
 (a) the intuitively correct judgments about Nicod's criterion and the equivalence condition are recovered or appropriately qualified, and
 (b) the apparent absurdity of "observing a white sock confirms that all ravens are black" is explained or dissolved (for instance by quantifying the degree of confirmation, by restricting the class of admissible observations, or by rejecting one of the principles in a justified way).

State the framework, prove that it is consistent, and demonstrate within it how the paradox is resolved.

Hempel's raven paradox is a classical problem in the philosophy of science and confirmation theory. Bayesian treatments (e.g., by Hosiasson-Lindenbaum, Good, Earman, Fitelson & Hawthorne) show that observing a non-black non-raven does confirm "all ravens are black" but only to a tiny degree, which is widely regarded as a partial resolution. However, no single universally accepted formal resolution exists, and the problem continues to be discussed as open in the universal-induction / algorithmic confirmation literature.

Fix a countable set of observable objects (emeralds) indexed by the time at which they are observed, and let each observation assign to an object a colour from a finite set including at least the colours green and blue. Consider the two hypotheses about the data stream:

  H1: every observed emerald is green;
  H2: every emerald observed strictly before the calendar year 2020 is green, and every emerald observed at or after 2020 is blue.

Assume the available empirical evidence consists only of observations made strictly before 2020, all of which report the colour green; thus H1 and H2 are logically consistent with, and assign equal likelihood to, the evidence.

A theory of inductive inference is here taken to be a procedure that, given any finite sequence of observations and any hypothesis expressible in a chosen formal language, assigns a real-valued degree of confirmation (for instance via a prior probability and Bayesian conditioning, or via a complexity-based prior such as the Solomonoff prior relative to a fixed universal description language).

Define alternative primitive predicates by

  grue(x) := (x is observed before 2020 and green) or (x is observed at or after 2020 and blue),
  bleen(x) := (x is observed before 2020 and blue) or (x is observed at or after 2020 and green).

In the language whose primitive colour predicates are {green, blue}, hypothesis H1 has a shorter syntactic description than H2; in the language whose primitive colour predicates are {grue, bleen}, the translated hypothesis H2 ("all emeralds are grue") has a shorter syntactic description than the translated H1.

Problem. Formulate a precise theory of induction—specifying the hypothesis language, the prior or complexity measure, and the confirmation rule—that, given only pre-2020 green observations, assigns strictly higher posterior confirmation (or strictly lower description-length-based penalty) to H1 than to H2, and which does so in a way that is invariant under the relabelling of primitive predicates exchanging {green, blue} with {grue, bleen}. Equivalently, exhibit a principled criterion, internal to the formal theory, that breaks the symmetry between the pairs (green, blue) and (grue, bleen) and justifies preferring H1 over H2.

Let $X$ be a Euclidean (or reflexive Banach) space and let $g\colon X\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper lower semicontinuous function. For a parameter $\lambda>0$, recall the proximal (Moreau) envelope and the farthest envelope defined with respect to the halved Euclidean norm $q(x):=\tfrac12\|x\|^2$:
$$P_\lambda g(x)=\inf_{y\in X}\bigl\{g(y)+\tfrac{1}{\lambda}q(x-y)\bigr\},\qquad Q_\mu g(x)=\sup_{y\in X}\bigl\{-g(y)+\tfrac{1}{\mu}q(x-y)\bigr\}.$$
A "Chebyshev function" is a function $g$ such that for every $x\in X$ the proximal problem $\arg\min_y\{g(y)+\tfrac{1}{\lambda}q(x-y)\}$ admits a unique minimizer (the Chebyshev point of $g$ at $x$); a "Klee function" is defined analogously through the farthest map $Q_\mu g$.

Now replace the Euclidean discrepancy $q(x-y)$ by a Bregman distance
$$D_f(x,y):=f(x)-f(y)-\langle \nabla f(y),\,x-y\rangle,$$
generated by a Legendre function $f\colon X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ (i.e., $f$ is a proper lower semicontinuous convex function that is essentially smooth and essentially strictly convex on its domain).

Problem. Develop the theory of Chebyshev functions and Klee functions for proper lower semicontinuous $g\colon X\to[-\infty,+\infty]$ when the halved Euclidean distance $q(\cdot-\cdot)$ is replaced by the Bregman distance $D_f$. Specifically:
(a) Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the Legendre generator $f$ under which the Bregman analogues of the proximal map and farthest map associated with $g$ are well-defined and single-valued for every $x\in X$.
(b) Provide an intrinsic characterization of the Chebyshev point of $g$ (the unique minimizer of $y\mapsto g(y)+D_f(x,y)$ or $y\mapsto g(y)+D_f(y,x)$) in this Bregman setting, in terms of $f$, $\nabla f$, and the subdifferential of $g$.

Subsequent work has addressed parts of this problem. Klee sets with respect to the right Bregman distance have been shown to be singletons and Chebyshev centers characterized under suitable Legendre/coercivity hypotheses; convexity of Bregman Chebyshev sets has been obtained when f is Legendre and 1-coercive via maximal monotonicity arguments. Extensions removing coercivity (suns, Chebyshev sets, Klee sets) appear in later publications. However, a complete intrinsic characterization of admissible generators f and of the Chebyshev point in full generality for the function (rather than set) case does not appear to be fully settled.

The general question of constructing proper, reparametrization-invariant "objective" priors on non-compact parameter spaces remains an active area of research. Jeffreys' prior is invariant but is well known to be improper on non-compact spaces such as $\mathbb{R}$, and reference priors and related constructions inherit similar issues. No widely accepted solution providing a single principled, proper, symmetry-invariant prior for arbitrary infinite/non-compact hypothesis classes is reported in the literature surveyed.

representations.normalized:
Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space (or, more generally, a real Banach space), and let $f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be a proper lower semicontinuous function. For $x\in X$ define the proximal mapping
$$P_f(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in X}\Big(f(y)+\tfrac{1}{2}\|x-y\|^2\Big),$$
and the farthest-point (or remotest) mapping
$$Q_f(x)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{y\in X}\Big(f(y)-\tfrac{1}{2}\|x-y\|^2\Big).$$
Call $f$ a Chebyshev function if $P_f(x)$ is a singleton for every $x\in X$, and a Klee function if $Q_f(x)$ is a singleton for every $x\in X$. In the finite-dimensional Euclidean setting $X=\mathbb{R}^n$, characterizations are known: e.g., $f$ is a Klee function iff $f-\tfrac{1}{2}\|\cdot\|^2$ is, up to a constant, the Fenchel conjugate of a strictly convex function on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with full domain (and analogous results hold for Chebyshev functions and for Chebyshev points/centers).

Problem. Establish analogues, in an arbitrary real Hilbert space and in general real Banach spaces, of the finite-dimensional results on Chebyshev and Klee functions, namely:
(a) characterize when a proper lower semicontinuous function $f$ is a Chebyshev function (single-valuedness of $P_f$ everywhere) and when it is a Klee function (single-valuedness of $Q_f$ everywhere);
(b) determine in what generality such functions must be convex (resp. concave-like) — extending the classical Chebyshev-set convexity question to the function setting;
(c) extend the Chebyshev-point / Chebyshev-center theory for functions to these infinite-dimensional settings.
