Consider classical electrodynamics in Minkowski spacetime, where the source-free Maxwell equations are time-reversal invariant and the inhomogeneous Maxwell equations admit two equally valid Green's-function solutions: the retarded field $F^{\mathrm{ret}}$ (built from past sources) and the advanced field $F^{\mathrm{adv}}$ (built from future absorbers). Empirically, radiation in our universe is described by retarded fields: charges produce outgoing waves and shadows lie on the past-light-cone side of opaque bodies, while the time-reversed scenario — coherent incoming high-frequency radiation correlated so as to converge on emitters — does not occur.

A standard partial explanation invokes absorbers (including the matter content of the early universe) together with thermalization: an absorber in a low-entropy state with many available microstates effectively damps outgoing radiation and breaks the symmetry between $F^{\mathrm{ret}}$ and $F^{\mathrm{adv}}$. However, every individual absorber, whether on Earth, in stars, or in the cosmological plasma, absorbs in the same temporal direction.

Provide a derivation, within a precisely formulated dynamical and statistical-mechanical framework (e.g., a coupled field-plus-matter Hamiltonian system with an explicit choice of initial/final macroscopic constraints), of the following:

1. State sufficient conditions on initial data, boundary conditions, or constraints on phase-space measures under which all absorbers in the universe absorb in a single common temporal direction, rather than some absorbing toward the future and others toward the past, or all absorbing toward the past with advanced field correlations.

2. Determine whether this universal alignment of absorption directions can be deduced from a low-entropy past condition (a Past Hypothesis) on the joint matter+radiation state alone, or whether an independent posited absence of advanced correlations is required.

3. Quantify, in a suitable measure on initial conditions, the relative likelihood of (a) configurations with universal retarded absorption, (b) configurations with universal advanced absorption, and (c) mixed configurations, and reconcile this with the claim that absence of advanced correlations is generic while a special low-entropy past condition is not.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question is known to be independent of ZFC. Koszmider constructed (consistently with ZFC) a non-separable Banach space of the form C(K) with no uncountable semibiorthogonal sequence, hence with no support set, giving a consistent negative answer. Conversely, under various set-theoretic assumptions (e.g., consistent statements forcing every non-separable Banach space to have an uncountable biorthogonal system), every non-separable Banach space admits a support set. Consider a classical Hamiltonian system with phase space $\Gamma$, Liouville measure $\mu$, and Hamiltonian flow $\phi_t:\Gamma	o\Gamma$ preserving $\mu$. A coarse-graining (Zwanzig projection) is specified by a partition $\mathcal{P}=\{C_\alpha\}$ of $\Gamma$ into measurable cells, or equivalently by a projection $P_{\mathcal{P}}$ on $L^1(\Gamma,\mu)$ that averages a probability density $ho$ over each cell. The associated Boltzmann/coarse-grained entropy of a state $ho$ is
$$S_{\mathcal{P}}(ho)\;=\;-\!\int_\Gamma (P_{\mathcal{P}}ho)\,\log(P_{\mathcal{P}}ho)\,d\mu,$$
and for a microstate $x\in\Gamma$ one sets $S_{\mathcal{P}}(x)=\log\mu(C_{\alpha(x)})$ where $C_{\alpha(x)}$ is the cell containing $x$.

Different choices of $\mathcal{P}$ (different "relevance concepts") yield different entropy functions, and a state that is low-entropy with respect to one projection can be high-entropy with respect to another. Suppose the universe is modeled by such a system and that at an initial time $t_0$ its microstate $x_0$ (or initial density $ho_0$) gives rise to a thermodynamic arrow of time, in the sense that for a broad class of physically natural projections $\mathcal{P}$ the function $t\mapsto S_{\mathcal{P}}(\phi_t x_0)$ is nondecreasing on $[t_0,\infty)$.

Problem. Identify a projection-independent property $\mathcal{L}(x_0)$ of the initial microstate (or initial density) such that:
(i) $\mathcal{L}$ is defined intrinsically from $(\Gamma,\mu,\phi_t)$ without reference to any particular partition $\mathcal{P}$;
(ii) whenever $\mathcal{L}(x_0)$ holds, $S_{\mathcal{P}}(\phi_t x_0)$ is nondecreasing for every projection $\mathcal{P}$ in a specified broad class;
(iii) conversely, if a thermodynamic arrow of time exists at $x_0$ with respect to that class of projections, then $\mathcal{L}(x_0)$ holds.

In other words, give a precise, coarse-graining-invariant characterization of "low-entropy initial condition" that underwrites temporal asymmetry, or prove that no such projection-independent characterization exists.

In general relativistic cosmology, the thermodynamic arrow of time is widely attributed to a very low-entropy initial state of the universe. One proposal identifies this initial low-entropy condition with the spatial homogeneity of the early universe; a sharper formulation, due to Penrose, postulates that the Weyl curvature tensor vanishes on all past (initial) singularities, while no analogous restriction is imposed on future singularities.

(a) Determine whether the appropriate "special" low-entropy condition characterizing the early universe is best formulated as (i) primordial spatial homogeneity, (ii) Penrose's vanishing-Weyl-tensor condition on all past singularities, or (iii) some closely related geometric/statistical condition, and give a precise mathematical statement of the chosen condition together with a justification that it captures the required low-entropy property.

(b) In the analogy with electromagnetism, the use of purely retarded radiation (excluding incoming free fields) can be derived from the presence of a sufficient distribution of absorbing matter (the Sommerfeld/Wheeler–Feynman absorber argument). Decide whether the Weyl curvature condition in (a) admits an analogous derivation from a dynamical mechanism (e.g.\ from properties of matter fields in general relativity), or whether instead it must be imposed as an independent law-like postulate. In the latter case, show that this postulate is necessary and sufficient to establish the causal asymmetry of the universe in the sense of excluding initial correlations that would be relevant to the future evolution.

Let $X$ be a (real or complex) Banach space. The density of $X$ is the smallest cardinality of a norm-dense subset of $X$. A sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ of nonzero vectors in $X$ is called an unconditional basic sequence if it is a Schauder basis of its closed linear span $\overline{\mathrm{span}}\{x_n:n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ and, in addition, there exists a constant $C\geq 1$ such that for every finitely supported sequence of scalars $(a_n)$ and every choice of signs $\varepsilon_n\in\{-1,+1\}$,
$$\Big\|\sum_n \varepsilon_n a_n x_n\Big\|\leq C\,\Big\|\sum_n a_n x_n\Big\|.$$
Let $\mathfrak{c}=2^{\aleph_0}$ denote the cardinality of the continuum.

(a) Determine whether every Banach space $X$ whose density is strictly greater than $\mathfrak{c}$ contains an infinite unconditional basic sequence.

(b) If the answer to (a) is negative in general, determine whether the conclusion holds under the additional assumption that $X$ is reflexive.

Let $p$ be a prime number. Recall that a central simple algebra $A$ over a field $F$ is called a division algebra if every nonzero element of $A$ is invertible, and that the degree of $A$ is $\sqrt{\dim_F A}$. Such an algebra $A$ of degree $p$ is called cyclic if it contains a maximal subfield $K \supset F$ with $[K:F]=p$ such that $K/F$ is a cyclic Galois extension; equivalently, $A \cong (K/F,\sigma,a)$ for some generator $\sigma$ of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ and some $a \in F^\times$. By a classical theorem of Wedderburn, every division algebra of degree $2$ or $3$ over any field is cyclic.

Problem: For each prime $p \geq 5$, exhibit a field $F$ together with an explicit central division algebra $D$ over $F$ of degree $p$ such that $D$ is not cyclic, i.e., $D$ contains no maximal subfield that is a cyclic Galois extension of $F$ of degree $p$.

For primes $p=2,3$ all degree-$p$ division algebras are cyclic (Wedderburn). For primes $p\ge 5$ the question of constructing a non-cyclic division algebra of degree $p$ has long been a central open problem. A 2020 preprint by E. Matzri (arXiv:2009.05772, "Non cyclic division algebras of prime degree") claims to produce examples of non-cyclic division algebras of prime degree as primary components of generic crossed products. Background and setup. In a Lorentzian 4-manifold (M,g) modelling a spacetime in a quantum-gravitational regime, let C_{abcd} denote the Weyl conformal curvature tensor of g. A "Weyl curvature condition" at a spacelike singularity Σ ⊂ ∂M is the requirement that, in a suitable limit toward Σ, an appropriate scalar invariant of the Weyl tensor (e.g. C_{abcd}C^{abcd} relative to the Ricci scalar squared, or a similar measure of Weyl anisotropy) vanishes, so that Σ is conformally regular. The classical Weyl curvature hypothesis imposes this only on initial (past) spacelike singularities, thereby providing a low-entropy past boundary condition while permitting generic high-Weyl future singularities inside black holes.

Consider instead the time-symmetric Weyl curvature condition: require that C_{abcd} satisfies the same vanishing/regularity condition on every spacelike singularity of M, both past and future, on the grounds that in quantum gravity past and future singularities cannot be sharply distinguished and that the interior of a black hole is causally inaccessible to external observers.

Problems.
(a) Determine whether the time-symmetric Weyl curvature condition is mathematically consistent with the known classical and semiclassical observational constraints on cosmological and astrophysical spacetimes (in particular, with the existence of the observed CMB low-entropy initial state and with the exterior geometry of astrophysical black holes).

(b) Determine whether imposing this time-symmetric condition forces, at the level of the allowed quantum-gravitational spacetimes, the absence of genuine event horizons and trapped black-hole interiors — i.e. whether all apparent black-hole-like regions must be replaced by horizonless, information-preserving configurations.

(c) Decide whether such a condition provides a consistent statistical-mechanical account of black-hole entropy (e.g. reproducing the Bekenstein–Hawking area law as a coarse-grained entropy) while avoiding any genuine information-loss paradox in the global evolution.

State and prove (or disprove) the precise theorems answering (a), (b), and (c) within a chosen rigorous framework for semiclassical or quantum gravity.

Consider instead the time-symmetric Weyl curvature condition: require that C_{abcd} satisfies the same vanishing/regularity condition on every spacelike singularity of M, both past and future, on the grounds that in quantum gravity past and future singularities cannot be sharply distinguished and that the interior of a black hole is causally inaccessible to external observers.

Problems.
(a) Determine whether the time-symmetric Weyl curvature condition is mathematically consistent with the known classical and semiclassical observational constraints on cosmological and astrophysical spacetimes (in particular, with the existence of the observed CMB low-entropy initial state and with the exterior geometry of astrophysical black holes).

(b) Determine whether imposing this time-symmetric condition forces, at the level of the allowed quantum-gravitational spacetimes, the absence of genuine event horizons and trapped black-hole interiors — i.e. whether all apparent black-hole-like regions must be replaced by horizonless, information-preserving configurations.

(c) Decide whether such a condition provides a consistent statistical-mechanical account of black-hole entropy (e.g. reproducing the Bekenstein–Hawking area law as a coarse-grained entropy) while avoiding any genuine information-loss paradox in the global evolution.

State and prove (or disprove) the precise theorems answering (a), (b), and (c) within a chosen rigorous framework for semiclassical or quantum gravity.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question concerns a foundational proposal in quantum gravity: whether a time-symmetric Weyl curvature condition on all spacelike singularities is consistent and whether it eliminates horizons and information loss. No definitive resolution exists; the black-hole information paradox and the status of the Weyl curvature hypothesis remain active open problems, with ongoing work on island formulas, firewalls, and Penrose's CCC, but no rigorous theorem settling the time-symmetric variant proposed here.

Let $F$ be a field and let $D$ be a finite-dimensional central division algebra over $F$. Recall that $D$ represents a class $[D]$ in the Brauer group $\mathrm{Br}(F)$, and the period (or exponent) of $D$ is the order of $[D]$ in $\mathrm{Br}(F)$. The algebra $D$ is called a crossed product if it contains a maximal subfield $K \subset D$ such that $K/F$ is a Galois extension; equivalently, $D$ arises from the standard crossed-product construction associated with some finite Galois extension $K/F$ and a 2-cocycle in $H^2(\mathrm{Gal}(K/F), K^\times)$.

Consider canonical quantum gravity in the Wheeler–DeWitt formulation. Let configuration space be superspace, the space of Riemannian 3-metrics h_{ab} on a spatial slice (together with non-gravitational matter fields φ), modulo spatial diffeomorphisms. A physical state is described by a wave functional Ψ[h_{ab}, φ] satisfying the Wheeler–DeWitt constraint

   H Ψ[h_{ab}, φ] = 0,

where H is the Hamiltonian constraint operator (a hyperbolic second-order functional differential operator on superspace whose kinetic term involves the DeWitt supermetric, which has indefinite signature with one negative direction associated with the local scale of h_{ab}). Because Ψ has no explicit dependence on any external parameter t, the equation contains no a priori notion of time evolution and no a priori arrow of time.

Problem. Formulate precise assumptions on (i) the structure of Ψ (for example, a WKB/semiclassical ansatz Ψ ≈ C[h] exp(i S[h]/ℏ) χ[h, φ] with respect to a suitable expansion parameter, such as an inverse power of the Planck mass), (ii) boundary conditions on Ψ in superspace (for instance, conditions imposed in the limit of vanishing three-volume), and (iii) the decomposition of degrees of freedom into "heavy/geometric" and "light/matter" sectors, under which one can:

(a) derive an effective Schrödinger-type equation iℏ ∂_τ χ = H_matter χ for the light sector, where τ is an intrinsic parameter constructed from the heavy variables (e.g. along integral curves of ∇S on superspace), so that τ plays the role of a physical, emergent time;

(b) identify a mechanism — for example, a low-entropy/simplicity condition on Ψ at the boundary corresponding to small three-volume together with decoherence between semiclassical branches — that singles out a preferred direction along τ, thereby producing an arrow of time correlated with the growth of suitable entropy functionals.

State explicitly the minimal set of assumptions on H, on Ψ, and on the boundary behaviour in superspace, and exhibit the construction of τ and of the asymmetry of correlations along τ that yields both an effective physical time and its arrow from a fundamentally timeless equation HΨ = 0.

Consider canonical quantum gravity coupled to matter, in which physical states $|\Psi\rangle$ are annihilated by the Hamiltonian constraint, yielding the timeless Wheeler–DeWitt equation
$$\hat{\mathcal{H}}\,\Psi[h_{ij},\phi] = 0,$$
where $h_{ij}$ denotes a spatial 3-metric on a closed 3-manifold and $\phi$ collectively denotes matter fields. In a semiclassical (WKB) regime far from a putative initial singularity, one expands
$$\Psi[h,\phi] \approx \sum_{\alpha} A_{\alpha}[h]\, e^{i S_{\alpha}[h]/\hbar}\, \chi_{\alpha}[h,\phi],$$
where each phase $S_\alpha$ satisfies the gravitational Hamilton–Jacobi equation, defining a congruence of quasi-classical 4-geometries, and the matter wave functional $\chi_\alpha[h,\phi]$ obeys, to leading order in $\hbar$, an effective Schrödinger equation
$$i\hbar\, \nabla S_\alpha \cdot \delta_{h}\chi_\alpha = \hat{H}_{\text{matter}}[h,\phi]\,\chi_\alpha$$
along the integral curves of $\nabla S_\alpha$. Each $\chi_\alpha$ is a "partial Schrödinger wave" associated with one branch of the global superposition.

Problem: Determine whether the intrinsic global dynamics encoded by the Wheeler–DeWitt equation, together with any natural boundary condition on $\Psi$ at small 3-geometries (the "big-bang" boundary of superspace), uniquely fixes the initial data $\chi_\alpha[h_0,\phi]$ for every partial Schrödinger wave $\chi_\alpha$ on a hypersurface of constant $S_\alpha$ in the WKB region. Equivalently, give a derivation that selects, from the timeless quantum state $\Psi$, a canonical assignment of initial conditions for each branch-dependent matter wave $\chi_\alpha$, or prove that no such derivation exists within the framework, so that additional postulates beyond the Wheeler–DeWitt dynamics are required.

Let $F$ be a field. The cohomological dimension of $F$, denoted $\mathrm{cd}(F)$, is the smallest non-negative integer $n$ (or $\infty$) such that $H^i(\mathrm{Gal}(F^{\mathrm{sep}}/F), M) = 0$ for every $i > n$ and every finite discrete torsion $\mathrm{Gal}(F^{\mathrm{sep}}/F)$-module $M$ whose order is invertible in $F$ (equivalently, the cohomological dimension of the absolute Galois group of $F$, in the sense of Serre, when $F$ is perfect; otherwise one uses the standard extension to the imperfect case).

A central simple $F$-algebra is a finite-dimensional associative $F$-algebra $A$ with center exactly $F$ and no two-sided ideals other than $0$ and $A$. By Wedderburn's theorem, $A \cong M_n(D)$ for a unique (up to isomorphism) central division $F$-algebra $D$, and $\dim_F A$ is a perfect square; write $\dim_F A = d^2$ and call $d$ the degree of $A$.

A central simple $F$-algebra $A$ of degree $d$ is called a crossed product if it contains a (commutative) maximal subfield $K \supseteq F$ with $[K:F] = d$ such that $K/F$ is a Galois extension. Equivalently, $A$ is Brauer equivalent to a cocycle algebra $(K/F, G, c)$ for some finite Galois extension $K/F$ with Galois group $G$ and some 2-cocycle $c \in Z^2(G, K^{\times})$, with $[K:F] = \deg(A)$.

Question: If $F$ is a field with $\mathrm{cd}(F) \le 2$, is every central simple $F$-algebra a crossed product?

representations.normalized:
In the Wheeler–DeWitt formulation of quantum cosmology for a homogeneous and isotropic universe with scale factor a, the wavefunction Ψ(a, φ) (with φ a matter field) is governed by a hyperbolic-type constraint equation that admits, in suitable regimes, a WKB form Ψ ≈ A(a, φ) exp(iS(a, φ)/ℏ) from which a notion of classical "WKB time" emerges via the gradient of S. The classical configuration variable a is taken to be nonnegative, but the Wheeler–DeWitt equation is naturally defined for all real a, and one may attempt to extend solutions and the dynamics through a = 0 to negative values of a.

Loop quantum cosmology refines this picture by replacing the differential operator in a by a difference operator on a discrete lattice in a (or in volume), and the resulting quantum dynamics is also formally defined for negative values of a.

Address the following questions in this setting:

(a) Determine whether negative values of the scale factor a admit a consistent physical interpretation after extending the (Wheeler–DeWitt or loop quantum cosmology) dynamics through a = 0, and in particular whether they can represent a "pre-big-bang" epoch.

(b) Establish whether, and in what precise sense, the WKB time function S can be continued through the locus a = 0 so as to provide a classical-time interpretation on both sides.

(c) In an oscillating-universe interpretation in which a < 0 is identified with a pre-big-bang phase, decide whether it is possible to have a low-entropy state at a = 0 preceded by an even lower-entropy state at a < 0 without forcing a reversal of the thermodynamic arrow of time, and reconcile this with the second law of thermodynamics.

Provide a precise mathematical and physical resolution, or demonstrate that no consistent extension is possible.

Let $F$ be a field and let $n$ be a positive integer. The Brauer group $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is the group of equivalence classes of finite-dimensional central simple $F$-algebras under Brauer equivalence (where $A \sim B$ iff $M_r(A) \cong M_s(B)$ for some positive integers $r,s$), with multiplication induced by tensor product over $F$. Let ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F) := \{[A] \in \mathrm{Br}(F) : n\cdot[A] = 0\}$ denote the $n$-torsion subgroup. A central simple $F$-algebra $A$ of degree $m$ (so $\dim_F A = m^2$) is called cyclic if it contains a maximal subfield $K \subset A$ with $K/F$ a cyclic Galois extension of degree $m$; equivalently, $A$ is isomorphic to a cyclic algebra $(K/F,\sigma,a)$ for some generator $\sigma$ of $\mathrm{Gal}(K/F)$ and some $a \in F^\times$.

Question: Is ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F)$ generated, as an abelian group, by Brauer classes $[A]$ of cyclic $F$-algebras $A$ whose degree divides $n$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem is classical and goes back to Albert (1936). By the Merkurjev–Suslin theorem, when $n$ is invertible in $F$ and $F$ contains a primitive $n$-th root of unity, ${}_n\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is generated by classes of cyclic algebras of degree $n$. Without the root-of-unity hypothesis the question is open in general, although affirmative answers are known in various special cases (e.g. small torsion, certain types of fields). The general problem remains open.

$$\ell_F(p^r,p^s)=\sup_A \ell(A),$$

$$\ell_F(m,n) \;=\; \sup\Bigl\{\, r \;:\; \text{some class in } {}_m\mathrm{Br}(F) \text{ requires at least } r \text{ degree-}n \text{ cyclic symbol algebras to express}\,\Bigr\},$$
i.e.\ the smallest integer $\ell$ (or $\infty$) such that every element of ${}_m\mathrm{Br}(F)$ is Brauer-equivalent to a tensor product of at most $\ell$ cyclic algebras of degree $n$ over $F$. Equivalently, via the Merkurjev–Suslin theorem, $\ell_F(m,n)$ is the minimum number of symbols $(a,b)_{\zeta_n}$ needed to write any element of ${}_m\mathrm{Br}(F)$.

Assume $F$ has finite Brauer $p$-dimension, so that $\ell_F(p,p)$ and $\ell_F(p^2,p)$ are known to be finite. The problem asks: for every prime $p \geq 3$, prove a finite upper bound for the symbol lengths
$$\ell_F(p,\, p^2) \quad \text{and} \quad \ell_F(p^2,\, p^2),$$
i.e.\ bound the number of degree-$p^2$ cyclic symbol algebras needed to express an arbitrary element of $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ of exponent dividing $p$ (resp.\ dividing $p^2$), in terms of invariants of $F$.

For a field $F$, let $\mathrm{Br}(F)$ denote its Brauer group. For each central simple $F$-algebra $A$, let $\mathrm{ind}(A)$ and $\mathrm{per}(A)$ denote its index and period (exponent), respectively. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact connected Riemannian manifold, let $U\colon M\to\mathbb{R}$ be a smooth potential, and consider the natural mechanical Hamiltonian
$$H\colon T^*M\to\mathbb{R},\qquad H(q,p)=\tfrac{1}{2}\,g^{-1}_q(p,p)+U(q),$$
associated with the Riemannian kinetic energy and the potential $U$. For each discount parameter $\alpha>0$, consider the modified (discounted) Hamilton–Jacobi equation
$$H(du_\alpha(q))-\alpha\,u_\alpha(q)=c(\alpha),\qquad q\in M,$$
where $c(\alpha)\in\mathbb{R}$ is a constant determined by the requirement that a solution exists, and $u_\alpha\in C^2(M)$ is sought as a smooth solution (the graph of $du_\alpha$ being an invariant Lagrangian submanifold of $T^*M$ for the Hamiltonian flow of $H-\alpha u_\alpha$). At $\alpha=0$ the equation reduces to the standard stationary Hamilton–Jacobi equation
$$H(du(q))=c,\qquad q\in M,$$
which in general does not admit smooth solutions and must be interpreted in a generalized (viscosity / weak KAM) sense.

Describe the behaviour of the family $\{u_\alpha\}_{\alpha>0}$ as $\alpha\downarrow 0$: does $u_\alpha$ (after suitable normalization) converge uniformly on $M$ to a distinguished generalized solution $u_0$ of the critical equation $H(du)=c(0)$, and if so identify this limit (for instance via Peierls' barrier and Mather measures).

For a field F, let Br(F) denote its Brauer group. For a central simple F-algebra A, let per(A) denote the order of the class of A in Br(F) (the period) and let ind(A) denote the index of A (the degree of the unique central division F-algebra Brauer-equivalent to A). It is classical that per(A) divides ind(A) and that the two integers share the same prime factors. Define the Brauer dimension of F by

  Br.dim(F) := inf { n ∈ ℤ_{≥0} : ind(A) divides per(A)^n for every central simple F-algebra A and every finite extension of F },

with Br.dim(F) = ∞ if no such n exists.

Problem. Define a notion of "dimension" dim(F), assigning a value dim(F) ∈ ℤ_{≥0} ∪ {∞} to fields F belonging to some natural and useful class, such that the following two properties hold:

 (i) Br.dim(F) ≤ dim(F) − 1 for every F in the class;
 (ii) dim(F(t)) = dim(F) + 1 for every F in the class, where F(t) is the rational function field in one variable over F.

Equivalently, exhibit a field-theoretic dimension function on a substantial class of fields that simultaneously bounds the Brauer dimension from above (shifted by one) and increases by exactly one upon adjoining a transcendental.

Setup. Let $M$ be a smooth manifold (not assumed compact and possibly equipped with a smooth nonholonomic distribution $\mathcal{D}\subset TM$). Let $L:TM\to\mathbb{R}$ be a smooth Lagrangian (in the constrained case, defined on $\mathcal{D}$), and fix a discount factor $\alpha>0$. For each initial state $q\in M$, consider the infinite-horizon discounted action

$$J_q(\gamma)=\int_0^{\infty} e^{-\alpha t}\, L(\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))\,dt,$$

where $\gamma:[0,\infty)\to M$ is an absolutely continuous curve with $\gamma(0)=q$ (and, in the nonholonomic case, $\dot\gamma(t)\in\mathcal{D}_{\gamma(t)}$ for a.e. $t$).

The problem is said to be well-posed if for every $q\in M$ there exists a unique minimizer $\gamma_q^\ast$ of $J_q$ over admissible curves, and a smooth optimal synthesis is said to exist if there is a smooth dynamical system on $M$ (or on $\mathcal{D}$) whose positive semi-trajectories are exactly the minimizers $\gamma_q^\ast$.

Question. Develop verifiable sufficient conditions, and a corresponding theory of smooth optimal synthesis, for the well-posedness of such infinite-horizon discounted variational problems in the following two generalizations beyond the case of a compact Riemannian manifold with a natural mechanical Hamiltonian $H(q,p)=\tfrac12 |p|_q^2 + U(q)$:

(a) general smooth Lagrangians $L:TM\to\mathbb{R}$ on a (possibly non-compact) manifold $M$;

(b) variational problems subject to smooth nonholonomic constraints given by a bracket-generating distribution $\mathcal{D}\subset TM$.

In each setting, identify intrinsic curvature-type or convexity-type conditions on $(L,\alpha)$ (respectively on $(L,\mathcal{D},\alpha)$) ensuring that every initial state admits a unique minimizing trajectory and that the family of minimizers is generated by a smooth flow.

Subsequent work has addressed parts of this program. The compact Riemannian/mechanical case with curvature-negativity criteria was treated in the ESAIM:COCV and Steklov papers establishing smooth optimal synthesis. A 2024 preprint (arXiv:2403.16979) explicitly tackles infinite-horizon nonholonomic and discounted nonlinear control problems, providing a regularized optimal solution but showing that for the discounted case asymptotic stability of the terminal set is only local (not global), indicating only partial resolution. No fully general curvature-type theory of smooth synthesis for arbitrary Lagrangians and nonholonomic constraints appears to be established.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem is classical and remains open in general. Known partial results: $Z(F,n)$ is known to be rational for $n \le 4$ (Sylvester, Procesi, Formanek for $n=3,4$), and stably rational for $n=5$ and $n=7$ (Bessenrodt–Le Bruyn, Beneish, Saltman). For general $n$ (in particular composite $n$ with several prime factors), rationality, stable rationality, and even retract rationality are open. Saltman introduced retract rationality in this context and gave reductions, but no general answer is known.

Let $F$ be a base field and $n\ge 2$ an integer. For any field extension $K/F$, let $\mathrm{Alg}_n(K)$ denote the set of isomorphism classes of central simple $K$-algebras of degree $n$, and let $\mathrm{CPAlg}_n(K)\subseteq \mathrm{Alg}_n(K)$ denote the subset of those algebras that are crossed products (i.e., contain a maximal subfield Galois over $K$). For a finite group $G$ whose order divides $n$, let $\mathrm{Alg}_G(K)$ denote the set of isomorphism classes of central simple $K$-algebras of degree $n$ that are $G$-crossed products (i.e., contain a maximal subfield that is Galois over $K$ with Galois group isomorphic to $G$).

Recall that the essential dimension $\mathrm{ed}(\mathcal F)$ of a covariant functor $\mathcal F:\mathrm{Fields}/F \to \mathrm{Sets}$ is the smallest integer $d$ such that every element of $\mathcal F(K)$, for every $K/F$, descends to a subfield $K_0\subseteq K$ with $\mathrm{trdeg}_F(K_0)\le d$. The essential dimension $\mathrm{ed}(G)$ of an algebraic group $G$ is the essential dimension of the functor $K\mapsto H^1(K,G)$. In particular, $\mathrm{ed}(\mathrm{PGL}_n)=\mathrm{ed}(\mathrm{Alg}_n)$.

Address the following:

(1) Establish nontrivial upper and lower bounds for $\mathrm{ed}(\mathrm{CPAlg}_n)$ and for $\mathrm{ed}(\mathrm{Alg}_G)$ as functions of $n$ and $G$.

(2) Compute the difference $\mathrm{ed}(\mathrm{Alg}_G) - \mathrm{ed}(G)$ for finite groups $G$ of order dividing $n$.

(3) Suppose that $\mathrm{ed}(\mathrm{CPAlg}_n) = \mathrm{ed}(\mathrm{PGL}_n)$. Does it follow that every central simple algebra of degree $n$ over every field extension of $F$ is a crossed product?

Suppose $\sigma$ is anisotropic. For every finite field extension $L/F$ of odd degree, consider the involution $\sigma_L=\sigma\otimes\mathrm{id}_L$ on the central simple $L$-algebra $A\otimes_F L$.

Question: Must $\sigma_L$ be anisotropic for every such odd-degree extension $L/F$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The analogue of Springer's theorem for involutions on central simple algebras is known in several cases (e.g., for hermitian forms over quaternion algebras with orthogonal involutions, and Karpenko's result that an orthogonal involution becoming isotropic over every splitting field becomes isotropic over a finite odd-degree extension), and the Hermitian Springer Conjecture has been shown equivalent to a Generic Isotropicity Conjecture by Karpenko. Let $F$ be a field and let $G$ be an absolutely almost simple linear algebraic group defined over $F$ (i.e., $G$ is connected, semisimple, and $G_{\bar F}$ is almost simple, having no nontrivial connected normal subgroups). Recall that $G$ is called isotropic over $F$ if it contains a nontrivial $F$-split torus $\mathbb{G}_{m,F}\hookrightarrow G$, and anisotropic over $F$ otherwise.

Associated to $G$ there is a finite set of primes $S(G)$, the set of homological (torsion) primes of $G$, defined as the set of primes $p$ such that $H^*(G_{\bar F};\mathbb{Z})$ has $p$-torsion (equivalently, the set of torsion primes of the underlying root datum of $G$). For example, for type $A_n$ and $C_n$ one has $S(G)=\emptyset$ relative to torsion (only depending on isogeny class), for type $B_n$, $D_n$ ($n\ge 3$), and $G_2$ one has $2\in S(G)$, for type $F_4$, $E_6$, $E_7$ one has $S(G)\subseteq\{2,3\}$, and for type $E_8$ one has $S(G)\subseteq\{2,3,5\}$.

Question: Suppose $G$ is anisotropic over $F$. Must $G$ remain anisotropic over every finite field extension $K/F$ whose degree $[K:F]$ is not divisible by any prime in $S(G)$?

Let $X$ be a geometrically connected, smooth, projective surface over a finite field $k$, and let $\mathrm{Br}(X)$ denote its cohomological Brauer group $H^2_{\mathrm{ét}}(X,\mathbb{G}_m)$. Write $\mathrm{Br}(X)(2)$ for the 2-primary torsion subgroup of $\mathrm{Br}(X)$. The Artin–Tate construction (analogous to the Cassels–Tate pairing) provides a non-degenerate skew-symmetric pairing
$$ \mathrm{Br}(X)(2) \times \mathrm{Br}(X)(2) \longrightarrow \mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z} $$
on the (finite) non-divisible 2-primary part of $\mathrm{Br}(X)$. Determine whether this pairing is alternating; equivalently, whether $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ for every $x \in \mathrm{Br}(X)(2)$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The question (originally posed by Tate) was answered affirmatively by Tony Feng, who used Steenrod operations in étale cohomology to construct Stiefel–Whitney classes and prove an étale analogue of Wu's formula, showing the obstruction to the pairing being alternating on 2-torsion vanishes. The result also extends to higher Brauer groups.

Let $F$ be a field and let $A$ and $B$ be (associative, finite- or infinite-dimensional) division algebras over $F$, each containing $F$ in its center. Form the tensor product $A \otimes_F B$ as an $F$-algebra. It is known that $A \otimes_F B$ need not be a division algebra: for example, $\mathbb{H} \otimes_{\mathbb{R}} \mathbb{H} \cong M_4(\mathbb{R})$ has many zero divisors, while in other cases $A \otimes_F B$ remains a division algebra.

Provide a structural criterion, formulated in terms of intrinsic invariants of the pair $(A,B)$ over $F$ (such as their centers, splitting fields, maximal subfields, Brauer classes, or other algebraic data), that is necessary and sufficient for $A \otimes_F B$ to contain a nonzero zero divisor; equivalently, for $A \otimes_F B$ to fail to be a division algebra.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of giving a structural criterion for when the tensor product of two F-division algebras contains a zero divisor remains an active area of research. Partial results exist (e.g., Rowen–Saltman provided examples where A⊗_F B fails to be a domain even when F is algebraically closed in the centers, and there are splitting criteria for Brauer classes over products of curves), but no general structural criterion is known. The question, originating with M. Schacher and studied by Bergman and others, appears to still be open.

For a central simple $F$-algebra $A$ of degree $n$ (so $\dim_F A = n^2$), let $\operatorname{SB}(A)$ denote its Severi–Brauer variety, the $F$-form of $\mathbb{P}^{n-1}$ that parametrizes right ideals of $A$ of reduced dimension $1$. Let $F(A)$ denote the function field of $\operatorname{SB}(A)$; this is a generic splitting field of $A$.

Suppose $A$ and $B$ are central simple $F$-algebras of the same degree $n$ such that the classes $[A]$ and $[B]$ generate the same subgroup of $\operatorname{Br}(F)$, i.e. $\langle [A]\rangle = \langle [B]\rangle$ in $\operatorname{Br}(F)$.

Question: Must the generic splitting fields $F(A)$ and $F(B)$ be isomorphic as $F$-algebras? Equivalently, must the Severi–Brauer varieties $\operatorname{SB}(A)$ and $\operatorname{SB}(B)$ be birationally equivalent over $F$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The conjecture is known in several cases: it holds when the index is not a prime power, and Roquette settled it when the algebra splits over a solvable Galois extension. The general case, particularly for central simple algebras of prime power index, remains open. Recent work (e.g. preprints from 2025) continues to investigate the conjecture, indicating it is still an active open problem.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem (the "genus" problem for division algebras) is partially understood. For quaternion algebras over number fields, the Albert–Brauer–Hasse–Noether theorem implies the answer is yes. However, counterexamples exist for cubic division algebras over the rationals where division algebras share the same maximal subfields but generate different cyclic subgroups in the Brauer group, and recent work (e.g., on the genus of a division algebra and unramified Brauer group, and arXiv:2409.19321 on fields of infinite transcendence degree) continues to refine the picture. The general question for arbitrary fields and the indicated classes of extensions remains open.

The question of whether two quaternion division algebras over a finitely generated field sharing the same maximal subfields must be isomorphic appears to be still open in general. Garibaldi and Saltman, and subsequent surveys by Chernousov, Rapinchuk and Rapinchuk, established the implication for "transparent" fields including number fields, global fields, local fields, and certain function fields, and showed finiteness of the genus over finitely generated fields, but the full conjecture for arbitrary finitely generated fields (or fields finitely generated over an algebraically closed field) remains unresolved.

Define the "genus" gen'(D) to be the set of Brauer classes [D'] in the Brauer group Br(F) of finite-dimensional central division algebras D' over F such that, for every finite field extension L/F, L splits D if and only if L splits D'.

Prove that gen'(D) is finite; equivalently, show that there are only finitely many isomorphism classes of finite-dimensional central division algebras over F (other than D itself) that have exactly the same collection of finite splitting fields as D.

Define the "genus" gen'(D) to be the set of Brauer classes [D'] in the Brauer group Br(F) of finite-dimensional central division algebras D' over F such that, for every finite field extension L/F, L splits D if and only if L splits D'.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Krashen and McKinnie ("Distinguishing division algebras by finite splitting fields", manuscripta math. 2011) establish an inductive transfer result: if for a prime p ≠ char K every class in the p-torsion of Br(K) has finite genus gen', then the same holds over K(t). This yields finiteness in many cases (e.g., over fields finitely generated over algebraically closed fields, and partial results over global/local fields), but a complete proof of the finiteness statement for all division algebras over arbitrary fields finitely generated over a prime field appears to remain open in full generality. Subsequent work (e.g., Chernousov–Rapinchuk–Rapinchuk, and recent papers on the genus of division algebras) addresses related cases.

Let $F$ be a field. A finite-dimensional central simple $F$-algebra $A$ is called a $G$-crossed product (for a finite group $G$) if $A$ contains a maximal subfield $K$ that is a Galois extension of $F$ with Galois group isomorphic to $G$. A finite group $G$ is said to be $F$-admissible if there exists an $F$-central division algebra that is a $G$-crossed product.

Problem: Given a field $F$, determine all finite groups $G$ that are $F$-admissible.

Let $F$ be a field. A finite-dimensional central simple $F$-algebra $A$ is called a $G$-crossed product (for a finite group $G$) if $A$ contains a maximal subfield $K$ that is a Galois extension of $F$ with Galois group isomorphic to $G$. A finite group $G$ is said to be $F$-admissible if there exists an $F$-central division algebra that is a $G$-crossed product.

Problem: Given a field $F$, determine all finite groups $G$ that are $F$-admissible.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The general admissibility problem, posed by Schacher in 1968, remains open. Substantial progress has been made for specific fields: over $\mathbb{Q}$, Schacher proved that admissible groups must be Sylow-metacyclic and conjectured the converse; many partial results exist (e.g., for solvable groups by Sonn, and specific simple groups like $M_{11}$, $\mathrm{PSL}(2,q)$). Patching techniques by Harbater–Hartmann–Krashen have settled admissibility for function fields over complete discretely valued fields. However, no complete classification is known for $\mathbb{Q}$, general number fields, or arbitrary base fields, and recent work (e.g., on admissibility and field relations, 2024) continues to investigate the problem.

Recall that a finite-dimensional division algebra $D$ with center a field $K$ is called a crossed product for $G$ if $D$ contains a maximal subfield $L$ which is Galois over $K$ with $\mathrm{Gal}(L/K) \cong G$. The group $G$ is said to be $\mathbb{Q}$-admissible if there exists a finite-dimensional central division algebra $D$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ that is a crossed product for $G$ (equivalently, $G$ occurs as the Galois group of a maximal subfield of some central division algebra over $\mathbb{Q}$).

A finite group is called Sylow-metacyclic if every one of its Sylow subgroups is metacyclic (i.e., is an extension of a cyclic group by a cyclic group). It is known that every $\mathbb{Q}$-admissible finite group is necessarily Sylow-metacyclic.

Prove or disprove: every Sylow-metacyclic finite group is $\mathbb{Q}$-admissible.

Let $F$ be a field and let $A$ be a central simple algebra over $F$. Recall that $A \cong M_n(D)$ for a unique (up to isomorphism) central division $F$-algebra $D$, and the index of $A$ is $\mathrm{ind}(A) = \deg(D) = \sqrt{\dim_F D}$. The reduced Whitehead group of $A$ is $SK_1(A) = \ker(\mathrm{Nrd}\colon A^\times \to F^\times)/[A^\times, A^\times]$, where $\mathrm{Nrd}$ denotes the reduced norm. A positive integer $n$ is called square-free if it is not divisible by the square of any prime.

Prove or disprove: if $SK_1(A \otimes_F L) = 0$ for every field extension $L/F$, then $\mathrm{ind}(A)$ is square-free.

While partial empirical mass-loss laws for Population II giants have been derived from Spitzer-IRAC and globular-cluster surveys (Origlia et al. 2007, 2014; McDonald & Zijlstra 2015; Tailo et al. 2021), and a 2025 study reports that RGB mass loss decreases with metallicity, no fully physics-based description with established driving mechanisms, timescales, and metallicity dependence has been agreed upon. representations.normalized:
Let $(\Omega, T)$ be a discrete-time dynamical system (or let $(\Omega, \Phi^t)$ be a continuous-time flow) on a Riemannian manifold $\Omega$, and let $H \subset \Omega$ be a measurable subset (the "hole"). Define the survival probability after time $t$ by
$$P(t) = \mu_0\bigl(\{x \in \Omega : T^k(x) \notin H \text{ for all } 0 \le k \le t\}\bigr),$$
where $\mu_0$ is a chosen reference (e.g. Lebesgue) probability measure on $\Omega$, and define the escape rate
$$\gamma = -\lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{1}{t} \ln P(t),$$
when this limit exists. Assume there exists a natural conditionally invariant measure on the survivor set whose conditioning produces a $T$-invariant probability measure $\nu$ supported on the repeller $\Lambda = \bigcap_{k\ge 0} T^{-k}(\Omega \setminus H)$. Let $\lambda_1 \ge \lambda_2 \ge \cdots$ denote the Lyapunov exponents of $T$ with respect to $\nu$, and let $h_{\mathrm{KS}}(\nu)$ denote the Kolmogorov–Sinai entropy of $T$ with respect to $\nu$.

The escape-rate formula asserts
$$\gamma = \sum_{i:\,\lambda_i > 0} \lambda_i - h_{\mathrm{KS}}(\nu). \qquad (\ast)$$

Determine the most general classes of maps $T$ and flows $\Phi^t$ (in particular, beyond the uniformly hyperbolic setting, including non-uniformly hyperbolic maps, systems with intermittency or singularities, and continuous-time flows) for which the identity $(\ast)$ holds. Establish $(\ast)$ in these classes, or exhibit counterexamples delineating its range of validity.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The escape-rate formula is classically known for uniformly hyperbolic open systems (Eckmann–Ruelle, Young). Recent work has extended it to certain non-uniformly hyperbolic settings (e.g. intermittent maps, polynomial escape rates via maximal large deviations, 2024–2025), but no general result covers arbitrary non-uniformly hyperbolic maps, systems with singularities, or general flows. The question of how broadly $(\ast)$ holds remains an active research problem with only partial progress.

Consider stars evolving along the red giant branch (RGB) phase, during which they lose mass through stellar winds before reaching the horizontal branch. Two questions concerning RGB mass loss in stellar (in particular globular) clusters are posed:

(1) Is RGB mass loss a continuous process operating throughout the ascent of the giant branch, or is it instead an episodic phenomenon concentrated in discrete events?

(2) Is the integrated RGB mass loss (or its efficiency) significantly correlated with the metallicity [Fe/H] of the host cluster, and if so, what is the sign and strength of this correlation?

Provide a quantitative characterization of the temporal nature of RGB mass loss and of its dependence (or lack thereof) on cluster metallicity.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The questions remain active research topics. Recent studies (e.g., MNRAS 2015, 448, 502; MNRAS 2020, 498, 5745; arXiv:2505.12794) provide partial answers: mass loss appears not to be uniformly continuous along the RGB and shows differences between first- and second-generation populations, while the metallicity dependence is debated — some works find weak/no dependence, others find a positive correlation in metal-poor clusters and a negative one near solar metallicity. No consensus closed-form law is established.

Let $D \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a planar billiard table (a bounded domain with piecewise smooth boundary), and let the billiard flow be the geodesic flow inside $D$ with elastic reflections at $\partial D$, equipped with its natural invariant measure. Fix a measurable subset $H \subset \partial D$ (the "hole") of arclength size $h > 0$, and define the survival probability at time $t > 0$ by
$$P_h(t) \;=\; \mu\bigl\{\, x \in D : \text{the trajectory starting from } x \text{ has not yet crossed } H \text{ by time } t\,\bigr\},$$
where $\mu$ is the normalized phase-space measure (so $P_h(0) = 1$).

Characterize the classes of billiard tables $D$ and the joint asymptotic regimes of $t \to \infty$ and $h \to 0^+$ for which there exists a nontrivial limiting function $F : (0,\infty) \to (0,1]$ such that, along the chosen joint limit with the product $h\,t$ held fixed,
$$\lim_{\substack{t \to \infty,\; h \to 0^+ \\ h t = s}} P_h(t) \;=\; F(s)$$
for all $s > 0$. In particular, identify for which families of billiards (with a one-parameter family of holes of variable size $h$) the survival probability collapses, in such a joint scaling limit, to a function of the single combined variable $h t$.

Recent literature (e.g., works on open spherical billiards, lemon billiards, and entropy/scaling-law analyses up through 2025) provides numerical and partial analytic evidence that survival probabilities can be collapsed onto a universal curve through rescaling involving the hole size, particularly when the hole overlaps stability islands or in hyperbolic regimes. The treatment of the third dredge-up in TPAGB stars remains an open problem in stellar astrophysics. Recent reviews and modeling papers (e.g., Karakas & Lattanzio 2014; Cinquegrana & Karakas 2022; Marigo et al. 2013, 2020) continue to describe 3DU efficiency as one of the largest uncertainties in AGB modeling, still parametrized via overshooting or diffusive-mixing free parameters. No first-principles, parameter-free 1D treatment of convective boundary mixing across the composition/opacity discontinuity has been established.

Let P be a simple polygon in the Euclidean plane (in particular, P may be taken to be a triangle). A billiard trajectory in P is a piecewise linear path traced by a point particle moving with unit speed inside P, reflecting off the sides of P according to the law of equal angles (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection), with the convention that trajectories hitting a vertex are undefined. Such a trajectory is called periodic if, after finitely many reflections, the particle returns to its initial position with its initial direction.

Question: Does every polygonal billiard table P admit at least one periodic billiard trajectory? In particular, does every triangle admit at least one periodic billiard trajectory?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem remains open in general. Periodic orbits are known to exist in all rational polygons, all acute triangles, all right triangles (Holt 1993; Galperin–Stepin–Vorobets 1991), and all triangles whose angles are at most 100 degrees (Schwartz). The case of general obtuse triangles, and of general (irrational) polygons, is still unresolved.

Consider stellar evolution models of the thermally pulsing Asymptotic Giant Branch (TP-AGB) phase, in which a low- or intermediate-mass star develops a degenerate carbon–oxygen core surrounded by helium- and hydrogen-burning shells and an extended convective envelope. During this phase, repeated third dredge-up episodes can transport carbon to the surface, so that the surface number ratio C/O exceeds unity and the envelope becomes carbon-rich. The structure of such an envelope, and in particular its photospheric effective temperature T_eff, is highly sensitive to the low-temperature (T ≲ 5000 K) Rosseland mean opacity κ_R(ρ,T;X_i), which depends on the detailed molecular chemistry (CN, C2, HCN, C2H2, etc.) set by the elemental abundances X_i.

(a) Quantify how replacing a fixed-composition (scaled-solar) low-temperature opacity table with a table that consistently accounts for the variable C/O ratio in carbon-rich envelopes shifts the effective-temperature track T_eff(t) of TP-AGB models as a function of initial mass M (1 M_⊙ ≤ M ≤ 5 M_⊙) and metallicity Z (0.0001 ≤ Z ≤ 0.02). Specifically, determine the magnitude (in K) and sign of ΔT_eff at the moment C/O first exceeds 1, and along the subsequent C-star evolution, and characterize how ΔT_eff scales with Z and with the surface carbon excess (C − O).

(b) Propagate these revised T_eff tracks through a stellar population synthesis (SPS) framework that integrates isochrones weighted by an initial mass function and a star-formation history. Determine the resulting changes in: (i) the integrated bolometric and near-infrared (J, H, K) luminosities contributed by the TP-AGB component, (ii) broad-band colours such as V−K and J−K of single-burst stellar populations of ages 0.1–2 Gyr, and (iii) the inferred mass-to-light ratios at fixed observed colours.

Provide explicit quantitative predictions and identify the regimes (in age, metallicity, and mass) where the use of carbon-consistent opacities produces the largest deviations from models employing scaled-solar opacities.

Subsequent work (Marigo & Aringer 2009; Marigo et al. 2013, 2017 COLIBRI/PARSEC; Ventura et al.) implemented variable-composition low-temperature opacities in TP-AGB models and quantified that C-rich opacities lower T_eff by several hundred K (more strongly at higher Z, nearly vanishing for Z ≲ 0.0004), enhance mass loss, and shift integrated near-IR colours and TP-AGB contributions in SPS predictions. Hence the qualitative question is largely addressed, although precise quantitative SPS predictions continue to be refined and calibrated against resolved-population data.

Let $Q \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a polygonal billiard table, i.e., a compact connected planar domain whose boundary is a finite union of line segments. Consider the billiard flow on $Q$: a point particle moves with unit speed along straight lines and reflects elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) upon hitting the boundary, with trajectories that hit a vertex left undefined. Fix an open subset $H \subset Q$ (a "hole"); a trajectory is said to escape at time $t$ if it first enters $H$ at time $t$. Starting from the uniform (Liouville) probability measure on the unit tangent bundle of $Q \setminus H$, let
$$P(t) = \mathrm{Prob}\{\text{the trajectory has not entered } H \text{ by time } t\}$$
denote the survival probability. Let $\mathcal{N} \subset Q$ denote the set of points lying on periodic billiard orbits that never enter $H$ ("non-escaping periodic orbits").

Question: Is the asymptotic behavior of $P(t)$ as $t \to \infty$ entirely determined by arbitrarily small neighborhoods of $\mathcal{N}$? Equivalently, for every $\varepsilon > 0$, is the contribution to $P(t)$ from initial conditions whose orbits remain at distance $\geq \varepsilon$ from $\mathcal{N}$ asymptotically negligible compared with the full survival probability $P(t)$ as $t \to \infty$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is stated as an open problem in surveys on open billiards, and related sub-questions (e.g., whether every polygon admits a periodic orbit) remain unresolved. No subsequent work was found that establishes or refutes that the long-time asymptotics of P(t) in polygonal billiards is determined by neighborhoods of non-escaping periodic orbits; numerical evidence (e.g., C/t decay in irrational polygons with periodic orbits, finite-time vanishing in rational directional flows without them) is consistent with the conjecture but does not prove it.

Synthetic Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB) models are simplified, parametric prescriptions of the late evolutionary phase of low- and intermediate-mass stars (roughly 0.8–8 solar masses) in which key uncertain physical processes—third dredge-up efficiency, hot bottom burning, mass-loss rates, the treatment of convective boundaries, and nucleosynthetic yields—are encoded by a finite set of free parameters. These parameters are typically calibrated by tuning their values so that the resulting synthetic stellar populations reproduce selected observational constraints (for example, the carbon-star luminosity functions of the Magellanic Clouds, AGB lifetimes, or initial–final mass relations) for stellar populations of given metallicity, age, and mass distribution.

Assess the predictive power of such calibrated synthetic AGB models when they are applied outside the region of parameter space (in metallicity, initial mass, age, and environment) covered by the calibrating populations. Specifically:

(a) Quantify the extent to which observables predicted by a synthetic AGB model calibrated on one stellar population (e.g., Magellanic Cloud C-star luminosity functions) remain reliable when the model is extrapolated to populations with substantially different metallicities, ages, or mass ranges.

(b) Determine whether, given that synthetic models inherit the same unresolved physical uncertainties as full evolutionary AGB calculations and require multiple hand-tuned parameters, their extrapolations can be expected to be predictive in any rigorous sense, or whether they should be regarded as interpolating descriptions valid only within their calibration domain.

Consider a planar billiard whose boundary is a stadium-like curve, namely a smooth curve consisting of two parallel straight segments joined by two focusing (curved) arcs, so that the table contains a one-parameter family of "bouncing-ball" periodic orbits perpendicular to the parallel segments. These bouncing-ball orbits form a family of marginally unstable periodic orbits (MUPOs): orbits whose linearized Poincaré map has eigenvalue 1 with a nontrivial Jordan block, so that nearby trajectories drift away only polynomially in time.

A trajectory near such a family eventually leaves a tubular neighborhood of the MUPO family, wanders through the chaotic component of phase space, and is later "reinjected" back into the neighborhood of the MUPOs with some distribution of incoming angles and positions; this stochastic-like return mechanism is called the reinjection dynamics, and it depends on the curvature properties of the boundary near the endpoints of the bouncing-ball segments.

Problem. Provide a comprehensive characterization of the dynamical properties of the marginally unstable periodic orbits in stadium-like billiards — including, in particular, the long-time statistics of trajectories near the MUPO family, decay of correlations, the algebraic tail of the distribution of consecutive collisions in the bouncing-ball region, and escape-rate / survival-probability asymptotics when a hole is opened in the table — purely in terms of the reinjection dynamics (the distribution of return positions, angles, and times of trajectories that leave and later re-enter a neighborhood of the MUPO family). Specifically, identify which features of the reinjection mechanism (depending on the curvature of the boundary near the endpoints of the parallel segments) determine these dynamical and escape properties, and derive quantitative predictions for them from properties of the reinjection map alone.

In one-dimensional stellar evolution modeling, convective energy transport in the outer envelope of a star is commonly described by mixing-length theory (MLT), in which the characteristic length scale of convective elements is parametrized as ℓ = α_MLT · H_p, where H_p is the local pressure scale height and α_MLT > 0 is a free parameter. The standard practice is to fix α_MLT by "solar calibration": one chooses α_MLT so that a stellar model of one solar mass and chemical composition equal to that of the present Sun reproduces, at the solar age, the observed solar radius (and luminosity and effective temperature). The value obtained depends on the other input physics adopted in the code, in particular the equation of state, the low-temperature opacities, the surface boundary conditions (for instance gray Eddington atmosphere versus integration of a detailed atmosphere model), and the assumed initial helium and metal abundances.

Consider stars on the Red Giant Branch (RGB) — low-mass stars (≈ 0.7–1.0 solar masses) after central hydrogen exhaustion, ascending the giant branch with deep convective envelopes — across a range of metallicities [Fe/H] from roughly −2.3 to solar. For such stars, the predicted effective temperature T_eff at fixed luminosity along the RGB depends sensitively on α_MLT.

Question: Is it the case that, for every reasonable choice of input physics (equation of state, low-T opacities, outer boundary conditions, heavy-element mixture, treatment of atomic diffusion), the solar-calibrated α_MLT obtained with that same input physics, when used unchanged to compute RGB tracks of low-mass stars at all metallicities in the above range, yields RGB effective-temperature predictions consistent with empirical RGB T_eff scales derived from observations of Galactic globular clusters and field giants? Equivalently: does there exist an empirical RGB T_eff scale that all internally consistent, solar-calibrated stellar codes reproduce simultaneously, or must α_MLT on the RGB be recalibrated separately (and possibly metallicity-dependently) for at least some choices of input physics?

Recent literature indicates that the adequacy of a solar-calibrated α_MLT for RGB stars across metallicities remains unsettled. Let $Q \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a planar billiard table (a bounded domain with piecewise smooth boundary) whose associated billiard map $T$ on the phase space $M$ (unit tangent bundle restricted to the boundary, with the standard invariant measure $\mu$) has mixed phase space: $M$ contains both a positive-measure set of chaotic orbits and a positive-measure set of invariant elliptic islands surrounded by KAM tori. Open the billiard by designating a measurable subset $H \subset \partial Q$ (a "hole") through which trajectories escape, and define the survival probability up to time $n$ by
$$P(n) = \mu\{x \in M : T^k(x) \notin H \text{ for all } 0 \le k \le n\}.$$
It is known that, due to the sticky behavior of orbits near the boundaries of the elliptic islands, $P(n)$ generically decays as a power law $P(n) \sim C\, n^{-\alpha}$ as $n \to \infty$.

Question: Is there a universal exponent $\alpha > 0$ such that, for every "generic" open billiard with mixed phase space (independent of the geometry of $Q$ and the choice of hole $H$), the survival probability satisfies $P(n) \sim C\, n^{-\alpha}$ as $n \to \infty$? In particular, does the conjectured value $\alpha \approx 2.57$ for area-preserving maps with stickiness near elliptic islands extend to all such open billiards?

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ ($n \ge 2$) be a bounded domain with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$, and let $T>0$. Consider the initial-boundary value problem for an incompressible viscoelastic medium of Jeffreys' type with an objective (frame-indifferent) constitutive law:

(i) Momentum balance and incompressibility:
$$\partial_t v + (v\cdot\nabla)v - \mathrm{Div}\,\sigma = f, \qquad \mathrm{div}\,v = 0 \quad \text{in } \Omega\times(0,T),$$
where $v:\Omega\times(0,T)\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is the velocity field, $f$ is a given external body force, and $\sigma$ is the stress tensor of the form
$$\sigma = -p\,I + 2\mu_0\, E(v) + 2\mu_1\, \tau,$$
with pressure $p$, deformation-rate tensor $E(v) = \tfrac12(\nabla v + (\nabla v)^\top)$, and $\mu_0,\mu_1>0$.

(ii) Constitutive law of Jeffreys' type with an objective derivative: the extra-stress $\tau$ satisfies
$$\tau + \lambda\, \frac{\mathcal{D}\tau}{\mathcal{D}t} = E(v),$$
where $\lambda>0$ is a relaxation time and $\frac{\mathcal{D}}{\mathcal{D}t}$ denotes an objective tensor derivative of the form
$$\frac{\mathcal{D}\tau}{\mathcal{D}t} = \partial_t \tau + (v\cdot\nabla)\tau + \tau\, W(v) - W(v)\,\tau + a\,(\tau\, E(v) + E(v)\,\tau),$$
with vorticity tensor $W(v) = \tfrac12(\nabla v - (\nabla v)^\top)$ and parameter $a\in[-1,1]$.

(iii) Boundary and initial conditions: $v=0$ on $\partial\Omega\times(0,T)$, $v(\cdot,0)=v_0$ in $\Omega$, and $\tau(\cdot,0)=\tau_0$ in $\Omega$.

Question. Does this initial-boundary value problem admit a global strong solution $(v,\tau,p)$ on $\Omega\times(0,T)$ for every $T>0$, in every dimension $n\ge 2$, without imposing any smallness or structural restrictions on the coefficients $\mu_0,\mu_1,\lambda,a$, on the external force $f$, or on the initial data $(v_0,\tau_0)$?

Consider planar mushroom billiards: a billiard table consisting of a semicircular "cap" of radius $R$ joined to a rectangular "stem" of width $2r < 2R$, in which a point particle moves in straight lines and reflects elastically off the boundary. Such billiards have a sharply divided phase space, consisting of an integrable region (orbits confined to the cap that never enter the stem) and a chaotic region (orbits that visit the stem), separated by a clean regular–chaotic interface. Embedded in the chaotic component there can be families of marginally unstable periodic orbits (MUPOs), whose presence depends on Diophantine properties of $r/R$.

Now introduce a hole in the boundary or in phase space that lies in the chaotic component, and let $P(t)$ denote the survival probability that a trajectory, started from an initial condition distributed according to the Liouville measure restricted to the chaotic component, has not escaped through the hole by time $t$. It is known that $P(t)$ can decay subexponentially due to (i) stickiness produced by MUPOs and (ii) stickiness produced by the regular–chaotic boundary itself.

Problem. Characterise quantitatively the escape properties of the regular–chaotic boundary in mushroom billiards and in similar billiards with a sharply divided mixed phase space. In particular, determine the asymptotic behaviour of $P(t)$ as $t \to \infty$ that is induced solely by the regular–chaotic interface (independently of the MUPO contribution), identify the geometric and number-theoretic features of the billiard that govern this contribution, and describe how the interface and the MUPO families combine to produce the observed slow decay of $P(t)$.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded domain with smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$, $n \ge 2$, and let $T>0$. Consider the Jeffreys-type integro-differential system for an incompressible viscoelastic fluid: find a velocity field $v:[0,T]\times\Omega \to \mathbb{R}^n$ and a pressure $p:[0,T]\times\Omega \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfying
$$
\frac{\partial v}{\partial t} + (v\cdot\nabla) v \;-\; \mu_0 \Delta v \;-\; \int_0^t e^{-(t-s)/\lambda}\,\mu_1\,\Delta v(s,x)\,ds \;+\; \nabla p \;=\; f(t,x),
$$
$$
\operatorname{div} v = 0 \quad \text{in } (0,T)\times\Omega,
$$
together with the no-slip boundary condition
$$
v\big|_{(0,T)\times\partial\Omega} = 0
$$
and the initial condition
$$
v\big|_{t=0} = v_0(x) \quad \text{in } \Omega,
$$
where $\mu_0,\mu_1,\lambda$ are positive constants (representing viscosity, elastic modulus, and relaxation time), $f \in L^2(0,T;V^*)$ is an external force, and $v_0 \in H$, with $H$ and $V$ the standard divergence-free Sobolev spaces $H = \overline{\{u \in C_0^\infty(\Omega)^n : \operatorname{div} u = 0\}}^{L^2}$ and $V = \overline{\{u \in C_0^\infty(\Omega)^n : \operatorname{div} u = 0\}}^{H^1_0}$.

A weak solution is a function $v \in L^\infty(0,T;H) \cap L^2(0,T;V)$ that satisfies the system in the standard distributional/variational sense.

Question: Without imposing any smallness or structural restrictions on the coefficients $\mu_0, \mu_1, \lambda$, on the external force $f$, or on the initial datum $v_0$, can one prove that every weak solution of the above initial-boundary value problem is regular (i.e. belongs, on $(0,T]\times\Omega$, to higher-order Sobolev or classical function spaces, in particular is unique and smooth) for all dimensions $n \ge 2$?

representations.normalized: Consider a family of billiard-like transport models in which point particles move in a $d$-dimensional domain (for example $\mathbb{R}^d$ or a periodic box) containing a configuration of fixed scatterers (obstacles), undergoing free motion between elastic collisions with the scatterers. Examples include the periodic Lorentz gas, Lorentz gases with randomly placed non-overlapping obstacles, and Ehrenfest wind-tree gases. Let $x_t$ denote the position of a tagged particle at time $t$, and consider the rescaled trajectory $X^\varepsilon_t = \varepsilon\, x_{t/\varepsilon^2}$ in the diffusive scaling limit $\varepsilon \to 0$.\n\nDetermine the minimal microscopic dynamical properties of such a model that are necessary and/or sufficient to ensure a "chaotic" macroscopic limit. Specifically, identify the weakest hypotheses on the microscopic dynamics (e.g. recurrence of typical trajectories, ergodicity of the billiard flow with respect to the natural invariant measure, existence and finiteness of a normal diffusion coefficient $D = \lim_{t\to\infty} \frac{1}{2dt}\, \mathbb{E}\,\|x_t - x_0\|^2$, mixing properties, or decay of correlations) under which the rescaled process $X^\varepsilon_t$ converges in distribution, as $\varepsilon \to 0$, to a Wiener process with covariance $2D\,t\,\mathrm{Id}$. Determine which of these properties are independent, which imply others, and which are individually necessary for normal diffusive behavior in the macroscopic limit.

The question of minimal microscopic conditions guaranteeing a diffusive (Wiener) macroscopic limit in billiard-like transport models is widely regarded as an open problem in mathematical physics. While diffusive limits are established for specific models (finite-horizon periodic Lorentz gas by Bunimovich–Sinai and refinements; some results for infinite-horizon and certain wind-tree models), no general characterization in terms of minimal dynamical hypotheses is known, and several natural cases (random non-overlapping obstacles, generic Ehrenfest gases) remain unresolved.

Consider an open two-dimensional quantum billiard: a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ consisting of the exterior of a finite collection of compact obstacles (so that classical particles may escape to infinity). For wavenumber $k \in \mathbb{C}$, consider the Helmholtz equation
$$(\nabla^2 + k^2)\psi = 0 \quad \text{on } \Omega,$$
with Dirichlet boundary conditions $\psi = 0$ on $\partial\Omega$ and outgoing radiation conditions at infinity. The values $k_n \in \mathbb{C}$ for which a nontrivial outgoing solution exists are called resonances; for an open system they have $\mathrm{Im}(k_n) < 0$.

Let the classical non-escaping set (the trapped set) be the set of phase-space points whose forward and backward billiard trajectories remain in a bounded region forever, and let $d_H$ denote the partial Hausdorff dimension of this trapped set (the Hausdorff dimension of its intersection with an energy shell, transverse to the flow direction).

For a fixed constant $C > 0$, let
$$N(k, C) := \#\{ n : \mathrm{Re}(k_n) < k,\ \mathrm{Im}(k_n) > -C \}.$$

Prove or disprove: as $k \to \infty$,
$$N(k, C) \asymp k^{d_H + 1}.$$

The fractal Weyl conjecture for open chaotic systems remains an active research problem. Rigorous fractal Weyl upper bounds have been proved in various settings (e.g., Nonnenmacher–Sjöstrand–Zworski for open quantum chaotic maps, and for several-convex-obstacle scattering under a no-eclipse condition), and the conjectured asymptotic has been tested numerically in many models. Consider an open (or generalized) billiard system: a domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ (possibly with additional dynamical generalizations such as nontrivial scatterers, intermittency, or modified reflection rules) whose boundary $\partial\Omega$ contains one or more "holes" through which trajectories may escape. Let an initial probability measure on the phase space (positions and unit velocity directions) be fixed (for instance, the uniform Liouville measure on a chosen energy shell), and let a point particle move along straight lines and reflect specularly off $\partial\Omega \setminus H$, where $H$ denotes the holes. Define the survival probability
$$P(t) = \operatorname{Prob}\big(\text{the trajectory has not yet exited through } H \text{ by time } t\big).$$
It is known in many examples that $P(t)$ admits a leading asymptotic behavior as $t \to \infty$ (algebraic decay $\sim C/t$ for typical chaotic billiards with holes, exponential decay in dispersing cases, etc.). The problem is the following:

For a given open or generalized billiard, determine whether $P(t)$ can be computed in closed form for all $t$, and if not, derive an asymptotic expansion of $P(t)$ as $t \to \infty$ that captures terms beyond the leading order (e.g., explicit subleading constants, correction terms, or full series expansions), with rigorous control of the remainder.

Let $T:M\to M$ be a measure-preserving dynamical system on a phase space $M$ equipped with a reference probability measure $\mu$, and let $H\subset M$ be a measurable subset called the hole. Define the survivor set up to time $n$ by
$$S_n(H)=\{x\in M:T^k(x)\notin H\text{ for all }0\le k\le n\},$$
and (when the limit exists) the escape rate
$$\gamma(H)=-\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\log\mu(S_n(H)).$$
Assume that $T$ exhibits little or no hyperbolicity (e.g. parabolic, intermittent, polygonal-billiard, or mixed phase-space systems with elliptic islands or marginally unstable periodic orbits).

Provide a general theory describing how the escape rate $\gamma(H)$, the asymptotics of $\mu(S_n(H))$, and the geometry of the survivor set are influenced by the recurrent structures of $T$, including:
(i) periodic orbits intersecting or lying near the hole $H$;
(ii) periodic orbits and more general recurrent sets (e.g. invariant tori, neutral fixed points, sticky regions) located elsewhere in phase space;
(iii) the interplay between such recurrent structures and the position, shape, and size of $H$.

In particular, characterize quantitatively how proximity of $H$ to short periodic orbits or to non-hyperbolic recurrent sets modifies $\gamma(H)$ relative to the hyperbolic case, and identify the corrections to the standard escape-rate formulas in the absence of uniform hyperbolicity.

The problem of describing escape in non-hyperbolic or mixed systems with recurrent structures (periodic orbits, sticky islands, marginally unstable orbits) remains an active research area. Partial results exist for specific cases — local escape rates near periodic vs. non-periodic points in hyperbolic settings (Keller–Liverani, Ferguson–Pollicott), polynomial decay due to marginally unstable periodic orbits in stadium billiards, and stickiness phenomena — but no general theory covers systems with little or no hyperbolicity. The question is consistently listed as open in surveys on open dynamical systems.

representations.normalized:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded planar domain with piecewise smooth boundary $\partial\Omega$, and consider the billiard flow on $\Omega$: a point particle moves in straight lines at unit speed inside $\Omega$ and reflects elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) upon hitting $\partial\Omega$. Fix a nonempty open subset $H \subset \partial\Omega$ ("the hole"), and define the escape time $\tau_H(x,v)$ of an initial condition $(x,v) \in \Omega \times S^1$ as the first time the trajectory reaches $H$. Equip the phase space with the Liouville measure and let the escape measurement consist of the data of the escape-time distribution $\mu_H(t) = \mathrm{Prob}(\tau_H > t)$ together with, possibly, the joint distribution of exit points and exit directions on $H$ for randomly chosen initial conditions.

The inverse escape problem asks:

(a) What features of the billiard dynamics on $\Omega$ (e.g., escape rate, Lyapunov spectrum, presence and measure of stability islands, topological entropy, periodic-orbit data) can be reconstructed from the escape measurements associated with one or several holes $H$?

(b) To what extent do these escape measurements determine the geometric shape of $\Omega$? In particular, do there exist non-isometric domains $\Omega_1, \Omega_2$ that produce identical escape measurement data for all admissible choices of holes, or does the escape data uniquely determine $\Omega$ up to isometry (an "escape" analogue of the question "Can one hear the shape of a drum?")?

Provide a systematic theory characterizing the maps $\Omega \mapsto \mu_H$ and identifying their injectivity properties and reconstruction algorithms.

A systematic solution to the inverse escape problem for billiards does not appear in the literature. While there is active research on escape rates, survival probabilities, and escape basins for open billiards (including studies relating hole placement to chaotic vs. regular dynamics), no general theory establishes which dynamical or geometric features of a billiard domain can be reconstructed from escape measurements, nor whether the shape of the domain is determined by such data. The problem appears to remain open.

The universality of the weak-coupling slope $m_\alpha$ (its dependence only on $\alpha$) is established (Caravenna–Giacomin–Toninelli; Caravenna–Giacomin 2010, Annals of Probability). The best known bounds give $1/(1+\alpha)\le m_\alpha\le 1$, and the explicit value of $m_\alpha$ for $\alpha\in(0,1)$ remains an open problem; no formula has been published. The $\alpha=0$ regime has separately been resolved (Berger–Giacomin–Lacoin, 2018), but this does not address $\alpha\in(0,1)$.

Lions and Masmoudi announced global existence of weak solutions for the corotational Oldroyd-B model in 2D and 3D, and this result is widely cited. However, the question of whether the proof's compactness argument is fully rigorous (in particular whether the identity for the defect measure at the initial time holds) has been raised as a concern in the Russian-language viscoelasticity literature, and no published refutation or independent complete verification specific to this gap appears in the standard search results. The status of this validation question therefore remains unclear.

Setting. Let $S=(S_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be the simple symmetric random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ starting from $0$, and let $\omega=(\omega_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be a sequence of i.i.d. real random variables, independent of $S$, with $\mathbb{E}[\omega_1]=0$, $\mathbb{E}[\omega_1^2]=1$, and finite exponential moments. For parameters $\lambda\ge 0$ and $h\in\mathbb{R}$, define the (quenched) copolymer Gibbs measure of length $N$ by the Radon–Nikodym derivative
$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbb{P}}(S)\;=\;\frac{1}{Z_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}}\exp\!\Big(\lambda\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\omega_n+h)\,\mathrm{sign}(S_n)\Big),$$
with the convention $\mathrm{sign}(0)=\mathrm{sign}(S_{n-1})$. The quenched free energy
$$\mathrm{f}(\lambda,h)\;=\;\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log Z_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}\right]$$
exists and is non-negative; it satisfies $\mathrm{f}(\lambda,h)\ge \lambda h$, and the (quenched) critical curve is
$$h_c(\lambda)\;=\;\inf\{h\ge 0:\mathrm{f}(\lambda,h)=\lambda h\}.$$
More generally, replacing $S$ by a recurrent renewal process whose inter-arrival law has a regularly varying tail with exponent $1+\alpha$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, one has
$$\lim_{\lambda\downarrow 0}\frac{h_c(\lambda)}{\lambda}\;=\;m_\alpha\in(0,\infty),$$
a universal constant depending only on $\alpha$. It is known that $\tfrac{1}{1+\alpha}\le m_\alpha\le 1$; in particular $m_{1/2}\ge \tfrac{2}{3}$.

Problem. Prove the strict inequality
$$m_{1/2}\;>\;\tfrac{2}{3}.$$

The slope $m_\alpha$ of the copolymer critical curve at weak coupling is known to lie in $[1/(1+\alpha),1]$, and Caravenna–Giacomin (and subsequent work by Berger–Caravenna–Poisat–Sun–Zygouras, arXiv:1301.5308) established universality of $m_\alpha$ as the slope of a continuum copolymer model, refuting the Monthus-type conjecture $m_\alpha=1/(1+\alpha)$ in some regimes. However, no source located explicitly establishes the strict inequality $m_{1/2}>2/3$ for the simple-random-walk/$\alpha=1/2$ copolymer; the question appears to remain open, although it is closely related to disproving $m_\alpha=1/(1+\alpha)$ at $\alpha=1/2$. Status is therefore reported as unknown.

Consider the random copolymer model defined as follows. Let S = (S_n)_{n≥0} be a simple random walk on ℤ, and let ω = (ω_n)_{n≥1} be an i.i.d. sequence of centered random variables with unit variance and finite exponential moments, independent of S. For parameters λ ≥ 0 and h ≥ 0, define the polymer measure of length N by

  dP_{N,λ,h}^{ω}/dP(S) = (1/Z_{N,λ,h}^{ω}) · exp( -2λ Σ_{n=1}^{N} (ω_n + h) Δ_n ),

where Δ_n = 1 if (S_{n-1}, S_n) lies in the lower half-plane (i.e. max(S_{n-1}, S_n) ≤ 0) and Δ_n = 0 otherwise, and Z_{N,λ,h}^{ω} is the normalizing partition function.

The model exhibits a localization–delocalization phase transition along a critical curve h = h_c(λ), which for the simple random walk satisfies a polynomial tail exponent α = 1/2 of the underlying return-time distribution; more generally one considers an analogous model where the underlying renewal/return-time distribution has regularly varying tails with index 1+α for some α > 0. It is known that the limit

  m_α := lim_{λ ↓ 0} h_c(λ)/λ

exists (under suitable hypotheses), and satisfies the universal bounds

  1/(1+α) ≤ m_α ≤ 1   for every α > 0.

Question: Does there exist any α > 0 for which the equality m_α = 1/(1+α) holds, i.e., for which the lower bound is attained?
