Let $S$ be a closed orientable surface of genus at least $2$, and let $\mathcal{T}(S)$ denote its Teichmüller space, i.e. the space of isotopy classes of hyperbolic metrics on $S$. Consider $M = S \times \mathbb{R}$, equipped with globally hyperbolic maximal compact (GHMC) anti-de Sitter (AdS) structures: Lorentzian metrics of constant sectional curvature $-1$ such that $M$ is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface $S \times \{0\}$ and is maximal among such Lorentzian structures. Each such structure $h$ has a convex core $C(h) \subset M$, whose boundary (when $h$ is not Fuchsian) consists of two connected components, each carrying an induced hyperbolic metric in $\mathcal{T}(S)$.

Question: Given any two metrics $m_-, m_+ \in \mathcal{T}(S)$, does there exist a unique GHMC anti-de Sitter structure $h$ on $M$ such that the induced metrics on the two connected components of the boundary of the convex core of $h$ are exactly $m_-$ and $m_+$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The existence (realization) part of the conjecture was established by Diallo, showing that any pair $(m_-,m_+) \in \mathcal{T}(S)^2$ is realized as the induced metrics on the convex core boundary of some GHMC AdS structure. The uniqueness (rigidity) part remains open in general; recent work by Chen–Schlenker and Prosanov (2025/2026) proves rigidity locally near the Fuchsian locus for strictly convex spacelike boundaries (smooth or polyhedral), but the global uniqueness statement is not known.

Consider a many-fermion quantum system (e.g. an atomic nucleus) described by a microscopic Hamiltonian H acting on a fermionic Fock space. At zero temperature, large-amplitude collective motion (LACM) can be formulated by selecting, within the time-dependent Hartree–Fock(–Bogoliubov) manifold of generalized Slater determinants, a low-dimensional collective submanifold M parametrized by collective coordinates q = (q^1, …, q^n) and conjugate momenta p, on which the dynamics is approximately self-consistent (e.g. via the adiabatic self-consistent collective coordinate method or the constrained HFB + local QRPA approach). The collective Hamiltonian H_coll(q,p) is then derived from H by requiring decoupling of collective and non-collective modes.

Develop an analogous microscopic theory at finite temperature T > 0. Concretely:

(a) Replace pure Slater determinants by thermal (mixed) states ρ(q,p;T) — for instance generalized thermal HFB density operators — and define a finite-temperature collective submanifold M_T in the space of such density operators that is invariant (to a controlled approximation) under the Liouville–von Neumann evolution iℏ∂_t ρ = [H, ρ]. Provide a self-consistent variational principle that determines M_T and the collective coordinates (q,p) as functions of T, reducing to the zero-temperature theory as T → 0.

(b) From this construction, derive a transport equation for the collective variables of the form
   M_{ij}(q,T) q̈^j + Γ_{ij}(q,T) q̇^j + ∂V(q,T)/∂q^i = ξ_i(t),
identifying microscopically the collective inertia M_{ij}, the friction (dissipation) tensor Γ_{ij}, the collective potential V, and the random force ξ_i, together with a fluctuation–dissipation relation linking Γ and the covariance of ξ.

(c) Identify and quantify the microscopic mechanisms responsible for the damping of collective motion — couplings of the collective degrees of freedom to non-collective one-particle–one-hole, two-particle–two-hole, …, and to thermally excited quasiparticles — and describe how the dominant mechanism evolves as the excitation energy increases from yrast (cold, near-ground) configurations toward the compound-nucleus regime (high level density, statistical equilibrium).

Consider a many-fermion quantum system (e.g. an atomic nucleus) described by a microscopic Hamiltonian H acting on a fermionic Fock space. At zero temperature, large-amplitude collective motion (LACM) can be formulated by selecting, within the time-dependent Hartree–Fock(–Bogoliubov) manifold of generalized Slater determinants, a low-dimensional collective submanifold M parametrized by collective coordinates q = (q^1, …, q^n) and conjugate momenta p, on which the dynamics is approximately self-consistent (e.g. via the adiabatic self-consistent collective coordinate method or the constrained HFB + local QRPA approach). The collective Hamiltonian H_coll(q,p) is then derived from H by requiring decoupling of collective and non-collective modes.

Develop an analogous microscopic theory at finite temperature T > 0. Concretely:

(a) Replace pure Slater determinants by thermal (mixed) states ρ(q,p;T) — for instance generalized thermal HFB density operators — and define a finite-temperature collective submanifold M_T in the space of such density operators that is invariant (to a controlled approximation) under the Liouville–von Neumann evolution iℏ∂_t ρ = [H, ρ]. Provide a self-consistent variational principle that determines M_T and the collective coordinates (q,p) as functions of T, reducing to the zero-temperature theory as T → 0.

(b) From this construction, derive a transport equation for the collective variables of the form
   M_{ij}(q,T) q̈^j + Γ_{ij}(q,T) q̇^j + ∂V(q,T)/∂q^i = ξ_i(t),
identifying microscopically the collective inertia M_{ij}, the friction (dissipation) tensor Γ_{ij}, the collective potential V, and the random force ξ_i, together with a fluctuation–dissipation relation linking Γ and the covariance of ξ.

(c) Identify and quantify the microscopic mechanisms responsible for the damping of collective motion — couplings of the collective degrees of freedom to non-collective one-particle–one-hole, two-particle–two-hole, …, and to thermally excited quasiparticles — and describe how the dominant mechanism evolves as the excitation energy increases from yrast (cold, near-ground) configurations toward the compound-nucleus regime (high level density, statistical equilibrium).

A complete solution consists of: (i) a mathematically well-posed definition of M_T and the finite-T collective Hamiltonian; (ii) explicit microscopic formulas for M_{ij}, Γ_{ij}, V, with proof of the appropriate fluctuation–dissipation relation; and (iii) a classification of damping mechanisms with quantitative criteria for their relative importance as a function of temperature.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem is posed as a long-term, largely unexplored research program: constructing a microscopic finite-temperature theory of large-amplitude collective motion and identifying the microscopic mechanisms of damping/dissipation between yrast and compound-nucleus regimes. While various partial approaches exist (finite-temperature HFB, linear response, dissipative TDHF, Kramers-type modeling of fission), no comprehensive, generally accepted microscopic theory has been established, so the problem is considered open.

A 3-dimensional anti-de Sitter (AdS) manifold is a Lorentzian 3-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$. Consider compact AdS 3-manifolds $N$ diffeomorphic to $S \times [0,1]$ whose boundary $\partial N$ consists of two connected components, each a smooth space-like strictly convex surface (so that the induced metric on each boundary component is Riemannian). Label the two boundary components so that the induced metrics on them are $g_-$ and $g_+$, respectively.

Question: Does there exist exactly one such AdS 3-manifold $N$ (up to isometry isotopic to the identity) for which $g_- = h_-$ and $g_+ = h_+$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Existence of such an AdS 3-manifold for any pair of metrics with curvature less than −1 was established by Tamburelli (2018). Uniqueness in the original two-induced-metrics formulation is not yet fully proved; however, Chen–Schlenker (2024) proved a closely related uniqueness result, showing that a quasifuchsian AdS spacetime is uniquely determined by the left (Mess) metric together with the induced metric on one past-convex Cauchy surface, via infinitesimal rigidity. The exact uniqueness statement asked here therefore appears partially resolved rather than fully settled.

In the microscopic theory of large-amplitude collective motion (LACM) in atomic nuclei, consider the tunneling decay of a high-K isomeric state to states of lower K, where K denotes the projection of the total angular momentum on the body-fixed symmetry axis of a deformed nucleus. Two competing collective decay pathways have been proposed:

(i) a path that proceeds through large-amplitude collective motion in the triaxial shape degree of freedom (i.e., tunneling through the γ degree of freedom of the nuclear shape, via shapes departing from axial symmetry);

(ii) a path that proceeds through large-amplitude collective motion in the orientation degree of freedom of the angular-momentum vector with respect to the principal axes of the body-fixed frame (i.e., reorientation of the angular momentum at fixed intrinsic shape, associated with K-mixing).

Determine which of these two pathways dominates the tunneling decay rate from a high-K isomer to low-K states. More precisely, identify the conditions (in terms of nuclear deformation parameters, the softness of the potential energy surface in γ, the height and shape of the relevant collective barriers, and the angular momentum) under which one pathway dominates over the other, and provide a microscopic, self-consistent description of the dominant collective tunneling mode and the associated decay rate.

A hyperbolic metric with cone singularities on $S$ is a metric of constant curvature $-1$ on the complement of a finite set of points $p_1,\dots,p_n\in S$, such that near each $p_i$ the metric is locally isometric to the model hyperbolic cone of some cone angle $\theta_i>0$.

A $(2+1)$-dimensional anti-de Sitter (AdS) manifold is a Lorentzian $3$-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$. Consider a globally hyperbolic maximal compact AdS manifold $M$ homeomorphic to $S\times(-1,1)$ that contains a convex compact subset $K$ whose boundary $\partial K$ consists of two spacelike polyhedral surfaces (each a finite union of totally geodesic spacelike triangles), a past component and a future component, each homeomorphic to $S$. The induced intrinsic metrics on these two boundary components are then hyperbolic metrics on $S$ with cone singularities (the cone points being the vertices of the polyhedral surfaces).

Given two hyperbolic metrics $h_-$ and $h_+$ on $S$ with cone singularities all of whose cone angles are strictly greater than $2\pi$, decide whether there exists a unique (up to isometry) such AdS manifold $M$ together with a convex compact subset whose past polyhedral boundary has induced metric isometric to $h_-$ and whose future polyhedral boundary has induced metric isometric to $h_+$.

Consider a rapidly rotating atomic nucleus with a triaxial shape, modeled microscopically (e.g., by a cranked mean-field plus quasiparticle description). In the small-amplitude limit, fluctuations of the angular-momentum vector around the uniformly rotating axis give rise to the wobbling mode, a collective rotational excitation describable within the random-phase approximation built on the cranked mean field. Two regimes lie outside this small-amplitude treatment:

(a) Large-amplitude wobbling. Suppose the amplitude of the wobbling mode grows so large that linear-response (small-amplitude) theory ceases to be valid, and the uniformly rotating mean-field state becomes unstable with respect to this collective rotational degree of freedom.

(b) Chiral vibrations. In a triaxially deformed rotating nucleus, the angular-momentum vector may tunnel between two configurations of opposite handedness (left-handed and right-handed orientations of the angular-momentum vector relative to the three principal axes), producing a collective vibrational mode that connects these two chiral configurations.

Develop a microscopic large-amplitude collective-motion (LACM) theory — that is, a theory of self-consistent collective coordinates and momenta extracted from the time-dependent mean-field (TDHF/TDHFB) dynamics in the rotating frame, valid beyond the harmonic/RPA regime — and apply it to:

1. Describe the dynamics of the wobbling degree of freedom beyond the small-amplitude regime, including the fate of the uniformly rotating state once it becomes unstable against large-amplitude wobbling.
2. Describe chiral vibrations as large-amplitude collective motion connecting the left- and right-handed triaxial rotating configurations.

Provide a microscopic determination of the relevant collective coordinate(s), the corresponding collective potential and inertia, and the resulting spectra and transition properties for both phenomena.

Let $S$ be a closed oriented surface of genus $g\ge 2$. A globally hyperbolic maximal compact (GHMC) anti-de Sitter 3-manifold $M$ diffeomorphic to $S\times\mathbb{R}$ is a maximal Lorentzian 3-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ admitting a Cauchy surface homeomorphic to $S$. By Mess's parameterization, the moduli space of such structures is identified with $\mathcal{T}(S)\times\mathcal{T}(S)$, where $\mathcal{T}(S)$ is the Teichmüller space of $S$; the two factors $(h_L,h_R)$ are the "left" and "right" hyperbolic metrics associated with $M$.

Inside $M$ there is a unique inclusion-minimal nonempty closed convex subset $C(M)$, the convex core, whose two boundary components carry intrinsic hyperbolic metrics $m_+,m_-\in\mathcal{T}(S)$. Let $V(M)$ denote the total volume of $M$ (when finite/appropriately normalized) and $V(C(M))$ the volume of the convex core.

Two nonnegative functions $F,G$ on $\mathcal{T}(S)\times\mathcal{T}(S)$ are called quasi-equivalent if there exist constants $A\ge 1,B\ge 0$ such that $A^{-1}G - B \le F \le AG + B$.

Question: Does there exist a natural distance $d$ on $\mathcal{T}(S)$, such as the Teichmüller distance $d_{\mathcal{T}}$ or the Weil–Petersson distance $d_{WP}$, such that either $V(M)$ or $V(C(M))$ is quasi-equivalent (as a function of $M$) to $d(m_+,m_-)$, or equivalently to $d(h_L,h_R)$?

Bonsante, Seppi and Tamburelli (arXiv:1703.01068) established partial results: the convex core volume is bounded above by the exponential of Thurston's Lipschitz asymmetric distance and below by (a function of) the Weil–Petersson distance, and is coarsely equivalent to the minimum L^1-energy and to the length of the earthquake lamination. The question as posed (a single natural Teichmüller-type distance quasi-equivalent to V(M) or V(C(M))) thus remains only partially resolved.

representations.normalized:
Consider the nuclear shell model in which an effective Hamiltonian acts in a truncated valence model space and is derived from an underlying microscopic nucleon-nucleon (NN) interaction (for example, a low-momentum NN potential obtained by renormalization-group decimation of a realistic high-precision NN force). The standard derivation (e.g., via the Q-box folded-diagram expansion or many-body perturbation theory in the valence space) produces a two-body effective interaction V_eff that, when applied to A>2 valence nucleons, omits two distinct kinds of many-body contributions:

(i) "induced" three- and higher-body forces in the valence space generated by the medium and by the projection onto the model space (i.e., effective many-body operators that arise from the NN interaction even when the underlying free-space Hamiltonian contains only two-body terms), and

(ii) "genuine" three-nucleon forces (3NFs) present in the underlying free-space Hamiltonian (for instance, the chiral N2LO 3NF), together with the effective valence-space operators they induce.

Problem. Develop a systematic and tractable framework for constructing realistic shell-model effective Hamiltonians for medium- and heavy-mass nuclei that consistently incorporates both induced and genuine three-body (and, where relevant, higher-body) contributions. Specifically:

(a) Give a perturbative or non-perturbative procedure (analogous to the folded-diagram / Q-box expansion for the two-body case) that produces an effective three-body interaction in the chosen valence space starting from a given NN + 3N free-space Hamiltonian, and prove or numerically demonstrate its convergence.

(b) Quantify, for representative medium-mass and heavy-mass isotopic chains, the size and structure (monopole, multipole, isospin dependence) of the induced and genuine three-body contributions to V_eff, and determine to what extent shell evolution, single-particle energies, spin-orbit splittings, drip-line locations, and spectra computed from the resulting Hamiltonian agree with experiment and with ab initio benchmarks.

(c) Identify under what conditions the three-body effective interaction can be accurately replaced by a density-dependent (normal-ordered two-body) approximation, and bound the error of such a reduction.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Substantial progress has been made since the question was posed. Three-body forces have been included in shell-model effective interactions for p-shell and sd-shell nuclei using chiral N2LO 3NFs and Q-box/folded-diagram techniques (e.g., Phys. Rev. C 98, 044305 (2018); Prog. Part. Nucl. Phys. review (2023)). Valence-space in-medium SRG and coupled-cluster methods now include 3NFs (often via normal-ordered two-body approximation) for nuclei up to mass A~100 and recently A~208. However, fully consistent inclusion of both induced and genuine three-body components in shell-model effective interactions for general medium- and heavy-mass nuclei, beyond the normal-ordered two-body approximation, remains an active area of research and is not fully solved.

representations.normalized:
Let S be a closed orientable surface of genus at least 2, and let T(S) denote its Teichmüller space, i.e. the space of isotopy classes of hyperbolic metrics on S. For each pair (h_l, h_r) in T(S) × T(S), there exists a unique (up to isometry) globally hyperbolic maximal Cauchy-compact (GHMC) anti-de Sitter 3-manifold M(h_l, h_r) homeomorphic to S × R, whose holonomy representation, viewed in PSL(2,R) × PSL(2,R) = Isom_0(AdS^3), has left and right components with hyperbolic quotients (S, h_l) and (S, h_r) respectively. Such a manifold contains a smallest non-empty closed convex subset C(M(h_l, h_r)), called its convex core, which has finite volume.

Fix h_l ∈ T(S) and consider the two functions on T(S):
   F(h_r) = Vol(M(h_l, h_r)),    G(h_r) = Vol(C(M(h_l, h_r))).

Determine whether each of F and G:
(i) is convex on T(S) (with respect to a natural geometric structure such as the Weil–Petersson structure or some canonical convexity structure),
(ii) is proper as a function T(S) → R,
(iii) attains a unique minimum, and that minimum is attained at h_r = h_l (i.e. the Fuchsian locus).

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent work has partially addressed the question. Bonsante–Seppi and collaborators showed that the volume of a GHMC anti-de Sitter 3-manifold and the volume of its convex core are coarsely equivalent to the L^1-energy between the two hyperbolic surfaces, which yields properness. More recently, it has been proved that Fuchsian manifolds (h_r = h_l) minimize the volume of GHMC AdS 3-manifolds (Vol(M) ≥ π²|χ(S)|, with equality iff Fuchsian), and analogous statements are known for the convex core. However, the strict convexity of these functions on Teichmüller space, and uniqueness of the minimum in full generality, do not appear to be completely settled in the literature.

Consider the framework of low-momentum nucleon-nucleon interactions $V_{\mathrm{low}\text{-}k}$ obtained by integrating out high-momentum modes (above a sharp or smooth cutoff $\Lambda$) of a realistic, phase-shift equivalent two-nucleon potential $V_{NN}$, so that all $V_{\mathrm{low}\text{-}k}(\Lambda)$ reproduce the same on-shell two-nucleon data and the deuteron binding energy below $\Lambda$. Let $V_{\mathrm{eff}}(\Lambda)$ denote the shell-model effective interaction in a chosen valence space, derived from $V_{\mathrm{low}\text{-}k}(\Lambda)$ via a many-body perturbation expansion of the $\hat{Q}$-box (e.g., the Kuo–Lee–Ratcliffe folded-diagram series), and let $\mathcal{O}(\Lambda)$ stand for resulting shell-model observables (binding energies relative to a closed core, low-lying excitation spectra, electromagnetic transition matrix elements, etc.) computed by diagonalizing $V_{\mathrm{eff}}(\Lambda)$ in the valence space.

(a) Quantify, as a function of $\Lambda$ varied over a physically reasonable window (e.g., $\Lambda \in [1.8, 3.0]\ \mathrm{fm}^{-1}$), the variation $\Delta\mathcal{O}(\Lambda)$ of representative shell-model observables, and determine to what extent this variation is suppressed when only two-nucleon forces are retained at the $V_{\mathrm{low}\text{-}k}$ level versus when induced three- and higher-body forces generated by the renormalization-group transformation are systematically included.

(b) Provide a principled characterization or control scheme of the residual $\Lambda$-dependence: identify the dominant operator structures responsible for it, propose a method (e.g., consistent inclusion of induced many-body forces, smooth regulators, or order-by-order perturbative resummation) that renders shell-model observables approximately $\Lambda$-independent within a quantified theoretical uncertainty, and give an estimate of the residual cutoff sensitivity that should be attributed as a systematic theoretical error to realistic shell-model predictions.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Empirical and theoretical work indicates that for cutoffs near $\Lambda \approx 2\ \mathrm{fm}^{-1}$, low-lying shell-model spectra derived from $V_{\mathrm{low}\text{-}k}$ depend only weakly on $\Lambda$, and the residual cutoff dependence is understood to originate from omitted short-range induced three- and higher-body forces generated by the renormalization-group transformation. Including such induced many-body forces (or using SRG-evolved consistent NN+3N interactions) substantially reduces the dependence, but a fully systematic, quantitative characterization and control of the residual cutoff sensitivity for shell-model observables across mass regions remains an active research problem.

representations.normalized:
Let $n\geq 2$ and consider the model space $\mathrm{AdS}^{n+1}$, the anti–de Sitter space of dimension $n+1$ (the Lorentzian symmetric space of constant sectional curvature $-1$). A Lorentzian manifold $M$ of dimension $n+1$ is said to be locally modeled on $\mathrm{AdS}^{n+1}$ if it is a $(G,X)$-manifold with $X = \mathrm{AdS}^{n+1}$ and $G$ its isometry group. Such an $M$ is globally hyperbolic maximal compact (GHMC) if it admits a compact spacelike Cauchy hypersurface (a compact spacelike hypersurface met exactly once by every inextendible causal curve) and is maximal among such manifolds for inclusion.

For integers $p,q\geq 1$ with $p+q=n$, let $\mathbb{H}^p$ and $\mathbb{H}^q$ denote real hyperbolic spaces of those dimensions, and let $\mathrm{SO}(1,p)\times\mathrm{SO}(1,q)$ act diagonally by isometries on $\mathbb{H}^p\times\mathbb{H}^q$. A uniform lattice $\Gamma$ in $\mathrm{SO}(1,p)\times\mathrm{SO}(1,q)$ is a discrete subgroup acting properly discontinuously and cocompactly.

Question: Must every Cauchy hypersurface of every GHMC manifold $M$ locally modeled on $\mathrm{AdS}^{n+1}$ be diffeomorphic to a quotient $\Gamma\backslash(\mathbb{H}^p\times\mathbb{H}^q)$ for some such $p,q$ with $p+q=n$ and some uniform lattice $\Gamma\subset\mathrm{SO}(1,p)\times\mathrm{SO}(1,q)$?

The question has been answered negatively. Counterexamples in dimensions (p+q)+1 with p+q between 4 and 8 were constructed by Lee–Marquis, and more recent work using Gromov–Thurston manifolds produces quasi-Fuchsian GHMC AdS spacetimes whose Cauchy hypersurfaces are not diffeomorphic to any quotient of $\mathbb{H}^p\times\mathbb{H}^q$ by a uniform lattice, since the fundamental group of a Gromov–Thurston manifold of dimension $\geq 4$ is not commensurable to a lattice in any Lie group.

representations.normalized:
Setup. In the derivation of effective shell-model interactions from a realistic nucleon–nucleon potential, one decomposes the full Hilbert space into a model space P and its complement Q = 1 − P. Following the Kuo–Lee–Ratcliffe folded-diagram formalism, the energy-independent effective interaction V_eff acting in P can be written as

   V_eff = Q̂ − Q̂' ∫ Q̂ + Q̂' ∫ Q̂ ∫ Q̂ − Q̂' ∫ Q̂ ∫ Q̂ ∫ Q̂ + … ,

where Q̂(ε) is the so-called Q̂-box, defined as the sum of all linked, non-folded, irreducible valence-linked Goldstone diagrams with at least one Q-space intermediate state, evaluated as a function of the starting energy ε; Q̂' denotes the Q̂-box with the zeroth-order term removed; the integral symbols stand for the folded-diagram operation (energy derivatives evaluated on shell); and the alternating series sums folded diagrams to all orders. In practice Q̂ is itself computed perturbatively in the residual interaction (typically the Brueckner G-matrix) and truncated at some finite order n in the interaction.

Problem. Establish rigorous convergence properties of the perturbative Q̂-box expansion used to construct V_eff. Specifically:

(a) Determine whether, for realistic low-momentum nucleon–nucleon interactions, the order-by-order expansion of Q̂(ε) (in powers of the residual interaction) converges, and characterize quantitatively the magnitude and operator structure of contributions beyond second order.

(b) Quantify the extent to which the all-orders folded-diagram resummation appearing in the formula above attenuates the differences between V_eff computed from Q̂-boxes truncated at different perturbative orders; in particular, prove or disprove that this resummation is sufficient to render second-order Q̂-box truncations adequate, or alternatively establish that third-order (and higher) Q̂-box terms produce non-negligible residual effects on V_eff.

(c) Provide criteria (on the model-space choice, the single-particle spectrum, and the underlying interaction) under which the combined Q̂-box plus folded-diagram series for V_eff is convergent, together with bounds on the truncation error.

Recent literature on realistic shell-model effective interactions continues to treat the convergence of the Q̂-box perturbative expansion as an unresolved issue: practical calculations are limited to third order because going beyond is computationally very difficult and no rigorous proof of convergence exists. Fix integers $p,q\ge 1$ with $n=p+q$, and consider the anti-de Sitter space $\mathrm{AdS}^{n+1}$, i.e. the model Lorentzian manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ realized as a quadric in $\mathbb{R}^{p+1,q+1}$. Its isometry group contains the subgroup $\mathrm{SO}(1,p)\times\mathrm{SO}(1,q)$ (via the natural decomposition $\mathbb{R}^{p+1,q+1}=\mathbb{R}^{p+1,0}\oplus\mathbb{R}^{0,q+1}$). There is a canonical convex domain $\Omega\subset\mathrm{AdS}^{n+1}$, invariant under this subgroup, that is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy hypersurface diffeomorphic to $\mathbb{H}^p\times\mathbb{H}^q$.

A globally hyperbolic maximal Cauchy-compact (GHMC) anti-de Sitter manifold of dimension $n+1$ is a Lorentzian $(n+1)$-manifold of constant curvature $-1$ that is globally hyperbolic with a closed Cauchy hypersurface and is maximal (with respect to isometric embedding) among such manifolds.

representations.normalized:
In the microscopic derivation of the nuclear shell-model effective interaction, one starts from an A-nucleon Hamiltonian
H = T + V = (T + U) + (V − U) ≡ H_0 + H_1,
where T is the intrinsic kinetic energy, V is a realistic nucleon–nucleon interaction, and U is an auxiliary one-body potential introduced so that H_0 = T + U defines a convenient single-particle basis. The effective interaction V_eff acting in a chosen valence model space is then obtained as a perturbative (folded-diagram) expansion in H_1 = V − U, whose Goldstone-type diagrams include both "V-insertions" and "−U-insertions," together with self-energy ("bubble") insertions on internal and external single-particle lines.

It is a standard observation that if U is chosen to be the Hartree–Fock self-consistent one-body potential, then to each order in the expansion the diagrams containing explicit −U vertices exactly cancel the corresponding bubble (Hartree–Fock self-energy) insertions, so that both classes of diagrams may be omitted from V_eff without loss.

Suppose instead that U is taken to be a harmonic-oscillator potential U(r) = (1/2) m ω² r² (the conventional choice for generating the single-particle basis in shell-model calculations), so that U is no longer the Hartree–Fock potential of V in the chosen model space. In the perturbative expansion of V_eff with this non-self-consistent U:

(a) Determine whether the omission of all diagrams containing −U vertices and all bubble self-energy insertions remains a justified approximation, i.e. whether the sum of these omitted diagrams still cancels (exactly or to a controlled accuracy) order by order.

(b) If the cancellation fails, quantify the size of the contribution of the omitted U- and bubble-insertion diagrams to V_eff and assess whether this contribution is significant compared with the diagrams that are retained.

Reviews of realistic shell-model effective interactions note that the cancellation between −U vertex diagrams and bubble (Hartree–Fock) self-energy insertions is exact only when U is the Hartree–Fock self-consistent potential. With a harmonic-oscillator U—the standard choice in practice—the justification of omitting these diagrams is acknowledged as not established, and a systematic quantitative assessment has not been reported in the available literature, so the question appears to remain open.

Let $M$ be a globally hyperbolic maximal compact (GHMC) anti-de Sitter manifold of arbitrary dimension $n+1 \geq 3$; that is, $M$ is a Lorentzian manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ which is globally hyperbolic with compact Cauchy hypersurfaces and which is maximal among such manifolds with respect to isometric embeddings preserving Cauchy hypersurfaces. The convex core $C(M)$ of $M$ is the smallest non-empty closed convex subset of $M$ whose inclusion is a homotopy equivalence. Let $P(M)$ denote the past of $C(M)$ in $M$.

A K-time on $P(M)$ is a smooth time function $\tau : P(M) \to I \subset \mathbb{R}$ (i.e., a smooth function whose gradient is everywhere timelike past-directed) such that:
(i) each level set $\tau^{-1}(t)$ is a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface of $P(M)$ whose Gauss–Kronecker curvature (the determinant of its shape operator) is constant equal to some value $K(t)$; and
(ii) the function $t \mapsto K(t)$ is strictly increasing in $t$.

Question: Does $P(M)$ always admit a K-time?

representations.normalized:
Setting. In the nuclear shell model, one starts from a doubly magic closed-shell core and treats nucleons in a finite valence model space outside the core. From an underlying realistic nucleon–nucleon (and possibly three-nucleon) interaction, an effective shell-model Hamiltonian H_eff is derived for the valence space using many-body perturbation theory, typically through the Kuo–Lee–Suzuki Q̂-box folded-diagram expansion. The Q̂-box is a sum of irreducible, valence-linked diagrams whose external lines lie in the valence space; one usually truncates the Q̂-box at second order in the residual interaction, retaining all folded diagrams to all orders. Diagonalizing H_eff in the valence space yields binding energies, level schemes, and other observables along isotopic (fixed Z, varying N) or isotonic (fixed N, varying Z) chains.

Empirical observation. For two-valence-nucleon systems near a doubly magic core, ground-state energies are accurately reproduced. As one moves along an isotopic or isotonic chain by adding valence nucleons, the calculated ground-state energies become progressively more bound than experiment, producing a systematic overbinding that grows with the number of valence nucleons.

Problem. Provide a quantitative theoretical explanation of this systematic overbinding by determining the relative contributions of:
(a) genuine three-nucleon forces in the underlying interaction;
(b) effective (induced) three-body forces generated by the many-body interaction of valence nucleons with core excitations and excluded states;
(c) higher-order terms of the Q̂-box, in particular third- and higher-order diagrams beyond the standard second-order truncation.

Specifically, decompose the discrepancy between calculated and experimental ground-state energies along long isotopic/isotonic chains into the contributions (a), (b), and (c), and identify which mechanism is dominant in producing the growth of overbinding with valence-nucleon number.

Subsequent work has made substantial progress: derivations of effective shell-model Hamiltonians from chiral two- plus three-nucleon forces (including induced three-body contributions from valence-space correlations and Pauli-violating terms) have been carried out and applied to p-shell, sd-shell, calcium, titanium and tin chains, demonstrating that genuine and effective 3N forces are essential to cure monopole defects and reduce overbinding (e.g., flattening of separation energies in neutron-rich Ca, Ti). However, residual overbinding (up to ~1 MeV/nucleon by Sn with some chiral interactions) persists, and a systematic, fully quantitative separation between 3N-force effects and higher-order Q̂-box (third-order and beyond) contributions has not been definitively established. The problem is therefore partially solved but remains an active area of investigation.

Let $M$ be a globally hyperbolic maximal anti-de Sitter 3-manifold with particles, where each particle is a cone singularity along a time-like line with cone angle strictly less than $\pi$. A space-like surface $\Sigma \subset M$ is said to be maximal if its mean curvature vanishes identically on the smooth part, and it is said to be orthogonal to the particles if at every intersection point of $\Sigma$ with a singular time-like line, the tangent plane to $\Sigma$ is orthogonal to that line.

Prove or disprove: there exists exactly one maximal space-like surface in $M$ that is orthogonal to all the particle singularities.

representations.normalized:
In the realistic nuclear shell model, an effective two-body interaction acting within a chosen valence space is derived from a realistic nucleon-nucleon potential (typically via a $\hat{Q}$-box / folded-diagram or similar perturbative construction). For a given doubly-closed-shell core, valence nucleons can be classified as particles (occupying single-particle orbitals above the Fermi surface of the core) or holes (occupying single-hole orbitals below it). Accordingly, the matrix elements of the effective interaction split into three classes: particle-particle (pp), particle-hole (ph), and hole-hole (hh).

Empirically, when realistic shell-model calculations are compared to experimental spectra and other observables across chains of nuclei, the level of agreement is systematically of high quality for nuclei whose low-lying structure is dominated by pp or ph matrix elements, but is noticeably and consistently worse for nuclei in which hh matrix elements play a significant role.

Problem. Identify and justify the physical and/or methodological origin of this asymmetry. Specifically, determine whether the discrepancy stems from (a) the perturbative derivation of the effective interaction (e.g. truncations of the $\hat{Q}$-box, treatment of folded diagrams, or core-polarization contributions) treating hole orbitals less accurately than particle orbitals, (b) intrinsic features of the underlying realistic nucleon-nucleon (and possibly three-nucleon) interaction in hole channels, (c) limitations of the chosen model space when hole excitations are involved, or (d) some combination thereof, and provide a quantitative explanation that accounts for the observed systematic degradation of agreement in hh-dominated nuclei.

representations.normalized:
Let $S$ be a closed orientable surface, let $x_1,\dots,x_n\in S$ be distinct marked points, and fix angles $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_n\in(0,\pi)$. A hyperbolic metric with cone singularities of angle $\theta_i$ at $x_i$ is a smooth metric of constant curvature $-1$ on $S\setminus\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ such that near each $x_i$ the metric is, in suitable local coordinates, isometric to a model hyperbolic cone of total angle $\theta_i$. Given two such metrics $h$ and $h'$ on $S$ (with the same marked points and the same prescribed cone angles), a diffeomorphism $\Phi:(S,h)\to(S,h')$ that fixes each $x_i$ is called minimal Lagrangian if it is area-preserving and its graph is a minimal surface in the Riemannian product $(S\times S,\,h\oplus h')$; equivalently, $\Phi^*h' = h(b\cdot,b\cdot)$ for some $h$-self-adjoint, positive, $h$-divergence-free bundle endomorphism $b$ of $TS$ with $\det b=1$.

Question: For every choice of $S$, marked points $x_1,\dots,x_n$, angles $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_n\in(0,\pi)$, and two hyperbolic cone metrics $h,h'$ on $S$ with cone angle $\theta_i$ at $x_i$, does there exist a unique minimal Lagrangian diffeomorphism $\Phi:(S,h)\to(S,h')$ that is isotopic to the identity (relative to the marked points) and fixes each $x_i$?

Develop a framework for realistic shell-model calculations of atomic nuclei near the proton and neutron drip lines that explicitly incorporates the coupling of bound single-particle configurations to the scattering continuum. More precisely:

(i) Starting from a realistic nucleon–nucleon interaction V (e.g., derived from a high-precision potential or chiral effective field theory) and using a many-body renormalization procedure to construct an effective two-body (and, where needed, three-body) interaction H_eff in a chosen model space, formulate a configuration-interaction shell-model scheme in which the single-particle basis includes bound states, narrow resonances (Gamow states), and non-resonant scattering states on equal footing — for instance via a Berggren completeness relation
   1 = Σ_b |b⟩⟨b| + Σ_r |r⟩⟨r̃| + ∫_{L^+} dk |k⟩⟨k̃|,
where L^+ is a contour in the complex momentum plane enclosing the selected resonances.

(ii) Specify how the effective Hamiltonian H_eff, originally constructed for a discrete bound-state model space, must be modified (renormalized) to remain consistent when the model space is extended to include resonant and continuum single-particle states, ensuring that the resulting many-body eigenvalue problem yields physically meaningful (complex) energies and widths for weakly bound and unbound nuclear states.

(iii) Demonstrate that the resulting realistic continuum-coupled shell model reproduces, in a controlled and systematic way, the known structure and spectroscopy of weakly bound or unbound nuclei near the drip lines (binding energies, one- and two-nucleon separation energies, resonance widths, decay thresholds, and threshold-related effects on spectra), and provides predictive power for nuclei beyond current experimental reach.

Provide such a construction, prove (or numerically establish) its convergence with respect to the truncation of the Berggren contour and many-body model space, and quantify the impact of continuum coupling on observables relative to standard bound-state shell-model calculations using the same realistic interaction.

Substantial progress has been made via the Realistic Gamow Shell Model, which uses the Berggren basis to incorporate bound, resonant, and scattering states on equal footing together with effective interactions derived from realistic potentials (e.g., CD-Bonn, chiral EFT). Calculations for neutron-rich oxygen, calcium, and other drip-line isotopes have been published, showing that continuum coupling significantly affects spectra and separation energies. However, a fully systematic, convergent ab initio treatment for heavier drip-line systems and a complete renormalization of three-body and higher continuum couplings remain active research; the broader program is partially solved rather than closed.

Let $M$ be a three-dimensional globally hyperbolic anti–de Sitter manifold with particles, that is, a Lorentzian cone-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ that is globally hyperbolic and whose singular locus consists of finitely many time-like geodesic lines along each of which the metric has a conical singularity of fixed cone angle in $(0,\pi)$. A constant-mean-curvature (CMC) time function on $M$ is a smooth function $\tau\colon M\to\mathbb{R}$ whose level sets are space-like Cauchy surfaces of constant mean curvature equal to $\tau$, and the slices are required to meet the singular locus orthogonally at each intersection point.

Question: Does every such $M$ admit a CMC time function as above, and if so, is it unique?

Chen and Schlenker (arXiv:1705.03674, published in Geometriae Dedicata, 2018) prove that every convex globally hyperbolic maximal (2+1)-spacetime of constant curvature (Minkowski, de Sitter, or anti-de Sitter) with particles—cone singularities of angles less than π along time-like geodesics—admits a unique CMC foliation, with slices orthogonal to the singular locus. This resolves the question affirmatively in the anti-de Sitter case.

representations.normalized:
Consider neutron-rich atomic nuclei lying near the neutron drip line, whose outermost neutron density extends to values far below the saturation density of normal nuclear matter (ρ₀ ≈ 0.16 fm⁻³). Such nuclei exhibit two characteristic features: (i) a neutron halo, in which one or a few weakly bound neutrons form a low-density tail extending well beyond the nuclear core, and (ii) a neutron skin, defined as the difference Δr_np = ⟨r²⟩_n^{1/2} − ⟨r²⟩_p^{1/2} between the root-mean-square radii of the neutron and proton density distributions. The symmetry energy S(ρ) of asymmetric nuclear matter is the coefficient governing the isospin-asymmetry dependence of the energy per particle, E(ρ,δ)/A = E(ρ,0)/A + S(ρ)δ² + O(δ⁴), where δ = (ρ_n − ρ_p)/ρ.

Address the following:

1. Determine to what extent the observed properties of neutron halos and neutron skins in finite drip-line nuclei can be used to infer the equation of state of dilute (sub-saturation) pure neutron matter.

2. Determine whether, and how quantitatively, measurements of neutron skin thicknesses and halo structures can constrain the symmetry energy S(ρ) of asymmetric nuclear matter, especially at sub-saturation densities, including its magnitude S(ρ₀) and slope L = 3ρ₀ (dS/dρ)|_{ρ₀}.

3. Quantify the degree to which low-density nuclear matter properties are manifested in the structural observables of finite neutron-rich nuclei whose outer neutron density is far below ρ₀, and identify the observables most sensitive to this dilute regime.

The question of extracting the dilute-neutron-matter equation of state and the symmetry energy (and its slope L) from neutron skins and halos remains an active and unresolved research problem. Recent work (2024–2025), including analyses reconciling PREX-II (208Pb) and CREX (48Ca) parity-violating measurements, dipole polarizability data, and EDF studies, continues to debate how tightly such observables constrain S(ρ) at sub-saturation densities. No consensus determination has been achieved.

Let $M$ be a globally hyperbolic maximal anti-de Sitter 3-manifold with particles, that is, a Lorentzian 3-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ which is globally hyperbolic and which carries cone singularities of fixed cone angles, each strictly less than $\pi$, along a finite collection of time-like curves. Let $C(M) \subset M$ denote the convex core of $M$ (the smallest non-empty closed convex subset that is a deformation retract of $M$, taken in the complement of the singular locus and extended in the standard way across the singularities). The complement $M \setminus C(M)$ has two connected components, the past component $\mathrm{Past}(C(M))$ and the future component $\mathrm{Fut}(C(M))$. By a "constant Gauss curvature surface" we mean a space-like, locally convex surface $S \subset M$ (orthogonal to the singular locus where it meets it) whose induced Riemannian metric has constant intrinsic Gauss curvature.

Prove or disprove: each of $\mathrm{Past}(C(M))$ and $\mathrm{Fut}(C(M))$ admits a unique foliation by surfaces of constant Gauss curvature.

Soc., 2020) proves that for any convex globally hyperbolic maximal anti-de Sitter 3-manifold with particles of cone angles less than π, the complement of the convex core admits a unique foliation by constant Gauss curvature surfaces. representations.normalized:
Consider infinite dilute nuclear matter and infinite dilute neutron matter at very low density. In such systems, theory predicts characteristic low-density correlations, including BCS–BEC crossover behavior of nucleon pairs, strong di-neutron spatial correlations at low density, and alpha-particle (four-nucleon) clustering when the density falls below a critical value of order one fifth of nuclear saturation density.

Now consider finite nuclei in which similar low-density regions or low-density limits occur, such as:
(i) two-neutron-halo nuclei (e.g. ^6He, ^11Li, ^14Be), where the two valence neutrons inhabit a dilute halo and exhibit a spatially compact "di-neutron" configuration;
(ii) neutron-rich isotopes whose surfaces and skins constitute a low-density neutron environment, in which a "surface di-neutron correlation" is conjectured;
(iii) the second 0^+ state of ^12C (the Hoyle state), interpreted as a dilute three-alpha cluster configuration.

Establish whether the exotic low-density correlations predicted in dilute infinite nuclear/neutron matter (di-neutron pairing in the BCS–BEC crossover regime and low-density alpha condensation) are actually realized in finite nuclei, and if so, give a quantitative theoretical and experimental link between these infinite-matter correlations and the observed finite-nucleus signatures listed above. Specifically:

(a) Define a precise correlation observable (e.g. the two-neutron pair-density or the alpha-particle four-body density correlation) that interpolates between the dilute-matter and finite-nucleus regimes.
(b) Determine whether the observed di-neutron spatial correlations in halo and neutron-rich nuclei, and the observed dilute alpha-cluster structure of the Hoyle state, are manifestations of the same low-density correlations expected in dilute infinite matter.

Let S be the interior of a compact orientable surface with finitely many boundary components and negative Euler characteristic. Let h_l and h_r be two complete convex cocompact hyperbolic metrics on S, and let

  ρ_l, ρ_r : π_1(S) → PSL(2, R)

denote their holonomy representations. Consider the diagonal representation

  (ρ_l, ρ_r) : π_1(S) → PSL(2, R) × PSL(2, R) ≅ Isom_0(AdS^3),

where AdS^3 is 3-dimensional anti-de Sitter space. The image group acts on AdS^3 by isometries; its action on AdS^3 may or may not be properly discontinuous.

For each of the two convex cocompact hyperbolic surfaces (S, h_l) and (S, h_r), the convex core is bounded by a collection of pleated surfaces (here, the funnels are removed); on each such boundary one has an induced hyperbolic metric on the boundary components and a bending measured geodesic lamination.

Problem. Provide a characterization of when the action of (ρ_l, ρ_r)(π_1(S)) on AdS^3 is properly discontinuous purely in terms of geometric data attached to the convex cores of (S, h_l) and (S, h_r), namely:

(a) in terms of the induced hyperbolic metrics on the boundary components of the two convex cores; and/or

(b) in terms of the bending measured laminations on the boundary components of the two convex cores.

Consider an atomic nucleus consisting of A nucleons (Z protons and N = A − Z neutrons) governed by a non-relativistic many-body Hamiltonian of the form

  H = Σ_i T_i + Σ_{i<j} V_{ij}^{(2)} + Σ_{i<j<k} V_{ijk}^{(3)},

where T_i is the single-nucleon kinetic energy, V^{(2)} is a realistic two-nucleon interaction containing both short-range repulsion and intermediate/long-range attraction, and V^{(3)} is a genuine three-nucleon interaction (e.g. of the Fujita–Miyazawa type, arising from intermediate Δ-isobar excitation in two-pion exchange). Suppose the nucleus lies at the neutron (or proton) drip line, meaning that the separation energy of the last nucleon(s) is positive but small enough that coupling to the single-particle continuum is non-negligible.

Formulate, and analyze, a microscopic many-body framework that simultaneously incorporates:

  (i) short-range nucleon–nucleon correlations induced by the hard core of V^{(2)};
  (ii) long-range collective/many-body correlations involving particle–hole excitations into the continuum (resonant and non-resonant scattering states);
  (iii) pairing correlations among weakly bound nucleons; and
  (iv) the three-body force V^{(3)}.

Within this framework, address the following:

(a) Anti-halo effect. Let ρ_n(r) denote the one-body density of the valence weakly bound neutrons, and let ⟨r^2⟩^{1/2} be its rms radius. Determine, as a function of the pairing gap Δ and the single-particle separation energy ε, whether switching on the pairing interaction reduces ⟨r^2⟩^{1/2} relative to the unpaired (Hartree–Fock) value. In particular, identify the regime (in Δ, ε, and orbital angular momentum ℓ of the valence orbit) in which pairing produces a localizing "anti-halo" effect versus the regime in which a spatially extended halo persists.

(b) Role of three-body forces. Quantify the extent to which the three-nucleon interaction V^{(3)} shifts the position of the neutron and proton drip lines (i.e., the largest N for fixed Z, and the largest Z for fixed N, with positive one- and two-nucleon separation energies), and the extent to which it modifies halo structure, spatial distributions, and continuum coupling at the drip line.

Provide either rigorous results, controlled approximations, or a precise conjecture with supporting analysis.

Formulate, and analyze, a microscopic many-body framework that simultaneously incorporates:

  (i) short-range nucleon–nucleon correlations induced by the hard core of V^{(2)};
  (ii) long-range collective/many-body correlations involving particle–hole excitations into the continuum (resonant and non-resonant scattering states);
  (iii) pairing correlations among weakly bound nucleons; and
  (iv) the three-body force V^{(3)}.

Within this framework, address the following:

(a) Anti-halo effect. Let ρ_n(r) denote the one-body density of the valence weakly bound neutrons, and let ⟨r^2⟩^{1/2} be its rms radius. Determine, as a function of the pairing gap Δ and the single-particle separation energy ε, whether switching on the pairing interaction reduces ⟨r^2⟩^{1/2} relative to the unpaired (Hartree–Fock) value. In particular, identify the regime (in Δ, ε, and orbital angular momentum ℓ of the valence orbit) in which pairing produces a localizing "anti-halo" effect versus the regime in which a spatially extended halo persists.

(b) Role of three-body forces. Quantify the extent to which the three-nucleon interaction V^{(3)} shifts the position of the neutron and proton drip lines (i.e., the largest N for fixed Z, and the largest Z for fixed N, with positive one- and two-nucleon separation energies), and the extent to which it modifies halo structure, spatial distributions, and continuum coupling at the drip line.

Provide either rigorous results, controlled approximations, or a precise conjecture with supporting analysis.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The microscopic description of drip-line nuclei combining short-range correlations, continuum coupling, pairing, and three-nucleon forces remains an active research frontier. Ab initio approaches (no-core shell model, coupled-cluster, Gorkov–Green's function, in-medium SRG with chiral 2N+3N forces) and Gamow shell-model / continuum-shell-model techniques have made substantial progress, and three-nucleon forces are known to significantly affect drip-line locations (e.g. for oxygen and calcium isotopes). The anti-halo effect of pairing has been demonstrated in specific cases but is not universal. No complete, unified solution exists; the problem is considered open.

Let $\Sigma$ be a closed oriented surface of genus at least $2$, and let $\mathcal{T} = \mathcal{T}(\Sigma)$ denote its Teichmüller space, equipped with the Weil–Petersson symplectic form $\omega_{WP}$. Let $T^*\mathcal{T}$ denote the cotangent bundle of $\mathcal{T}$, equipped with its canonical (Liouville) symplectic form $\omega_{can}$.

Recall two parameterizations of the deformation space $\mathcal{MGH}(\Sigma)$ of maximal globally hyperbolic Cauchy-compact anti-de Sitter (AdS) 3-manifolds homeomorphic to $\Sigma\times\mathbb{R}$:

(i) (Krasnov–Schlenker) Each $M\in\mathcal{MGH}(\Sigma)$ contains a unique embedded maximal (mean-curvature-zero) Cauchy surface; the induced conformal class $c$ on $\Sigma$ together with the holomorphic quadratic differential $q$ associated with the second fundamental form yields a parameterization $\mathcal{MGH}(\Sigma) \to T^*\mathcal{T}$, $M \mapsto (c, q)$.

(ii) (Mess) The holonomy of $M$ decomposes into a pair of Fuchsian representations whose quotients are two hyperbolic surfaces, giving $\mathcal{MGH}(\Sigma) \to \mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}$, $M\mapsto (m_\ell, m_r)$.

Composing the inverse of (i) with (ii) defines a homeomorphism
$$\varphi: T^*\mathcal{T} \longrightarrow \mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}.$$

Question: Is $\varphi$ symplectic? Equivalently, does there exist a nonzero constant $C$ such that
$$\varphi^*\bigl(\pi_1^*\omega_{WP} - \pi_2^*\omega_{WP}\bigr) = C\,\omega_{can}$$
on $T^*\mathcal{T}$, where $\pi_1,\pi_2:\mathcal{T}\times\mathcal{T}\to\mathcal{T}$ are the two projections?

The question appears to have been answered affirmatively. Mazzoli, Seppi, and Tamburelli (arXiv:2107.10363, "Para-hyperKähler geometry of the deformation space of MGHC anti-de Sitter three-manifolds," published in J. Geom. Anal., 2024) develop a para-hyperKähler structure on the deformation space MGH(Σ) that simultaneously incorporates the Mess identification with T×T (carrying the difference of Weil-Petersson forms) and the Krasnov-Schlenker identification with T*T (carrying the canonical cotangent symplectic form), implying that the map φ is symplectic up to a constant. An analogous statement for the universal Weil-Petersson Teichmüller space is established in arXiv:2412.06498.

Consider an atomic nucleus in the medium- to heavy-mass region (mass number A in roughly the range 60–250) lying close to the neutron drip line, i.e., having so large a neutron-to-proton ratio N/Z that the neutron Fermi level is nearly at zero binding energy. In such systems several weakly bound single-particle orbitals can be simultaneously occupied by many neutrons, the spatial extent of the neutron density exceeds that of the proton density (forming a neutron skin or halo), and the neutron and proton Fermi momenta k_F^(n) and k_F^(p) differ substantially.

(a) Identify and characterize the new many-body correlations (e.g., pairing among loosely bound orbitals, di-neutron correlations, continuum coupling effects) and the new collective excitation modes (e.g., soft dipole / pygmy modes, novel isovector or compressional modes) that should arise specifically because of the large neutron excess and the proximity of several orbitals to the continuum threshold.

(b) Determine whether the strong neutron–proton asymmetry causes the low-lying collective dynamics to depart from the predominantly isoscalar pattern familiar in β-stable nuclei, and in particular whether it yields collective modes in which the excess neutrons oscillate (partly) independently of the proton–neutron core, producing genuine "decoupled" neutron collective motion distinct from the standard isovector giant dipole resonance.

Provide a quantitative theoretical prediction of the existence, energy, transition strengths, and microscopic structure of such modes, together with criteria distinguishing them from known collective excitations in stable nuclei.

Let $\mathbb{H}^2$ denote the hyperbolic plane (the Poincaré disk model), with ideal boundary at infinity $S^1 = \partial_\infty \mathbb{H}^2$. A homeomorphism $\psi : S^1 \to S^1$ is called quasisymmetric if there exists $M \geq 1$ such that for every triple of distinct points $a,b,c \in S^1$ with $|a-b|=|b-c|$ (in arc length on the circle), one has $\tfrac{1}{M} \leq \tfrac{|\psi(a)-\psi(b)|}{|\psi(b)-\psi(c)|} \leq M$. A diffeomorphism $\varphi : \mathbb{H}^2 \to \mathbb{H}^2$ is harmonic if it is a critical point of the Dirichlet energy with respect to the hyperbolic metric (equivalently, its tension field vanishes), and quasiconformal if there exists $K \geq 1$ such that the dilatation $\frac{|\partial_z \varphi| + |\partial_{\bar z}\varphi|}{|\partial_z\varphi|-|\partial_{\bar z}\varphi|} \leq K$ almost everywhere.

Question: Given an orientation-preserving quasisymmetric homeomorphism $\psi : S^1 \to S^1$, does there exist a unique quasiconformal harmonic diffeomorphism $\varphi : \mathbb{H}^2 \to \mathbb{H}^2$ which extends continuously to $\overline{\mathbb{H}^2} \cup S^1$ with boundary restriction equal to $\psi$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

This is the Schoen conjecture in dimension 2. Existence was established by V. Markovic (J. Amer. Math. Soc., 2017), who proved that every quasisymmetric homeomorphism of $S^1$ admits a quasiconformal harmonic extension to $\mathbb{H}^2$. Uniqueness had been established earlier (Li–Tam, and others). Thus the question is affirmatively resolved.

A halo nucleus is a weakly bound nuclear system whose ground state can be modeled as a tightly bound core with one or more loosely bound valence nucleons forming an extended spatial distribution. In Coulomb dissociation, a halo projectile passes by a high-Z target and is excited by the time-dependent Coulomb field into the continuum, releasing its valence nucleon(s).

For a one-neutron halo nucleus, the low-energy electric-dipole (E1) strength distribution measured in Coulomb dissociation is well described as a single-particle transition of the valence neutron from its weakly bound bound-state orbital to low-energy continuum orbitals of the core+neutron system, with the differential cross section determined by the corresponding dB(E1)/dE strength function.

For a two-neutron halo nucleus (a Borromean three-body system consisting of a core C and two valence neutrons n_1, n_2, in which no two-body subsystem is bound), the two valence neutrons may be spatially and dynamically correlated (e.g., a "dineutron" configuration versus a "cigar"-like configuration, plus final-state n-n and n-C interactions in the continuum).

Develop a theoretical description of the Coulomb dissociation cross section of a two-neutron halo nucleus that incorporates the n-n correlation in both the initial bound state and the three-body continuum final state. Specifically:

(a) Define a framework that expresses the differential dissociation cross section, and in particular the low-lying E1 strength distribution dB(E1)/dE_x and the invariant-mass / relative-energy spectra of the (n,n) and (C,2n) subsystems, in terms of a correlated three-body wave function of the projectile and a correlated three-body continuum final state.

(b) Determine the role of the two-neutron correlation: quantify how the shape, magnitude, and energy location of the soft E1 strength and of the n-n and C-2n relative-energy distributions depend on the presence and form of n-n correlations (including pairing and final-state interactions) versus an uncorrelated independent-particle treatment.

(c) Identify observables in Coulomb dissociation that uniquely fix the form of the two-neutron correlation in the halo ground state and in the dissociation process.

Consider the three-dimensional anti-de Sitter space $\mathrm{AdS}^3$, the Lorentzian symmetric space of constant sectional curvature $-1$, and its conformal boundary at infinity $\partial_\infty \mathrm{AdS}^3$, which contains a distinguished family of projective lines isomorphic to $\mathbb{RP}^1$. Let $\phi : \mathbb{RP}^1 \to \mathbb{RP}^1$ be a quasisymmetric homeomorphism, and let $\Lambda \subset \partial_\infty \mathrm{AdS}^3$ denote the graph of $\phi$, regarded as an acausal topological circle in the boundary. Let $C \subset \mathrm{AdS}^3$ be the convex hull of $\Lambda$, and let $D \subset \mathrm{AdS}^3$ be the associated domain of dependence (the maximal globally hyperbolic open region admitting $\Lambda$ as boundary at infinity).

A spacelike surface $\Sigma \subset D$ is said to have constant mean curvature (CMC) if its mean curvature with respect to the induced Lorentzian normal is constant on $\Sigma$, and its principal curvatures are uniformly bounded if the eigenvalues of its shape operator are bounded by a constant independent of the point.

Question: Does there exist a unique foliation of $D$ by spacelike CMC surfaces, each with uniformly bounded principal curvatures and asymptotic boundary equal to $\Lambda$, such that the value of the mean curvature parametrizes the leaves?

representations.normalized:
In the framework of nuclear structure, consider neutron-rich nuclei whose neutron-to-proton ratio is large enough that a low-density neutron skin develops at the surface. In the electric-dipole (E1) response of such nuclei, in addition to the well-known isovector giant dipole resonance, additional low-energy E1 strength is observed below or at the particle-emission threshold; this concentration of strength is known as the pygmy dipole resonance (PDR).

Determine the physical nature of the pygmy dipole resonance in neutron-rich nuclei, in particular as the neutron separation energy decreases toward the neutron drip line. Specifically:

(a) Quantify the degree of collectivity of the low-energy E1 strength: to what extent do many nucleons contribute coherently to these excitations, both in the isoscalar and isovector channels?

(b) Identify the microscopic mechanism that generates the PDR. Possibilities to be discriminated include (i) a coherent vibration of the neutron skin against an essentially inert isospin-saturated core, (ii) a superposition of weakly collective single-particle excitations of loosely bound neutrons, and (iii) a mode whose structure is strongly shaped by pairing and di-neutron correlations in the dilute neutron skin.

(c) Determine how the PDR connects, as one approaches the drip line, to the soft low-energy dipole mode that emerges in nuclei containing very weakly bound neutrons (halo-like systems), and whether these are continuously related manifestations of the same underlying excitation or qualitatively distinct modes.

Provide a reliable theoretical description and quantitative prediction (energy centroid, transition densities, B(E1) distribution, and collectivity measures) capable of discriminating among (i)–(iii) and reproducing systematic data along isotopic chains toward the neutron drip line.

Possibilities to be discriminated include (i) a coherent vibration of the neutron skin against an essentially inert isospin-saturated core, (ii) a superposition of weakly collective single-particle excitations of loosely bound neutrons, and (iii) a mode whose structure is strongly shaped by pairing and di-neutron correlations in the dilute neutron skin.

(c) Determine how the PDR connects, as one approaches the drip line, to the soft low-energy dipole mode that emerges in nuclei containing very weakly bound neutrons (halo-like systems), and whether these are continuously related manifestations of the same underlying excitation or qualitatively distinct modes.

Provide a reliable theoretical description and quantitative prediction (energy centroid, transition densities, B(E1) distribution, and collectivity measures) capable of discriminating among (i)–(iii) and reproducing systematic data along isotopic chains toward the neutron drip line.

Recent reviews and conference contributions (e.g., a 2023 Progress in Particle and Nuclear Physics review on pygmy resonances and 2024 talks) emphasize that the collectivity of the PDR remains strongly debated, that no coherent description of its nature has yet been achieved, and that recent results challenge the simple "neutron-skin-against-core" picture. The connection to soft dipole modes near the drip line and the role of pairing/di-neutron correlations are still active research questions, indicating the problem remains open.

Develop an extension of the nuclear energy density functional (an energy functional E[ρ_n, ρ_p, τ, J, ...] of neutron and proton densities and associated currents whose minimization yields ground-state binding energies, radii, and pairing properties of finite nuclei) that is reliable for predicting nuclei at both the proton and neutron drip lines. The extension must satisfy the following requirements:

(a) Wigner energy. For nuclei with equal neutron and proton numbers (N = Z), there is an additional binding contribution, known as the Wigner energy, which is not reproduced by standard energy density functionals containing only isovector (T = 1) pairing and conventional Skyrme- or Gogny-type particle–hole channels. Construct a functional that quantitatively reproduces this extra binding near the proton drip line, and decide whether incorporating an explicit isoscalar (T = 0) neutron–proton pairing channel is necessary and sufficient to account for it.

(b) Low-density regime. Near the drip lines nucleonic matter exhibits clustering (e.g. α-like or dineutron correlations) at low densities, for which the underlying many-body physics is not fully constrained. Provide a parameterization of the functional in the low-density limit consistent with available constraints (nuclear matter equation of state at subsaturation densities, halo and weakly bound systems).

(c) High-density regime. The functional must remain physically meaningful at densities above saturation, where the many-body interaction is poorly known, in such a way that empirical data on finite nuclei near the drip lines can be used to constrain its form without spurious instabilities.

State explicitly the analytic form of the proposed functional, prove that its minimization is well-defined, and demonstrate via fits to measured masses and separation energies that it predicts both drip lines with controlled, quantified theoretical uncertainty.

representations.normalized:
Let $S$ be a closed orientable surface of genus at least $2$, and let $M = S \times \mathbb{R}$. A globally hyperbolic maximal compact (GHMC) anti–de Sitter structure on $M$ is a maximal Lorentzian structure of constant curvature $-1$ that is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy surface diffeomorphic to $S$. Such a structure admits a nonempty inclusion-minimal compact totally convex subset $C(h)$, the convex core, whose topological boundary (when $h$ is not Fuchsian) consists of two pleated surfaces, each carrying a transverse measured geodesic lamination on $S$, called the upper and lower measured bending laminations $\beta_+(h)$ and $\beta_-(h)$.

A weighted multicurve on $S$ is a finite formal sum $l = \sum_i a_i \gamma_i$ where the $\gamma_i$ are pairwise disjoint simple closed geodesics on $S$ and $a_i > 0$; it is regarded as a measured lamination. Two measured laminations $l_-, l_+$ on $S$ are said to fill $S$ if for every nontrivial simple closed curve $c$ on $S$, $i(l_-, c) + i(l_+, c) > 0$.

Question: Given any two weighted multicurves $l_-$ and $l_+$ on $S$ that together fill $S$, does there exist a unique (up to isotopy) GHMC anti–de Sitter structure $h$ on $M$ such that $\beta_-(h) = l_-$ and $\beta_+(h) = l_+$?

Existence of a GHMC AdS structure realizing a given pair of filling measured laminations as bending laminations of the convex core boundary was established by Bonsante–Schlenker. Uniqueness has been proved only in partial settings: near the Fuchsian locus (e.g., recent work of Prosanov, 2025–2026) and for sufficiently small filling pairs $t\lambda, t\mu$ with $t$ small. The general uniqueness question for arbitrary filling weighted multicurves appears to remain open.

In nuclear density functional theory, a self-bound nucleus is described by an energy density functional whose total energy is decomposed into a particle-hole part depending on the neutron and proton normal densities ρ_n(r), ρ_p(r) and a pairing (particle-particle) part depending additionally on the neutron and proton pair (anomalous) densities ρ̃_n(r), ρ̃_p(r). Determine the functional form of the pairing energy contribution

   E_pair[ρ_n, ρ_p, ρ̃_n, ρ̃_p]

such that the resulting pair correlations are described consistently and accurately across the entire density range relevant to finite nuclei: from the very low-density regime of dilute neutron matter, where strong-coupling effects (large scattering length, possible BCS–BEC crossover behavior) become important, up to ordinary nuclear saturation density ρ_0 ≈ 0.16 fm⁻³. The functional must be quantitatively reliable for nuclei near the neutron and proton drip lines, where the coupling between bound states and the continuum mediated by pairing is essential. Identify a closed-form expression (or a systematic construction) for E_pair[ρ_n, ρ_p, ρ̃_n, ρ̃_p] meeting these requirements.

Consider a self-bound quantum many-body system of A nucleons (protons and neutrons) described within a nuclear energy-density functional framework. Let ρ_q(x,t) denote the normal one-body density and ρ̃_q(x,t) the pairing (anomalous) density for q ∈ {n,p}, and let E_pair[ρ_n, ρ_p, ρ̃_n, ρ̃_p] be a pairing energy functional included in the total energy. The time-dependent Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov (TDHFB) equations are the equations of motion for the generalized density matrix obtained by variation of the total energy functional, generalizing time-dependent Hartree–Fock to incorporate pair correlations.

Formulate and solve the following problems:

(a) Develop a numerical and analytical framework to solve the TDHFB equations for medium-mass and heavy weakly-bound (drip-line) nuclei, with boundary conditions that enforce the correct asymptotic behavior of the quasiparticle wave functions in the continuum (including outgoing-wave conditions for emitted particles).

(b) Extend time-dependent many-body dynamics so that nuclear reactions producing more than three outgoing fragments/particles can be treated, including the proper continuum asymptotic behavior of the many-body wave function.

(c) Within time-dependent density functional theory (TDDFT) for nuclei, give a prescription for computing exclusive (channel-resolved) reaction cross sections that does not suffer from spurious cross-channel correlations of the type known to occur when one extracts exclusive cross sections directly from a single TDHF trajectory.

Prove that the proposed framework is well-posed, derive the associated cross-section formulas, and establish their correctness (absence of spurious cross-channel correlations and correct asymptotics).

Setup. An anti-de Sitter (AdS) 3-manifold is a Lorentzian 3-manifold of constant sectional curvature −1. A tachyon singularity along a smooth space-like curve is a cone-type Lorentzian singularity modeled, in suitable local coordinates, on the quotient of a wedge of AdS_3 by a space-like rotation; the "tachyon mass" is the cone angle parameter measuring the rotational defect transverse to the singular curve.

Let N be a closed 3-manifold equipped with an AdS structure that has tachyon singularities along a link L ⊂ N (the singular locus is a disjoint union of finitely many simple closed space-like curves), with prescribed tachyon masses m_1, …, m_k along the components of L. Assume that the complement N ∖ L is atoroidal, i.e. every embedded incompressible torus in N ∖ L is boundary-parallel.

Question. Under the above atoroidal hypothesis, is the AdS structure on N rigid relative to the tachyon masses? Equivalently, is every continuous deformation of the singular AdS structure on N that preserves the tachyon masses (m_1, …, m_k) trivial up to isotopy?

Develop a quasiparticle random phase approximation (QRPA) for atomic nuclei near the drip lines that simultaneously incorporates: (i) pairing correlations on top of a Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov (HFB) ground state, (ii) an explicit treatment of single-particle continuum states, (iii) intrinsic shape (axial and/or triaxial) deformation, and (iv) full self-consistency of all residual fields, namely the residual particle–hole, particle–particle, and rearrangement interactions derived from the same effective Hamiltonian/energy density functional used to obtain the HFB ground state.

The formal task is to formulate the linear response of the time-dependent HFB equations under an external perturbing field in such a way that the formally infinite quasiparticle phase space arising when continuum orbitals are kept explicitly is handled rigorously (e.g., via Green's function / response-function techniques in coordinate space, exact boundary conditions for the outgoing continuum, or controlled discretization). The construction must be applicable both to finite deformed nuclei and to inhomogeneous nuclear matter (e.g., neutron-star inner crust pasta phases).

The accompanying computational task is to design numerical methods and algorithms for solving the resulting large-scale QRPA problem that are suitable for massively parallel computation, and to demonstrate convergence and full self-consistency of the residual interaction with the underlying HFB mean field and pairing field.

Question: Construct such a fully self-consistent deformed continuum QRPA framework, including its mathematical formulation, its numerical/algorithmic realization, and a demonstration of its applicability to drip-line nuclei and to inhomogeneous nuclear matter.

Substantial progress exists: continuum QRPA on coordinate-space HFB has been developed for spherical nuclei, and deformed QRPA with discretized continuum and pairing has been applied to neutron-rich Mg isotopes. An AdS structure on $N$ with a tachyon singularity of mass $m>0$ along $\Sigma$ is, by definition, a smooth AdS structure on $N \setminus \Sigma$ whose geodesic completion is homeomorphic to $N$, such that the metric near each component of $\Sigma$ is locally modeled on the Lorentzian cone manifold obtained from $\mathrm{AdS}^3$ by a Lorentzian holonomy fixing a spacelike geodesic, with rotation parameter (mass) $m$ along that geodesic; equivalently, the singular locus is a spacelike geodesic and a meridian linking $\Sigma$ has hyperbolic holonomy with translation length $m$.

Question: Given the pair $(N,\Sigma)$ as above, do there exist AdS structures on $N$ with tachyon singularities along $\Sigma$ that are arbitrarily close (in the deformation space of $(G,X)$-structures on $N$) to the given nonsingular AdS structure? What topological conditions on the pair $(N,\Sigma)$ are necessary or sufficient for the existence of such deformations? What geometric conditions (e.g. on the homotopy class or on the geometry of $\Sigma$ inside $N$) are necessary or sufficient?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question asks for a general criterion (topological/geometric conditions on $(N,\Sigma)$) under which a nonsingular AdS structure on a closed 3-manifold can be deformed to nearby AdS structures with tachyon singularities along a prescribed link. Existing work establishes such deformations in specific examples (e.g. unit tangent bundles of $(2,m,m)$ triangle orbifolds for $m\ge 5$, via geometric transitions through half-pipe geometry from hyperbolic cone structures), but no general necessary/sufficient conditions on $(N,\Sigma)$ have been found in the literature surveyed. The problem appears to remain open in full generality.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) exhibit a prompt high-energy emission phase whose spectrum is typically well fit by a smoothly broken power law with a non-thermal appearance, but whose underlying radiative origin remains uncertain. Determine the physical radiation process that produces the prompt high-energy emission in GRBs. Specifically:

(a) Identify which mechanism is responsible for the non-thermal component of the prompt spectrum among the following candidates:
 (i) optically thin synchrotron radiation by relativistic electrons in a tangled or ordered magnetic field within the relativistic jet,
 (ii) jitter radiation, i.e. radiation by relativistic electrons traversing small-scale, randomly oriented magnetic field fluctuations whose coherence length is much smaller than the electron Larmor radius, or
 (iii) synchrotron self-Compton emission, in which synchrotron photons are inverse-Compton scattered by the same population of relativistic electrons.

(b) Determine whether the prompt emission spectrum also contains a photospheric thermal component, namely (quasi-)blackbody radiation released at the Thomson photosphere of the relativistic outflow, in addition to the non-thermal component identified in (a).

Provide a definitive identification of the dominant non-thermal mechanism and decide the presence (or absence) of a thermal photospheric contribution in the prompt emission of GRBs.

Let $S$ be a closed orientable surface of genus at least $2$, and let $\widetilde{S}$ denote its universal cover. Let $\rho_l, \rho_r : \pi_1(S) \to \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ be two quasi-Fuchsian representations.

Let $X_{\mathbb{C}}$ denote the complex anti-de Sitter space, defined as $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ equipped with its bi-invariant complex pseudo-Riemannian metric coming from (a complex multiple of) the Killing form, on which $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C}) \times \mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ acts isometrically by left and right multiplication: $(g_l, g_r)\cdot x = g_l \, x \, g_r^{-1}$. A smooth embedding $f : \widetilde{S} \to X_{\mathbb{C}}$ is called $(\rho_l, \rho_r)$-equivariant if
$$ f(\gamma \cdot p) = \rho_l(\gamma) \, f(p) \, \rho_r(\gamma)^{-1} \quad \text{for all } \gamma \in \pi_1(S), \ p \in \widetilde{S},$$
and is called space-like if the pullback by $f$ of the (real part of the) ambient pseudo-Riemannian metric is a Riemannian metric on $\widetilde{S}$.

(a) Does there always exist a $(\rho_l, \rho_r)$-equivariant space-like embedding $f : \widetilde{S} \to X_{\mathbb{C}}$?

(b) When such an embedding exists, can it be chosen so that the induced metric on $\widetilde{S}$ has constant curvature?
