Background. Classically, an equivariant map algebra is constructed from the following data: a scheme (or algebraic variety) X, a finite-dimensional Lie algebra g over a field of characteristic zero, and a finite group Γ acting on both X (by automorphisms of schemes) and g (by Lie algebra automorphisms). The equivariant map algebra is the Lie algebra

  M(X,g)^Γ = { f : X → g : f is a regular morphism and f(γ·x) = γ·f(x) for all γ ∈ Γ, x ∈ X },

with pointwise Lie bracket. Its finite-dimensional irreducible representations and extension theory have been classified in the algebraic setting.

Problem. Develop an analytic counterpart of this theory. Specifically, let X be a (real or complex) Banach manifold, let a be a Banach algebra (or, more generally, a Banach Lie algebra), and let Γ be a (topological, possibly compact or finite) group acting smoothly on X and by continuous algebra automorphisms on a. Consider the space

  C^∞_Γ(X, a) = { f : X → a : f is differentiable (in the Banach-manifold sense) and Γ-equivariant },

equipped with pointwise operations and a suitable topology making it a topological Banach–Lie algebra (or topological algebra).

(1) Construct the analytic theory of such equivariant map algebras: define an appropriate category, identify natural topologies, and establish basic structural properties (e.g. ideals, central extensions, completions).

(2) Develop a representation theory for C^∞_Γ(X, a): introduce a class of admissible (continuous, topological, or Banach) representations, prove an analogue of the evaluation-representation construction, and classify the irreducible objects in this class under reasonable assumptions on X, a, and Γ.

(3) Compare the resulting analytic theory with the known algebraic theory of equivariant map algebras when X is taken to be an algebraic variety (regarded as a Banach manifold) and a a finite-dimensional Lie algebra.

Consider a phase-field model of solidification consisting of a non-conserved order parameter \(\varphi(x,t)\) (distinguishing solid and liquid phases) coupled to a diffusion field \(u(x,t)\) (a dimensionless temperature or supersaturation). A standard formulation takes the coupled stochastic evolution equations
\[
\tau\,\partial_t \varphi = W^2\nabla^2\varphi - f'(\varphi) - \lambda\, g'(\varphi)\,u + \eta_\varphi(x,t),
\]
\[
\partial_t u = D\nabla^2 u + \tfrac{1}{2}\partial_t h(\varphi) + \nabla\!\cdot \boldsymbol{\eta}_u(x,t),
\]
where \(W\) sets the diffuse-interface thickness, \(\tau\) is a relaxation time, \(D\) is a diffusion coefficient, \(f\) is a symmetric double-well potential, and \(g,h\) are standard interpolation functions. The noises \(\eta_\varphi\) and \(\boldsymbol{\eta}_u\) are Gaussian with covariances chosen to satisfy a fluctuation–dissipation relation at temperature \(T\), regularized by a microscopic cutoff length \(a\ll W\).

In the regime where \(W\) is comparable to the capillary length \(d_0\), the dimensionless fluctuation amplitudes \(F_\varphi := T/(W^{d}\,\text{(energy scale)})\) and the analogous \(F_u\) are of order unity, so the bare parameters \((W,\tau,\lambda,D,f,g,h)\) are renormalized by the noise into effective (physical) parameters \((W_{\rm eff},\tau_{\rm eff},\lambda_{\rm eff},D_{\rm eff},\dots)\) that depend on the cutoff \(a\). Moreover, the deterministic sharp-interface limit \(W\to 0\) must be reformulated because the cutoff \(a\) introduces an additional length scale.

Problem. Construct a quantitative stochastic phase-field model, calibrated to a given material with prescribed bulk thermodynamics, interface free energy, kinetic coefficient, and nucleation barrier, satisfying all of the following:
(i) An explicit renormalization map relating the bare parameters \((W,\tau,\lambda,D,f,g,h;a)\) to physically measured (renormalized) bulk free-energy density, interface stiffness, mobility, and nucleation rate, valid when \(F_\varphi, F_u = O(1)\).
(ii) A modified asymptotic (thin-interface) analysis, taking simultaneous limits of \(W,a\to 0\) with a controlled ratio \(a/W\), that recovers the correct stochastic sharp-interface free-boundary problem (Gibbs–Thomson condition with fluctuating curvature-driven kinetics and a noisy Stefan condition) with material-specific coefficients.
(iii) Quantitative agreement, in this asymptotic regime, between the model's predictions for equilibrium interface fluctuations (capillary-wave spectrum), bulk thermal fluctuations, and homogeneous/heterogeneous nucleation rates and the corresponding values for the target material.

Provide such a construction, or prove obstructions showing that no choice of \((f,g,h,\lambda,\tau,W,a)\) within this class can simultaneously achieve (i)–(iii).

Let $X$ be an affine scheme of finite type over $\mathbb{C}$, let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over $\mathbb{C}$, and let $\Gamma$ be a finite group acting on both $X$ (by automorphisms of schemes) and $\mathfrak{g}$ (by Lie algebra automorphisms). The equivariant map algebra is defined as
$$M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma} = \{\, \alpha \in \mathfrak{g} \otimes_{\mathbb{C}} \mathcal{O}(X) : (\gamma\cdot\alpha) = \alpha \text{ for all } \gamma \in \Gamma\,\},$$
with the pointwise Lie bracket, where $\Gamma$ acts diagonally on $\mathfrak{g} \otimes \mathcal{O}(X)$.

A multiloop algebra is the special case where $X = (\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n}$, $\Gamma = \mathbb{Z}/m_1\mathbb{Z} \times \cdots \times \mathbb{Z}/m_n\mathbb{Z}$ acts on $X$ by roots of unity, and $\Gamma$ acts on $\mathfrak{g}$ by commuting finite-order automorphisms.

Problem: Classify equivariant map algebras $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$ up to isomorphism of Lie algebras in substantial generality. Concretely:

1. Generalize the known isomorphism classification of (twisted) loop algebras (corresponding to $n=1$) to all multiloop algebras with $n \geq 2$, giving necessary and sufficient conditions on the data $(\mathfrak{g}_1, m_1^{(1)},\dots,m_n^{(1)}, \sigma_1^{(1)},\dots,\sigma_n^{(1)})$ and $(\mathfrak{g}_2, m_1^{(2)},\dots,m_n^{(2)}, \sigma_1^{(2)},\dots,\sigma_n^{(2)})$ for the corresponding multiloop algebras to be isomorphic as Lie algebras.

2. Extend the classification beyond the multiloop case to general equivariant map algebras $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$, providing invariants of the triple $(X,\mathfrak{g},\Gamma)$ that determine $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$ up to isomorphism.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The isomorphism problem for equivariant map algebras is highlighted as a fundamental open problem in surveys on the topic. While the isomorphism classification is known for (twisted) loop algebras and certain multiloop cases, no general classification of equivariant map algebras $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^\Gamma$ up to isomorphism is available; the data $(X,\mathfrak{g},\Gamma)$ is known to not be uniquely determined by the algebra in general, and the problem remains open in the multiloop case for $n\geq 2$ and beyond.

Let $\Gamma$ be a group acting on an algebraic variety (or scheme) $X$ and on a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{a}$ (over a field $k$ of characteristic zero) by automorphisms. Let $M(X,\mathfrak{a}) = \mathcal{O}(X) \otimes_k \mathfrak{a}$ denote the Lie algebra of regular maps from $X$ to $\mathfrak{a}$, equipped with the diagonal $\Gamma$-action $(\gamma \cdot f)(x) = \gamma \cdot f(\gamma^{-1} x)$. The equivariant map algebra is the fixed-point Lie subalgebra
$$M(X,\mathfrak{a})^{\Gamma} = \{ f \in M(X,\mathfrak{a}) : \gamma \cdot f = f \text{ for all } \gamma \in \Gamma\}.$$
This class includes (twisted) loop algebras, (twisted) multiloop algebras, current algebras, and generalized current algebras as special cases.

Problem: Determine the group of Lie algebra automorphisms $\mathrm{Aut}(M(X,\mathfrak{a})^{\Gamma})$ in broad generality. In particular, give an explicit description of this automorphism group for the twisted loop algebras (where $X = \mathbb{G}_m$, $\mathfrak{a}$ is a finite-dimensional simple Lie algebra, and $\Gamma$ is a finite cyclic group acting by a diagram automorphism) and for the multiloop algebras (where $X = (\mathbb{G}_m)^n$ and $\Gamma = (\mathbb{Z}/m_1\mathbb{Z}) \times \cdots \times (\mathbb{Z}/m_n\mathbb{Z})$ acts by commuting finite-order automorphisms), and relate these descriptions to the classification of equivariant map algebras up to isomorphism.

representations.normalized:
Let $X$ be a scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic zero, let $\mathfrak{a}$ be a finite-dimensional associative $k$-algebra, and let $\Gamma$ be a finite group acting on $X$ by automorphisms of schemes and on $\mathfrak{a}$ by $k$-algebra automorphisms. The equivariant map algebra is
$$M(X,\mathfrak{a})^\Gamma = \{\,\alpha\colon X \to \mathfrak{a} \mid \alpha \text{ is a regular morphism and } \alpha(\gamma\cdot x) = \gamma\cdot\alpha(x)\ \forall\gamma\in\Gamma,\ x\in X\,\},$$
viewed as an associative algebra under pointwise multiplication.

For a finite set $\mathbf{x} = \{x_1,\dots,x_n\}$ of $\Gamma$-orbits in the rational points of $X$, with chosen representatives, evaluation gives an algebra homomorphism
$$\mathrm{ev}_{\mathbf{x}}\colon M(X,\mathfrak{a})^\Gamma \longrightarrow \mathfrak{a}^{\Gamma_{x_1}}\otimes\cdots\otimes \mathfrak{a}^{\Gamma_{x_n}},$$
where $\Gamma_{x_i}$ is the stabilizer of $x_i$.

Now assume in addition that $\mathfrak{a}$ carries the structure of an associative bialgebra, with coproduct $\Delta\colon \mathfrak{a}\to \mathfrak{a}\otimes \mathfrak{a}$ compatible with the $\Gamma$-action. Using $\Delta$ together with the evaluation map at multiple orbits, one can define a class of "multi-orbit evaluation representations" of $M(X,\mathfrak{a})^\Gamma$: given a finite-dimensional $\mathfrak{a}$-module $V$, pull $V$ back along the iterated coproduct followed by evaluation at $\mathbf{x}$ to obtain an $M(X,\mathfrak{a})^\Gamma$-module structure on $V$.

Problem: Construct this family of multi-orbit evaluation representations precisely, determine their structure (in particular their decomposition, irreducibility criteria, isomorphism classes, and extension/Ext groups), and describe the role they play in classifying the finite-dimensional representations of $M(X,\mathfrak{a})^\Gamma$ when $\mathfrak{a}$ is an associative bialgebra.

Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, let X be a scheme of finite type over k with coordinate ring A, let g be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over k, and let Γ be a group acting on both X and g by automorphisms. The equivariant map algebra is

   M(X,g)^Γ = (g ⊗_k A)^Γ = { x ∈ g ⊗_k A : (γ·x) = x for all γ ∈ Γ },

with Lie bracket induced from g. Assume that with respect to a chosen triangular decomposition (or weight grading) one has well-defined notions of global Weyl modules W(λ) and local Weyl modules W_loc(λ) attached to dominant integral weights λ, generalizing the construction known for current algebras g ⊗ k[t] and loop algebras g ⊗ k[t,t^{-1}].

Address the following:

(a) For an arbitrary equivariant map algebra M(X,g)^Γ as above (in particular, beyond the cases where g is simple, X is affine of finite type, and Γ is abelian acting freely on X), determine the length, the dimension, and the graded (or weighted) character of each local Weyl module W_loc(λ).

(b) Formulate and decide a suitable analog of BGG reciprocity in this setting: namely, identify a category of M(X,g)^Γ-modules possessing a notion of standard (Weyl) modules Δ(λ) and simple/costandard modules L(μ), and determine whether the multiplicities [P(μ) : Δ(λ)] of standard modules in projective covers (or their analogs) coincide with the multiplicities [Δ(λ) : L(μ)] of simples in standard modules, in the form

   [P(μ) : Δ(λ)] = [Δ(λ) : L(μ)],

generalizing the BGG reciprocity established for current algebras and certain map algebras.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Significant progress has been made: local Weyl modules for equivariant map algebras with free abelian group actions were studied (Feigin–Loktev type results, arXiv:1103.5766), and global Weyl modules for equivariant map algebras were developed (arXiv:1303.4437, IMRN 2015). Extensions to equivariant map Lie superalgebras appeared recently (arXiv:2511.01631), and BGG reciprocity has been established for current algebras (arXiv:1307.1440). However, a fully general theory for arbitrary equivariant map algebras (general schemes/groups, complete length/dimension/character results, and a fully general BGG reciprocity) does not appear to be completely settled, so the program is partially solved.

Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over a field $k$ of characteristic $0$, let $A$ be a unital commutative associative $k$-algebra, and let $\Gamma$ be a finite group acting by Lie algebra automorphisms on $\mathfrak{g}$ and by algebra automorphisms on $A$. Let $\Gamma$ act diagonally on the tensor product Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}\otimes A$ (i.e. $\gamma\cdot(x\otimes a)=(\gamma\cdot x)\otimes(\gamma\cdot a)$), and consider the equivariant map algebra
$$M=(\mathfrak{g}\otimes A)^{\Gamma}=\{u\in\mathfrak{g}\otimes A:\gamma\cdot u=u\text{ for all }\gamma\in\Gamma\}.$$
For a perfect Lie algebra $L$ (i.e. $L=[L,L]$), let $\operatorname{uce}(L)\to L$ denote its universal central extension.

Assume $M$ is perfect.

(a) Describe the central extensions of $M$, and in particular determine the universal central extension $\operatorname{uce}(M)=\operatorname{uce}((\mathfrak{g}\otimes A)^{\Gamma})$ explicitly.

(b) The action of $\Gamma$ on $\mathfrak{g}\otimes A$ lifts uniquely to an action of $\Gamma$ on $\operatorname{uce}(\mathfrak{g}\otimes A)$. Determine, in broad generality (i.e. for as wide a class of triples $(\mathfrak{g},A,\Gamma)$ as possible), whether the natural comparison map yields an isomorphism
$$\operatorname{uce}\bigl((\mathfrak{g}\otimes A)^{\Gamma}\bigr)\;\cong\;\bigl(\operatorname{uce}(\mathfrak{g}\otimes A)\bigr)^{\Gamma},$$
and identify hypotheses on $\mathfrak{g}$, $A$, and $\Gamma$ under which this holds or fails.

A population-based metaheuristic optimization algorithm is an iterative stochastic search procedure that maintains, at each step t = 0, 1, 2, ..., a population X_t = (X_t^{(1)}, ..., X_t^{(N)}) of N search agents in a (possibly continuous) search space S, with the joint sequence {X_t}_{t≥0} forming a Markov chain on S^N whose transition kernel encodes the algorithm's selection, variation, and interaction rules. Examples include genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, ant colony optimization, differential evolution, firefly algorithms, cuckoo search, and similar schemes; in each case the individual agent trajectories are not independent Markov chains but interact through the population update rule.

Develop a general mathematical framework for such interacting-Markov-chain population metaheuristics that:

(1) Establishes sufficient conditions on the transition kernel under which the algorithm converges, in a precise probabilistic sense (e.g., almost-sure convergence, convergence in probability, or convergence in distribution of best-so-far value), to the global optimum of a given objective function f : S → ℝ.

(2) Provides quantitative estimates of the rate of convergence — for instance, bounds on P(f(X_t^{best}) - f^* > ε) as a function of t, N, and characteristics of f and of the kernel — applicable broadly to the class of population-based metaheuristics rather than to any single specific algorithm.

The problem is to formulate and prove such a unified convergence and convergence-rate theory for the entire class of population-based metaheuristics with interacting agents.

A metaheuristic algorithm for solving a global optimization problem $\min_{x\in\Omega} f(x)$ (with $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ and $f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$) is an iterative stochastic search procedure that, at each step, generates candidate solutions using two complementary mechanisms:

(i) Local intensification (exploitation): operations that concentrate the search in a neighborhood of currently promising candidates, in order to refine them.

(ii) Global diversification (exploration): operations that spread the search broadly over $\Omega$, in order to discover previously unexplored regions and avoid premature convergence to local minima.

Let a metaheuristic be parameterized by a control $\alpha\in[0,1]$ (or, more generally, by a schedule $\alpha_t$ over iterations $t=1,2,\dots,T$) that quantifies the relative weight given to intensification versus diversification, where $\alpha=0$ corresponds to pure diversification and $\alpha=1$ to pure intensification. Let $\mathcal{F}$ denote a class of objective functions $f$, and let $E_f[\alpha,T]$ denote the expected optimality gap after $T$ iterations of the metaheuristic with control $\alpha$ on objective $f$.

Address the following:

(a) Does there exist, for a sufficiently general class $\mathcal{F}$, an optimal value $\alpha^\star$ (or optimal schedule $\{\alpha_t^\star\}$) that minimizes $\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}} E_f[\alpha,T]$, providing a universally optimal trade-off between local intensification and global diversification?

(b) If such an optimal balance exists, give a constructive characterization of $\alpha^\star$ (or of $\{\alpha_t^\star\}$) and a method by which a metaheuristic algorithm can attain it.

(c) If no such universally optimal balance exists, determine the best achievable trade-off: identify tight bounds on $\inf_{\alpha}\sup_{f\in\mathcal{F}} E_f[\alpha,T]$ and exhibit strategies (possibly adaptive in $f$ or $t$) that attain these bounds.

The question of an optimal exploration–exploitation trade-off in general-purpose metaheuristics is widely regarded as a long-standing open problem. No-Free-Lunch theorems (Wolpert–Macready) imply that no universally optimal balance can exist over all objective functions, but for restricted function classes the question of optimal or near-optimal schedules remains open and is the subject of ongoing research in adaptive and hyper-heuristic methods.

Consider the class of iterative search algorithms for global optimization of an objective function f : X → R on a (possibly large, discrete or continuous) search space X. Such an algorithm produces a sequence of candidate solutions x_1, x_2, ... by repeatedly applying an update rule that may depend on (i) deterministic information derived from previously evaluated points (e.g. gradients, finite differences, or rules exploiting current best solutions), and (ii) random perturbations drawn from some probability distribution. Three idealized regimes can be distinguished: (a) a purely deterministic algorithm, in which the update rule is a deterministic function of the history; (b) a purely random algorithm, in which each new candidate is drawn independently from a fixed distribution on X without using past evaluations; and (c) a hybrid metaheuristic, in which each update is a balanced mixture of a deterministic exploitation component and a stochastic exploration component.

Provide a rigorous theoretical explanation, supported by quantitative bounds, of the following empirical observation: across broad classes of objective functions f (for instance, multimodal functions on bounded domains satisfying mild regularity assumptions), a suitably balanced hybrid algorithm of type (c) converges to a global optimum (or to an ε-approximate global optimum) substantially faster, in terms of expected number of function evaluations, than any algorithm of type (a) or type (b).

More precisely, formulate and prove a theorem of the following form: identify a class F of objective functions and a family H of hybrid algorithms parametrized by a randomization level p ∈ [0,1] (with p = 0 corresponding to purely deterministic and p = 1 to purely random search) such that the expected hitting time T_p(f, ε) to reach an ε-approximate optimum satisfies

   inf_{p ∈ (0,1)} sup_{f ∈ F} E[T_p(f, ε)]  ≪  min{ sup_{f ∈ F} E[T_0(f, ε)],  sup_{f ∈ F} E[T_1(f, ε)] },

and characterize the optimal balance p* and the mechanism by which the interplay between deterministic exploitation and stochastic exploration produces this efficiency gain.

A metaheuristic optimization algorithm is an iterative stochastic procedure that searches a (typically large, discrete or continuous) solution space $\mathcal{S}$ for an approximate optimizer of an objective function $f:\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}$. Such algorithms are typically built from several interacting search components, most notably:

- an exploration (diversification) component, which generates candidate solutions far from the current population so as to broadly sample $\mathcal{S}$;
- an exploitation (intensification) component, which refines promising candidate solutions in a local neighborhood so as to improve objective values;
- and possibly additional components governing selection pressure, memory, randomization, parameter adaptation, etc.

The algorithm's overall performance is widely believed to depend on a suitable balance between these components: too much exploration prevents convergence, while too much exploitation causes premature stagnation in local optima.

Problem. Formulate a quantitative, algorithm-independent framework for measuring the balance among the interacting search components of a metaheuristic algorithm during its execution on a given problem instance. Specifically:

(a) Define a measurable quantity (or family of quantities) $B(t)$, computable from the trajectory of populations $\{P_t\}_{t\ge 0}$ produced by the algorithm and from the objective function $f$, that captures the relative contributions of exploration and exploitation (and any other components) at iteration $t$.

(b) Provide a statistical test, with explicit null hypothesis and rejection criterion, that decides whether a given run (or ensemble of runs) of the algorithm has reached a "proper" balance among its components, in a sense made precise by the framework.

(c) Show that the proposed measure and test are consistent in the following sense: on benchmark families of objective functions where ground-truth optimal balance can be characterized (for example, via theoretical convergence-rate analysis on convex quadratics, on needle-in-a-haystack functions, or on no-free-lunch style ensembles), the measure correctly identifies imbalance and the test has controlled type-I and type-II error rates.

Let X be an infinite-dimensional (real or complex) Banach space. A sequence (e_n)_{n=1}^∞ in a Banach space Y is called a Schauder basis of Y if every y ∈ Y has a unique norm-convergent expansion y = Σ_{n=1}^∞ a_n e_n with scalar coefficients a_n. A quotient of X is a Banach space of the form X/M, where M ⊂ X is a closed linear subspace, equipped with the quotient norm.

Question: Does every infinite-dimensional Banach space X admit a closed subspace M ⊂ X such that the quotient space X/M is infinite-dimensional and possesses a Schauder basis?

Background. The No-Free-Lunch (NFL) theorems for optimization assert, roughly, that when performance is averaged uniformly over all objective functions f : X → Y with X and Y finite, every pair of (non-revisiting) black-box search algorithms has identical average performance under any performance measure depending only on the sequence of observed objective values. NFL theorems are known to hold in this finite single-objective setting and are known to fail in general for continuous infinite search domains.

Now consider the multiobjective setting. Let X be a finite search space and let Y₁, …, Y_k be finite totally ordered value sets (k ≥ 2). A multiobjective problem is a function F : X → Y₁ × ⋯ × Y_k. A black-box multiobjective algorithm A produces, for each F, a sequence of distinct query points x₁, x₂, … ∈ X chosen adaptively based on previously observed vector values F(x₁), …, F(x_{i−1}). Fix a performance measure φ depending only on the sequence of observed value vectors (for example, hypervolume of the dominated region after m steps, or time to first hit the Pareto-optimal set).

Question. Determine whether the following analogue of the NFL theorem holds:

For every pair of black-box multiobjective algorithms A and B, and every such performance measure φ and horizon m,
   Σ_{F : X → Y₁×⋯×Y_k} φ(A, F, m) = Σ_{F : X → Y₁×⋯×Y_k} φ(B, F, m).

If the equality holds, identify the precise hypotheses on the class of problems, on the algorithms, and on φ under which it holds, and describe the implications for the design and comparison of multiobjective optimization algorithms. If the equality fails, characterize natural sub-classes of multiobjective problems (for example, those defined by a fixed Pareto front, by closure under permutation of X, or by a fixed shape of Pareto front) on which an NFL-type identity does or does not hold, and describe the consequences for algorithm development.

The question has been substantially addressed. Corne and Knowles (2003) showed "free leftovers" can exist for multiobjective optimization in the presence of an archiver, indicating NFL does not always hold in the standard multiobjective formulation. Conversely, Service (2010) proved an NFL theorem for multi-objective optimization showing that, with appropriate definitions, the classical NFL identity does extend: NFL holds over the set of multiobjective problems sharing a fixed Pareto front, and more generally over classes structurally closed under permutation. Thus the problem is partially solved: precise hypotheses under which NFL holds or fails for multiobjective optimization have been identified, although a unified picture and full implications for algorithm design continue to be discussed.

A metaheuristic algorithm is a (typically stochastic) iterative procedure A that, given an optimization problem instance P = (f, X) with objective f : X → ℝ on a search space X, produces a sequence of candidate solutions x_1, x_2, … ∈ X aiming to approximate min_{x∈X} f(x). Common empirical measures used to compare two such algorithms A and B on a benchmark family of instances are: (i) the absolute best objective value reached after a fixed budget, and (ii) the number of objective-function evaluations needed to reach a prescribed accuracy.

Develop a formal theoretical framework for comparing the performance of metaheuristic algorithms that goes beyond these empirical measures. Specifically:

1. Propose a mathematically rigorous definition of "performance" of a metaheuristic A on a class C of optimization problems, taking into account stochasticity (e.g., expectations and tail bounds over the algorithm's random choices), convergence rate, solution quality, robustness, and computational cost.

2. Define an agreed set of comparison measures M_1, …, M_k (functionals on pairs (A, C)) such that: (a) each M_i is well-defined and computable or estimable; (b) the measures collectively induce a meaningful preorder on metaheuristic algorithms relative to a problem class; (c) the framework is consistent with no-free-lunch–type results, in the sense that universal dominance across all problem classes is precluded but class-relative dominance is captured.

3. Prove that within this framework one can derive non-trivial theoretical comparison theorems between standard metaheuristics (for example, simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization, differential evolution) on identifiable problem classes.

Provide either such a framework with proofs, or a rigorous argument that no such framework satisfying (1)–(3) can exist.

Recall that for an ordinal $\gamma$, a transfinite Schauder basis of length $\gamma$ for a Banach space $Y$ is a family $(y_\alpha)_{\alpha<\gamma}$ in $Y$ such that every $y\in Y$ admits a unique expansion $y=\sum_{\alpha<\gamma} a_\alpha y_\alpha$ converging in the natural transfinite sense, with the partial-sum projections uniformly bounded by some constant $C\ge 1$.

Determine, as a function of $X$, the supremum of the ordinals $\gamma$ such that some quotient of $X$ admits a transfinite Schauder basis of length $\gamma$. In particular, characterize this supremum for general infinite-dimensional Banach spaces $X$, and decide whether it can always be attained.

Consider the infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system on the lattice $\mathbb{Z}^d$ given, in action–angle variables $(I_j,\phi_j)_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$, by
$$H \;=\; \sum_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d} \omega_j\, I_j \;+\; \varepsilon \sum_{\langle i,j\rangle} f_{i,j}(I_i,I_j;\phi_i,\phi_j),$$
with symplectic form $\sum_j dI_j\wedge d\phi_j$, where:
- the frequencies $(\omega_j)_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ are weakly correlated (e.g. independent and identically distributed in a fixed bounded interval, or otherwise satisfy standard Diophantine-type non-resonance conditions almost surely);
- the perturbation is of short range or finite range, in the sense that the sum runs over pairs $\langle i,j\rangle$ of nearby lattice sites and each $f_{i,j}$ is a real-analytic function of the listed variables;
- $\varepsilon>0$ is sufficiently small.

By an infinite-dimensional KAM torus we mean an invariant torus of the perturbed flow, parametrised by all angle variables $(\phi_j)_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d}\in\mathbb{T}^{\mathbb{Z}^d}$, on which the dynamics is conjugate to a linear flow with Diophantine-type frequency vector close to $(\omega_j)$, and which is obtained as a small perturbation of the unperturbed torus $\{I_j = I_j^0\}_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$ for a prescribed initial action profile $(I_j^0)_{j\in\mathbb{Z}^d}$.

Existence of such tori is known when the initial actions $I_j^0$ are strongly localized (e.g. exponentially decaying) and even for slower decay of the form $I_j^0 \sim \exp\!\big(-(\log|j|)^{1+\alpha}\big)$ for some $\alpha>0$.

Question: Does there exist an infinite-dimensional KAM torus of the above Hamiltonian system whose initial action profile decays only polynomially, i.e. satisfying
$$I_j^0 \;\asymp\; |j|^{-M}, \qquad |j|\to\infty,$$
for some sufficiently large constant $M>0$?

Question: Does such a Hamiltonian system possess KAM tori? Consider an infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system on a lattice (for example, a Hamiltonian network of oscillators with short-range coupling) whose equations of motion can be linearized about an equilibrium. Suppose the linearized operator — concretely, an operator of the form $L = -\Delta_f + v$, where $\Delta_f$ is a (possibly weighted) discrete Laplacian on the lattice and $v$ is a multiplication (potential) operator — has spectrum that contains a non-degenerate interval of continuous spectrum (i.e., the spectrum is not pure point and includes an absolutely continuous or singular continuous component filling some interval $[\beta,\beta+1]$).

Question: Under these hypotheses, can the full nonlinear Hamiltonian system support any KAM tori, that is, invariant tori carrying quasi-periodic motion with Diophantine frequency vectors that persist under the nonlinear perturbation? Address this in particular for Hamiltonians with short-range interactions, where the standard KAM machinery for quasi-periodic breathers relies on pure point spectrum of the linearization. Consider an infinite-dimensional Hamiltonian system on a lattice (for example, a Hamiltonian network of oscillators with short-range coupling) whose equations of motion can be linearized about an equilibrium. Suppose the linearized operator — concretely, an operator of the form $L = -\Delta_f + v$, where $\Delta_f$ is a (possibly weighted) discrete Laplacian on the lattice and $v$ is a multiplication (potential) operator — has spectrum that contains a non-degenerate interval of continuous spectrum (i.e., the spectrum is not pure point and includes an absolutely continuous or singular continuous component filling some interval $[\beta,\beta+1]$).

Address this in particular for Hamiltonians with short-range interactions, where the standard KAM machinery for quasi-periodic breathers relies on pure point spectrum of the linearization. Either construct such KAM tori in the presence of an interval of continuous spectrum, or prove a general non-existence (obstruction) theorem showing that an interval of continuous spectrum in the linearization precludes the existence of KAM tori.

The literature on quasi-periodic breathers in Hamiltonian lattices consistently treats pure point spectrum of the linearized operator as essential for KAM constructions, and identifies continuous spectrum as an obstruction; recent works (e.g., on granular chains and coupled map lattices) still operate under pure-point or finite-multiplicity assumptions, and no general theorem either constructing KAM tori under an interval of continuous spectrum or proving their non-existence in this setting has been located. Let Y ⊂ ℝ² be a smooth, strictly convex billiard table, i.e., a planar domain bounded by a smooth strictly convex closed curve ∂Y. Consider the billiard flow inside Y, defined by the motion of a point particle traveling along straight lines in the interior of Y and reflecting elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) upon hitting ∂Y. This flow can be regarded as a Hamiltonian system with two degrees of freedom on the unit tangent bundle, and its dynamics is encoded by the billiard map on the annulus of inward-pointing unit vectors based on ∂Y. The system is called (Liouville) integrable if there exists a smooth first integral, independent of the energy on an open dense set, that is invariant under the billiard map (equivalently, the phase space is foliated by invariant curves on which the dynamics is conjugate to a rotation, away from a set of measure zero).

Prove or disprove: if the billiard flow inside such a smooth, strictly convex domain Y is integrable, then ∂Y must be an ellipse.

Let $\mathfrak{c}$ denote the cardinality of the continuum. Recall that an infinite sequence $(x_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ in a Banach space $X$ is called a basic sequence if it is a Schauder basis of its closed linear span, and it is called sub-symmetric if it is unconditional and equivalent to each of its infinite subsequences (equivalently, there is a constant $C\geq 1$ such that for every strictly increasing sequence of indices $n_1<n_2<\cdots$ and every choice of scalars $(a_k)$, $C^{-1}\bigl\|\sum_k a_k x_k\bigr\|\leq \bigl\|\sum_k a_k x_{n_k}\bigr\|\leq C\bigl\|\sum_k a_k x_k\bigr\|$, with unconditionality of $(x_n)$). The density of a Banach space $X$ is the smallest cardinality of a norm-dense subset of $X$.

Answer the following two questions:

(a) Does every Banach space of density strictly greater than $\mathfrak{c}$ contain an infinite sub-symmetric basic sequence?

(b) Does every reflexive Banach space of density strictly greater than $\aleph_1$ contain an infinite sub-symmetric basic sequence?

Let $\gamma\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth closed convex curve with perimeter $|\gamma|$. For each real number $\ell>|\gamma|$, the string (gardener's) construction associates to $\gamma$ a closed convex curve $G(\gamma,\ell)$ defined as follows: wrap a closed inextensible loop of length $\ell$ around $\gamma$, pull it taut at a point $P$ outside $\gamma$, and let $P$ trace out a curve as it moves around $\gamma$ keeping the loop taut. The resulting locus is $G(\gamma,\ell)$; it is a closed convex curve containing $\gamma$ in its interior, and $\gamma$ is a caustic of the billiard inside $G(\gamma,\ell)$.

When $\gamma$ is an ellipse, the integrability of the billiard inside an ellipse implies the following transitivity property: for any $\ell_1>|\gamma|$ and any $\ell_2>|G(\gamma,\ell_1)|$, there exists a unique $\ell_3>|\gamma|$ such that
$$G igl(G(\gamma,\ell_1),\,\ell_2 igr)=G(\gamma,\ell_3).$$

Problem. Prove or disprove: ellipses are the only smooth closed convex curves $\gamma$ for which this transitivity property of the string construction holds.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The transitivity (nesting) property of the string construction is known to hold for ellipses by integrability of elliptic billiards, and Poritsky (1950) showed ellipses are the only curves with the related "string property" / Poritsky property in the plane. However, the specific characterization stated as Problem 1b — that ellipses are the only closed convex curves for which the string construction is transitive in this two-step sense — does not appear to have been resolved; recent work on curves with the Poritsky property (e.g., Glutsyuk 2022) addresses related rigidity questions but does not settle this exact problem. Status appears open.

The classical Tsirelson space $T$ is constructed as follows. Let $(e_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be the unit-vector basis of $c_{00}(\mathbb{N})$. The Schreier family is
$$\mathcal{S} = \{F\subseteq\mathbb{N} : F \text{ is finite and } |F|\le \min F\}\cup\{\emptyset\}.$$
Two finite subsets $E,F\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ are admissible if $E<F$ (i.e.\ $\max E<\min F$); a sequence $E_1<E_2<\cdots<E_k$ of finite subsets is admissible if there exists $F=\{n_1<\cdots<n_k\}\in\mathcal{S}$ with $n_i\le \min E_i$ for all $i$. The norm $\|\cdot\|_T$ on $c_{00}(\mathbb{N})$ is the unique norm satisfying the implicit equation
$$\|x\| = \max\Bigl(\|x\|_\infty,\; \tfrac{1}{2}\sup\sum_{i=1}^k \|E_ix\|\Bigr),$$
where the sup is over all admissible sequences $E_1<\cdots<E_k$, and $T$ is the completion of $(c_{00}(\mathbb{N}),\|\cdot\|_T)$. The space $T$ is reflexive and contains no isomorphic copy of any $\ell_p$ ($1\le p<\infty$) or $c_0$.

Question. Does there exist a non-separable Banach space $X$ produced by an analogous construction—based on a non-separable analogue of the Schreier family $\mathcal{S}$ defined on an uncountable index set $\Gamma$, together with a corresponding admissibility relation on finite subsets of $\Gamma$—such that $X$ is non-separable, has a long (uncountable) Schauder-type basis $(e_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\Gamma}$, and shares the essential structural feature of the Tsirelson space that no subspace is isomorphic to $c_0$ or to any $\ell_p$ for $1\le p<\infty$?

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded planar domain whose boundary $\partial\Omega$ is a simple closed curve. The billiard flow inside $\Omega$ is defined by the free motion of a point particle that reflects elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) at $\partial\Omega$. The associated billiard map $T$ acts on the set of unit inward-pointing tangent vectors based on $\partial\Omega$, sending an outgoing reflection to the next reflection. The metric (Kolmogorov–Sinai) entropy $h_\mu(T)$ is defined with respect to the natural invariant measure $d\mu = \sin\varphi\, d\varphi\, ds$, where $s$ is arclength on $\partial\Omega$ and $\varphi \in (0,\pi)$ is the angle of reflection.

Recall: $\Omega$ is called convex if it equals the intersection of a family of half-planes; it is called strictly convex if its boundary contains no line segment. The boundary regularity refers to the regularity of an arclength parametrization of $\partial\Omega$.

(a) Construct a strictly convex billiard table $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with $C^1$-smooth boundary such that the billiard map $T$ has positive metric entropy.

(b) Construct a convex billiard table $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ with $C^2$-smooth boundary such that the billiard map $T$ has positive metric entropy.

representations.normalized:
Let $Y \subset \mathbb{R}^d$ be a piecewise smooth billiard table, i.e. a domain whose boundary is a finite union of smooth hypersurfaces meeting transversally, in which a point particle moves along straight lines and reflects elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) upon hitting the smooth part of the boundary. Let $\Phi$ denote the phase space of the associated billiard map, consisting of unit vectors based at boundary points and pointing inward, equipped with the canonical invariant Liouville measure $\mu$ (normalized to be finite). For an integer $n \geq 2$, let $P_n \subset \Phi$ be the set of periodic points of period $n$ for the billiard map, and let
$$P = \bigsqcup_{n=2}^{\infty} P_n$$
be the set of all periodic points. Note that $\mu(P) = \sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \mu(P_n)$, so $\mu(P) = 0$ if and only if $\mu(P_n) = 0$ for every $n \geq 2$.

Prove or disprove:
(i) $\mu(P) = 0$;
(ii) $\mu(P_n) = 0$ for every integer $n \geq 2$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Ivrii's conjecture (1978) remains open in general for smooth/piecewise smooth billiards. It is established in several special cases: real-analytic convex boundaries, period-3 (triangular) orbits for piecewise smooth planar billiards, and period-4 (quadrilateral) orbits for planar billiards with piecewise C^4 boundary (Glutsyuk–Kudryashov). Recent work has proven the conjecture for generic complex algebraic billiards of degree d ≥ 2 for all periods, and in some cases for outer and symplectic billiards. Counterexamples exist in the broader class of projective billiards. The general non-analytic case remains unresolved.

representations.normalized:
Let $Y \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a compact connected planar region whose boundary $\partial Y$ is a finite union of smooth curves meeting at finitely many corner points. Assume each smooth boundary component is either:

(i) a "dispersive" component, meaning a smooth curve that is strictly convex inward (i.e., its curvature, taken with respect to the inward normal pointing into $Y$, is strictly negative everywhere, so the boundary bulges into the table), or

(ii) a "neutral" component, meaning a straight line segment (zero curvature).

Consider the billiard flow on $Y$: a point particle moves with unit speed inside $Y$ along straight lines and reflects elastically (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection) upon hitting $\partial Y$. The phase space is the unit tangent bundle of $Y$, equipped with the natural invariant Liouville measure $\mu$.

Call $Y$ a semi-dispersive billiard table if its boundary consists only of components of types (i) and (ii), with at least one component of type (i). Call the billiard flow on $Y$ hyperbolic if its Lyapunov exponents are nonzero almost everywhere with respect to $\mu$ (i.e., the flow is non-uniformly hyperbolic in the sense of Pesin theory).

Question: Is the billiard flow on every semi-dispersive billiard table $Y$ (in the above sense) hyperbolic?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Hyperbolicity and ergodicity of semi-dispersive billiards is a longstanding research area (Sinai, Bunimovich, Krámli–Simányi–Szász, Chernov–Dolgopyat). While hyperbolicity is established in many particular semi-dispersive systems (hard-ball gases, Lorentz gas, stadia, falling balls), the general question of whether every planar semi-dispersive billiard table (dispersive arcs together with neutral segments) is hyperbolic does not appear to have a complete proof in the literature, and surveys treat full hyperbolicity in this generality as still open.

For uniformly hyperbolic systems, the exponential growth rate of periodic points equals the topological entropy (classical results of Bowen, Katok). For general (nonuniformly) hyperbolic billiards the equality of the periodic-orbit growth rate and topological entropy is not established in full generality; recent work (e.g., on Sinai billiards and on generic convex billiards) addresses positivity and lower bounds for entropy, but a complete answer to whether the limit, when it exists, must coincide with topological entropy for arbitrary hyperbolic billiards has not been confirmed in the sources found.

Fix a combinatorial type of simple planar polygon with $n \geq 3$ vertices (i.e., a cyclic ordering of the vertices and the resulting edge structure), and let $T(n)$ denote the moduli space of all simple Euclidean $n$-gons of this combinatorial type, parametrized in the natural way (for example, by the locations of the vertices, modulo Euclidean similarities), so that $T(n)$ is an open subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Let $\lambda$ denote Lebesgue measure on $T(n)$. For each polygon $P \in T(n)$, consider the billiard flow on $P$: the geodesic flow on the unit tangent bundle of $P$ with elastic reflection at the boundary, preserving Liouville measure. Call $P$ ergodic if this billiard flow is ergodic with respect to Liouville measure, and let $E(n) \subset T(n)$ denote the set of ergodic $n$-gons. It is known (Kerckhoff–Masur–Smillie) that $E(n)$ is residual in $T(n)$ in the sense of Baire category. Determine whether
\[
\lambda(E(n)) > 0.
\]

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether almost every polygon (with respect to Lebesgue measure on the moduli space of n-gons) has ergodic billiard flow is widely cited as an open problem. The known result of Kerckhoff–Masur–Smillie establishes only Baire-genericity of E(n), and recent surveys and papers on polygonal billiards (e.g., on weak mixing in rational billiards, 2024) still describe positive-measure ergodicity as unresolved. No proof of λ(E(n)) > 0 appears in the literature.

\[
\Phi_i = \{(x,v) \in \Phi : x \in a_i\},
\]
so that $\Phi = \bigsqcup_{i=1}^n \Phi_i$ is a disjoint decomposition.

Call $P$ an irrational $n$-gon if at least one of its interior angles is an irrational multiple of $\pi$.

Question: Suppose $P$ is an irrational $n$-gon, and let $M \subset \Phi$ be a measurable set that is invariant under the billiard flow and has positive Liouville measure. If $\Phi_i \subset M$ for some $1 \le i \le n$, must it follow that $M = \Phi$?

$$c_*(P)\,\ell^2 \;\le\; f_P(\ell) \;\le\; c^*(P)\,\ell^2$$
for all sufficiently large $\ell$. The numbers $c_*(P)$ and $c^*(P)$ are called the quadratic constants of $P$.

Problem: Provide efficient (effective and quantitatively sharp) estimates for the quadratic constants $c_*(P)$ and $c^*(P)$ in terms of the geometry of $P$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of efficiently estimating the quadratic constants for counting periodic billiard orbits in rational polygons remains open. Existence of the bounds is due to Masur (with ineffective constants) and effective constants were later obtained by Vorobets, but sharp/efficient estimates in terms of polygon geometry are still being sought, and the equality $c_*(P)=c^*(P)$ (existence of a quadratic limit) is itself unresolved beyond Veech/lattice cases.

Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a polygonal billiard table. A billiard orbit from $x \in \Omega$ to $y \in \Omega$ is a continuous broken-line trajectory in $\Omega$ starting at $x$ and ending at $y$, whose interior segments hit only the (open) edges of $\partial\Omega$ (avoiding the vertices) and reflect there according to the law of equal angles. Let $\Gamma(x,y)$ denote the set of all billiard orbits from $x$ to $y$.

A pair $\{x,y\}$ with $x,y \in \Omega$ is called secure if there exists a finite set $\{z_1, \dots, z_n\} \subset \Omega \setminus \{x,y\}$ such that every $\gamma \in \Gamma(x,y)$ passes through some $z_i$. The polygon $\Omega$ is called secure if every pair of points $x,y \in \Omega$ is secure.

The polygon $\Omega$ is called rational if all of its interior angles are rational multiples of $\pi$.

Problem: Characterize the secure polygons. In particular, give a criterion that decides whether a given rational polygon is secure.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The problem remains open in general. Known partial results include: among regular polygons, only the square, equilateral triangle, and regular hexagon have the finite blocking (security) property; among Veech surfaces, only torus branched covers are secure; and a lattice polygon is secure iff it is arithmetic. A standing conjecture asserts that a polygon is secure iff it is "almost integrable" (in particular rational), but no full characterization—nor a complete criterion for arbitrary rational polygons—has been established.

Let $P \subset \mathbb{R}^2$ be a (simple) polygon, and consider the billiard flow inside $P$: a point particle moves in straight lines and reflects off the boundary $\partial P$ according to the law of equal angles, with the trajectory undefined if it hits a vertex. Code each trajectory by the cyclic sequence of sides of $P$ that it strikes. The full billiard complexity $p(n)$ of $P$ is defined as the number of distinct words of length $n$ over the alphabet of sides of $P$ that arise as factors of some such bi-infinite billiard coding (equivalently, the number of equivalence classes of orbit segments crossing exactly $n$ sides, where two segments are equivalent if and only if they hit the same ordered sequence of sides).

Prove or disprove the following conjecture: there exists an integer $d \geq 3$ such that for every polygon $P$, there exist constants $c_1(P), c_2(P) > 0$ and $n_0(P)$ with
$$ c_1(P)\, n^3 \;\leq\; p(n) \;\leq\; c_2(P)\, n^d \qquad \text{for all } n \geq n_0(P). $$

Consider polygonal billiards in the Euclidean plane. A polygon is called integrable if it is one of the following: the equilateral triangle, the right isosceles triangle, the 30-60-90 triangle, or any rectangle. A polygon P is called almost integrable if the group generated by reflections in the sides of one of the integrable polygons Q tiles the plane in such a way that P is a union of tiles in this tiling (equivalently, P is tiled under reflections by Q).

For two points x, y in the interior of a polygon P, a billiard trajectory from x to y is a polygonal path inside P from x to y whose reflections at the boundary obey the law of equal angles (and which avoids the corners). A finite set B ⊂ P \ {x, y} is said to block all billiard trajectories from x to y if every billiard trajectory from x to y passes through some point of B. The polygon P is called secure (or has finite blocking property) if for every pair of points x, y in the interior of P there exists such a finite blocking set B.

Question: Is it true that a polygon P is secure if and only if P is almost integrable?

It is known that every compact flat Riemannian manifold is secure. Prove or disprove the following: a compact smooth Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is secure if and only if it is flat (i.e., has identically zero sectional curvature).

The converse has been established in several special cases: Bangert and Gutkin (2008) proved that secure 2-dimensional Riemannian tori are flat, and Burns–Gutkin and Lafont–Schmidt verified the conjecture for compact Riemannian manifolds with nonpositive sectional curvature. Let $\mathcal{T}$ be a metric tree graph: a connected metric graph with no cycles, consisting of a finite or countable family of edges (each identified isometrically with an interval of $\mathbb{R}$, finite or half-infinite) joined at vertices. On each edge, equip the function space with the Lebesgue measure inherited from the edge parametrization, and define
$$L^2(\mathcal{T}) = \bigoplus_{e \in E(\mathcal{T})} L^2(e), \qquad H^1(\mathcal{T}) = \{u \in C(\mathcal{T}) : u|_e \in H^1(e) \text{ for all } e\}.$$
Let $-\Delta_{\mathcal{T}}$ be a self-adjoint realization of the Laplacian on $\mathcal{T}$ (for instance the Kirchhoff Laplacian, defined on functions $u$ that are continuous at every vertex $v$ and satisfy $\sum_{e \succ v} \partial_e u(v) = 0$, where the sum runs over edges incident to $v$ and the derivatives are taken in the outgoing direction).

Consider the Cauchy problem for the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on $\mathcal{T}$:
$$ i\,\partial_t u(t,x) = -\Delta_{\mathcal{T}} u(t,x) + \lambda \, |u(t,x)|^{2\sigma} u(t,x), \quad x \in \mathcal{T},\ t \in \mathbb{R},$$
$$ u(0,\cdot) = u_0 \in H^1(\mathcal{T}), $$
with $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ and power $\sigma > 0$.

Question: Establish a rigorous well-posedness theory for this Cauchy problem on a general metric tree graph $\mathcal{T}$ analogous to the one available on the star graph (a single vertex with finitely many half-infinite edges). Specifically, prove local well-posedness in the energy space $H^1(\mathcal{T})$, conservation of mass and energy, and global well-posedness in the subcritical regime (e.g., $0 < \sigma < 2$ in the focusing case under suitable mass thresholds, and all $\sigma > 0$ in the defocusing case), together with the appropriate Strichartz-type dispersive estimates for the linear propagator $e^{it\Delta_{\mathcal{T}}}$ on the tree.

For the linear case, norm-resolvent convergence of Schrödinger operators on shrinking fat graphs to operators on metric graphs with various self-adjoint vertex conditions is established (e.g., Cacciapuoti–Exner, Berkolaiko–Latushkin–Sukhtaiev). For NLS, rigorous results are limited: a strong-confinement / thin-waveguide limit in a single 2D tube has been derived (Cacciapuoti–Finco–Noja, Ann. Henri Poincaré 2017), and numerical/asymptotic studies of solitons in shrinking tubular networks (Uzdin et al.) suggest Kirchhoff-type vertex conditions in some regimes. The general nonlinear question on networks with junctions, the dependence of limiting vertex conditions on the scaling and on Neumann vs. Dirichlet wall conditions, is not fully settled.

representations.normalized:
Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a metric graph (for concreteness, take either (i) the real line $\mathbb{R}$ viewed as two half-lines joined at a single vertex $v=0$ ("line with a defect"), or (ii) the Y-junction consisting of three half-lines $[0,\infty)$ joined at a common vertex $v$). On $\mathcal{G}$ consider an $N$-body bosonic Hamiltonian acting on the symmetric tensor power of $L^2(\mathcal{G})$, of the form
$$ H_N \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^N \bigl(-\Delta_{\mathcal{G},i} + V_{\mathrm{ext}}(x_i)\bigr) \;+\; \sum_{1\le i<j\le N} N^{2}\, v\bigl(N(x_i-x_j)\bigr), $$
where $-\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}$ is the Laplacian on $\mathcal{G}$ equipped with a chosen self-adjoint vertex condition at $v$ (e.g.\ Kirchhoff, $\delta$-type, or more general) and $v\ge 0$ is a sufficiently regular pair-interaction potential of scattering length $a$. Let $\psi_{N,0}$ be a sequence of $N$-body bosonic states that exhibit complete Bose–Einstein condensation onto a one-particle wave function $\varphi_0\in L^2(\mathcal{G})$, and let $\psi_{N,t} = e^{-itH_N}\psi_{N,0}$.

Prove or disprove: in the limit $N\to\infty$ with the Gross–Pitaevskii scaling above, the reduced one-particle density matrices of $\psi_{N,t}$ converge to $|\varphi_t\rangle\langle\varphi_t|$, where $\varphi_t:\mathcal{G}\to\mathbb{C}$ solves a quasi–one-dimensional cubic nonlinear Schrödinger / Gross–Pitaevskii equation
$$ i\partial_t \varphi_t \;=\; -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}\varphi_t \;+\; V_{\mathrm{ext}}\varphi_t \;+\; 8\pi a\,|\varphi_t|^2 \varphi_t \quad\text{on each edge of }\mathcal{G}, $$
supplemented by an effective self-adjoint vertex condition at $v$ that is to be identified explicitly from the microscopic data $(H_N, v, \text{vertex condition of }-\Delta_{\mathcal{G}})$. In particular, identify the correct effective vertex/boundary condition obtained in the limit, already in the simplest case of the line with a single defect (two edges meeting at one vertex).

representations.normalized:
Consider the nonlinear Schrödinger equation
$$ i\,\partial_t \psi = -\Delta_{\mathcal G}\psi - |\psi|^{p-1}\psi $$
posed on a metric graph $\mathcal G$, where $\Delta_{\mathcal G}$ denotes the Laplacian acting on functions $\psi:\mathcal G\to\mathbb C$ defined edge-wise, with Kirchhoff (or other natural self-adjoint) vertex conditions. A standing wave is a solution of the form $\psi(t,x)=e^{i\omega t}\phi_\omega(x)$ with $\omega>0$ and $\phi_\omega$ a real-valued bound state satisfying
$$ -\Delta_{\mathcal G}\phi_\omega + \omega\phi_\omega - |\phi_\omega|^{p-1}\phi_\omega = 0. $$
Linearizing the equation about $\phi_\omega$ produces self-adjoint operators $L_1, L_2$ on $L^2(\mathcal G)$ with
$$ L_1 = -\Delta_{\mathcal G} + \omega - p\,\phi_\omega^{p-1}, \qquad L_2 = -\Delta_{\mathcal G} + \omega - \phi_\omega^{p-1}. $$
The classical Grillakis–Shatah–Strauss framework reduces the orbital (in)stability of $\phi_\omega$ to:
(i) counting the number $n(L_1)$ of negative eigenvalues of $L_1$, and
(ii) verifying the Vakhitov–Kolokolov slope condition, namely the sign of $\frac{d}{d\omega}\|\phi_\omega\|_{L^2(\mathcal G)}^2$.

Suppose $\mathcal G$ is a metric graph more complicated than a star graph — for instance a tree with several internal vertices, or a graph containing one or more loops — and suppose that no explicit closed-form expression for the bound state $\phi_\omega$ is available.

Develop a general method that, in this setting, allows one to:
(a) determine $n(L_1)$ for the standing wave $\phi_\omega$ on $\mathcal G$, and
(b) determine the sign of $\frac{d}{d\omega}\|\phi_\omega\|_{L^2(\mathcal G)}^2$,
and thereby establish orbital stability or orbital instability of $\phi_\omega$ on such graphs without relying on explicit formulas for the standing wave.

representations.normalized:
Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a metric graph (a finite or infinite graph whose edges are identified with intervals of $\mathbb{R}$, possibly including half-lines), equipped with the Lebesgue measure on each edge and Kirchhoff (or other self-adjoint) vertex conditions at the vertices. Consider the nonlinear Schrödinger equation
$$ i\,\partial_t \psi = -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}} \psi - |\psi|^{p-1}\psi, \qquad p>1, $$
where $\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}$ denotes the self-adjoint Laplacian on $L^2(\mathcal{G})$ associated with the chosen vertex conditions. A nonlinear bound state of frequency $\omega>0$ is a solution of the form $\psi(t,x)=e^{i\omega t}\varphi(x)$ with $\varphi\in H^1(\mathcal{G})$ satisfying the stationary equation
$$ -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}\varphi + \omega\varphi = |\varphi|^{p-1}\varphi $$
together with the vertex conditions. A branch of nonlinear bound states $\{\varphi_\omega\}$ is said to have a linear counterpart if $\|\varphi_\omega\|_{H^1}\to 0$ as $\omega$ approaches some eigenvalue $-\omega_0$ of $-\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}$, in which case the branch bifurcates from the corresponding linear eigenfunction.

Develop a general method, applicable to nontrivial metric graphs $\mathcal{G}$ (for instance star graphs, tadpole graphs, and graphs with loops), that constructs and identifies branches of nonlinear bound states which do not have a linear counterpart in the above sense — in particular, branches of nonlinear excited states known to exist on star graphs — characterizing the topological or geometric features of $\mathcal{G}$ responsible for their existence and providing criteria to detect such branches.

Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a metric graph (a connected metric space obtained by identifying endpoints of finitely many edges, each isometric to an interval of $\mathbb{R}$, possibly with half-lines). Consider the nonlinear Schrödinger equation on $\mathcal{G}$,
$$ i\partial_t u(t,x) = H u(t,x) - |u(t,x)|^{2p} u(t,x), \qquad x\in\mathcal{G},\ t\in\mathbb{R}, $$
where $H = -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}$ is the self-adjoint Laplacian on $\mathcal{G}$ associated to a chosen set of vertex conditions (e.g. Kirchhoff or $\delta$-type), and $p>0$ is subcritical. A standing wave is a solution of the form $u_\omega(t,x) = e^{i\omega t}\Phi_\omega(x)$, where $\Phi_\omega\in H^1(\mathcal{G})$ solves $H\Phi_\omega - |\Phi_\omega|^{2p}\Phi_\omega = -\omega \Phi_\omega$. Linearizing around $\Phi_\omega$ yields a (non-self-adjoint, non-skew-adjoint) Hamiltonian operator $JL$ acting on real-vector-valued perturbations.

Question: Are such standing waves asymptotically stable in the following sense? For every initial datum $u_0\in H^1(\mathcal{G})$ sufficiently close, in the energy norm, to $\Phi_\omega$, does the corresponding solution $u(t)$ admit, for $t\to\infty$, a decomposition
$$ u(t,x) = e^{i\theta(t)}\Phi_{\omega_\infty}(x) + e^{-itH}\psi_\infty(x) + r(t,x), $$
with $\omega_\infty$ near $\omega$, a dispersive component $e^{-itH}\psi_\infty$ evolving under the linear graph Hamiltonian, and a remainder satisfying $\|r(t)\|_{L^2(\mathcal{G})}\to 0$ as $t\to\infty$?

Equivalently: can one establish sufficiently sharp spectral and dispersive estimates for the non-self-adjoint linearized Hamiltonian $JL$ on $\mathcal{G}$, and control the nonlinear remainder, to prove this asymptotic relaxation onto a nearby standing wave?

The general problem of asymptotic stability of NLS standing waves on metric graphs appears to remain open. Recent literature (through 2025–2026) on NLS on graphs focuses primarily on existence and orbital (Lyapunov) stability of ground states, including stability transitions on general metric graphs. Asymptotic stability results in the soliton-resolution sense are available only in restricted models with concentrated nonlinearities (point interactions on the line or in 3D), not for general metric graphs with extended nonlinearities, where dispersive estimates for the linearized non-self-adjoint operator $JL$ are not yet established.

Consider the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation on a star graph $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of $N\geq 2$ semi-infinite half-lines (edges) $e_1,\ldots,e_N$ joined at a single vertex $v$. On each edge identified with $[0,\infty)$, the wavefunction $\psi_j(t,x)$ satisfies
$$ i\partial_t \psi_j = -\partial_x^2 \psi_j - |\psi_j|^2 \psi_j, \qquad x>0,\; j=1,\ldots,N, $$
with Kirchhoff (or, more generally, $\delta$-type) coupling at the vertex:
$$ \psi_1(t,0)=\cdots=\psi_N(t,0), \qquad \sum_{j=1}^N \partial_x \psi_j(t,0) = \alpha\,\psi_1(t,0), $$
for some fixed $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$.

A "fast soliton" on edge $e_j$ is an incoming profile of the form $\psi_j(0,x)=e^{i v x}\,\mathrm{sech}(x-x_0)$ with $|v|$ large and $x_0\ll 0$ (so it travels toward the vertex). Existing results describe the scattering of a single fast soliton arriving at $v$ and produce reflected/transmitted solitonic components on the outgoing edges.

Question:
(a) Do there exist genuine multisoliton solutions of this cubic NLS on the star graph $\mathcal{G}$ (i.e., solutions that, in suitable asymptotic regimes, decompose into several spatially separated soliton-like profiles propagating on the edges)?

$$ i\partial_t \psi_j = -\partial_x^2 \psi_j - |\psi_j|^2 \psi_j, \qquad x>0,\; j=1,\ldots,N, $$

$$ \psi_1(t,0)=\cdots=\psi_N(t,0), \qquad \sum_{j=1}^N \partial_x \psi_j(t,0) = \alpha\,\psi_1(t,0), $$
for some fixed $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}$.

A "fast soliton" on edge $e_j$ is an incoming profile of the form $\psi_j(0,x)=e^{i v x}\,\mathrm{sech}(x-x_0)$ with $|v|$ large and $x_0\ll 0$ (so it travels toward the vertex). Existing results describe the scattering of a single fast soliton arriving at $v$ and produce reflected/transmitted solitonic components on the outgoing edges.

Question: 
(a) Do there exist genuine multisoliton solutions of this cubic NLS on the star graph $\mathcal{G}$ (i.e., solutions that, in suitable asymptotic regimes, decompose into several spatially separated soliton-like profiles propagating on the edges)?

(b) If several fast solitons are launched simultaneously on (possibly different) edges so that they all reach the vertex $v$ at the same time, what is the dynamical outcome of the collision at $v$? In particular, characterize the asymptotic state for $t\to+\infty$ in terms of reflected/transmitted soliton components, radiation, and any nonlinear interaction at the vertex.

$$ i\,\partial_t\psi = -\partial_x^2\psi - |\psi|^2\psi, $$
supplemented at every vertex $v$ by Kirchhoff (or more general self-adjoint) matching conditions: $\psi$ is continuous at $v$ and $\sum_{e
i v}\partial_x\psi_e(v)=0$, where the sum is over edges incident to $v$ taken with the outgoing orientation.

A soliton on a single edge (line) is the family $\phi_{c,v,x_0,\gamma}(t,x)=\sqrt{2}c\,\operatorname{sech}(c(x-vt-x_0))\,e^{i(vx/2-(v^2/4-c^2)t+\gamma)}$ with amplitude $c>0$, velocity $v$, position $x_0$, phase $\gamma$. (a) For an arbitrary finite tree graph $\mathcal{G}$ (with semi-infinite leaves) equipped with Kirchhoff vertex conditions, prove that an incoming high-velocity soliton entering along one semi-infinite edge propagates through the tree, splitting at each interior vertex, and that on each outgoing edge the resulting wave is, up to errors that vanish as the velocity tends to infinity, a sum of solitons whose parameters and reflection/transmission amplitudes are determined recursively by the linear scattering matrices at each vertex.

(c) Quantify the influence of the topology of $\mathcal{G}$ (presence of loops, cycles, branching structure) on the persistence, decay, or trapping of solitons.

Consider the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger equation on a star graph $\mathcal{G}$ consisting of $N$ half-lines joined at a single vertex, with a Kirchhoff-type (or more general self-adjoint) coupling at the vertex and an external potential $V$ on the edges:
$$ i\partial_t \psi = -\Delta\psi + V\psi - |\psi|^2\psi, \qquad \psi(t,\cdot)\in L^2(\mathcal{G}). $$
Let $\phi_v(x-vt)$ denote a standing soliton of the underlying line equation boosted to velocity $v$, and consider an initial datum given by such a fast solitary wave $\psi_0$ supported on one incoming edge and traveling toward the vertex with large velocity $v$. After scattering at the vertex, the solution decomposes into outgoing components on the various edges. It is known that there is a time interval of order $\log v / v$ (logarithmic in the velocity) on which each outgoing component is approximated, in $H^1$, by a solitary wave whose amplitude is determined by the linear scattering coefficients at the vertex.

Question: Can the timescale on which this solitary-wave approximation of the outgoing components remains accurate be extended beyond the $\log v / v$ scale? Specifically, determine whether (and under which assumptions on the initial datum $\psi_0$ and on the external potential $V$) the validity time of the outgoing-soliton approximation can be improved to a longer (e.g.\ polynomial in $v$, or velocity-independent) timescale, and characterize how the maximal such timescale depends on $\psi_0$ and $V$.

Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a metric graph with at least one semi-infinite edge, and consider the nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation
$$ i\partial_t \psi = -\partial_x^2 \psi + f(|\psi|^2)\psi $$
on each edge of $\mathcal{G}$, with Kirchhoff (or otherwise self-adjoint) coupling conditions at every vertex. In the integrable case $f(s)=-s$ (cubic focusing NLS on the line), it is known that a fast soliton incoming along a semi-infinite edge of $\mathcal{G}$ scatters at the vertex and produces, on each outgoing edge, a wave that remains close in $H^1$ to a (rescaled) soliton over a timescale $T_v$ depending logarithmically (or polynomially) on the soliton velocity $v$.

Now suppose the nonlinearity $f$ is a smooth perturbation of the cubic one,
$$ f(s) = -s + \varepsilon\, g(s), $$
with $g$ smooth and bounded on compact sets, and $\varepsilon>0$ small. Prove or disprove the following: there exist $\varepsilon_0>0$ and a timescale $T_v'$ comparable to $T_v$ such that, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,\varepsilon_0)$ and every sufficiently fast incoming soliton, the outgoing waves on each semi-infinite edge of $\mathcal{G}$ remain close in $H^1$ to solitons (of the unperturbed cubic NLS, with appropriately determined parameters) up to time $T_v'$.

Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a metric graph consisting of a finite number of edges (half-lines or finite segments) joined at one or more vertices, equipped with a self-adjoint realization $H$ of the Laplacian $-\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}$ (e.g., Kirchhoff or $\delta$-type coupling at the vertices). Consider the cubic (or, more generally, focusing power-type) nonlinear Schrödinger equation on $\mathcal{G}$,
$$ i\,\partial_t \psi(t,x) = H\psi(t,x) - |\psi(t,x)|^{2\sigma}\psi(t,x), \qquad x\in\mathcal{G},\ t\in\mathbb{R}, $$
with initial datum $\psi(0,\cdot)=\psi_0\in H^1(\mathcal{G})$. On each edge identified with $\mathbb{R}^+$, recall that the free NLS on the line admits soliton solutions of the form $\phi_{c,v}(t,x)=e^{i(vx/2-(v^2/4-c)t)}\,\eta_c(x-vt-x_0)$, where $\eta_c$ is the ground-state profile with parameter $c>0$ and $v\in\mathbb{R}$ is the velocity.

Two regimes are well studied: (i) the "near standing wave" regime, in which $\psi$ stays close to a stationary nonlinear bound state of $H$, and (ii) the "fast-soliton scattering" regime, in which a soliton of large velocity $v\gg 1$ impinges on a vertex and the scattering through the junction can be approximated by the linear scattering matrix of $H$.

Problem: For initial data consisting of one or several solitons incident on a vertex of $\mathcal{G}$ in dynamical regimes that are neither close to a standing wave nor in the fast-soliton scattering limit, provide a rigorous mathematical description of:
(a) the mechanism by which a soliton can be trapped (captured) at a vertex or graph defect, producing a long-lived localized state at the vertex; and
(b) the mechanism by which new solitons, carrying nontrivial mass and momentum, can be generated and emitted along the outgoing edges from such an interaction.

Specifically, identify quantitative conditions on $\mathcal{G}$, $H$, the nonlinearity exponent $\sigma$, and the parameters $(c,v)$ of the incoming soliton(s) under which capture and/or generation occur, and prove asymptotic decomposition theorems of the form
$$ \psi(t,\cdot) = \sum_{j} \phi_{c_j,v_j}(t,\cdot) + \chi(t,\cdot) + r(t,\cdot), \qquad \|r(t)\|_{H^1(\mathcal{G})}\to 0, $$
where $\chi$ is a localized state attached to the vertex and the $\phi_{c_j,v_j}$ are outgoing solitons.

Let $M$ be a 3-dimensional smooth manifold and consider single-input control-affine systems of the form
$$\dot q = f(q) + u\, g(q), \qquad q \in M, \quad |u(t)| \le 1,$$
where $f, g$ are smooth vector fields on $M$ and admissible controls $u(\cdot)$ are measurable functions with values in $[-1,1]$. Given two points $q_0, q_1 \in M$, a trajectory connecting $q_0$ to $q_1$ is called time-optimal if it minimizes the transfer time among all admissible trajectories with the same endpoints.

A trajectory is called piecewise smooth if it is smooth except at finitely many switching points where the optimal control changes regime.

Question: Is it true that for a generic pair $(f,g)$ of smooth vector fields on $M$ (in the sense of Whitney $C^\infty$ topology), every time-optimal trajectory of the above system is piecewise smooth?

Consider a single-input affine control system on a smooth manifold $M$ of dimension $n \geq 3$:
$$\dot q = f(q) + u\, g(q), \qquad |u(t)| \leq 1,$$
where $f, g$ are smooth vector fields on $M$. For fixed initial and terminal states, a time-optimal trajectory is an admissible trajectory steering the initial to the terminal state in minimum time. By Pontryagin's Maximum Principle, every time-optimal trajectory is the projection of an extremal, i.e.\ a curve $(q(t),p(t))$ in $T^*M$ satisfying the Hamiltonian system associated with the maximized Hamiltonian $H(q,p,u) = \langle p, f(q)\rangle + u\,\langle p, g(q)\rangle$, and the optimal control satisfies $u(t) = \mathrm{sgn}\,\langle p(t), g(q(t))\rangle$ at points where the switching function $\varphi(t) := \langle p(t), g(q(t))\rangle$ is nonzero.

A switching point is an instant $t$ at which $\varphi(t)=0$ and the control changes sign. There exist constructed examples of extremals of such systems whose switching points accumulate (chattering / Fuller-type extremals) and whose qualitative structure is stable under small smooth perturbations of the vector fields $f$ and $g$.

Question: For such structurally stable chattering extremals, are the corresponding trajectories actually time-optimal (at least locally) between their endpoints?

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold equipped with a sub-Riemannian structure, that is, a smooth bracket-generating distribution $\mathcal{D}\subset TM$ together with a smoothly varying inner product on $\mathcal{D}$. An absolutely continuous path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$ is called admissible (horizontal) if $\dot\gamma(t)\in\mathcal{D}_{\gamma(t)}$ for almost every $t$, and its length is $\ell(\gamma)=\int_0^1\|\dot\gamma(t)\|\,dt$.

Let $\gamma_0,\gamma_1:[0,1]\to M$ be two smooth admissible paths with common starting point $\gamma_0(0)=\gamma_1(0)=q_0$, and assume that their initial velocities are linearly independent: $\dot\gamma_0(0)\wedge\dot\gamma_1(0)\neq 0$. Consider the broken (corner) path obtained by concatenating $\bar\gamma_0$ (the reversal of $\gamma_0$) with $\gamma_1$, going from $\gamma_0(1)$ through $q_0$ to $\gamma_1(1)$, of total length $\ell(\gamma_0)+\ell(\gamma_1)$.

Question: does there always exist an admissible path joining $\gamma_0(1)$ to $\gamma_1(1)$ whose length is strictly less than $\ell(\gamma_0)+\ell(\gamma_1)$?

Hakavuori and Le Donne (Inventiones Math., 2016, "Non-minimality of corners in subriemannian geometry") proved that admissible curves with a corner are never length minimizing in any sub-Riemannian manifold. This affirmatively resolves the question: a strictly shorter admissible path between the endpoints always exists, so the problem is solved.

Let $(M,\Delta,g)$ be a sub-Riemannian manifold, where $M$ is a smooth connected manifold, $\Delta\subset TM$ is a smooth bracket-generating distribution, and $g$ is a smooth metric on $\Delta$. Fix a base point $q_0\in M$ and let
$$\Omega_{q_0} = \{\gamma\in H^1([0,1],M) : \dot\gamma(t)\in\Delta_{\gamma(t)}\text{ for a.e. }t,\ \gamma(0)=q_0\}$$
be the Hilbert manifold of horizontal (admissible) paths starting at $q_0$. Define the endpoint map
$$\mathrm{End}_{q_0}:\Omega_{q_0}\to M,\qquad \mathrm{End}_{q_0}(\gamma)=\gamma(1).$$
A horizontal path $\gamma\in\Omega_{q_0}$ is called singular (or abnormal) if it is a critical point of $\mathrm{End}_{q_0}$, i.e.\ the differential $d\mathrm{End}_{q_0}(\gamma)$ is not surjective. A point $q\in M$ is a regular value of $\mathrm{End}_{q_0}$ if every $\gamma\in\mathrm{End}_{q_0}^{-1}(q)$ is a regular point.

Question: Must the endpoint map $\mathrm{End}_{q_0}$ always admit at least one regular value in $M$? Equivalently, is it impossible that the singular horizontal curves issuing from $q_0$ fill the whole manifold $M$?

This is a form of the Sard conjecture in sub-Riemannian geometry: the set of endpoints of singular horizontal curves from a fixed point should have measure zero (in particular cannot fill M). It has been established in important special cases — e.g. on Martinet surfaces (Belotto da Silva–Rifford, 2018) and the strong Sard conjecture for analytic rank-two distributions on 3-manifolds (Belotto da Silva–Figalli–Parusiński–Rifford, Inventiones 2022, showing the singular reachable set has Hausdorff dimension ≤ 1) — but the general conjecture remains open.

Let $M$ be a 3-dimensional smooth manifold and let $D \subset TM$ be a rank-2 distribution which is of Martinet type, i.e. there exists a smooth 1-form $\omega$ with $D = \ker\omega$ such that the Martinet surface
$$\Sigma = \{q \in M : \omega \wedge d\omega = 0\}$$
is a smooth 2-dimensional submanifold of $M$, and at each point of $\Sigma$ the distribution $D$ is transverse to $\Sigma$. Equip $D$ with a smooth Riemannian metric $g$, so that $(M, D, g)$ is a sub-Riemannian structure of Martinet type. For a base point $q_0 \in M$ and $r > 0$, define the sub-Riemannian sphere
$$S(q_0, r) = \{ q \in M : d_{SR}(q_0, q) = r \},$$
where $d_{SR}$ is the sub-Riemannian distance. A horizontal curve $\gamma : [0,T] \to M$ tangent to $D$ is called a singular (abnormal) curve if it is a critical point of the endpoint map restricted to horizontal curves with fixed initial point; in the Martinet case the singular curves through $q_0$ are the integral curves of $D \cap T\Sigma$ contained in $\Sigma$, and such a singular curve is called optimal if it is locally length-minimizing for $g$.

Consider the class of generic sub-Riemannian metrics $g$ on a Martinet distribution. Let $r>0$ be small enough that $S(q_0,r)$ meets an optimal singular curve issuing from $q_0$, and let $\bar q$ be a point of intersection of $S(q_0,r)$ with this optimal singular curve.

Problem. Provide a complete classification, up to germs of $C^1$-diffeomorphisms of $\mathbb{R}^3$, of the germ of the sub-Riemannian sphere $S(q_0,r)$ at the point $\bar q$.

representations.normalized:
In thermal quantum field theory in the imaginary-time (Matsubara) formalism, loop integrals are replaced by "sum-integrals" of the form

    ∑∫_P f(P) := T ∑_{p_0} ∫ d^{d-1}p/(2π)^{d-1} f(p_0, p),

where p_0 ranges over discrete Matsubara frequencies (p_0 = 2π n T for bosons, p_0 = (2n+1)π T for fermions, n ∈ ℤ), T > 0 is the temperature, and dimensional regularization is used in the spatial directions. In perturbative finite-temperature QCD and related field theories, higher-order computations require evaluation of multi-loop master sum-integrals that depend on the additional scale T and that mix ultraviolet and infrared divergent regions in a nontrivial way.

Develop a systematic, computer-algebraic algorithm for the evaluation of arbitrary multi-loop thermal sum-integrals with the following properties:

1. It handles the discretized Matsubara frequencies and the temperature scale T together with the continuous spatial loop momenta in a uniform framework.
2. It goes beyond purely integration-by-parts (IBP) reductions on Matsubara summands by incorporating additional analytic techniques known to be effective for zero-temperature multi-loop integrals (e.g., differential equations, dimensional shifts, Mellin–Barnes representations, sector decomposition, symbolic summation, etc.).
3. It produces a reusable, automated procedure for separating ultraviolet and infrared divergent contributions of any given sum-integral, so that the divergent parts can be isolated algorithmically rather than case by case.
4. It reduces the evaluation of any multi-loop master sum-integral occurring in higher-order thermal perturbation theory to a finite, mechanizable set of operations, as opposed to the case-by-case treatments currently used beyond two loops.

Construct such an algorithm and prove its correctness and termination, or else establish a precise obstruction showing that no such uniform algorithmic treatment is possible.

Let $\Delta$ be a smooth Engel distribution on $\mathbb{R}^4$, that is, a rank-2 distribution such that, denoting $\Delta^1=\Delta$ and $\Delta^{k+1}=\Delta^k+[\Delta,\Delta^k]$, one has $\dim\Delta^2(q)=3$ and $\dim\Delta^3(q)=4$ for every $q\in\mathbb{R}^4$. Equip $\Delta$ with a smooth sub-Riemannian metric $g$, and define the sub-Riemannian distance $d(q_0,q)$ as the infimum of the $g$-lengths of horizontal (i.e. tangent to $\Delta$) Lipschitz curves joining $q_0$ to $q$. For small $r>0$, the sub-Riemannian sphere $S_r(q_0)=\{q:d(q_0,q)=r\}$ is a 3-dimensional hypersurface in $\mathbb{R}^4$.

It is known that through every point $q_0$ there passes a unique (up to reparametrization) singular (abnormal) horizontal curve $\gamma$, and that sufficiently short subarcs of $\gamma$ are length-minimizing. Hence $\gamma$ meets each small sphere $S_r(q_0)$ at distinguished points.

Problem: provide a complete local classification, up to smooth diffeomorphism of $(\mathbb{R}^4,q_0)$, of the singularities of $S_r(q_0)$ at the points where the optimal singular curve $\gamma$ through $q_0$ meets the sphere $S_r(q_0)$. Equivalently, describe all possible local diffeomorphism types of the germ $(S_r(q_0),p)$ at such intersection points $p=\gamma(\pm r)$.
