Consider thermal field theory at temperature $T$ in the imaginary-time (Matsubara) formalism, where bosonic sum-integrals are defined by
$$\sumint_P f(P) \;=\; T\sum_{p_0\in 2\pi T\mathbb{Z}} \int\!\frac{d^{d-1}\mathbf p}{(2\pi)^{d-1}}\, f(p_0,\mathbf p),$$
with Euclidean four-momentum $P=(p_0,\mathbf p)$ and $P^2=p_0^2+\mathbf p^2$. In the evaluation of three-loop massless bosonic vacuum sum-integrals contributing to the next-to-next-to-leading-order Debye screening mass of hot QCD, after applying a standard ultraviolet/infrared subtraction procedure and a coordinate-space transformation, four convergent residual contributions, denoted
$$B^{\mathrm{I}}_N,\quad B^{\mathrm{II}}_N,\quad B^{\mathrm{III}}_N,\quad B^{\mathrm{IV}}_N,$$
parametrized by a positive integer $N$ (an exponent appearing on certain bosonic propagators), can be reduced to one-dimensional integrals over the positive real axis whose integrands are products of polylogarithms, ordinary logarithms, and hyperbolic functions of a single variable.

Problem. Find closed-form analytic expressions, valid for arbitrary integer $N\ge 1$, for the four families
$$B^{\mathrm{I}}_N,\ B^{\mathrm{II}}_N,\ B^{\mathrm{III}}_N,\ B^{\mathrm{IV}}_N,$$
or equivalently provide a systematic evaluation procedure that produces such expressions as explicit functions of $N$ (rather than a case-by-case numerical evaluation at fixed values such as $N=2$ and $N=3$).

Let $f_0$ and $f_1$ be smooth vector fields on a neighborhood of a point $q_0\in\mathbb{R}^2$. Consider the control system
$$\dot q = u_0 f_0(q) + u_1 f_1(q), \qquad u_0^2 + u_1^2 \le 1,$$
and define the associated almost-Riemannian distance from $q_0$ by
$$S_{q_0}(q) = \inf\{\, T \ge 0 : \exists\, \text{admissible controls } (u_0,u_1) \text{ with } u_0^2+u_1^2 \le 1 \text{ steering } q_0 \text{ to } q \text{ in time } T\,\}.$$
For each $q$ near $q_0$, let $\Delta(q)=\mathrm{span}\{f_0(q),f_1(q)\}$, and let $\Delta^k(q)$ denote the $k$-th step of the flag obtained by iterated Lie brackets of $f_0,f_1$. Set
$$n_k(q)=\dim\Delta^k(q).$$
Assume that at $q_0$ the vectors $f_0(q_0)$ and $f_1(q_0)$ are collinear and that
$$n_2(q_0)=1,\qquad n_3(q_0)=2$$
(so $q_0$ is a tangency-type singular point where the distribution is one-dimensional, the first bracket does not generate, but the second bracket does).

Provide a $C^1$-classification of the germs at $q_0$ of the distance function $S_{q_0}$ for generic pairs $(f_0,f_1)$ satisfying the conditions $n_2(q_0)=1$ and $n_3(q_0)=2$. That is, exhibit a list of model germs such that, for an open dense set of pairs $(f_0,f_1)$ in the appropriate $C^\infty$ topology, the germ of $S_{q_0}$ is $C^1$-equivalent to one of these models, and prove that distinct models are not $C^1$-equivalent.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold and let $\Delta \subset TM$ be a smooth vector distribution on $M$ (a smooth subbundle, or more generally a smooth submodule of the tangent sheaf). A singular curve of $\Delta$ is, in the sense of sub-Riemannian/control geometry, an absolutely continuous horizontal curve $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$ (i.e. $\dot\gamma(t)\in\Delta_{\gamma(t)}$ a.e.) which is a critical point of the endpoint map among horizontal curves with fixed endpoints. Call $\Delta$ singular transitive if any two points of $M$ can be joined by a concatenation of finitely many singular curves of $\Delta$. The symmetry group of $\Delta$ is
$$\mathrm{Sym}(\Delta)=\{\Phi\in\mathrm{Diff}(M):\Phi_*\Delta=\Delta\}.$$
Question: Does singular transitivity of $\Delta$ imply that $\mathrm{Sym}(\Delta)$ carries the structure of a finite-dimensional Lie group (acting smoothly on $M$)?

A smooth closed curve $\gamma:S^1\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is called nondegenerate (locally convex) if for every $t\in S^1$ the derivatives $\gamma'(t),\gamma''(t),\dots,\gamma^{(n)}(t)$ are linearly independent in $\mathbb{R}^n$ (equivalently, the Frenet frame is well defined and all generalized curvatures are nowhere vanishing).

Given a strictly convex closed curve $c$ in a plane $\mathbb{R}^2\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ and an integer $m\geq 1$, let $c^{(m)}$ denote the curve obtained by traversing $c$ exactly $m$ times. Define $\mu(n)$ to be the smallest positive integer $m$ with the following property: for every strictly convex closed plane curve $c$ and every $\varepsilon>0$, there exists a smooth closed curve $\tilde\gamma:S^1\to\mathbb{R}^n$ that is nondegenerate in the above sense and is $\varepsilon$-close (in the $C^0$, or equivalently $C^k$ for any fixed $k$) to $c^{(m)}$.

It is known that $\mu(2)=1$ and $\mu(3)=2$. Determine $\mu(n)$ for every integer $n>3$.

Consider the incompressible Navier-Stokes system with periodic boundary conditions
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot
abla)u - 
u\,\Delta u + 
abla p = \eta(t,x), \qquad \mathrm{div}\, u = 0,$$
with viscosity $

$$V_D = \overline{\{u \in V : \mathrm{supp}\, u \subset D\}}$$

The question of approximate controllability of the periodic Navier-Stokes system by a localized, finite-dimensional, viscosity-independent forcing supported in a fixed open subset of the torus is, to our knowledge, still open. Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes system on the two-dimensional torus $\mathbb{T}^2 = \mathbb{R}^2/2\pi\mathbb{Z}^2$:
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = h(t,x) + \eta(t,x), \qquad \mathrm{div}\,u = 0, \qquad u(0,\cdot)=u_0,$$
where $\nu>0$ is the viscosity, $h$ is a fixed external force, $u_0 \in V$, and $V$ denotes the space of divergence-free, mean-zero vector fields on $\mathbb{T}^2$ of class $H^1$. Fix a non-empty open set $D\subset \mathbb{T}^2$ and let
$$V_D = \overline{\{u\in V : \mathrm{supp}\,u \subset D\}}.$$
The control $\eta$ is required to take values in a finite-dimensional subspace $E\subset V_D$ that is chosen independently of $\nu$.

The system is said to be controllable in finite-dimensional projections in time $T>0$ if for every finite-dimensional subspace $F\subset V$, every $u_0\in V$, and every $\hat u\in V$ there exists a control $\eta\in L^2([0,T];E)$ such that the corresponding solution $u$ satisfies $\mathsf{P}_F u(T,\cdot) = \mathsf{P}_F \hat u$, where $\mathsf{P}_F$ is the orthogonal projection onto $F$.

Question: Does there exist a finite-dimensional subspace $E\subset V_D$, independent of the viscosity $\nu$, such that the system above is controllable in finite-dimensional projections in every time $T>0$? If so, give an explicit construction of such $E$.

Let $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$. A numerical semigroup is a submonoid $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ (containing $0$ and closed under addition) such that $\mathbb{N} \setminus S$ is finite. Every numerical semigroup $S \neq \mathbb{N}$ admits a unique minimal system of generators $\{n_1, n_2, \dots, n_e\}$ with $\gcd(n_1, \dots, n_e) = 1$; the integer $e = e(S)$ is called the embedding dimension of $S$. The Frobenius number of $S$ is defined as
$$F(S) = \max(\mathbb{Z} \setminus S),$$
i.e., the largest integer that does not belong to $S$.

For $e = 2$, with minimal generators $n_1 < n_2$, one has the classical formula $F(S) = n_1 n_2 - n_1 - n_2$.

Problem: For numerical semigroups $S$ with embedding dimension $e(S) \geq 3$, give a general closed-form formula expressing $F(S)$ as a function of a minimal system of generators $\{n_1, n_2, \dots, n_e\}$ of $S$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem of finding a general closed-form formula for the Frobenius number of a numerical semigroup with embedding dimension at least 3 is a long-standing open problem. F. Curtis (1990) proved that the Frobenius number cannot be expressed as a finite-arithmetic-step closed formula (in particular as a polynomial) in the generators when e ≥ 3, and Ramírez Alfonsín showed that the corresponding decision problem is NP-hard. Partial results exist for special families (e.g., arithmetic, almost arithmetic, geometric, or symmetric/pseudo-symmetric semigroups, and the e=3 case has explicit semi-algorithmic descriptions), but no general formula is known.

The general problem of determining the type of a numerical semigroup from its multiplicity, embedding dimension, genus, and/or Frobenius number remains open. $$a x \bmod b \;\le\; x,$$
and let
$$S(a,b,1) \;=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{N} : a x \bmod b \le x \,\}.$$
It is known that $S(a,b,1)$ is a numerical semigroup, i.e. a submonoid of $(\mathbb{N},+)$ whose complement $\mathbb{N}\setminus S(a,b,1)$ is finite. For a numerical semigroup $S$ define:

- the Frobenius number $F(S) = \max(\mathbb{Z}\setminus S)$;
- the multiplicity $m(S) = \min(S\setminus\{0\})$;
- the embedding dimension $e(S)$, the cardinality of the (unique) minimal system of generators of $S$;
- the type $t(S) = \#\{\, z \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus S : z + s \in S \text{ for all } s \in S\setminus\{0\}\,\}$ (the number of pseudo-Frobenius numbers of $S$).

Find closed-form expressions, in terms of the parameters $a$ and $b$ only, for
$$F(S(a,b,1)),\qquad m(S(a,b,1)),\qquad t(S(a,b,1)),\qquad e(S(a,b,1)).$$

A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}_0$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}_0$. For such an $S$, define:
- the Frobenius number $F(S) = \max(\mathbb{N}_0 \setminus S)$,
- the genus $g(S) = |\mathbb{N}_0 \setminus S|$,
- the embedding dimension $e(S)$, the cardinality of the unique minimal system of generators of $S$.

Given positive integers $a < b$ with $\gcd(a,b)=1$, the modular numerical semigroup associated with the pair $(a,b)$ is
$$S(a,b) \;=\; \{\, x \in \mathbb{N}_0 : ax \bmod b \le x \,\},$$
where $ax \bmod b$ denotes the remainder of $ax$ upon division by $b$. A numerical semigroup is called modular if it equals $S(a,b)$ for some such pair.

Wilf's conjecture asserts that for every numerical semigroup $S$,
$$e(S)\, g(S) \;\le\; (e(S)-1)\,(F(S)+1).$$

Question: Does Wilf's conjecture hold for every modular numerical semigroup?

Let $p$ be an odd prime. Let $K_\infty/K$ be a $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension of a number field $K$ with Galois group $\Gamma\cong\mathbb{Z}_p$, and let $\Lambda=\mathbb{Z}_p[[\Gamma]]$ denote the associated Iwasawa algebra (a complete regular local Noetherian ring isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}_p[[T]]$). A finitely generated $\Lambda$-module $M$ is said to have Property F if it is a submodule of a free $\Lambda$-module of finite rank and, in addition, satisfies the following rigidity condition: for every height-one prime $\mathfrak{p}$ of $\Lambda$, the localization $M_\mathfrak{p}$ is a reflexive $\Lambda_\mathfrak{p}$-module, and $M$ admits a canonical decomposition $M=\bigoplus_{\chi}M(\chi)$ into isotypic components under any continuous action of a finite group commuting with $\Gamma$, with each component itself embedding as a submodule of a free $\Lambda$-module.

The standard Iwasawa class-group modules (e.g.\ the projective limits of $p$-parts of class groups along $K_\infty/K$, suitably modified) are known to enjoy Property F.

Problem. Provide intrinsic structural criteria — formulated purely in terms of $\Lambda$-module-theoretic invariants such as Fitting ideals, characteristic ideals, depth, or behavior under localization at height-one primes — that are necessary and sufficient (or at least sufficient under natural hypotheses) for a finitely generated $\Lambda$-module $M$ that arises as a projective limit of finite $p$-groups along $K_\infty/K$ to have Property F. Equivalently, identify general conditions on a submodule $M\subset\Lambda^n$ guaranteeing Property F, and exhibit further natural classes of $\Lambda$-modules (beyond the classical Iwasawa class-group modules) that satisfy Property F.

A numerical semigroup is a subset $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$. The elements of $\mathbb{N}\setminus S$ are called the gaps of $S$; the largest gap is the Frobenius number $F(S)$, and the number of gaps is the genus $g(S)$. The type $t(S)$ is the cardinality of the set $\{x\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus S : x+s\in S\text{ for every }s\in S\setminus\{0\}\}$ (the pseudo-Frobenius numbers). Every numerical semigroup admits a unique finite minimal system of generators.

For positive integers $a,b,c,d$ with $a/b<c/d$, set $I=[a/b,c/d]$ and define
$$S(I)\;=\;\mathbb{N}\cap\bigsqcup_{n\ge 0} nI\;=\;\{x\in\mathbb{N}:\exists n\in\mathbb{N},\ na/b\le x\le nc/d\}.$$
Then $S(I)$ is a numerical semigroup, and a numerical semigroup is called proportionally modular if it equals $S(I)$ for some such interval $I$.

Problem. Provide explicit closed-form formulas, depending only on the unique minimal system of generators $\{n_1<n_2<\cdots<n_e\}$ of a proportionally modular numerical semigroup $S$, that compute each of the following invariants of $S$:
(i) the Frobenius number $F(S)$,
(ii) the genus $g(S)$,
(iii) the type $t(S)$.

For each $n$, let $S_n$ denote the set of primes of $K_n$ lying above $p$, and let $\mathrm{Cl}'(K_n)$ be the ideal class group of the ring of $S_n$-integers (the $p$-integers) of $K_n$. Define
$$A'(K_n) := \mathrm{Cl}'(K_n)\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Z}_p,$$
the $p$-part of the $p$-integer class group, and form the projective limit
$$A' := \varprojlim_{n} A'(K_n)$$
with respect to the norm maps. Then $A'$ is a finitely generated module over the Iwasawa algebra $\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}_p[[T]] \cong \mathbb{Z}_p[[\mathrm{Gal}(K_\infty/K)]]$, where $T = \gamma - 1$ for a topological generator $\gamma$ of $\mathrm{Gal}(K_\infty/K)$. Let
$$A'[T] := \{x\in A' : Tx = 0\}$$
denote the $T$-torsion submodule.

Question: Is $A'[T]$ finite for every Galois number field $K$ and every prime $p$? Equivalently, does the generalized Gross–Kuz'min conjecture hold for all such $K$ and $p$?

Let $\mathcal{O}_K^\times$ denote the group of global units of $K$, and let $E := \mathcal{O}_K^\times / (\text{torsion})$, so by Dirichlet's unit theorem $E$ is a free abelian group of rank $r := r_1 + r_2 - 1$.

For each prime $\mathfrak{p}$ of $K$ above $p$, let $K_\mathfrak{p}$ denote the completion and $U_\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_{K_\mathfrak{p}}^\times$ the group of principal local units (i.e., those congruent to $1$ modulo $\mathfrak{p}$). Set
$$U := \prod_{\mathfrak{p} \mid p} U_\mathfrak{p},$$
which is a finitely generated $\mathbb{Z}_p$-module. The diagonal embedding $\mathcal{O}_K^\times \hookrightarrow U$ induces a homomorphism $\iota_p : E \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{Z}_p \to U$. Let $K$ be a number field of degree $n = r_1 + 2r_2$ over $\mathbb{Q}$, where $r_1$ is the number of real embeddings and $r_2$ the number of pairs of complex embeddings, and let $p$ be a fixed rational prime. For each prime $\mathfrak{p}$ of $K$ above $p$, let $K_\mathfrak{p}$ denote the completion and $U_\mathfrak{p} \subset \mathcal{O}_{K_\mathfrak{p}}^\times$ the group of principal local units (i.e., those congruent to $1$ modulo $\mathfrak{p}$). Set 
$$U := \prod_{\mathfrak{p} \mid p} U_\mathfrak{p},$$
which is a finitely generated $\mathbb{Z}_p$-module. The diagonal embedding $\mathcal{O}_K^\times \hookrightarrow U$ induces a homomorphism $\iota_p : E \otimes_\mathbb{Z} \mathbb{Z}_p \to U$. Define the closure $\overline{E} \subset U$ to be the topological closure of the image of $E$ under this embedding, and define the Leopoldt defect
$$D(K) := \mathrm{rk}_\mathbb{Z}(E) - \mathrm{rk}_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(\overline{E}) = r - \mathrm{rk}_{\mathbb{Z}_p}(\overline{E}).$$
Equivalently, $D(K)$ equals the dimension of the kernel of $\iota_p$ as a $\mathbb{Q}_p$-vector space.

Prove or disprove: for every number field $K$ and every prime $p$, one has $D(K) = 0$.

For general number fields, however, the conjecture remains open as of 2026; recent works (e.g., Allen–Calegari–Gee–Newton on potential automorphy and Leopoldt, and ongoing efforts via representation-theoretic and unit-theoretic methods) continue to attack it without a complete resolution.

A numerical semigroup is a subset S of the nonnegative integers N that contains 0, is closed under addition, and has finite complement in N. For such an S, let:
- m(S) = min(S \ {0}) be the multiplicity,
- F(S) = max(N \ S) be the Frobenius number (assume S ≠ N),
- n(S) = #{ s ∈ S : s < F(S) },
- e(S) = the embedding dimension, i.e. the cardinality of the unique minimal system of generators of S.

Wilf's conjecture asserts that for every numerical semigroup S ≠ N,
  F(S) + 1 ≤ e(S) · n(S).
Define the half of S by
  S/2 = { x ∈ N : 2x ∈ S }.
It is known that S/2 is again a numerical semigroup.

Question: If a numerical semigroup S satisfies Wilf's conjecture, must its half S/2 also satisfy Wilf's conjecture?

Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $K$ be a CM number field containing the $p$-th roots of unity, with maximal totally real subfield $K^+$. Let $j$ denote the complex conjugation, which acts on $G = \mathrm{Gal}(K/\mathbb{Q})$-modules; for a $\mathbb{Z}_p[j]$-module $M$ on which $2$ is invertible, write $M^- = \{m \in M : j(m) = -m\}$ for the minus part.

Fix a finite set $T$ of primes of $K^+$ containing all $p$-adic primes and all archimedean primes, and let $T$ also denote the corresponding set of primes of $K$. Let $\mathcal{O}_{K,T}$ be the ring of $T$-integers of $K$ and let $A'_K$ denote the $p$-part of the $T$-class group of $K$ (the ideal class group of $\mathcal{O}_{K,T}$, tensored with $\mathbb{Z}_p$).

Let $K_\infty/K$ be the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-extension, with intermediate fields $K_n$, and define
$$A' := \varprojlim_n A'_{K_n},$$
a module over $\Lambda = \mathbb{Z}_p[[\mathrm{Gal}(K_\infty/K)]]$. Let $T \subset \Lambda$ also denote (by abuse of notation) the augmentation-type element such that $M[T]$ denotes the $T$-torsion submodule, equivalently the submodule of $\Gamma$-coinvariants viewed as a torsion piece, i.e., $(A')^-[T] = \{x \in (A')^- : Tx = 0\}$.

Question: Is it true that
$$(A')^-[T] = \{1\}\,?$$

Equivalently, does the minus part of the inverse limit of $p$-parts of $T$-class groups along the cyclotomic $\mathbb{Z}_p$-tower of $K$ have no nontrivial $T$-torsion?

A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$. Given positive integers $a$ and $b$, the modular numerical semigroup $S(a,b)$ is defined as
$$S(a,b) = \{ x \in \mathbb{N} : a x \bmod b \le x \}.$$
More generally, for positive integers $a,b,c$, the proportionally modular numerical semigroup $S(a,b,c)$ is
$$S(a,b,c) = \{ x \in \mathbb{N} : a x \bmod b \le c x \}.$$
A numerical semigroup $S$ is said to admit a Toms decomposition if it can be expressed as a finite intersection
$$S = \bigcap_{i=1}^{n} S(a_i, b_i, c_i)$$
of proportionally modular numerical semigroups. The Frobenius number of $S$ is $F(S) = \max(\mathbb{N}\setminus S)$, and $S$ is called contracted if $\frac{F(S)+1}{2} \notin S$ (equivalently, $S$ contains no element strictly between $F(S)/2$ and $F(S)$ other than as required, in the sense used for contracted semigroups).

Question: Is it true that every contracted modular numerical semigroup admits a Toms decomposition?

Consider the disordered copolymer model on $\mathbb{Z}$ defined as follows. Let $S=(S_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a simple symmetric random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ starting at $0$, with law $\mathbf{P}$, and let $\omega=(\omega_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be an i.i.d. sequence of standard Gaussian random variables (the disorder) with law $\mathbb{P}$, independent of $S$. For parameters $\lambda\ge 0$ and $h\ge 0$ and length $N\in\mathbb{N}$, define the polymer measure
$$\frac{d\mathbf{P}_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}}{d\mathbf{P}}(S)=\frac{1}{Z_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}}\exp\!\left(\lambda\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\omega_n+h)\,\mathrm{sign}(S_n)\right),$$
with the convention $\mathrm{sign}(0)=\mathrm{sign}(S_{n-1})$ when $S_n=0$, and $Z_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}$ the normalizing partition function. The free energy
$$\mathrm{f}(\lambda,h)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\,\mathbb{E}\log Z_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}$$
exists, is non-negative, and is non-increasing in $h$. The (quenched) critical curve is
$$h_c(\lambda)=\inf\{h\ge 0:\mathrm{f}(\lambda,h)=0\},\qquad \lambda>0,$$
and corresponds to the boundary between the localized phase $\{\mathrm{f}>0\}$ and the delocalized phase $\{\mathrm{f}=0\}$.

For the simple random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$, the return time to $0$ has tail exponent $\alpha=1/2$. It is known that the limit
$$m_{1/2}:=\lim_{\lambda\downarrow 0}\frac{h_c(\lambda)}{\lambda}$$
exists and satisfies $m_{1/2}\in[2/3,1]$.

Prove that this weak-coupling critical slope satisfies the strict inequality
$$m_{1/2}>\frac{2}{3}.$$

Consider the disordered copolymer model on $\mathbb{Z}$ defined as follows. Let $S=(S_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a simple symmetric random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ starting at $0$, with law $\mathbf{P}$, and let $\omega=(\omega_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be an i.i.d. sequence of standard Gaussian random variables (the disorder) with law $\mathbb{P}$, independent of $S$. For parameters $\lambda\ge 0$ and $h\ge 0$ and length $N\in\mathbb{N}$, define the polymer measure
$$\frac{d\mathbf{P}_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}}{d\mathbf{P}}(S)=\frac{1}{Z_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}}\exp\!\left(\lambda\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\omega_n+h)\,\mathrm{sign}(S_n)\right),$$
with the convention $\mathrm{sign}(0)=\mathrm{sign}(S_{n-1})$ when $S_n=0$, and $Z_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}$ the normalizing partition function. The free energy
$$\mathrm{f}(\lambda,h)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\,\mathbb{E}\log Z_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}$$
exists, is non-negative, and is non-increasing in $h$. The (quenched) critical curve is
$$h_c(\lambda)=\inf\{h\ge 0:\mathrm{f}(\lambda,h)=0\},\qquad \lambda>0,$$
and corresponds to the boundary between the localized phase $\{\mathrm{f}>0\}$ and the delocalized phase $\{\mathrm{f}=0\}$.

For the simple random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$, the return time to $0$ has tail exponent $\alpha=1/2$. It is known that the limit
$$m_{1/2}:=\lim_{\lambda\downarrow 0}\frac{h_c(\lambda)}{\lambda}$$
exists and satisfies $m_{1/2}\in[2/3,1]$.

Prove that this weak-coupling critical slope satisfies the strict inequality
$$m_{1/2}>\frac{2}{3}.$$

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Subsequent work by Berger, Caravenna, Poisat, Sun and Zygouras (Comm. Math. Phys. 2014) proved the Bolthausen–den Hollander–Opoku conjecture identifying the weak-coupling slope $m_\alpha$ with the critical slope of a continuum copolymer model for $\alpha\in(0,1)$, but the search results do not explicitly confirm a strict inequality $m_{1/2}>2/3$ at the level of the discrete model. The status of this specific strict bound could not be definitively verified from the available sources.

A proportionally modular Diophantine inequality is an expression of the form a x mod b ≤ c x, where a, b, c are positive integers; the set S(a,b,c) = { x ∈ ℕ : a x mod b ≤ c x } is a numerical semigroup, called a proportionally modular numerical semigroup. When c = 1 the inequality is called modular, and the corresponding semigroup S(a,b,1) is called a modular numerical semigroup. A numerical semigroup S is said to admit a Toms decomposition if there exist positive integers q_1,…,q_n, m_1,…,m_n, and L with gcd(q_i, m_i) = gcd(L, m_i) = gcd(L, q_i) = 1 for every i, such that S can be written as a finite intersection of proportionally modular numerical semigroups arising from this data; equivalently, S is a finite intersection of proportionally modular numerical semigroups.

Question: Is every finite system of proportionally modular Diophantine inequalities equivalent (i.e., defining the same numerical semigroup as the intersection of solution sets) to a finite system of modular Diophantine inequalities (those with proportion c = 1)? Equivalently, can every numerical semigroup that admits a Toms decomposition be expressed as an intersection of finitely many modular numerical semigroups?

Let $S=(S_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a simple symmetric random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ starting at $0$, and let $\omega=(\omega_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be an i.i.d. sequence of standard Gaussian random variables, independent of $S$. For parameters $\lambda\ge 0$ (coupling) and $h\in\mathbb{R}$ (bias), and for each $N\in\mathbb{N}$, define the copolymer Gibbs measure with quenched disorder $\omega$ by

$$\frac{d\mathbf{P}_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}}{d\mathbf{P}}(S)=\frac{1}{Z_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}}\exp\!\Big(\lambda\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\omega_n+h)\,\mathrm{sign}(S_n)\Big),$$

with the convention $\mathrm{sign}(S_n)=\mathrm{sign}(S_{n-1})$ when $S_n=0$, where $\mathbf{P}$ is the law of $S$ and $Z_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}$ is the normalizing partition function. The quenched free energy is

$$\textsf{f}(\lambda,h)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\,\mathbb{E}\big[\log Z_{N,\lambda,h}^{\omega}\big]\ge 0,$$

and the model exhibits a localization/delocalization transition along a critical curve $h_c(\lambda)=\inf\{h\ge 0:\textsf{f}(\lambda,h)=0\}$, which is known to satisfy $h_c(\lambda)/\lambda\to m\in[1/2,1]$ as $\lambda\downarrow 0$ for some constant $m$ (the weak-coupling critical slope).

More generally, replace the simple random walk by a discrete renewal process whose inter-arrival law has a regularly varying tail with index $1+\alpha$ for $\alpha\in(0,1)$ (so that the return-time distribution satisfies $\mathbf{P}(\tau_1=n)=n^{-(1+\alpha)}L(n)$ for a slowly varying $L$), and define analogously the copolymer free energy and critical curve. It is known that
$$\lim_{\lambda\downarrow 0}\frac{h_c(\lambda)}{\lambda}=:m_\alpha\in\Big[\frac{1}{1+\alpha},\,1\Big].$$

Question: Does there exist some $\alpha\in(0,1)$ for which
$$m_\alpha=\frac{1}{1+\alpha}\,?$$

A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and whose complement $\mathbb{N}\setminus S$ is finite. The elements of $\mathbb{N}\setminus S$ are called the gaps of $S$. A positive integer $n$ is a fundamental gap of $S$ if $n \notin S$ but $kn \in S$ for every integer $k \geq 2$; the set of fundamental gaps is denoted $\mathrm{FG}(S)$.

Equivalently, ordering the positive integers by divisibility ($a \preceq b$ iff $a \mid b$), the fundamental gaps are the maximal elements of the set of gaps of $S$. The set $\mathrm{FG}(S)$ uniquely determines $S$, since
$$ S = \mathbb{N} \setminus \{ d \in \mathbb{N} : d \mid x \text{ for some } x \in \mathrm{FG}(S)\}. $$

Problem. Find simple, easily checkable sufficient conditions on a finite subset $X \subseteq \mathbb{N} \setminus \{0\}$ which guarantee the existence of a numerical semigroup $S$ such that $X = \mathrm{FG}(S)$.

Consider the general copolymer model defined as follows. Let $S=(S_n)_{n\ge 0}$ be a recurrent random walk on $\mathbb{Z}$ starting at $0$, whose return time to $0$ has a distribution with polynomial tail of exponent $1+\alpha$ for some $\alpha\in(0,1]$ (i.e., $P(\tau_1=n)=n^{-(1+\alpha)}L(n)$ for a slowly varying $L$). Let $\omega=(\omega_n)_{n\ge 1}$ be an i.i.d. sequence of centered, unit-variance random variables with finite exponential moments of all orders, independent of $S$. For parameters $\lambda\ge 0$ and $h\in\mathbb{R}$, define the quenched partition function
$$Z_{N,\omega}(\lambda,h)=E\!\left[\exp\!\left(\lambda\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\omega_n+h)\,\mathrm{sign}(S_n)\right)\right],$$
with the convention $\mathrm{sign}(S_n)=\mathrm{sign}(S_{n-1})$ if $S_n=0$. The quenched free energy is
$$F(\lambda,h)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\log Z_{N,\omega}(\lambda,h)\right]\ge 0,$$
and the critical curve is $h_c(\lambda)=\inf\{h\ge 0:F(\lambda,h)=0\}$.

It is known that for every $\lambda>0$ there exists a finite constant $c(\lambda)$ such that
$$F(\lambda,h_c(\lambda)+\delta)\le (1+\alpha)\,c(\lambda)\,\delta^{2}\qquad\text{for every }\delta>0. \qquad (\star)$$

Question: Can the smoothing bound $(\star)$ be improved by replacing the exponent $2$ with a strictly larger exponent? More precisely, does there exist $\gamma>2$ such that for every $\lambda>0$ one has $F(\lambda,h_c(\lambda)+\delta)\le C(\lambda)\,\delta^{\gamma}$ for all sufficiently small $\delta>0$?

Subsequent work by Caravenna and den Hollander (2013) sharpened the constant in the smoothing inequality and established asymptotic optimality of the constant in the weak-coupling regime, but kept the quadratic exponent. A numerical semigroup is a subset $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement $\mathbb{N}\setminus S$ (the gaps of $S$). The Frobenius number $F(S)$ is the largest gap of $S$ (with $F(\mathbb{N})=-1$ by convention).

For numerical semigroups $S$ and $T$, define the quotient
$$T/2 \;=\; \{\, n\in\mathbb{N}\ :\ 2n\in T\,\}.$$
This $T/2$ is again a numerical semigroup. When $T/2=S$, we say that $T$ is a double of $S$. For every numerical semigroup $S$ the set
$$\mathcal{D}(S)\;=\;\{\,T\subseteq\mathbb{N}\ :\ T \text{ is a numerical semigroup with } T/2=S\,\}$$
is nonempty and finite.

Problem. Find a closed-form expression, depending only on invariants of $S$, for
$$\min\{\,F(T)\ :\ T\in\mathcal{D}(S)\,\},$$
the minimum Frobenius number among all doubles of $S$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

A related problem—the minimum genus among doubles of a numerical semigroup $S$—was solved by Strazzanti (arXiv:1512.00638), who proved that for $d$-folds the minimum genus equals $g(S)+\lceil (d-1)F(S)/2\rceil$. However, that work treats only the genus and does not provide a formula for the minimum Frobenius number among doubles. No source located in the search gives such a closed-form formula for $\min\{F(T):T/2=S\}$, so the status of this specific question appears unresolved based on available evidence.

Consider the random copolymer model at a selective interface defined as follows. Let $\tau=\{\tau_n\}_{n\ge 0}$ be a renewal process on $\mathbb{N}$ with $\tau_0=0$ and inter-arrival law $P(\tau_1=n)=L(n)\,n^{-(1+\alpha)}$ for some slowly varying function $L$ and exponent $\alpha>0$. Let $\omega=\{\omega_n\}_{n\ge 1}$ be an i.i.d. sequence of centered random variables with unit variance and finite exponential moments (the disorder, or charge sequence). For parameters $\lambda\ge 0$ (coupling strength) and $h\ge 0$ (asymmetry bias), define the polymer measure of length $N$ by
$$\frac{dP_{N,\omega}^{\lambda,h}}{dP}(\tau) = \frac{1}{Z_{N,\omega}^{\lambda,h}}\exp\Big(\lambda\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\omega_n+h)\Delta_n\Big)\mathbf{1}_{\{N\in\tau\}},$$
where $\Delta_n\in\{-1,+1\}$ is the sign of the excursion of the underlying walk between consecutive renewal points (interpreted via the standard copolymer construction), and $Z_{N,\omega}^{\lambda,h}$ is the partition function. The quenched free energy
$$\textsf{f}(\lambda,h)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}\log Z_{N,\omega}^{\lambda,h}$$
exists, equals zero in the delocalized phase, and is positive in the localized phase, giving a critical curve $h_c(\lambda)$. Let $\textsf{f}(\lambda,h)$ vanish like $(h_c(\lambda)-h)^{\nu(\alpha,\lambda)}$ (in a suitable sense) as $h\uparrow h_c(\lambda)$, with possible logarithmic corrections.

Determine the dependence of the near-critical behavior of $\textsf{f}(\lambda,h)$ on the tail exponent $\alpha$ and on the coupling parameter $\lambda$. In particular, decide which of the following holds: the critical exponent and near-critical asymptotics are (i) $\alpha$-dependent only, (ii) $\lambda$-dependent only, (iii) dependent on both $\alpha$ and $\lambda$, or (iv) universal (independent of both). Provide the corresponding critical exponent(s) and any logarithmic corrections.

$$\frac{dP_{N,\omega}^{\lambda,h}}{dP}(\tau) = \frac{1}{Z_{N,\omega}^{\lambda,h}}\exp\Big(\lambda\sum_{n=1}^{N}(\omega_n+h)\Delta_n\Big)\mathbf{1}_{\{N\in\tau\}},$$
where $\Delta_n\in\{-1,+1\}$ is the sign of the excursion of the underlying walk between consecutive renewal points (interpreted via the standard copolymer construction), and $Z_{N,\omega}^{\lambda,h}$ is the partition function. The quenched free energy
$$\textsf{f}(\lambda,h)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N}\mathbb{E}\log Z_{N,\omega}^{\lambda,h}$$
exists, equals zero in the delocalized phase, and is positive in the localized phase, giving a critical curve $h_c(\lambda)$. Let $\textsf{f}(\lambda,h)$ vanish like $(h_c(\lambda)-h)^{\nu(\alpha,\lambda)}$ (in a suitable sense) as $h\uparrow h_c(\lambda)$, with possible logarithmic corrections.

Determine the dependence of the near-critical behavior of $\textsf{f}(\lambda,h)$ on the tail exponent $\alpha$ and on the coupling parameter $\lambda$. In particular, decide which of the following holds: the critical exponent and near-critical asymptotics are (i) $\alpha$-dependent only, (ii) $\lambda$-dependent only, (iii) dependent on both $\alpha$ and $\lambda$, or (iv) universal (independent of both). Provide the corresponding critical exponent(s) and any logarithmic corrections.

Consider the copolymer model at a selective interface defined as follows. Let ω = (ω_n)_{n≥1} be a sequence of i.i.d. centered random variables with unit variance and finite exponential moments, with law P. For parameters λ ≥ 0 and h ≥ 0 and an integer N ≥ 1, let S = (S_n)_{n≥0} denote a simple random walk on ℤ starting at 0 with law 𝐏, and define the (quenched) partition function

  Z_{N,ω} = 𝐄[ exp( -2λ Σ_{n=1}^N (ω_n + h) Δ_n ) ],

where Δ_n = 1 if S_n ≤ 0 (or, more precisely, if the bond (S_{n-1}, S_n) lies in the lower half-plane) and Δ_n = 0 otherwise. The free energy is

  F(λ, h) = lim_{N→∞} (1/N) E log Z_{N,ω},

and the inverse correlation length is

  μ(λ, h) = − lim_{N→∞} (1/N) log E[ (1 + e^{−2λ Σ_{n=1}^N (ω_n + h)}) / Z_{N,ω} ].

Both limits exist (P-a.s. and in L¹) for λ > 0, h ≥ 0. There exists a critical curve h_c(λ) > 0 such that F(λ, h) > 0 for h < h_c(λ) (localized phase) and F(λ, h) = 0 for h ≥ h_c(λ) (delocalized phase); similarly μ(λ, h) > 0 in the localized phase and vanishes at h_c(λ).

Question: Fix λ > 0. Is it true that

  log μ(λ, h) ∼ log F(λ, h)   as h ↑ h_c(λ)  ?

That is, does the ratio log μ(λ, h) / log F(λ, h) tend to 1 as h approaches the critical point from below?

A numerical semigroup is a cofinite submonoid S of (N, +) containing 0. The embedding dimension of S is the cardinality of its unique minimal system of generators. A nonempty family F of numerical semigroups is called a Frobenius variety if (i) S ∩ T ∈ F whenever S, T ∈ F, and (ii) for every S ∈ F with S ≠ N there exists T ∈ F such that T ⊋ S and T \ S = {F(S)}, where F(S) = max(N \ S) is the Frobenius number of S.

A numerical semigroup S is said to admit a Toms decomposition if there exist numerical semigroups S_1, …, S_n, each of embedding dimension two, such that S = S_1 ∩ … ∩ S_n. Let V_T denote the family of all numerical semigroups admitting a Toms decomposition; it is known that V_T is a Frobenius variety, and that every numerical semigroup of embedding dimension two belongs to V_T.

Question: Is V_T the least Frobenius variety (with respect to inclusion) that contains every numerical semigroup of embedding dimension two? Equivalently, does every Frobenius variety containing all numerical semigroups of embedding dimension two contain V_T?

Let $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$. A numerical semigroup is a submonoid $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ (containing $0$, closed under addition) whose complement $\mathbb{N}\setminus S$ is finite. A (Frobenius) variety is a nonempty family $\mathcal{V}$ of numerical semigroups such that:
(i) if $S, T \in \mathcal{V}$ then $S \cap T \in \mathcal{V}$, and
(ii) if $S \in \mathcal{V}$ and $S \neq \mathbb{N}$, then $S \cup \{F(S)\} \in \mathcal{V}$, where $F(S) = \max(\mathbb{N}\setminus S)$ is the Frobenius number of $S$.

The variety $\mathcal{V}$ is called infinite if it contains infinitely many numerical semigroups.

Associated with $\mathcal{V}$ is a rooted directed tree $G(\mathcal{V})$: the vertex set is $\mathcal{V}$, the root is $\mathbb{N}$, and there is a directed edge from $S$ to $T$ whenever $T = S \cup \{F(S)\}$ (so $T$ is the parent of $S$). For $n \geq 0$, the $n$-th level of $G(\mathcal{V})$ is the set of vertices at directed distance $n$ from the root $\mathbb{N}$, and let $\ell_n(\mathcal{V})$ denote its cardinality.

Question: Is it true that for every infinite Frobenius variety $\mathcal{V}$ and every integer $n \geq 0$,
$$\ell_{n+1}(\mathcal{V}) > \ell_n(\mathcal{V})?$$

In the Standard Model of particle physics, the purely leptonic decay of the charged B meson, B+ → τ+ ν_τ, has a branching ratio that can be predicted from the CKM matrix element |V_ub|, the B-meson decay constant f_B, the B-meson mass and lifetime, and the τ mass via the formula

  BR(B+ → τ+ ν_τ) = (G_F^2 m_B m_τ^2 / 8π) (1 − m_τ^2/m_B^2)^2 f_B^2 |V_ub|^2 τ_B.

A global unitarity-triangle fit (using inputs such as |V_ub| from semileptonic decays, ε_K, Δm_d, Δm_s, sin 2β, and the angles α and γ) yields an indirect Standard-Model prediction for this branching ratio. The current experimental world average is

  BR_exp(B+ → τ+ ν_τ) = (1.64 ± 0.34) × 10^{−4},

while the indirect global-fit determinations differ from this experimental value by 2.6σ (CKMfitter) and 3.2σ (UTfit).

Question: Determine whether sufficiently precise future experimental measurements of BR(B+ → τ+ ν_τ), combined with improved theoretical inputs (in particular f_B and |V_ub|), can resolve this tension within the Standard Model, or whether the discrepancy persists and signals new physics beyond the Standard Model (for example, a charged-Higgs contribution that modifies the leptonic decay amplitude).

Updated Belle and BaBar measurements using hadronic and semileptonic tagging have lowered the experimental world average of BR(B+ → τ+ ν_τ) toward the Standard-Model expectation, and current CKMfitter/UTfit global fits report a much reduced discrepancy (typically below 2σ). Background and definitions.

Let $\mathbb{N}_0=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$. A numerical semigroup is a subset $S\subseteq\mathbb{N}_0$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement $\mathbb{N}_0\setminus S$. The cardinality $g(S)=|\mathbb{N}_0\setminus S|$ is the genus of $S$, and the largest integer not in $S$ is the Frobenius number $F(S)$.

A nonempty family $\mathcal{V}$ of numerical semigroups is called a Frobenius variety if:
(i) $S,T\in\mathcal{V}\Rightarrow S\cap T\in\mathcal{V}$, and
(ii) for every $S\in\mathcal{V}$ with $S\neq\mathbb{N}_0$, one has $S\cup\{F(S)\}\in\mathcal{V}$.

For a Frobenius variety $\mathcal{V}$, the associated tree $\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{V})$ has the elements of $\mathcal{V}$ as vertices, with $\mathbb{N}_0$ as the root, and an edge between $S$ and $S\cup\{F(S)\}$ whenever $S\in\mathcal{V}\setminus\{\mathbb{N}_0\}$. The level of a vertex $S\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{V})$ equals its genus $g(S)$, and the $n$-th level set is
$$\mathcal{V}_n=\{S\in\mathcal{V}:g(S)=n\}.$$

Say that $\mathcal{V}$ has the Bras-Amorós growth property if
$$|\mathcal{V}_{n+1}|>|\mathcal{V}_n|\qquad\text{for every }n\geq 0,$$
the analogue, restricted to $\mathcal{V}$, of the Bras-Amorós conjecture concerning the strict growth of the number of numerical semigroups by genus.

Problem. Give an explicit characterization of the Frobenius varieties $\mathcal{V}$ for which $|\mathcal{V}_{n+1}|>|\mathcal{V}_n|$ holds for all $n\geq 0$.

For a Frobenius variety $\mathcal{V}$, the associated tree $\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{V})$ has the elements of $\mathcal{V}$ as vertices, with $\mathbb{N}_0$ as the root, and an edge between $S$ and $S\cup\{F(S)\}$ whenever $S\in\mathcal{V}\setminus\{\mathbb{N}_0\}$. The level of a vertex $S\in\mathcal{T}(\mathcal{V})$ equals its genus $g(S)$, and the $n$-th level set is
$$\mathcal{V}_n=\{S\in\mathcal{V}:g(S)=n\}.$$

Say that $\mathcal{V}$ has the Bras-Amorós growth property if
$$|\mathcal{V}_{n+1}|>|\mathcal{V}_n|\qquad\text{for every }n\geq 0,$$
the analogue, restricted to $\mathcal{V}$, of the Bras-Amorós conjecture concerning the strict growth of the number of numerical semigroups by genus.

Problem. Give an explicit characterization of the Frobenius varieties $\mathcal{V}$ for which $|\mathcal{V}_{n+1}|>|\mathcal{V}_n|$ holds for all $n\geq 0$.

Subsequent literature on Frobenius varieties, pseudo-varieties, and Frobenius-restricted varieties studies their tree structure but does not give a general characterization of those Frobenius varieties whose level sequences are strictly increasing. representations.normalized:
Consider the purely leptonic decays B+ → ℓ+ν_ℓ (ℓ ∈ {μ, τ}) of a charged B meson. In the Standard Model the branching ratio is

  BR_SM(B+ → ℓ+ν_ℓ) = (G_F^2 m_B m_ℓ^2 / 8π) (1 − m_ℓ^2/m_B^2)^2 f_B^2 |V_ub|^2 τ_B,

where G_F is the Fermi constant, m_B and m_ℓ are the meson and lepton masses, f_B is the B-meson decay constant, V_ub is the relevant CKM element, and τ_B is the B+ lifetime.

In a type-II two-Higgs-doublet model (or in supersymmetric extensions sharing the same tree-level structure), exchange of a charged Higgs boson modifies this rate by a multiplicative factor depending on tan β (the ratio of the two Higgs vacuum expectation values) and the charged-Higgs mass M_H:

  BR(B+ → ℓ+ν_ℓ) = BR_SM · r_H,  with  r_H = (1 − tan^2 β · m_B^2 / M_H^2)^2.

Suppose a future high-luminosity B-factory program collects an integrated luminosity of 75 ab^(-1) and measures the branching ratios of B+ → τ+ν_τ and B+ → μ+ν_μ with their projected statistical and systematic uncertainties using both hadronic and semileptonic tagging methods. Determine, as a quantitative region in the (tan β, M_H) plane, the portion of parameter space that can be excluded at 95% confidence level by combining these two measurements assuming agreement with the Standard Model expectation, and identify the resulting lower bound on M_H as a function of tan β (and equivalently the upper bound on tan β / M_H).

A numerical semigroup is a cofinite submonoid S of (N, +) (with 0 ∈ S). For such an S, let g(S) = #(N \ S) be its genus, F(S) = max(Z \ S) its Frobenius number, and e(S) the cardinality of its (unique) minimal system of generators (the embedding dimension). Wilf's classical conjecture asserts e(S) g(S) ≤ (e(S) − 1)(F(S) + 1) for every numerical semigroup S.

A Frobenius variety V is a nonempty family of numerical semigroups satisfying:
(i) if S, T ∈ V, then S ∩ T ∈ V;
(ii) if S ∈ V and S ≠ N, then S ∪ {F(S)} ∈ V.
Within such a variety, every S ∈ V admits a unique minimal V-system of generators, whose cardinality is denoted e_V(S).

Problem: Characterize all Frobenius varieties V with the property that, for every S ∈ V,
   e_V(S) · g(S) ≤ (e_V(S) − 1) · (F(S) + 1).

Wilf's classical conjecture for numerical semigroups remains open in general, with only partial results (e.g., symmetric, pseudo-symmetric semigroups, low embedding dimension, and recently preservation under gluing). representations.normalized:
Consider a high-luminosity e+e- collider experiment operating at the Υ(4S) resonance, designed to study the rare leptonic decay B+ → ℓ+ν_ℓ (ℓ = e, μ, τ). The baseline detector is similar to a BaBar-style geometry but with the center-of-mass boost reduced from βγ = 0.56 to βγ = 0.28, which enlarges the geometric acceptance. Two optional sub-detectors are under consideration:

(i) a forward particle-identification device (Fwd-PID) covering the polar-angle range 17°–25°, providing K/π separation that improves tag-side kaon identification;
(ii) a backward electromagnetic calorimeter (Bwd-EMC) covering the polar-angle range 152°–167°, providing additional photon/energy veto capability.

Empirically determined per-component effects on the analysis of B+ → ℓ+ν_ℓ are:
- Reduced boost (βγ = 0.28 vs 0.56): signal efficiency multiplied by 1.07; background multiplied by 0.94.
- Fwd-PID inclusion: signal efficiency multiplied by 1.025; background multiplied by 1.025.
- Bwd-EMC inclusion: signal efficiency unchanged; background multiplied by 0.90.

Assuming the three modifications act independently and that the figure of merit for sensitivity to a rare branching fraction is S/√B (where S is signal yield ∝ signal efficiency and B is background yield), determine which of the eight possible configurations (each option on/off) maximizes S/√B, and compute the resulting multiplicative improvement factor relative to the baseline (βγ = 0.56, no Fwd-PID, no Bwd-EMC).

representations.normalized:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement $\mathbb{N}\setminus S$ (the gaps of $S$). The largest gap is called the Frobenius number $F(S)$. A numerical semigroup $S$ is pseudo-symmetric if $F(S)$ is even and, for every integer $x \in \mathbb{Z}\setminus\{F(S)/2\}$, one has $x \in S$ if and only if $F(S) - x \notin S$.

A Frobenius variety is a non-empty family $\mathcal{V}$ of numerical semigroups satisfying:
(i) if $S, T \in \mathcal{V}$, then $S \cap T \in \mathcal{V}$; and
(ii) if $S \in \mathcal{V}$ and $S \neq \mathbb{N}$, then $S \cup \{F(S)\} \in \mathcal{V}$.

The intersection of any family of Frobenius varieties is again a Frobenius variety, so given any set $\mathcal{F}$ of numerical semigroups there is a smallest Frobenius variety $\mathrm{Var}(\mathcal{F})$ containing $\mathcal{F}$, called the Frobenius variety generated by $\mathcal{F}$.

Problem: Give an explicit description (intrinsic membership characterization) of the Frobenius variety generated by the family of all pseudo-symmetric numerical semigroups.

representations.normalized:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$. Equivalently, $S = \langle n_1,\dots,n_e\rangle = \{a_1 n_1 + \cdots + a_e n_e : a_i \in \mathbb{N}\}$ for some positive integers $n_1,\dots,n_e$ with $\gcd(n_1,\dots,n_e)=1$.

Given a field $k$ and a numerical semigroup $S = \langle n_1,\dots,n_e\rangle$, let $k[S]=k[t^{n_1},\dots,t^{n_e}]$ be the associated semigroup ring, and let $\varphi:k[x_1,\dots,x_e]\to k[S]$ be the surjection sending $x_i\mapsto t^{n_i}$. The semigroup $S$ is called a complete intersection numerical semigroup if the ideal $\ker\varphi$ can be generated by $e-1$ elements (equivalently, by $e-1$ pure-difference binomials).

For a numerical semigroup $S$ and a positive integer $d$, the quotient of $S$ by $d$ is defined as
$$S/d = \{x \in \mathbb{N} : dx \in S\},$$
which is again a numerical semigroup.

Problem. Characterize, by intrinsic combinatorial or arithmetic conditions on a numerical semigroup $T$, exactly those $T$ for which there exist a complete intersection numerical semigroup $S$ and a positive integer $d$ such that $T = S/d$.

A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$. Every numerical semigroup $S 
eq \mathbb{N}$ has a unique minimal system of generators $\{n_1 < n_2 < \dots < n_e\}$; the integer $e = e(S)$ is called the embedding dimension of $S$, and $m(S) = n_1$ is the multiplicity. It is known that $e(S) \le m(S)$, and $S$ is said to have maximal embedding dimension (MED) if $e(S) = m(S)$.

Given two numerical semigroups $S_1$ and $S_2$ (both different from $\mathbb{N}$), with minimal generators $\{a_1,\dots,a_r\}$ and $\{b_1,\dots,b_s\}$ respectively, and given positive integers $\lambda \in S_2 \setminus \{b_1,\dots,b_s\}$ and $\mu \in S_1 \setminus \{a_1,\dots,a_r\}$ with $\gcd(\lambda,\mu)=1$, the gluing of $S_1$ and $S_2$ (with respect to $\lambda,\mu$) is the numerical semigroup
$$ S = \langle \lambda a_1, \dots, \lambda a_r,\ \mu b_1, \dots, \mu b_s angle. $$
A family $\mathcal{F}$ of numerical semigroups is said to be closed under gluing if every gluing of two members of $\mathcal{F}$ again belongs to $\mathcal{F}$.

Determine the smallest family $\mathcal{F}$ of numerical semigroups that
(i) contains every numerical semigroup of maximal embedding dimension, and
(ii) is closed under gluing.

That is, identify and characterize this minimum family explicitly.

representations.normalized:
A numerical semigroup is a subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ that is closed under addition, contains $0$, and has finite complement in $\mathbb{N}$. Every numerical semigroup $S \neq \{0\}$ admits a unique minimal system of generators $\{n_1 < n_2 < \cdots < n_e\}$; the integer $e = e(S)$ is called the embedding dimension of $S$. The Frobenius number $F(S)$ is the largest integer not belonging to $S$, and $S$ is said to be symmetric if for every integer $z$ one has $z \in S$ if and only if $F(S) - z \notin S$.

Given $S$ with minimal generators $n_1,\dots,n_e$, consider the surjective monoid homomorphism $\varphi : \mathbb{N}^e \to S$ defined by $\varphi(a_1,\dots,a_e) = a_1 n_1 + \cdots + a_e n_e$, and let $\sigma_S = \{(\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}) \in \mathbb{N}^e \times \mathbb{N}^e : \varphi(\mathbf{a}) = \varphi(\mathbf{b})\}$ be the kernel congruence. A presentation of $S$ is a generating set (as a congruence) of $\sigma_S$, and a minimal presentation is one of minimum cardinality, which is an invariant of $S$.

Question: Does there exist a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that for every symmetric numerical semigroup $S$ with embedding dimension $e$, the cardinality of a minimal presentation of $S$ is at most $f(e)$?

Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer and let $\mathbb{N} = \{0,1,2,\dots\}$. Consider the free commutative monoid $\mathbb{N}^n$ with the standard basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$. Given positive integers $c_1,\dots,c_n$ and nonnegative integers $a_{jk}$ (for $1 \le j \le n$ and $1 \le k \le n$ with $k \neq j$), define the finite subset $\sigma \subset \mathbb{N}^n \times \mathbb{N}^n$ by
$$\sigma = \big\{\,(c_i\, e_i,\; a_{i1}e_1+\cdots+\widehat{a_{ii}e_i}+\cdots+a_{in}e_n)\ :\ i=1,\dots,n\,\big\},$$
that is, the $i$-th relation pairs $c_i e_i$ with $\sum_{k\neq i} a_{ik} e_k$. Let $\langle\sigma\rangle$ denote the smallest monoid congruence on $\mathbb{N}^n$ containing $\sigma$, and let $\mathbb{N}^n/\langle\sigma\rangle$ be the corresponding quotient commutative monoid. A numerical semigroup is a submonoid $S$ of $(\mathbb{N},+)$ such that $\mathbb{N}\setminus S$ is finite.

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the integers $c_i$ and $a_{jk}$ for the quotient monoid $\mathbb{N}^n/\langle\sigma\rangle$ to be isomorphic, as a monoid, to a numerical semigroup.

representations.normalized:
A proportionally modular numerical semigroup is a set of the form
S(A,B,C) = { x ∈ ℤ_{≥0} : (A x) mod B ≤ C x },
where A, B, C are positive integers and "(Ax) mod B" denotes the remainder of Ax upon division by B. Equivalently, denoting this semigroup by ⟨A, B⟩·C·, one has the identity
⟨n₁, n₂⟩·n₃· = { x ∈ ℤ_{≥0} : u n₂ n₃ x mod (n₁ n₂) ≤ n₃ x }
for any positive integer u with u n₂ ≡ 1 (mod n₁).

Given pairwise coprime integers a, b, c ≥ 2 and an integer n ≥ 3, consider the proportionally modular numerical semigroup
T(a,b,c,n) = ⟨a^n, b^n⟩ · c^{n-1} ·.

It is known that T(a,b,c,n) contains a^n, b^n, and c^{n-1}, and the statement
"For all such (a,b,c,n), the set {a^n, c^{n-1}, b^n} is NOT a minimal system of generators of T(a,b,c,n)"
is logically equivalent to Fermat's Last Theorem (the assertion that a^n + b^n = c^n has no solution in positive integers when n ≥ 3).

Problem: Provide a proof of the above semigroup-theoretic statement — namely, that for every choice of pairwise coprime integers a, b, c ≥ 2 and every integer n ≥ 3 the proportionally modular numerical semigroup ⟨a^n, b^n⟩·c^{n-1}· is not minimally generated by {a^n, c^{n-1}, b^n} — without invoking Fermat's Last Theorem (in particular, without appealing to the modularity theorem of Wiles and Taylor–Wiles).

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a numerical semigroup, that is, a cofinite submonoid of $(\mathbb{N},+)$ containing $0$. Denote by $\mathrm{Ap}(S,n) = \{s \in S : s - n \notin S\}$ the Apéry set of $S$ with respect to $n \in S \setminus \{0\}$, and let $m = \min(S \setminus \{0\})$ be the multiplicity of $S$.

The type of $S$ is defined as
$$t(S) = \#\{x \in \mathbb{Z} \setminus S : x + s \in S \text{ for all } s \in S \setminus \{0\}\}.$$

For an element $s \in S \setminus \{0\}$, the $\omega$-primality of $s$ in $S$, denoted $\omega_S(s)$, is the smallest positive integer $k$ such that whenever $a_1 + \cdots + a_n - s \in S$ with $a_1, \ldots, a_n \in S \setminus \{0\}$, there exists a subset $I \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}$ with $|I| \le k$ such that $\sum_{i \in I} a_i - s \in S$ (and $\omega_S(s) = \infty$ if no such $k$ exists). The $\omega$-primality of $S$ is
$$\omega(S) = \max\{\omega_S(n) : n \in \text{minimal generators of } S\}.$$

It is known that $\omega(S) \ge t(S)$ holds for every numerical semigroup $S$, and that the strict inequality $\omega(S) \neq t(S)$ is rare.

Problem. Give a characterization of the numerical semigroups $S$ for which $\omega(S) \neq t(S)$.

A numerical semigroup is a cofinite submonoid H of (ℕ₀, +); equivalently, H ⊆ ℕ₀ contains 0, is closed under addition, and ℕ₀ ∖ H is finite. Let A(H) denote the (finite) set of atoms (irreducible elements) of H, i.e. the minimal generating set of H ∖ {0}. For an element s ∈ H ∖ {0}, a factorization of s is an expression s = a₁ + a₂ + ⋯ + aₖ with aᵢ ∈ A(H), and the length of such a factorization is k. The set of lengths of s is

  L(s) = { k ∈ ℕ : s admits a factorization of length k }.

Characterize the finite subsets L ⊆ ℕ that arise as L(s) for some numerical semigroup H and some element s ∈ H. That is, determine necessary and sufficient conditions on a finite set L ⊆ ℕ guaranteeing the existence of a numerical semigroup H and an element s ∈ H with L(s) = L.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a numerical semigroup, that is, a cofinite submonoid of $(\mathbb{N},+)$ minimally generated by $n_1,\dots,n_k$ with $\gcd(n_1,\dots,n_k)=1$. For $s\in S$, the set of factorizations of $s$ is $\mathsf{Z}(s)=\{(a_1,\dots,a_k)\in\mathbb{N}^k:\sum a_i n_i = s\}$. The distance between two factorizations $z=(a_i)$ and $z'=(b_i)$ is $\mathsf{d}(z,z')=\max\{\sum_i \max(a_i-b_i,0),\,\sum_i \max(b_i-a_i,0)\}$. For $N\ge 0$, an $N$-chain from $z$ to $z'$ is a sequence $z=z_0,z_1,\dots,z_t=z'$ in $\mathsf{Z}(s)$ with $\mathsf{d}(z_{j-1},z_j)\le N$ for all $j$. The catenary degree $c(s)$ is the least $N$ such that any two elements of $\mathsf{Z}(s)$ can be joined by an $N$-chain.

Determine whether the function $c\colon S\to\mathbb{N}$ is eventually periodic; that is, decide whether there exists $n\in S$ and an integer $M$ such that $c(s+n)=c(s)$ for every $s\in S$ with $s\ge M$.

Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be a numerical semigroup, i.e., a submonoid of $(\mathbb{N},+)$ whose complement in $\mathbb{N}$ is finite. Fix a system of generators $S = \langle n_1, \dots, n_k \rangle$. For $s \in S$, the set of factorizations of $s$ is
$$\mathsf{Z}(s) = \{(a_1,\dots,a_k) \in \mathbb{N}^k : a_1 n_1 + \cdots + a_k n_k = s\},$$
equipped with the distance $\mathsf{d}(a,b) = \max\!\left(\sum_i \max(a_i-b_i,0),\ \sum_i \max(b_i-a_i,0)\right)$.

For $s \in S$ and $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$, define the local tame degree
$$t_i(s) = \sup\{\,\mathsf{d}(z, \mathsf{Z}(s) \cap (\mathbb{N}^k_{\ge 0} \text{ with } a_i \ge 1))\, : z \in \mathsf{Z}(s),\ s - n_i \in S\,\},$$
and the tame degree
$$t(s) = \max_{i\,:\,s-n_i \in S} t_i(s).$$

Question: Is the function $t : S \to \mathbb{N}$, $s \mapsto t(s)$, eventually periodic? That is, do there exist integers $N \ge 0$ and $\pi \ge 1$ such that for every $s \in S$ with $s \ge N$, one has $s + \pi \in S$ and $t(s + \pi) = t(s)$?

representations.normalized:
Let $H$ be a separable complex Hilbert space and let $(A,B)$ be a bilinear quantum control system on $H$ of the form
$$\frac{d\psi}{dt}(t) = A\psi(t) + u(t)\,B\psi(t),$$
where $A$ is a skew-adjoint operator with purely discrete spectrum admitting a Hilbert basis $(\varphi_j)_{j\in\mathbb{N}}$ of eigenvectors with $A\varphi_j = i\lambda_j\varphi_j$, $\lambda_j\in\mathbb{R}$, and $B$ is a skew-symmetric operator on $H$. For $u\in L^1(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$, let $\Upsilon^u_{T,0}$ denote the propagator of the controlled equation between times $0$ and $T$ (assumed to be well-defined as a unitary operator on $H$ in the appropriate sense).

For an integer $k\ge 0$, the system $(A,B)$ is said to be $k$-weakly-coupled if the domain $D(|A|^{k/2})$ is invariant under the propagators $\Upsilon^u_{T,0}$ for every $u\in L^1(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ and every $T>0$, and there exists a constant $c_k\ge 0$ such that for every $\phi\in D(|A|^{k/2})$,
$$\bigl|\Re\langle |A|^k \phi, B\phi\rangle\bigr| \le c_k\,\bigl\langle |A|^{k/2}\phi,\,|A|^{k/2}\phi\bigr\rangle.$$

Assume that $(A,B)$ is $k$-weakly-coupled for every $k>0$.

Exhibit explicitly a state $\psi_b\in H$ which is not collinear to the first eigenvector $\varphi_1$, together with a control $u\in L^1(\mathbb{R},\mathbb{R})$ and a time $T>0$, such that
$$\Upsilon^u_{T,0}\,\varphi_1 = \psi_b.$$

The problem is posed as an open question in the literature on bilinear quantum control of infinite-dimensional Schrödinger systems. While general approximate-controllability results for weakly-coupled systems and some explicit-time exact controllability results on bounded 1D domains have been obtained, no explicit construction of a non-trivial reachable target state from $\varphi_1$ at the level of generality stated (any system $k$-weakly-coupled for all $k>0$) appears to have been provided. Setup. Let H be a separable complex Hilbert space with Hermitian inner product ⟨·,·⟩. Let A be a (possibly unbounded) skew-adjoint linear operator on H with discrete spectrum, and let (φ_n)_{n≥1} be a Hilbert basis of H consisting of eigenvectors of A, so that Aφ_n = i λ_n φ_n with real numbers λ_n. Let B be a skew-adjoint linear operator on H. Consider the bilinear control system

  (d/dt) ψ(t) = A ψ(t) + u(t) B ψ(t),  ψ(0) ∈ H, ‖ψ(0)‖ = 1,

where the control u: [0, T] → ℝ is piecewise constant. Denote by Υ^u_{t,0} the (well-defined) propagator associated with such a piecewise constant control, and let PC denote the set of all real-valued piecewise constant controls.

Assumptions on (A, B):
(i) Standard well-posedness assumption: A generates a C_0 group of unitary operators, B is skew-adjoint, and A + uB generates a unitary propagator for every u ∈ ℝ, with the resulting propagators leaving a suitable invariant subspace dense in H.
(ii) k-weakly-coupled property for every k > 0: for each k > 0 there exists a constant C_k such that, for every solution ψ of the controlled system with piecewise constant control u, one has ‖|A|^{k/2} ψ(t)‖ ≤ C_k (1 + ‖|A|^{k/2} ψ(0)‖) as long as the total variation of u stays bounded by a fixed constant (uniformly in k-th order moments of A).
(iii) A is unbounded.
(iv) B has no eigenvector in H.
(v) (A, B) admits a non-degenerate chain of connectedness: there is an ordering of the eigenstates such that consecutive pairs (φ_{n_j}, φ_{n_{j+1}}) satisfy ⟨B φ_{n_j}, φ_{n_{j+1}}⟩ ≠ 0 and the corresponding spectral gaps λ_{n_{j+1}} − λ_{n_j} are pairwise distinct from any other transition frequency, and the resulting graph connects every eigenstate.

Under (i)–(v), the union ⋃_{t ≥ 0} { Υ^u_{t,0} φ_1 : u ∈ PC } is dense in the unit sphere of H. Define

  ρ := inf { T ≥ 0 : ⋃_{0 ≤ t ≤ T} { Υ^u_{t,0} φ_1 : u ∈ PC } is dense in the unit sphere of H }.

Question. Does there exist a pair (A, B) satisfying (i)–(v) for which ρ > 0?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

The question concerns whether the minimal approximate-controllability time ρ for the ground state can be positive in a k-weakly-coupled bilinear quantum system with unbounded drift and a non-eigenvector control operator. Related works by Beauchard–Coron–Teismann, Coron, and more recently Duca–Pozzoli (2024) study positive minimal time and small-time approximate controllability for bilinear Schrödinger equations, providing both examples with positive minimal time (e.g., on degenerate cases) and new small-time controllability results. However, none of the located sources clearly settles the specific case of a k-weakly-coupled system (for every k>0) with unbounded A and B having no eigenvector. The status appears to remain open / unverified from public sources.

Assume in addition that (A,B) admits a non-degenerate chain of connectedness; that is, there exists an ordering of the eigenstates such that the graph with vertex set {φ_k} and edges {(j,k) : ⟨φ_j, B φ_k⟩ ≠ 0} is connected, and along some spanning subgraph the spectral gaps |λ_j − λ_k| corresponding to edges are pairwise distinct and different from any other spectral gap |λ_l − λ_m| with ⟨φ_l, B φ_m⟩ ≠ 0.

    ‖ Υ^{u_ε}_{T_ε,0} φ_1 − ψ_b ‖ < ε,
and moreover such u_ε can be chosen with a number N(ε) of discontinuities (switches between the values 0 and 1) of order O(1/ε) as ε → 0.

Setting. Let H be a separable complex Hilbert space and consider a bilinear control system of the form
    dψ/dt = A ψ + u(t) B ψ,    ψ(0) = ψ_0 ∈ H,
where A is a skew-adjoint operator on H with purely discrete spectrum (iλ_k)_{k∈ℕ} and an associated orthonormal basis (φ_k)_{k∈ℕ} of eigenvectors, B is a (possibly unbounded) skew-symmetric operator on H, and u : [0,T] → ℝ is a scalar control of bounded L^1 norm.

Standing hypothesis (Assumption 1). The pair (A,B) is such that A is skew-adjoint with discrete spectrum and eigenbasis (φ_k); B is skew-symmetric with domain containing the finite linear combinations of the (φ_k); and for every u ∈ ℝ the operator A + u B generates a strongly continuous unitary group on H, with well-posed propagators Υ^u_T solving the Cauchy problem for u ∈ L^1([0,T], ℝ).

k-weak coupling. For k > 0, write |A|^{k} for the spectral power of A acting on its domain. The system (A,B) is called k-weakly-coupled if the domain of |A|^{k} is invariant under A + uB for every u ∈ ℝ and there exists C_k > 0 such that
    | Re ⟨ |A|^{k} ψ , B ψ ⟩ | ≤ C_k ⟨ |A|^{k} ψ , ψ ⟩
for every ψ in the domain of |A|^{k}.

Galerkin truncations. For N ∈ ℕ, let π_N denote the orthogonal projection onto span(φ_1,…,φ_N) and define the N-th Galerkin approximation
    Υ^{(N),u}_T  :=  the propagator on π_N H of the truncated system  dψ/dt = π_N A π_N ψ + u(t) π_N B π_N ψ.

Uniform Galerkin approximation in L^1. The system (A,B) is said to admit good Galerkin approximations uniformly with respect to the L^1 norm of the control if, for every T > 0, every ψ_0 ∈ H, and every K, ε > 0, there exists N_0 such that for every N ≥ N_0 and every u ∈ L^1([0,T], ℝ) with ‖u‖_{L^1} ≤ K,
    ‖ Υ^u_T ψ_0  −  Υ^{(N),u}_T π_N ψ_0 ‖_H  <  ε.

Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on a bounded domain Ω ⊂ ℝ^d (d = 2 or 3) with suitable boundary conditions,
   ∂_t u + (u·∇)u = -∇p + ν Δu + f,    ∇·u = 0,
where ν > 0 is the kinematic viscosity and f is a (possibly time-independent) forcing chosen so that the dynamics are turbulent. View the resulting flow as a deterministic dynamical system on a phase space X (e.g., a divergence-free Sobolev space) with global attractor A.

Classical engineering practice studies turbulence via Reynolds averaging: one decomposes u = ⟨u⟩ + u′, takes a (time, ensemble, or filtered) mean, and obtains evolution equations for ⟨u⟩ that involve the unknown Reynolds stress ⟨u′ ⊗ u′⟩, leading to the closure problem (no finite system of equations for finitely many statistical moments of u closes without additional modeling assumptions).

Alternative deterministic descriptions of the attractor A include:
  (i) the (Hausdorff or box-counting) fractal dimension of A;
  (ii) Sinai–Ruelle–Bowen (SRB) measures, i.e. invariant probability measures on A that are absolutely continuous along unstable manifolds and whose time averages describe Lebesgue-typical initial conditions;
  (iii) shadowing: given a numerically computed pseudo-orbit {x_n} with one-step error at most δ, find a true orbit {y_n} of the dynamics with sup_n ‖x_n − y_n‖ ≤ ε(δ), and use such shadow orbits to compute statistics on A.

Problem. Construct a mathematically rigorous and computationally tractable effective description of the turbulent dynamics on A that
  (a) replaces Reynolds averaging and avoids the associated closure problem,
  (b) provides quantitatively more useful information for engineering predictions than the fractal dimension of A or an SRB measure on A, and
  (c) renders shadowing (or a related variational/inverse method based on true orbits) practical for the entire turbulent attractor at Reynolds numbers of engineering interest, i.e. produces, for any sufficiently long pseudo-orbit on A, a true orbit shadowing it within a controlled error using computational resources that scale feasibly with the attractor dimension.

Equivalently: exhibit such a description, or prove that no description satisfying (a)–(c) can exist within a specified class.

The problem remains open.

Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on a bounded domain (or on the torus) in two or three spatial dimensions,
  ∂_t u + (u·∇)u = -∇p + (1/Re) Δu,  ∇·u = 0,
with prescribed boundary/initial data, where Re is the Reynolds number; and the corresponding incompressible Euler equations obtained formally by setting 1/Re = 0. Let S_t^{Re} denote the solution map sending an initial datum u_0 (in a suitable Sobolev space such as H^s with s sufficiently large) to the solution u(·,t) at time t.

Definitions:
(i) The solution map exhibits "sensitive dependence on initial data" at u_0 if it is differentiable (or at least locally Lipschitz) and small initial perturbations grow exponentially in time at a rate independent of the size of the perturbation.
(ii) The solution map exhibits "rough dependence on initial data" at u_0 if for every t > 0 it is continuous but nowhere locally uniformly continuous and nowhere Fréchet differentiable, so that arbitrarily small perturbations of u_0 can produce order-one changes in the solution essentially instantaneously.

It is known that for the Euler equations the solution map S_t^{∞} (at any t ≠ 0) is continuous but nowhere locally uniformly continuous and nowhere differentiable, i.e. exhibits rough dependence. For the Navier–Stokes solution map S_t^{Re} one has the upper bound on the operator norm of its Fréchet derivative of the form ‖dS_t^{Re}‖ ≤ exp(C√(t·Re) + C_1 t).

Question: Prove or disprove that violent fully developed turbulence at sufficiently high Reynolds number is caused by rough dependence on initial data — concretely, that as Re → ∞ the operator norm of the derivative dS_t^{Re} of the Navier–Stokes solution map (acting on a suitable function space) tends to infinity for every fixed t > 0, and that this mechanism (rather than ordinary sensitive dependence on initial data, i.e. chaos with bounded Lyapunov exponents) is the cause of the rapid, short-time onset of violent turbulence in the high-Reynolds-number regime.

The conjecture, due to Y. Charles Li, is that high-Reynolds-number violent turbulence is caused by rough (rather than sensitive) dependence on initial data, with the supporting sub-conjecture that the norm of the derivative of the Navier–Stokes solution map blows up as Re → ∞. Subsequent works (Inci, Feng–Li, and numerical studies) provide partial support — bounds of the form exp(C√(tRe)+C_1 t) and numerical evidence of super-fast perturbation growth — but no proof that the derivative norm diverges as Re → ∞ or that this mechanism rigorously explains turbulence onset. The problem appears to remain open.

Consider a classical many-body Hamiltonian system whose microscopic dynamics are time-reversible: if $\{(q_i(t),p_i(t))\}_{i=1}^N$ is a solution of Hamilton's equations on the time interval $[0,T]$, then $\{(q_i(T-t),-p_i(T-t))\}$ is also a solution. Suppose furthermore that the dynamics are chaotic in the sense that the system has at least one positive Lyapunov exponent, so that infinitesimal perturbations of the initial phase-space point grow exponentially in time and any coarse-grained (macroscopic) observable rapidly loses memory of the initial microstate.

(a) Formulate precisely, and decide, whether the combination of microscopic time-reversibility with chaotic sensitivity to initial conditions and unavoidable external perturbations is sufficient to derive macroscopic thermodynamic irreversibility (an H-theorem-type monotone behavior of an appropriate coarse-grained entropy) for such systems.

(b) In a cosmological model in which matter evolves under such time-reversible but chaotic dynamics inside an expanding spatial geometry, determine whether reversing simultaneously the velocity of every particle (i.e. applying the time-reversal involution to the matter degrees of freedom while leaving the geometric expansion unchanged) yields a configuration that continues to expand, or one that contracts. Equivalently, decide whether the cosmological arrow of time (expansion vs. contraction) is determined by the matter's microscopic state in a way that is sensitive to the velocity-reversal operation, and characterize the role, if any, of chaotic amplification of perturbations in selecting the observed expanding branch.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The relationship between microscopic reversibility, dynamical chaos, and the emergence of macroscopic/thermodynamic and cosmological arrows of time is a long-standing foundational question. Chaos (mixing, positive Lyapunov exponents) is widely regarded as relevant to relaxation but is generally not accepted as a complete explanation of thermodynamic irreversibility, which most accounts attribute to low-entropy initial conditions (the "past hypothesis"). No consensus derivation is established, and the cosmological velocity-reversal question remains a matter of active discussion rather than a settled theorem.

Consider the Rosenzweig–MacArthur predator–prey model
\[
\frac{dN}{dT}=rN\!\left(1-\frac{N}{b}\right)-\frac{aNP}{h+N},\qquad \frac{dP}{dT}=\frac{eaNP}{h+N}-mP,
\]
where $N(T)\ge 0$ is the prey density, $P(T)\ge 0$ the predator density, and $r,b,a,h,e,m>0$ are the prey intrinsic growth rate, prey carrying capacity, maximal predation rate, half-saturation prey density, conversion efficiency, and predator mortality, respectively. The classical "paradox of enrichment" asserts that increasing the carrying capacity $b$ destabilizes the coexistence equilibrium and can drive both species to extinction through limit-cycle oscillations of growing amplitude.

(a) Nondimensionalize the system by introducing suitable dimensionless time and population variables, and show that, up to a rescaling, all dynamical behavior is governed by a reduced set of dimensionless parameters which includes the capacity–predation number
\[
H \;=\; \frac{h}{b}.
\]
Identify a complete minimal set of dimensionless parameters and write the rescaled system explicitly.

(b) Within this dimensionless formulation, determine whether varying $b$ (the prey carrying capacity) and varying $h$ (the half-saturation constant) act on the dynamics only through the single combination $H=h/b$, so that increasing $b$ and decreasing $h$ produce identical changes in the qualitative dynamics.

(c) Using the answer to (b), assess the following claim: the apparent destabilization caused by enrichment (increasing $b$) is the same mathematical effect as that caused by decreasing $h$, and the "paradox of enrichment" is therefore an artifact of comparing systems that differ in $b$ while holding the dimensional parameter $h$ fixed. Either prove this resolution rigorously from the structure of the nondimensionalized equations, or exhibit dynamical features (e.g., bifurcations, Hopf thresholds, or amplitudes of limit cycles) that depend on $b$ and $h$ separately and not solely through $H$.

Consider a pest species with population $H(t)$ and a natural predator with population $P(t)$ governed by a Lotka–Volterra-type system

$$\dot H = a H - b H P, \qquad \dot P = c H P - d P,$$

where $a,b,c,d>0$. Pesticide application is modeled by removing both species at a per-capita rate $q\ge 0$ during application, yielding the modified system

$$\dot H = a H - b H P - q H, \qquad \dot P = c H P - d P - q P,$$

which may be applied either continuously (constant $q$ over an interval) or impulsively (instantaneous fractional reductions $H\mapsto (1-\alpha)H$, $P\mapsto (1-\beta)P$ at prescribed times $t_k$, with $0\le \alpha,\beta\le 1$). Let $E>0$ denote a fixed economic threshold for the pest.

The "paradox of pesticides" is the phenomenon that, although such an application immediately decreases $H$, it can also disturb the predator–prey ratio so much that the pest later rebounds with $\sup_{t>t_0} H(t) > E$, i.e., to a level higher than would have occurred without intervention.

Problem. Develop and analyze a mathematical model of the above type that:
(i) captures the simultaneous suppression of pest and predator and the resulting change in their ratio;
(ii) characterizes, in terms of the parameters $a,b,c,d$, the application strength ($q$ or $\alpha,\beta$), and the state $(H(t_0),P(t_0))$ at the moment of application, necessary and sufficient conditions under which a single application (or a periodic schedule of applications) leads to a later resurgence with $H(t)>E$ for some $t>t_0$;
(iii) determines an optimal timing rule and dosage (as functions of the current state $(H,P)$) that minimize $\sup_{t\ge 0} H(t)$ — equivalently, that suppress the pest below $E$ for all subsequent time — and prove that such a rule indeed avoids the paradoxical resurgence.

Modified Lotka–Volterra and impulsive predator–prey models incorporating pesticide-induced mortality have been studied extensively, giving partial answers: equilibria analysis explains the paradox (pest equilibrium increases while predator equilibrium decreases when both species share a per-capita pesticide mortality), and impulsive/threshold-control schemes have been proposed showing that timing applications when the pest population is sufficiently high outperforms periodic spraying. Consider a fluid domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ in which $N$ species of phytoplankton compete for a single limiting nutrient. Let $f(t,x) \ge 0$ denote the density of the limiting nutrient and $\rho_n(t,x) \ge 0$, $n=1,\dots,N$, the densities of the species. Suppose the water has a prescribed turbulent velocity field $u(t,x)$ (divergence-free), and that each species $n$ drifts relative to the water with a species-specific velocity $v_n(t,x)$ (e.g. buoyancy- or motility-induced). Assume:

1. The nutrient is advected by the water, diffuses with coefficient $D_f \ge 0$, is consumed by species $n$ at a rate $g_n(f)\rho_n$, and is regenerated by a source/recycling term $S(t,x,f,\rho_1,\dots,\rho_N)$:
$$\partial_t f + u\cdot\nabla f - D_f\Delta f \;=\; -\sum_{n=1}^N g_n(f)\rho_n \;+\; S.$$
2. Each species is advected by $u+v_n$, diffuses with coefficient $D_n\ge 0$, grows at a per-capita rate $G_n(f)$ depending on the local nutrient, and dies at rate $m_n$:
$$\partial_t \rho_n + (u+v_n)\cdot\nabla \rho_n - D_n \Delta \rho_n \;=\; \big(G_n(f) - m_n\big)\rho_n, \qquad n=1,\dots,N.$$

Equip the system with appropriate initial data $f(0,\cdot), \rho_n(0,\cdot) \ge 0$ and either periodic or no-flux boundary conditions on $\partial\Omega$.

In a spatially homogeneous, well-mixed setting, the classical principle of competitive exclusion implies that at most one species (the one with the largest $G_n(f^*)/m_n$ at the equilibrium nutrient level $f^*$) survives at equilibrium.

Question: Within the above nonequilibrium reaction–advection–diffusion framework, exhibit conditions on the velocity field $u$, the species drifts $\{v_n\}$, the uptake/growth functions $\{g_n,G_n\}$, the recycling term $S$, and the diffusivities under which the system admits long-time solutions in which all $N$ species persist, in the sense that
$$\liminf_{t\to\infty}\frac{1}{|\Omega|}\int_\Omega \rho_n(t,x)\,dx \;>\; 0 \qquad \text{for every } n=1,\dots,N,$$
even when $N$ is arbitrarily large compared with the number of limiting nutrients (here, one). Equivalently, prove or disprove that turbulent advection together with species-specific drift, nutrient regeneration, and species-dependent uptake suffices to sustain coexistence of arbitrarily many competitors on a single limiting resource.

The paradox of the plankton, posed by Hutchinson (1961), has many proposed mechanistic resolutions but no single universally accepted one. Various models — including chaotic competition (Huisman–Weissing), spatial heterogeneity, turbulent/advective mixing in open flows, and fractal mixing along chaotic sets — produce sustained coexistence of many species on few resources, providing partial resolutions. A general rigorous theorem characterizing when reaction–advection–diffusion systems with one limiting nutrient sustain N-species coexistence remains open; surveys (e.g. Roy & Chattopadhyay 2007) describe the question as not fully resolved.

Let $M$ be a closed smooth oriented manifold of dimension $4k$. Its signature $\tau(M)\in\mathbb{Z}$ is defined as the signature of the symmetric nondegenerate intersection form
$$H^{2k}(M;\mathbb{R})\times H^{2k}(M;\mathbb{R})\to \mathbb{R},\qquad (\alpha,\beta)\mapsto \langle \alpha\smile\beta,[M]\rangle,$$
where $[M]$ is the fundamental class. Let $p_i(M)\in H^{4i}(M;\mathbb{Z})$ denote the Pontryagin classes of the tangent bundle of $M$, and let $L(M)=\prod_j \frac{\sqrt{x_j}}{\tanh\sqrt{x_j}}$ denote Hirzebruch's $L$-polynomial in the Pontryagin classes (the multiplicative sequence associated with the power series $\sqrt{x}/\tanh\sqrt{x}$). The Hirzebruch signature theorem states
$$\tau(M)=\langle L(p_1(M),p_2(M),\dots),[M]\rangle.$$
Associated to the signature one has a virtual signature/$L$-genus that, when extended appropriately, satisfies a functional equation analogous to that for $x/\tanh(x)$.

(a) Provide a proof of the above signature formula that proceeds by elementary means, avoiding the use of cobordism theory, the Atiyah–Singer index theorem, heat-kernel methods, or other deep machinery from algebraic and differential topology.

(b) Give a geometric interpretation of the functional equation satisfied by the virtual signature associated with the $L$-genus.

Let $H$ be a closed subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{R})$. An $H$-structure on a smooth $n$-dimensional manifold $M$ is a reduction of the structure group of the frame bundle of $M$ from $\mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{R})$ to $H$; equivalently, it is a principal $H$-subbundle $P \subset \mathrm{Fr}(M)$ of the bundle of linear frames. Such an $H$-structure is called integrable (or locally flat) if $M$ admits an atlas of charts $\{(U_\alpha,\varphi_\alpha)\}$ with $\varphi_\alpha : U_\alpha \to \mathbb{R}^n$ open such that on each $U_\alpha$ the local frame $(\partial/\partial x^1,\dots,\partial/\partial x^n)$ pulled back by $\varphi_\alpha$ is a section of $P$, and the transition maps $\varphi_\alpha \circ \varphi_\beta^{-1}$ have differentials lying in $H$ at every point.

Concrete examples include $H = \mathrm{GL}(n/2,\mathbb{C}) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{R})$ (almost complex versus complex structures), $H = \mathrm{Sp}(n,\mathbb{R})$ (almost symplectic versus symplectic structures), $H = \mathrm{GL}(k,\mathbb{R}) \times \mathrm{GL}(n-k,\mathbb{R})$ (almost product versus foliation structures), and $H = \mathrm{O}(n)$ (always integrable, by existence of Riemannian metrics with locally Euclidean charts).

Problem. Find a general criterion, formulated uniformly in $H$ and $M$, that decides whether the smooth $n$-manifold $M$ admits an integrable $H$-structure for an arbitrary prescribed closed subgroup $H \subset \mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{R})$, as opposed to a collection of ad hoc criteria specific to particular subgroups $H$.
