Let $k\ge 1$ be an integer and let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $2k+1$. A (globally defined) Pfaffian equation on $M$ is a smooth line subbundle of $T^*M$, equivalently (when trivializable) the kernel distribution determined by a nowhere-vanishing 1-form $\alpha\in\Omega^1(M)$. The class of a Pfaffian equation at a point $x\in M$ is the unique odd integer $2r+1$ such that, for any 1-form $\alpha$ defining the equation near $x$,
$$\bigl(\alpha\wedge(d\alpha)^{r}\bigr)(x)\neq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\bigl(\alpha\wedge(d\alpha)^{r+1}\bigr)(x)=0.$$
Fix an integer $r$ with $0\le r\le k$. Find a necessary and sufficient criterion (in terms of the topology and smooth structure of $M$) for $M$ to admit a globally defined Pfaffian equation whose class equals $2r+1$ at every point of $M$; equivalently, a criterion for the existence of a 1-form $\alpha\in\Omega^1(M)$ such that
$$\alpha\wedge(d\alpha)^{r}\;\text{is nowhere zero on }M,\qquad\alpha\wedge(d\alpha)^{r+1}\equiv 0\;\text{on }M.$$
The endpoint cases are: $r=k$, the contact case (existence of a contact structure on $M^{2k+1}$); and $r=0$, the existence of a nowhere-vanishing closed-mod-$\alpha$ 1-form, i.e. a codimension-one foliation defined by a global 1-form.

Let $k\ge 1$ be an integer and let $M$ be a smooth manifold of dimension $2k+1$. A (globally defined) Pfaffian equation on $M$ is a smooth line subbundle of $T^*M$, equivalently (when trivializable) the kernel distribution determined by a nowhere-vanishing 1-form $\alpha\in\Omega^1(M)$. The class of a Pfaffian equation at a point $x\in M$ is the unique odd integer $2r+1$ such that, for any 1-form $\alpha$ defining the equation near $x$,
$$\bigl(\alpha\wedge(d\alpha)^{r}\bigr)(x)\neq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\bigl(\alpha\wedge(d\alpha)^{r+1}\bigr)(x)=0.$$
Fix an integer $r$ with $0\le r\le k$. Find a necessary and sufficient criterion (in terms of the topology and smooth structure of $M$) for $M$ to admit a globally defined Pfaffian equation whose class equals $2r+1$ at every point of $M$; equivalently, a criterion for the existence of a 1-form $\alpha\in\Omega^1(M)$ such that
$$\alpha\wedge(d\alpha)^{r}\;\text{is nowhere zero on }M,\qquad\alpha\wedge(d\alpha)^{r+1}\equiv 0\;\text{on }M.$$
The endpoint cases are: $r=k$, the contact case (existence of a contact structure on $M^{2k+1}$); and $r=0$, the existence of a nowhere-vanishing closed-mod-$\alpha$ 1-form, i.e. a codimension-one foliation defined by a global 1-form.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem (attributed to S.-S. Chern) asks for a topological criterion for the global existence of a Pfaffian equation of constant class $2r+1$ on a $(2k+1)$-manifold. While the extremes are well studied — contact structures ($r=k$) and codimension-one foliations defined by a global 1-form ($r=0$) — no general criterion for intermediate $r$ appears in the literature, and the problem is generally regarded as open. The web search did not surface a published resolution.

representations.normalized:
Let $M^{2n}$ be a compact almost-complex manifold with almost-complex structure $J$. Choose a $J$-compatible Hermitian metric $g$ on $M$. The complexified exterior algebra decomposes by $J$ into $(p,q)$-forms, and the exterior derivative splits as $d=\mu+\partial+\bar\partial+\bar\mu$, where $\bar\partial:\mathcal A^{p,q}\to\mathcal A^{p,q+1}$. Using the Hermitian metric, define the Laplacian $\Delta_{\bar\partial}=\bar\partial\,\bar\partial^*+\bar\partial^*\bar\partial$ acting on $(p,q)$-forms, and set
$$h^{p,q}(M,J,g)=\dim_{\mathbb R}\ker\bigl(\Delta_{\bar\partial}\big|_{\mathcal A^{p,q}}\bigr).$$

(a) Is the integer $h^{p,q}(M,J,g)$ independent of the choice of $J$-compatible Hermitian metric $g$?

(b) If not, define numerical invariants $h^{p,q}(M,J)$ that depend only on the almost-complex structure $J$ (and not on any choice of metric) and that, when $J$ is integrable, recover the classical Dolbeault numbers $\dim_{\mathbb C} H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(M)$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The metric-independence part (a) has been answered negatively: Holt and Zhang exhibited an almost complex structure on the Kodaira–Thurston manifold for which $h^{1,1}$ depends on the choice of Hermitian metric. For part (b), Cirici and Wilson (2018+) introduced a Dolbeault cohomology for arbitrary almost complex manifolds with an associated spectral sequence converging to de Rham cohomology, providing metric-independent invariants extending the integrable Dolbeault numbers; subsequent work has continued to refine this theory and related Bott–Chern/Aeppli analogues, so the problem is generally regarded as partially solved with active ongoing developments.

Let $\mathbb{CP}^3$ denote complex projective 3-space, viewed as a smooth closed 6-manifold. A complex structure on $\mathbb{CP}^3$ is an integrable almost complex structure $J$ on this underlying smooth manifold; it endows $\mathbb{CP}^3$ with the structure of a (possibly non-standard, possibly non-Kähler) complex 3-fold, and hence with a holomorphic tangent bundle $T_J$ whose Chern classes $c_i(T_J) \in H^{2i}(\mathbb{CP}^3;\mathbb{Z})$ are defined.

Question: Does there exist a complex structure $J$ on the smooth manifold underlying $\mathbb{CP}^3$ such that the second Chern class vanishes, i.e. $c_2(T_J) = 0 \in H^4(\mathbb{CP}^3;\mathbb{Z})$?

(Equivalently, can one find an integrable almost complex structure on $\mathbb{CP}^3$ whose induced holomorphic tangent bundle has zero second Chern class? Such a complex structure would necessarily differ from the standard one, for which $c_2$ of the standard holomorphic tangent bundle is nonzero, and would in particular be non-Kähler.)

Let $n \geq 3$ and let $M$ denote the smooth manifold underlying the complex projective space $\mathbb{CP}^n$ (equipped with its standard differentiable structure). A complex structure on $M$ is an integrable almost complex structure $J: TM \to TM$, equivalently a maximal holomorphic atlas making $M$ into a complex manifold of complex dimension $n$. Two complex structures are equivalent if there is a diffeomorphism of $M$ intertwining them.

Determine, up to equivalence, all complex structures on $M$. In particular:

(a) Is the standard complex structure of $\mathbb{CP}^n$ the unique complex structure on $M$ that admits a compatible Kähler metric? (For $n\geq 3$ this is the question of whether every Kähler complex structure on the smooth manifold $\mathbb{CP}^n$ is biholomorphic to the standard one.)

(b) Does there exist a complex structure on $M$ that is not Kähler (i.e., admits no Kähler metric)? If so, classify all such non-Kähler complex structures on $M$ up to equivalence.

The problem (Hirzebruch's Problem 31, 1954) has been completely solved. Kotschick proved that a rational linear combination of Chern numbers of smooth complex projective varieties is an oriented diffeomorphism invariant iff it is a linear combination of the Euler number and the Pontryagin numbers; the homeomorphism and unoriented cases are also resolved. The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type if the position vector field admits a decomposition
$$x = c + x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k,$$
where $c \in \mathbb{E}^m$ is a constant vector, $k$ is a positive integer, and each $x_i: M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ is a non-constant smooth map satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for some real number $\lambda_i$, with the eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_k$ pairwise distinct.

Problem: Classify, up to rigid motion of the ambient Euclidean space, all finite-type hypersurfaces $M^n \subset \mathbb{E}^{n+1}$. In particular, give a complete classification of all finite-type surfaces in $\mathbb{E}^3$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The classification of finite-type hypersurfaces in Euclidean space, and even the classification of finite-type surfaces in E^3, is a long-standing open problem posed by B.-Y. Chen. Partial results are known: classifications have been obtained for special families such as ruled surfaces, quadrics, tubes, cyclides of Dupin, and spiral surfaces, where the only finite-type examples are the obvious ones (e.g., planes, spheres, circular cylinders). Chen's conjecture that spheres are the only compact finite-type surfaces in E^3 remains open, as does the case of surfaces of revolution, translation surfaces, and helicoidal surfaces in general.

$$x = x_0 + x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k, \qquad \Delta x_i = \lambda_i\, x_i \quad (i=1,\dots,k),$$
for some real numbers $\lambda_1<\lambda_2<\cdots<\lambda_k$. The smallest such integer $k$ is called the type of $M$.

Problem. Classify all finite-type hypersurfaces $M^{n}$ of the hypersphere $S^{n+1}\subset E^{n+2}$; that is, determine, up to congruence, all $n$-dimensional submanifolds of $S^{n+1}$ which, viewed as submanifolds of $E^{n+2}$, are of finite type.

Let $S^3 \subset \mathbb{E}^4$ denote the standard unit 3-sphere, viewed as a hypersurface of Euclidean 4-space with the induced metric. Let $M$ be a closed (compact, without boundary) smooth surface isometrically immersed in $S^3$, and consider $M$ as a submanifold of $\mathbb{E}^4$ via the standard embedding $S^3 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{E}^4$. Let $\Delta$ denote the Laplace–Beltrami operator on $M$ acting on smooth functions. The immersion $x: M \to \mathbb{E}^4$ is said to be of finite type if the position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{k} x_i,$$
where $x_0 \in \mathbb{E}^4$ is constant and each non-constant $\mathbb{E}^4$-valued component $x_i$ satisfies $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for some real number $\lambda_i$, with $k < \infty$. A surface $M$ in $S^3$ is called a finite-type surface if its standard immersion into $\mathbb{E}^4$ is of finite type.

Three classes of finite-type surfaces in $S^3$ are known:
(a) minimal surfaces of $S^3$ (which are precisely the 1-type surfaces with eigenvalue $2$);
(b) the standard (totally umbilical) 2-spheres in $S^3$;
(c) products of two plane circles, i.e. flat tori of the form
$$\bigl\{(r_1\cos\alpha, r_1\sin\alpha, r_2\cos\beta, r_2\sin\beta) : \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\bigr\} \subset S^3,$$
where $r_1^2 + r_2^2 = 1$ and $r_1, r_2 > 0$.

Prove or disprove: every finite-type surface in $S^3$ is one of the surfaces in (a), (b), or (c).

Let $S^{n+1} \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+2}$ denote the unit hypersphere, and let $M^n \subset S^{n+1}$ be a smooth, connected, oriented hypersurface. Recall:

(a) A curvature surface of $M$ is a connected submanifold $N \subset M$ such that for each $p \in N$, the tangent space $T_pN$ equals an eigenspace (principal direction space) of the shape operator of $M$. The hypersurface $M$ is called Dupin if along each curvature surface the corresponding principal curvature is constant, and is called proper Dupin if, in addition, the number $g$ of distinct principal curvatures is constant on $M$.

(b) $M$ is called isoparametric if all of its principal curvatures (as functions on $M$) are constant.

Let $x : M^n \to \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ be an isometric immersion of a connected $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold into Euclidean $(n+2)$-space. The immersion $x$ is said to be of finite type if its position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$x = x_0 + x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_k,$$
where $x_0 \in \mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ is a constant vector and $x_1, \ldots, x_k$ are non-constant $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$-valued maps satisfying $\Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i$ for some real numbers $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_k$, with $\Delta$ the Laplacian of the induced metric on $M^n$. The smallest such $k$ is the type of the immersion; when $k = 2$, the immersion is called of 2-type. A 2-type immersion is said to be of null 2-type if one of the eigenvalues $\lambda_1, \lambda_2$ equals zero, and of non-null 2-type otherwise. The mean curvature function of $x$ is the norm of the mean curvature vector field $H$, and $x$ is said to have constant mean curvature if $\|H\|$ is constant on $M^n$. The submanifold is called spherical if its image lies in some hypersphere of $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$.

Prove or disprove: every $n$-dimensional non-null 2-type submanifold of $\mathbb{E}^{n+2}$ with constant mean curvature is spherical.

Setup. Let $x : M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ be an isometric immersion of a compact surface $M$ into Euclidean $m$-space. Decompose the position vector via the spectral decomposition of the Laplacian $\Delta$ acting on $\mathbb{E}^m$-valued functions on $M$:
$$x = x_0 + \sum_{i \in I} x_i, \qquad \Delta x_i = \lambda_i x_i,$$
where $x_0$ is a constant vector, $I$ is a (possibly infinite) set of positive integers, and the $\lambda_i$ are distinct positive eigenvalues with the corresponding nonzero $\mathbb{E}^m$-valued eigencomponents $x_i$. The immersion (or the surface $M$) is said to be of $k$-type if $|I|=k$; in particular, $M$ is of $2$-type if $I=\{p,q\}$ with $\lambda_p\neq\lambda_q$. The surface $M$ is said to lie fully in a linear subspace $V\subset\mathbb{E}^m$ if $x(M)$ is contained in an affine translate of $V$ but not in any proper affine subspace of it. Let $S^{n-1}(r)\subset\mathbb{E}^n$ denote the round hypersphere of radius $r$ centered at the origin. A $2$-type surface $x:M\to S^{n-1}(r)\subset\mathbb{E}^n$ is called mass-symmetric in $S^{n-1}(r)$ if its center of mass coincides with the center of the hypersphere, equivalently $x_0=0$.

Question. Do there exist $2$-type surfaces $M$ that lie fully in an even-dimensional hypersphere $S^{2k-1}(r)\subset\mathbb{E}^{2k}$ of a Euclidean space? In particular, do there exist mass-symmetric $2$-type surfaces that lie fully in such an even-dimensional hypersphere?

status_assertions.value: open_status:unknown

Partial results are known: Barros and Chen showed that compact stationary mass-symmetric 2-type surfaces in a hypersphere are flat and lie fully in $S^5$ or $S^7$; in particular no mass-symmetric 2-type surface lies fully in $S^4$. status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

This is Chen's biharmonic conjecture (1991), which asserts that every biharmonic submanifold of Euclidean space is minimal. The conjecture remains open in general. It has been confirmed for surfaces ($n=2$, Chen and Jiang, late 1980s), for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^4$ ($n=3$, Hasanis–Vlachos 1995), and for hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^5$ ($n=4$, Fu–Hong–Zhan 2021). The case of hypersurfaces in $\mathbb{E}^m$ for $m \geq 6$ and the general submanifold case remain unresolved, though numerous partial results exist under additional curvature or codimension assumptions.

Let P be a finite set of points in the plane in general position (no three collinear, or more generally with the standard convention that two points see each other iff the open segment between them contains no other point of P). The point visibility graph G(P) has vertex set P, with two points adjacent if and only if they see each other in this sense. For a graph G, let χ(G) denote its chromatic number and ω(G) its clique number.

Question: Does there exist a function f : ℕ → ℕ such that for every finite planar point set P,
   χ(G(P)) ≤ f(ω(G(P)))?
Equivalently, is the class of point visibility graphs χ-bounded?

status_assertions.value: open_status:solved

The conjecture has been refuted. F. Pfender constructed point visibility graphs with clique number 6 whose chromatic number can be made arbitrarily large, showing that χ is not bounded by any function of ω for point visibility graphs. A subset C ⊆ S is called a visible clique if every pair of distinct points in C is mutually visible. A subset of S is called collinear if all its points lie on a common straight line.

Prove or disprove the following statement: for every pair of integers k ≥ 2 and ℓ ≥ 2, there exists an integer h(k, ℓ) such that every finite set S of at least h(k, ℓ) points in the Euclidean plane contains either ℓ collinear points or a visible clique of size k.

Let $N$ be an irreducible compact homogeneous Riemannian manifold. Recall that the eigenvalues of the Laplace–Beltrami operator $\Delta$ on $N$ form a discrete sequence $0 = \lambda_0 < \lambda_1 < \lambda_2 < \cdots$. For each positive eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ with eigenspace $V_{\lambda_i}$ of dimension $m_i$, there is, up to a positive constant, a canonical isometric immersion $x_i \colon N \to \mathbb{E}^{m_i}$ into Euclidean space whose components form an orthonormal basis of $V_{\lambda_i}$; this is the $i$-th standard immersion of $N$. When $i = 1$, $\varphi := x_1 \colon N \to \mathbb{E}^{m_1}$ is called the first standard immersion.

An isometric immersion $f \colon M \to \mathbb{E}^m$ of a (compact) Riemannian manifold $M$ is said to be of finite type if its position vector admits a finite spectral decomposition
$$f = f_0 + f_{t_1} + f_{t_2} + \cdots + f_{t_k},$$
where $f_0$ is a constant vector and $\Delta f_{t_j} = \lambda_{t_j} f_{t_j}$ for distinct positive eigenvalues $\lambda_{t_1}, \dots, \lambda_{t_k}$ of the Laplacian on $M$; the immersion is of $k$-type if exactly $k$ nonzero eigen-components appear. In particular, $f$ is of $1$-type (resp. $2$-type) if and only if $k = 1$ (resp. $k = 2$).

Now let $M \subset N$ be a submanifold of $N$, and consider the composed immersion $\varphi|_M \colon M \to \mathbb{E}^{m_1}$.

Problem. Characterize, in terms of intrinsic and extrinsic geometric conditions on $M \subset N$, all submanifolds $M$ of $N$ such that $\varphi|_M$ is of finite type. In particular, characterize those $M \subset N$ for which $\varphi|_M$ is of $1$-type, and those for which $\varphi|_M$ is of $2$-type.

The classical theorem of Lyusternik and Schnirelmann asserts that on the 2-sphere $S^2$ equipped with an arbitrary smooth Riemannian metric, there exist at least three geometrically distinct simple (i.e., without self-intersections) closed geodesics. The problem is to determine whether an analogous quantitative existence statement holds in higher dimensions. Specifically:

For every integer $n \ge 3$ and every smooth Riemannian metric $g$ on the $n$-sphere $S^n$ (with primary attention to the case $n = 3$), is there a finite lower bound $N(n) > 1$, depending only on $n$, such that $(S^n, g)$ always admits at least $N(n)$ geometrically distinct simple closed geodesics? Equivalently, does the Lyusternik–Schnirelmann theorem on the existence of multiple simple closed geodesics extend from $S^2$ to $S^n$ for $n \ge 3$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

For a general Riemannian metric on $S^n$ with $n \ge 3$, the only known multiplicity results are those that hold for arbitrary compact Riemannian manifolds; no Lyusternik–Schnirelmann-type extension guaranteeing multiple simple closed geodesics is currently known, and the question is listed as an open problem in geodesic problem surveys.

Let $M$ be a closed (compact, without boundary) smooth manifold of dimension $n \geq 2$. A Riemannian metric on $M$ is a smoothly varying positive-definite inner product on the tangent spaces of $M$; a Finsler metric on $M$ is a smooth function $F : TM \to [0, \infty)$ that is positive and smooth off the zero section, positively homogeneous of degree one in the fiber variable, and whose vertical Hessian $\tfrac{1}{2}\partial^2 F^2 / \partial v^i \partial v^j$ is positive definite. Either type of metric induces a geodesic flow $\varphi_t$ on the unit tangent bundle $SM$, which preserves a canonical smooth probability measure $\mu$ (the Liouville measure). The flow $(\varphi_t, \mu)$ is called ergodic if every $\varphi_t$-invariant measurable subset of $SM$ has $\mu$-measure $0$ or $1$.

Question: Does every closed smooth manifold $M$ of dimension at least $2$ admit a Riemannian metric or a Finsler metric whose geodesic flow on $SM$ is ergodic with respect to the Liouville measure?

A Finsler metric on a smooth manifold $M$ is a continuous function $F:TM\to[0,\infty)$ that is smooth on $TM\setminus\{0\}$, positively homogeneous of degree one (i.e., $F(x,\lambda v)=\lambda F(x,v)$ for all $\lambda>0$), and whose fiberwise Hessian $\tfrac{1}{2}\partial^2 F^2/\partial v^i\partial v^j$ is positive definite on $TM\setminus\{0\}$. Such a metric is called reversible if $F(x,-v)=F(x,v)$ for all $(x,v)\in TM$, and irreversible otherwise. A closed geodesic of $(M,F)$ is a non-constant smooth closed curve $\gamma:S^1\to M$ that is locally length-minimizing with respect to $F$ (parametrized with constant Finslerian speed). Two closed geodesics are considered the same if one is an orientation-preserving reparametrization of the other. A closed geodesic is called prime if it is not the $k$-fold iterate of another closed geodesic for any integer $k\ge 2$.

Prove or disprove: every irreversible Finsler metric on the 2-sphere $S^2$ has either exactly two or infinitely many distinct prime closed geodesics.

Let $X$ be the blow-up of the complex projective plane $\mathbb{P}^2$ at $r$ distinct (possibly general) points $p_1,\dots,p_r$, with exceptional divisors $E_1,\dots,E_r$, and let $H$ denote the pullback of the hyperplane class on $\mathbb{P}^2$. For integers $d, m_1,\dots,m_r$, consider the divisor
$$D = dH - m_1 E_1 - \cdots - m_r E_r$$
on $X$. Call $D$ special if $D$ is effective and $h^1(X, \mathcal{O}_X(D)) > 0$. Equivalently, the linear system of plane curves of degree $d$ with multiplicity at least $m_i$ at $p_i$ is non-empty and has dimension strictly greater than the expected dimension $\max\{-1, \binom{d+2}{2} - 1 - \sum_i \binom{m_i+1}{2}\}$.

The statement is referred to in the literature as a conjecture (sometimes attributed to Y. Long) about Finsler 2-spheres. Partial results are known: on every Finsler $S^2$ there are at least two prime closed geodesics, and either there are infinitely many prime closed geodesics or there are at least two irrationally elliptic prime closed geodesics; under positive flag curvature pinching or under the assumption that the number of prime closed geodesics is finite, existence (and even multiplicity) of elliptic prime closed geodesics has been established. No unconditional proof for arbitrary Finsler metrics on $S^2$ was found.

The question is known to have a positive answer in dimension 2 (Bangert, 1980), where in fact infinitely many geometrically distinct closed geodesics exist on any complete finite-volume surface. A Finsler metric on a smooth manifold $M$ is a continuous function $F: TM \to [0,\infty)$ that is smooth on $TM \setminus \{0\}$, positively homogeneous of degree one (i.e., $F(x, \lambda v) = \lambda F(x,v)$ for all $\lambda > 0$), and whose vertical Hessian $\frac{1}{2}\partial^2(F^2)/\partial v^i \partial v^j$ is positive definite on $TM \setminus \{0\}$. The Finsler metric $F$ is called irreversible if there exists $(x,v) \in TM$ with $F(x,v) \neq F(x,-v)$. The Finsler length of a piecewise smooth curve $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ is $L_F(\gamma) = \int_a^b F(\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))\,dt$, and a closed geodesic is a non-constant critical point of $L_F$ on the space of piecewise smooth loops in $M$ (equivalently, a non-constant smooth map $S^1 \to M$ that locally minimizes $F$-length up to forward reparametrization). The Finsler volume of $(M,F)$ is defined via the Busemann–Hausdorff (or Holmes–Thompson) volume form associated with $F$.

Question: Does there exist an irreversible Finsler metric $F$ on the cylinder $\mathbb{R} \times S^1$ such that the total Finsler volume of $(\mathbb{R} \times S^1, F)$ is finite and $(\mathbb{R} \times S^1, F)$ admits no closed geodesics?

Let $(M,g)$ be a closed connected Riemannian manifold and let $\sigma$ be a closed 2-form on $M$ (the magnetic form). The associated Lorentz force is the bundle endomorphism $Y:TM\to TM$ defined by $g(Y(u),v)=\sigma(u,v)$ for all $u,v\in T_pM$, $p\in M$. A magnetic geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma:\mathbb{R}\to M$ satisfying
$$\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=Y(\dot\gamma),$$
where $\nabla$ is the Levi-Civita connection of $g$. The kinetic energy $E(\gamma)=\tfrac{1}{2}|\dot\gamma|^2_g$ is constant along any magnetic geodesic, so its dynamics preserves the energy hypersurfaces $\Sigma_k=\{(p,v)\in TM:\tfrac12|v|_g^2=k\}$ for $k>0$. A closed magnetic geodesic of energy $k$ is a non-constant magnetic geodesic that is periodic.

Question: For every closed Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$, every closed 2-form $\sigma$ on $M$, and every $k>0$, does there exist at least one closed magnetic geodesic on the energy level $\Sigma_k$?

Let $M$ be a closed (compact, without boundary) smooth manifold. A Kropina metric on $M$ is a Finsler-type structure of the form
$$F(x,y) = \frac{\alpha(x,y)^2}{\beta(x,y)},\qquad y\in T_xM\setminus\{0\},$$
where $\alpha$ is a Riemannian metric on $M$ and $\beta$ is a nowhere-vanishing $1$-form on $M$, and $F$ is defined on the conic open subset $A=\{(x,y)\in TM:\beta_x(y)>0\}$. A geodesic of a Kropina metric is a smooth curve $\gamma:I\to M$ with $\dot\gamma(t)\in A$ for all $t$ that is a critical point of the energy functional associated with $F$ (equivalently, a solution of the Kropina geodesic equation). A closed geodesic is a non-constant geodesic $\gamma:\mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}\to M$ for some $T>0$.

Question: Does every Kropina metric on every closed manifold $M$ admit at least one closed geodesic?

For a topological space $X$ and a fixed coefficient field $\mathbb{F}$, let $b(X)=\sum_{i\ge 0}\dim_{\mathbb{F}} H_i(X;\mathbb{F})$ denote the sum of its Betti numbers.

$$b(\Lambda^T M)\quad\text{and}\quad b(\Omega^T(p,q)).$$
In particular, characterize, in terms of the Riemannian geometry and topology of $(M,g)$, when these growths are bounded, polynomial, or exponential, and identify the corresponding rates.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question concerning the growth of total Betti numbers of length-bounded free loop spaces and based path spaces on a closed Riemannian manifold is a classical question going back to Gromov and Paternain, related to topological entropy of the geodesic flow. While Gromov proved upper bounds via the Morse-theoretic relation to closed/connecting geodesics, and exponential lower bounds are known under hypotheses like rationally hyperbolic fundamental group, a complete characterization of the growth rates remains an open problem.

Let $M=S^n$ ($n\ge 2$) be the $n$-sphere equipped with a Riemannian metric $g$, and let $\Lambda M = C^\infty(S^1,M)$ denote the free loop space, endowed with the energy functional $E:\Lambda M\to[0,\infty)$, $E(\gamma)=\tfrac12\int_0^1 g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)\,dt$, whose nontrivial critical points are the closed geodesics of $(M,g)$. For a nonzero homology class $X\in H_*(\Lambda M;\mathbb{Z})$, define the minimax critical value
$$\mathrm{cr}(X)=\inf\bigl\{\,r\ge 0 : X\in\operatorname{im}\bigl(H_*(\{E\le r\})\to H_*(\Lambda M;\mathbb{Z})\bigr)\bigr\}.$$

This is the Burns–Katok marked length spectrum rigidity conjecture. It was proved in dimension 2 for negatively curved metrics by Otal (1990) and independently by Croke (1990). In higher dimensions it remains open in full generality, but substantial progress has been made: Guillarmou and Lefeuvre (2019) established local rigidity in any dimension for negatively curved metrics, and further results have been obtained in the Anosov setting. Thus the conjecture is partially solved.

Let X be a finite 2-dimensional simplicial complex equipped with a piecewise hyperbolic metric, in the following sense: every 2-simplex of X is isometric to a geodesic triangle in the hyperbolic plane H^2 (with geodesic edges), the metrics on adjacent simplices agree on common edges, and the resulting length metric on X is locally CAT(−1) (equivalently, the link of every vertex, equipped with its induced angular metric, has systole at least 2π).

For such an X, let Γ = π_1(X) and let C be the set of conjugacy classes of Γ. Because the universal cover of X is CAT(−1), each nontrivial conjugacy class [γ] ∈ C contains a unique closed local geodesic loop in X, of some length ℓ_X([γ]) > 0. The function ℓ_X : C \ {1} → (0, ∞) is called the marked length spectrum of X.

Question. Suppose X and X' are two such piecewise hyperbolic, locally CAT(−1) 2-complexes, and let φ : π_1(X) → π_1(X') be a group isomorphism such that ℓ_X([γ]) = ℓ_{X'}([φ(γ)]) for every conjugacy class [γ].

(a) If X' is assumed to be homeomorphic to X and to carry a piecewise hyperbolic metric of the above type with the same combinatorial structure, must X and X' be isometric?

(b) More generally, if one allows X' to be any locally CAT(−1) metric space homeomorphic to X (without restricting to piecewise hyperbolic structures), must X and X' be isometric?

In other words: does the marked length spectrum determine the metric on X within (a) the class of 2-dimensional piecewise hyperbolic simplicial complexes locally CAT(−1) and homeomorphic to X, and (b) the larger class of all locally CAT(−1) metrics on the space X?

Partial results are known. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected Riemannian manifold with non-empty boundary $\partial M$. The boundary distance function $d_g\colon\partial M\times\partial M\to[0,\infty)$ assigns to each pair $(x,y)$ of boundary points the Riemannian distance between them, taken inside $M$. The manifold $(M,g)$ is said to be boundary distance rigid (or simply boundary rigid) within a class $\mathcal{C}$ of Riemannian manifolds with boundary if, whenever $(N,h)\in\mathcal{C}$ admits a diffeomorphism $\varphi\colon\partial N\to\partial M$ with $d_h(p,q)=d_g(\varphi(p),\varphi(q))$ for all $p,q\in\partial N$, there exists an isometry $\Phi\colon(N,h)\to(M,g)$ with $\Phi|_{\partial N}=\varphi$.

A compact Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ with boundary is called simple if $\partial M$ is strictly convex with respect to $g$, and any two points of $M$ are joined by a unique minimizing geodesic depending smoothly on its endpoints.

Problem. Determine geometric and topological conditions on a compact Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ with boundary, on a candidate manifold $(N,h)$ with boundary, and on the metric $g$ itself, that suffice to guarantee that $(M,g)$ is boundary distance rigid; in particular, decide whether every simple compact Riemannian manifold is boundary distance rigid.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The C^0-conjugacy rigidity conjecture for compact negatively curved Riemannian manifolds is widely cited as an open problem in differential geometry. It is known to hold for surfaces (via results of Croke and Otal on nonpositively curved surfaces, combined with Hamenstädt's work linking marked length spectrum to C^0-conjugacy of geodesic flows), but remains open in dimensions ≥ 3. Surveys of open problems in geodesic flow rigidity (e.g. Burns–Matveev, Croke) list it as unresolved.

Consider a relaxed (cool-core) galaxy cluster whose central region hosts an active galactic nucleus (AGN) producing relativistic electrons. Surrounding the AGN, diffuse synchrotron radio emission with steep spectral index α > 1 (defined by flux density S_ν ∝ ν^{-α}) extends over a region of linear size on the order of several hundred kiloparsecs (a "radio mini-halo"). A direct difficulty is that, given the relativistic electrons' radiative (synchrotron + inverse Compton) cooling time and their diffusion/streaming speeds in the intracluster medium (ICM), the diffusion time across the mini-halo volume exceeds the electrons' radiative lifetime, so the seed electrons injected by the central AGN cannot, by transport alone, fill the observed volume before losing energy.

(a) Identify a physical mechanism that simultaneously explains (i) the spatial extent of the diffuse emission, (ii) the steep spectral index α > 1, and (iii) the fact that mini-halos appear preferentially in clusters that are dynamically relaxed yet show cold fronts in the ICM.

(b) Quantitatively determine whether subsonic gas sloshing in the cluster core, induced by minor gravitational perturbations and bounded by cold fronts, can drive turbulence of sufficient amplitude and on the right spatial scales (≲ 100 kpc) to re-accelerate seed electrons supplied by the central AGN — via stochastic Fermi-II processes such as transit-time damping of magnetosonic modes or non-resonant compression — up to Lorentz factors that reproduce the observed radio luminosity, morphology, and spectral steepening within the cooling time.

The turbulent re-acceleration scenario driven by core gas sloshing has accumulated substantial observational and theoretical support: MHD simulations (ZuHone et al. 2013) show sloshing-induced turbulence can re-accelerate seeds to produce mini-halo-like emission, and recent multi-frequency observations (e.g., RXCJ1558.3−1410 in 2024, Abell 795 in 2024, Abell 3558 in 2025, RX J1347.5–1145 in 2025) consistently find mini-halo emission confined within sloshing cold fronts and aligned with low-entropy spirals. However, alternative/complementary mechanisms (hadronic secondary models, AGN feedback, large-scale envelopes around mini-halos) remain viable, and the question of whether sloshing turbulence is universally sufficient quantitatively is not fully settled.

Let $(M,g)$ be a closed (compact, without boundary) Riemannian manifold of negative sectional curvature. Consider the geodesic flow $\varphi^t$ on the unit tangent bundle $SM$, which is an Anosov flow: there is a continuous, $D\varphi^t$-invariant splitting
$$T(SM) = E^s \oplus \mathbb{R}\cdot X \oplus E^u,$$
where $X$ is the geodesic spray, and $E^s$, $E^u$ are the stable and unstable subbundles, exponentially contracted by $D\varphi^t$ for $t\to+\infty$ and $t\to-\infty$ respectively. The metric $g$ is called $\tfrac14$-pinched if there exists a constant $K>0$ such that all sectional curvatures of $g$ lie in the interval $[-K,-K/4)$ (equivalently, the ratio of the maximum to minimum of $|K_\sigma|$ is strictly less than $4$).

Question: Does there exist such a closed Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ of negative sectional curvature with $\dim M > 2$ for which the stable and unstable subbundles $E^s$ and $E^u$ are $C^1$-smooth on $SM$, yet the metric $g$ is not $\tfrac14$-pinched?

The literature establishes that strict 1/4-pinching implies C^1 regularity of the stable/unstable subbundles, and Hasselblatt constructed metrics arbitrarily close to 1/4-pinched whose horospherical foliations fail to be C^1. Let $M$ be a closed Riemannian manifold of dimension $n \geq 3$ with strictly negative sectional curvature. The geodesic flow $\varphi_t$ on the unit tangent bundle $SM$ is then an Anosov flow, and the unstable subbundle $E^u \subset T(SM)$ has dimension $n-1$. With respect to the Liouville (Bowen–Margulis or any ergodic SRB) measure, Oseledets' theorem yields, for almost every $v \in SM$, positive Lyapunov exponents $0 < \lambda_1(v) \leq \lambda_2(v) \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_{n-1}(v)$ along $E^u$. For a typical (i.e. measure-generic) geodesic, these exponents are constants $\lambda_1 \leq \cdots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$.

Question: Does there exist a closed Riemannian manifold of negative curvature whose geodesic flow satisfies
$$\frac{\lambda_{n-1}}{\lambda_1} > 2$$
for the Lyapunov exponents associated with typical geodesics (as opposed to the analogous ratio computed only along exceptional closed geodesics)?

representations.normalized:
Galaxy clusters can host diffuse, megaparsec-scale synchrotron radio emission known as radio halos, believed to be powered by turbulent re-acceleration of relativistic electrons in the intra-cluster medium following cluster mergers. "Classical" giant radio halos are typically associated with massive, energetic cluster–cluster mergers and exhibit integrated radio spectral indices α (with flux density S_ν ∝ ν^α) around α ≈ −1.2 to −1.3, while "ultra-steep-spectrum" radio halos (USSRH) are defined by α < −1.5 and are predicted by turbulent re-acceleration models to arise in less energetic merger events (minor mergers and/or mergers of lower-mass clusters).

Address the following questions:

(a) Do less energetic cluster mergers — in particular, the common minor mergers expected to dominate hierarchical mass assembly in the Universe — produce a detectable signature of diffuse synchrotron emission in the radio band?

(b) If such signatures exist, are they preferentially manifested as ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos (α < −1.5) or as other classes of faint diffuse cluster radio sources, such that they are predominantly detectable by high-sensitivity low-frequency (∼ 100–300 MHz) observations while remaining strongly constrained (i.e., faint or undetected) at GHz frequencies?

Provide either a derivation from a physical model of merger-driven turbulent re-acceleration that predicts the occurrence rate, luminosity function, and spectral distribution of such diffuse sources as a function of cluster mass and merger energetics, or observational determinations of these quantities.

Consider the diffuse, extended synchrotron radio emission observed from the intracluster medium of galaxy clusters, classified into two morphological types: (i) radio halos, which are large (~Mpc-scale), centrally located, low-surface-brightness sources roughly coincident with the X-ray-emitting thermal gas, and (ii) radio relics, which are elongated, often peripheral sources frequently associated with merger shock fronts. Both types of source emit via synchrotron radiation from a population of relativistic electrons (Lorentz factor γ ≫ 1) gyrating in cluster-scale magnetic fields of order ~µG. The integrated radio spectrum of such a source is the function S(ν) giving total flux density as a function of frequency ν, conventionally fit (locally) by a power law S(ν) ∝ ν^{−α} with spectral index α, but possibly exhibiting curvature (a high-frequency steepening or a low-frequency flattening) that constrains the energy distribution N(E) ∝ E^{−δ} of the emitting electrons and any cooling, injection, or re-acceleration processes acting on them.

The problem is the following:

(a) For each known radio halo and radio relic, determine the integrated radio spectrum S(ν) over the frequency range from approximately 100 MHz to several GHz, with sufficient frequency coverage and accuracy to detect spectral curvature and to measure the spectral index α (and any spatial variations of α via spectral imaging).

(b) From the measured spectral shapes and spectral-index values, infer the energy distribution and maximum energy of the underlying relativistic electron population, and identify the physical re-acceleration mechanism (e.g., second-order Fermi turbulent re-acceleration in halos versus diffusive shock acceleration or shock re-acceleration in relics, as opposed to purely secondary models in which electrons arise from hadronic collisions of cosmic-ray protons with thermal nuclei) that is consistent with these spectra. In particular, characterize whether and at what frequency the integrated halo spectra exhibit a high-frequency cutoff/steepening predicted by stochastic re-acceleration models, and whether relic spectra are consistent with the spectral-index/Mach-number relation predicted by diffusive shock acceleration.

(b) From the measured spectral shapes and spectral-index values, infer the energy distribution and maximum energy of the underlying relativistic electron population, and identify the physical re-acceleration mechanism (e.g., second-order Fermi turbulent re-acceleration in halos versus diffusive shock acceleration or shock re-acceleration in relics, as opposed to purely secondary models in which electrons arise from hadronic collisions of cosmic-ray protons with thermal nuclei) that is consistent with these spectra. In particular, characterize whether and at what frequency the integrated halo spectra exhibit a high-frequency cutoff/steepening predicted by stochastic re-acceleration models, and whether relic spectra are consistent with the spectral-index/Mach-number relation predicted by diffusive shock acceleration.

Subsequent observations with LOFAR, MWA, uGMRT, and JVLA have substantially increased the number of halos and relics with measured integrated spectra from ~100 MHz to GHz, confirming features such as high-frequency steepening in some halos (e.g., the Coma cluster, A521) consistent with turbulent re-acceleration, and power-law/curved relic spectra broadly consistent with shock (re-)acceleration scenarios. Let $S$ be a closed (compact, boundaryless), orientable smooth surface of genus $g \geq 2$, equipped with a smooth Riemannian metric $g$ whose sectional (Gaussian) curvature satisfies $K \leq 0$ everywhere. Let $T^1 S$ denote the unit tangent bundle of $(S,g)$, and let $\varphi_t : T^1 S \to T^1 S$ denote the geodesic flow, defined by $\varphi_t(x,v) = (\gamma_{x,v}(t), \dot\gamma_{x,v}(t))$, where $\gamma_{x,v}$ is the unique geodesic with $\gamma_{x,v}(0) = x$ and $\dot\gamma_{x,v}(0) = v$. Let $\mu_L$ denote the Liouville measure on $T^1 S$ (the canonical smooth invariant probability measure induced by the Riemannian volume on $S$ together with the Lebesgue measure on the unit circle fibers). The flow $\varphi_t$ preserves $\mu_L$.

Question: Is the geodesic flow $(\varphi_t, \mu_L)$ ergodic, i.e., is every Borel set $A \subset T^1 S$ with $\varphi_t(A) = A$ for all $t \in \mathbb{R}$ necessarily of $\mu_L$-measure $0$ or $1$?

Consider a galaxy cluster hosting diffuse, low-surface-brightness synchrotron radio emission of two types: (i) a centrally located radio halo, roughly co-spatial with the X-ray emitting intracluster medium, and (ii) one or more peripheral radio relics. The synchrotron emission is produced by a population of relativistic electrons with energy distribution N(E) dE ∝ E^{-p} dE radiating in a magnetic field B that pervades the cluster volume; the resulting monochromatic emissivity at frequency ν scales as j_ν ∝ N_0 B^{(p+1)/2} ν^{-(p-1)/2}, so that the local spectral index α (defined by S_ν ∝ ν^{-α}) is α = (p-1)/2 at frequencies far from any spectral break, while energy losses (synchrotron and inverse-Compton) introduce a high-frequency cutoff ν_b that depends on B and on the age of the radiating electrons.

Tasks:

1. Determine the two-dimensional spatial distribution α(x, y) of the radio spectral index across the projected extent of cluster radio halos and relics, including any systematic radial gradients, fluctuations, and patches of spectral steepening or flattening.

2. Using multi-frequency spectral-index maps together with the integrated spectrum of the source, derive constraints on:
   (a) the energy spectrum of the radiating relativistic electrons throughout the source volume, including the location and shape of any high-frequency cutoff and the implications for the (re)acceleration or injection mechanism;
   (b) the three-dimensional distribution of the magnetic field strength B in the cluster volume, including its central value, its radial profile, and its degree of small-scale spatial fluctuation.

Specifically, provide a quantitative procedure that, given resolved spectral-index imaging α(x, y; ν_1, ν_2) at multiple frequency pairs and the integrated radio spectrum, recovers (i) the spatial profile of the electron energy distribution and its break energy, and (ii) the magnetic field distribution B(r) throughout the cluster, and identify the observational requirements (frequency coverage, sensitivity to low surface brightness, angular resolution) under which such a reconstruction is feasible.

Galaxy clusters frequently host extended, diffuse, polarized synchrotron sources at their peripheries known as radio relics. It is widely believed that relics trace merger-driven shock waves propagating through the intracluster medium, which (re)accelerate relativistic electrons. A "shock front" in this context is an X-ray–detected discontinuity in temperature and density (e.g., as identified with high-resolution X-ray imaging spectroscopy), characterized by a sonic Mach number M = v_s / c_s, where v_s is the shock speed and c_s is the upstream sound speed.

Problem. Compile the set of galaxy clusters in which (i) a shock front has been firmly detected through X-ray observations and (ii) a radio relic has been observed whose location, morphology, and polarization properties show a clear spatial and physical association with that shock front. For each such system, determine the Mach number of the shock from X-ray (and, where possible, radio spectral) measurements. Then decide whether the resulting sample is consistent with the hypothesis that radio relics are produced by merger-driven shocks with Mach numbers M ≲ 3, or whether it requires revising this expected Mach-number range.

Since 2011 the sample of clusters with both an X-ray–detected shock front and an associated radio relic has grown (e.g., A520, A754, A2163, CIZA J2242.8+5301, A3667, the Bullet Cluster, El Gordo). Thus the underlying observational program is ongoing and the Mach-number picture is partially confirmed but still under active investigation.

representations.normalized:
Galaxy clusters are gravitationally bound systems of galaxies whose intracluster medium (ICM) is a hot, magnetized, diffuse plasma that radiates synchrotron emission detectable as diffuse radio sources on Mpc scales. Such diffuse sources are commonly classified as: (i) radio halos — centrally located, roughly spherical, low-surface-brightness sources co-spatial with the X-ray emitting ICM; (ii) radio relics — elongated, often peripheral, polarized sources typically interpreted as tracers of shock fronts; and (iii) mini-halos — smaller central sources confined within cool cores. During cluster mergers, gravitational potential energy is dissipated into the ICM via shock waves (which can accelerate or re-accelerate relativistic electrons via diffusive shock acceleration) and via turbulence (which can re-accelerate electrons via second-order Fermi mechanisms and amplify magnetic fields).

Consider the empirical class C of merging galaxy clusters in which two or more distinct diffuse radio sources (e.g., a halo plus one or more relics, or multiple relics) are simultaneously detected. For a cluster in C, let the merger be characterized by parameters such as mass ratio q, impact parameter b, time since core passage t, and viewing geometry. Let the diffuse radio emission be characterized by the spatial distribution of surface brightness, integrated spectral index, spectral index maps, polarization fraction maps, and morphological correspondence with X-ray shocks and ICM turbulence indicators.

Problem. Develop a quantitative model of the spatio-temporal development of merger-driven shocks and turbulence throughout the cluster volume that:
(a) predicts the joint occurrence, relative locations, morphologies, and polarization properties of multiple diffuse radio sources within a single cluster as functions of (q, b, t) and the magnetic-field configuration;
(b) reproduces the observed statistical correlations (or lack thereof) between halo and relic properties in clusters of class C, including spectral-index distributions and surface-brightness profiles;
(c) specifies which features of the observed diffuse emission constitute robust diagnostics of the underlying shock strength distribution and turbulent energy spectrum in the ICM.

Equivalently: characterize, in a falsifiable way, the mapping from the merger dynamics and the resulting (shock, turbulence) fields in the ICM to the observed multi-component diffuse radio emission of clusters in C.

In the context of diffuse non-thermal radio emission from galaxy clusters, a giant radio halo is a Mpc-scale, low-surface-brightness, centrally located synchrotron source whose integrated radio spectrum follows a power law S_ν ∝ ν^α. A radio halo is called ultra-steep-spectrum (USSRH) if its spectral index satisfies α < −1.5 (equivalently, the spectrum is steeper than this value over the observed frequency range). Within the turbulent re-acceleration model, merger-driven magnetohydrodynamic turbulence in the intra-cluster medium re-accelerates relativistic electrons via stochastic (second-order Fermi) processes; the model generically predicts that a significant fraction of mergers (especially those involving lower-mass systems) should produce halos with α < −1.5, while flatter-spectrum halos are expected for the most energetic mergers.

Determine whether ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos constitute a genuine, statistically populated class of diffuse cluster radio sources (as opposed to a small number of isolated cases), and assess whether the observed abundance and statistical properties of such USSRHs—when compared to predictions of the turbulent re-acceleration model—provide quantitative observational support for that model of radio halo formation.

Subsequent low-frequency surveys with LOFAR, GMRT/uGMRT and MWA have substantially expanded the number of identified ultra-steep-spectrum radio halos. A 2024 LOFAR study reports that roughly 64% (7/11) of analyzed halos have α < −1.5, consistent with predictions of the turbulent re-acceleration model. This supports USSRHs as a real population and provides observational backing for turbulent re-acceleration, though precise statistics and full population-level confirmation across cluster mass and merger states are still being refined.

representations.normalized:
Let $\mathbb{T}^n = \mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{Z}^n$ be the $n$-dimensional torus. A Finsler metric on $\mathbb{T}^n$ is a continuous function $F : T\mathbb{T}^n \to [0,\infty)$ that is smooth on $T\mathbb{T}^n \setminus \{0\}$, positively homogeneous of degree one in the fiber variable (i.e. $F(x,\lambda v)=\lambda F(x,v)$ for $\lambda>0$), and whose vertical Hessian $\frac{1}{2}\partial^2(F^2)/\partial v^i\partial v^j$ is positive definite on $T\mathbb{T}^n\setminus\{0\}$. The Finsler metric $F$ is said to have no conjugate points if no geodesic of $F$ contains a pair of conjugate points. A locally Minkowski metric on $\mathbb{T}^n$ is a Finsler metric whose fundamental function $F(x,v)$ depends only on $v$ in the standard coordinates of $\mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{Z}^n$ (equivalently, $\mathbb{T}^n$ admits an atlas in which $F$ is translation-invariant). The geodesic flow $\varphi^F_t$ of $F$ is the flow on the unit tangent bundle $SF\mathbb{T}^n=\{(x,v)\in T\mathbb{T}^n : F(x,v)=1\}$ generated by the Finsler geodesic spray.

Question: Suppose $F$ is a smooth Finsler metric on $\mathbb{T}^n$ without conjugate points. Must the geodesic flow of $F$ on $SF\mathbb{T}^n$ be (smoothly, or topologically) conjugate to the geodesic flow of some locally Minkowski metric on $\mathbb{T}^n$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is widely cited as open. The Riemannian analogue (Hopf conjecture) was settled by Burago–Ivanov, but the Finsler version is more subtle: Finsler tori without conjugate points need not be locally Minkowski. Partial results exist (e.g., the analytic, k-basic case by Cui–Shen; transitivity results in the surface case by Bialy and others; recent work on canonical deformations toward flat Finsler metrics). No general affirmative or negative answer to the conjugacy question appears in the literature as of 2026.

Let $\alpha,\beta:[0,\infty)\to M$ be two distinct unit-speed geodesic rays with $\alpha(0)=\beta(0)$. Determine whether
$$\operatorname{dist}(\alpha(t),\beta(t))\longrightarrow\infty\quad\text{as }t\to\infty,$$
where $\operatorname{dist}$ denotes the Riemannian distance on $M$. (The case $\dim M=2$ is known; the question concerns dimensions $\geq 3$.)

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem—whether two geodesic rays from a common point in a complete simply connected Riemannian manifold without conjugate points must diverge to infinity—is known in dimension 2 but is reported as open in higher dimensions in the Burns–Matveev problem list, and no resolution in higher dimensions appears in subsequent literature. Counterexamples are known in the Finsler setting, but the Riemannian higher-dimensional case remains open.

Consider two counter-propagating bunched particle beams in a high-energy circular collider undergoing long-range (parasitic) beam–beam interactions at injection energy. Suppose the betatron tunes, the transverse beam–beam separation at the parasitic crossings, the longitudinal emittance, and the available physical aperture are all held fixed. Empirically, the fractional loss rate dN/dt of one beam is observed to depend on the parameters of the opposing ("opposing") beam in the following way:

(i) linearly in the opposing beam's bunch intensity N_opp,
(ii) quadratically in the opposing beam's transverse (rms) emittance ε_opp,
(iii) quadratically in the chromaticity ξ_opp of the opposing beam's lattice setting.

That is, dN/dt ∝ N_opp · ε_opp^2 · ξ_opp^2, with all other listed parameters fixed.

Problem. Develop a theoretical (analytic) model of long-range beam–beam-driven particle loss at injection that derives, from first principles of single-particle dynamics in the presence of long-range beam–beam kicks (with chromatic modulation and finite physical aperture), the scaling
   dN/dt  ∝  N_opp · ε_opp^2 · ξ_opp^2.
The model should identify the dynamical mechanism (e.g., resonance excitation, diffusion via chromatic tune modulation, or stochastic dynamic-aperture reduction) responsible for each of the three exponents (1, 2, 2), and should reproduce these dependencies in the appropriate parameter regime.

representations.normalized:
Consider a circular hadron collider in which two counter-rotating bunched beams interact at one or more interaction regions. Around each main interaction point the beams share a common beam pipe over a finite distance, so that in addition to the head-on beam-beam collision each test particle of one beam encounters the opposing bunch at several parasitic ("long-range") crossings per turn, where the two beams are transversely separated by a few r.m.s. beam sizes. Let N denote the bunch population (number of particles per bunch) of the opposing beam and ε its transverse normalized emittance. For a well-tuned machine whose betatron tunes are kept away from low-order resonances harmful to single-particle stability, empirical observations in existing colliders suggest that the rate of beam loss attributable to long-range beam-beam interactions depends on the opposing-beam parameters only through certain specific functional combinations of N and ε (a "long-range loss law").

(a) Determine whether these observed dependencies of the long-range loss rate on (N, ε) are nearly universal across well-tuned colliders operated away from harmful resonances, in the sense of being independent of the specific machine, optics, and number of long-range encounters per turn (up to an overall normalization).

(b) In particular, determine whether the same functional dependencies hold in a collider configuration with several long-range beam-beam encounters per interaction region per turn (such as a high-energy proton-proton collider with strong parasitic crossings), and identify the explicit scaling law L = f(N, ε) governing the long-range-induced loss rate in that regime.

Recent literature on long-range beam-beam effects in the LHC and HL-LHC continues to study scaling of losses and emittance growth with bunch intensity, emittance, and separation, and reports that observed scalings are consistent with simple assumptions but no universal closed-form law has been established. Mitigation via wire compensators is an active area, with first experimental evidence published in 2024. The question of universality of long-range loss laws across machines therefore appears to remain open.

In a high-energy hadron collider, the beam-beam parameter ξ characterizes the linear tune shift produced on a test particle by the electromagnetic field of the opposing bunch. A standard class of theoretical models describes long-term particle loss as arising from chaotic diffusion in action space due to the overlap of nonlinear betatron resonances driven by the beam-beam force. In such models, the local diffusion coefficient D(J) in action J scales as the square of the perturbation strength, so that

   D(J) ∝ ξ²,

and, under standard assumptions about the boundary conditions at the dynamic aperture, the resulting particle loss rate L (fractional intensity loss per unit time during a store) is also predicted to scale as

   L ∝ ξ².

In contrast, an empirical fit to proton intensity decay during collider stores has been found to be well represented by a relation of the form

   L ≈ a + b·ξ,

i.e. a loss rate that is approximately linear in ξ over the operational range of ξ.

Problem. Construct a quantitative dynamical model of beam loss for a stored proton beam under beam-beam perturbation that:

(a) Reproduces the quadratic scaling D ∝ ξ² of the diffusion coefficient in action space implied by resonance-overlap / Chirikov-type analyses of the beam-beam Hamiltonian, yet

(b) Yields, after solving the associated Fokker–Planck equation for the action distribution f(J,t) on a domain bounded by an absorbing aperture J = J_a,

   ∂f/∂t = ∂/∂J [ D(J) ∂f/∂J ],   f(J_a,t) = 0,

a long-time fractional loss rate L(ξ) = −(1/N) dN/dt that depends on ξ approximately linearly rather than quadratically over a realistic range of ξ.

Identify the physical and mathematical mechanisms (e.g. the ξ-dependence of the effective absorbing boundary, ξ-dependent tails of the initial distribution, halo repopulation, non-Gaussian core dynamics, or additional noise sources such as residual gas scattering, intra-beam scattering, or external tune ripple) that, when incorporated into the diffusive description, can rigorously reconcile the predicted ξ² scaling of D with an observed near-linear ξ scaling of L.

In a high-energy hadron collider, the beam-beam parameter ξ characterizes the linear tune shift produced on a test particle by the electromagnetic field of the opposing bunch. A standard class of theoretical models describes long-term particle loss as arising from chaotic diffusion in action space due to the overlap of nonlinear betatron resonances driven by the beam-beam force. In such models, the local diffusion coefficient D(J) in action J scales as the square of the perturbation strength, so that

   D(J) ∝ ξ²,

and, under standard assumptions about the boundary conditions at the dynamic aperture, the resulting particle loss rate L (fractional intensity loss per unit time during a store) is also predicted to scale as

   L ∝ ξ².

In contrast, an empirical fit to proton intensity decay during collider stores has been found to be well represented by a relation of the form

   L ≈ a + b·ξ,

i.e. a loss rate that is approximately linear in ξ over the operational range of ξ.

Problem. Construct a quantitative dynamical model of beam loss for a stored proton beam under beam-beam perturbation that:

(a) Reproduces the quadratic scaling D ∝ ξ² of the diffusion coefficient in action space implied by resonance-overlap / Chirikov-type analyses of the beam-beam Hamiltonian, yet

(b) Yields, after solving the associated Fokker–Planck equation for the action distribution f(J,t) on a domain bounded by an absorbing aperture J = J_a,

   ∂f/∂t = ∂/∂J [ D(J) ∂f/∂J ],   f(J_a,t) = 0,

a long-time fractional loss rate L(ξ) = −(1/N) dN/dt that depends on ξ approximately linearly rather than quadratically over a realistic range of ξ.

Identify the physical and mathematical mechanisms (e.g. the ξ-dependence of the effective absorbing boundary, ξ-dependent tails of the initial distribution, halo repopulation, non-Gaussian core dynamics, or additional noise sources such as residual gas scattering, intra-beam scattering, or external tune ripple) that, when incorporated into the diffusive description, can rigorously reconcile the predicted ξ² scaling of D with an observed near-linear ξ scaling of L.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The reconciliation between resonance-overlap diffusion predictions (loss rate ∝ ξ²) and the Tevatron empirical near-linear dependence on the beam-beam parameter is identified in the literature as an unresolved modeling challenge. Subsequent beam-beam studies (e.g. for LHC and Tevatron-era analyses) continue to discuss diffusion models and empirical loss scalings without providing a definitive derivation that yields linear ξ dependence from a ξ² diffusion coefficient. No widely accepted resolution was located.

Subsequent reports on KEKB crab-cavity operation acknowledge that the achieved vertical beam-beam parameter (~0.09) remained well below the simulated value (~0.15), and that the cause was not fully identified. Contributing factors discussed include operation near a synchro-betatron resonance, chromatic coupling (partly mitigated by skew sextupoles), and contradictions between simulated and measured beam lifetime. No definitive resolution has been published; the question remained open at KEKB shutdown, with investigations continuing in the SuperKEKB context.

Let $(\mathbb{R}^2, g)$ be a complete Riemannian metric on the plane. Suppose $g$ satisfies the following Riemannian version of Euclid's parallel postulate: for every complete geodesic $\gamma$ and every point $p \in \mathbb{R}^2$ not lying on $\gamma$, there exists exactly one complete geodesic $\gamma'$ passing through $p$ such that $\gamma' \cap \gamma = \emptyset$. (This condition is known to imply that $g$ has no conjugate points.)

Question: Must $(\mathbb{R}^2, g)$ be isometric to the flat Euclidean plane?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question (attributed to Bangert–Knieper, 1991, and also raised by Croke) asks whether a complete Riemannian metric on the plane satisfying the parallel postulate must be flat. The general problem appears still open. A partial affirmative answer was given by showing that if, in addition, the metric admits total curvature, then it is isometric to the Euclidean plane (Mathematische Annalen, 2020; arXiv:1611.07761).

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

This is a conjecture attributed to Spatzier asserting that closed higher-rank symmetric spaces of noncompact type are rigid among metrics without conjugate points. It generalizes the celebrated Hopf and Burns–Spatzier–Ballmann higher-rank rigidity results. Searches reveal active related work (e.g., higher-rank rigidity theorems for convex projective and CAT(0) settings, rigidity for products M×S¹) but no resolution of the full conjecture for general higher-rank symmetric spaces of noncompact type. It appears to remain open.

representations.normalized:
Consider two electron–positron colliders operating with crab-cavity collision schemes. In each ring, the linear single-particle transfer map through the interaction region is modeled by a symplectic 6×6 matrix that acts on transverse phase-space coordinates (x, p_x, y, p_y) coupled to the longitudinal coordinate (z, δ), where δ = ΔE/E is the relative momentum deviation. Sextupole magnets in the chromatic correction sections are assumed to have small rotational misalignments about the beam axis; such a roll angle θ in a sextupole of integrated strength K_2 induces, to leading order in θ, an additional skew-sextupole component of strength K_2·θ. When combined with linear horizontal–vertical dispersion and crab-cavity-induced z–x coupling, these skew-sextupole errors generate a δ-dependent x–y coupling, hereafter called chromatic coupling, characterized by the resonance driving terms

  c_±(δ) = ∮ ds [ K_1^s(s) + 2 K_2(s) θ(s) η_x(s) ] · √(β_x β_y) · exp{ i [ φ_x(s) ∓ φ_y(s) ] } · (1 + a_± δ + …),

where K_1^s is any residual skew quadrupole, η_x is horizontal dispersion, β_{x,y} are the Courant–Snyder beta functions, and φ_{x,y} are the betatron phases.

For the two colliders compare the following lattice-dependent quantities at the design tunes:
(i) the chromatic-coupling sensitivity ∂c_±/∂δ |_{δ=0} produced by a unit rotational sextupole misalignment,
(ii) the proximity of the working point (Q_x, Q_y, Q_x ± Q_y) to the difference and sum coupling resonances and their chromatic side-bands,
(iii) the amplification of (i) by the crab-cavity-induced z–x mixing matrix element.

Determine quantitatively which combination of these lattice properties (chromatic-coupling driving-term sensitivity, tune working point, crab-induced mixing, and IR optics asymmetry) makes one such collider far more susceptible to chromatic coupling from rotational sextupole misalignments than the other, and exhibit a closed-form criterion that predicts when crab-crossing operation in a given lattice is dynamically dominated by chromatic coupling generated from sextupole roll errors.

Consider a hadron collider in which a bunch of protons interacts head-on (and possibly through long-range encounters) with a bunch of anti-protons of equal energy. Each beam is characterized by a transverse rms emittance (ε_p for protons, ε_a for anti-protons) and the standard linear beam-beam tune-shift parameter ξ, which for round Gaussian beams is
  ξ = (N r_0) / (4 π ε_n),
where N is the opposing bunch population, r_0 is the classical proton radius, and ε_n is the normalized transverse emittance of the opposing beam. Single-particle proton motion in the presence of the nonlinear beam-beam kick from the anti-proton charge distribution is otherwise governed by the (weak-strong) Hamiltonian
  H(x,p_x,y,p_y;s) = H_lattice(x,p_x,y,p_y;s) + δ_p(s) U(x,y; σ_x(ε_a), σ_y(ε_a)),
where U is the Bassetti–Erskine potential of a Gaussian charge distribution with rms sizes σ_{x,y} determined by ε_a, and δ_p denotes periodic kicks at the interaction point(s).

Empirically, in regimes where the anti-proton emittance ε_a is large compared to the proton emittance ε_p, proton losses are dominated by relatively low-order betatron resonances n_x Q_x + n_y Q_y = p (with |n_x|+|n_y| small). When ε_a is reduced so that ε_a ≈ ε_p, observations show that proton losses become markedly more sensitive to high-order resonances (large |n_x|+|n_y|), even when this reduction in ε_a simultaneously decreases the beam-beam parameter ξ by roughly 40%.

Problem. Develop a quantitative theoretical model — in terms of the resonance driving terms generated by U at given ε_a/ε_p, the resulting nonlinear detuning, the dynamic-aperture or diffusion rate of proton trajectories under repeated kicks, and the proton phase-space density occupying these resonances — that predicts and explains why decreasing ε_a toward ε_p enhances the contribution of high-order resonances to proton losses despite the accompanying ~40% reduction in ξ. The model should yield a calculable loss rate (or diffusion coefficient) as a function of ε_a/ε_p and ξ that reproduces the observed crossover from low-order- to high-order-resonance-dominated loss as ε_a → ε_p.

Let $M$ be a closed orientable surface of genus at least $2$, and let $S^1$ denote the circle. Equip the product manifold $M \times S^1$ with a smooth Riemannian metric $g$ that has no conjugate points (i.e., along every geodesic, the only Jacobi field vanishing at two distinct points is the zero field). Consider the $\mathbb{Z}$-cover of $M \times S^1$ corresponding to the $S^1$ factor, namely $M \times \mathbb{R}$ with the lifted metric, which by abuse of notation is also denoted $g$.

Prove or disprove the following: there exists a Riemannian metric $g_1$ on $M$ such that
$$(M \times \mathbb{R},\, g) \;=\; (M, g_1) \times (\mathbb{R}, dt^2)$$
as Riemannian manifolds; that is, $g$ splits isometrically as a direct product of a metric on $M$ and the standard Euclidean metric on $\mathbb{R}$.

Let $(M,g)$ be a closed oriented Riemannian surface of genus $\geq 2$, and let $\Omega$ be a smooth $2$-form on $M$ (the "magnetic field"). The magnetic flow $\phi_t^k$ on the energy level $S_k M = \{(x,v)\in TM : \tfrac12|v|_g^2 = k\}$ is the flow generated by the vector field $X_k$ on $TM$ such that, for unit-speed parametrization, the trajectories $\gamma(t)$ satisfy
$$\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma = Y_x(\dot\gamma),$$
where $Y:TM\to TM$ is the bundle map determined by $\Omega_x(u,v) = \langle Y_x(u), v\rangle_g$. A magnetic geodesic $\gamma$ has no conjugate points if the linearised flow along $\gamma$ admits no nontrivial perpendicular Jacobi field that vanishes at two distinct times.

Suppose that on the energy level $S_k M$ the topological entropy $h_{\mathrm{top}}(\phi^k|_{S_kM})$ vanishes.

Prove or disprove: under this hypothesis, every magnetic geodesic on $S_k M$ has no conjugate points, and moreover the pair $(g,\Omega)$ is rigid in the following sense — $g$ has constant Gaussian curvature and $\Omega = c\,\omega_g$ is a constant multiple of the Riemannian area form $\omega_g$.

representations.normalized:
In a high-energy storage-ring collider, two counter-rotating bunched beams cross at an interaction point. The strength of the nonlinear electromagnetic perturbation that one beam exerts on a particle of the opposing beam at small transverse amplitude is characterized by the beam-beam parameter ξ, defined (for round Gaussian beams of rms transverse size σ, with N particles per opposing bunch, classical particle radius r_p, and relativistic factor γ) by

    ξ = (N r_p) / (4 π γ ε),

where ε is the transverse emittance of the test beam. Empirically, single-ring hadron colliders such as the SPS proton–antiproton collider operated stably at ξ ≈ 0.005 and the Tevatron at ξ ≈ 0.008, with relatively loose tolerances on the matching of the transverse rms sizes σ_1, σ_2 of the two colliding beams at the interaction point.

In the HERA electron–proton collider, by contrast, the beam-beam parameter acting on the proton beam was only about ξ ≈ 0.001, yet operational experience required that the transverse sizes of the proton beam and the opposing electron beam be matched to within roughly

    |σ_p − σ_e| / σ_p  ≲  20%

at the interaction point in order to keep proton beam losses at a tolerable level; larger size mismatches led to unacceptable losses.

Problem. Provide a quantitative dynamical explanation of this stringent ~20% beam-size matching tolerance at HERA. Specifically, identify the mechanism by which a transverse rms size mismatch between the proton beam and the opposing (electron) beam produces enhanced diffusion and particle losses in the proton beam, derive how the resulting loss rate depends on the size-mismatch ratio σ_e/σ_p and on ξ, and show why the tolerance on this mismatch can be much tighter at the smaller HERA value ξ ≈ 0.001 than at the larger values ξ ≈ 0.005–0.008 attained in the SPS and the Tevatron.

representations.normalized:
Consider two counter-rotating bunched hadron beams in a circular collider undergoing head-on beam-beam collisions. The transverse coherent dipole oscillation spectrum of the two-beam system contains two discrete modes: the σ-mode (0-mode), in which the two bunches oscillate in phase, and the π-mode, in which they oscillate out of phase. The σ-mode lies inside the incoherent betatron tune spread of single-particle frequencies and is therefore Landau-damped, whereas the π-mode is shifted outside the incoherent continuum (for nearly equal beams and beam-beam parameter ratios above roughly 0.6) and is, in classical rigid-bunch theory, undamped. An undamped coherent mode is generally expected to drive a transverse instability in the presence of machine impedance.

Experimentally, in the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) the π coherent beam-beam mode has been clearly observed lying outside the incoherent spectrum, yet no associated transverse instability developed.

Provide a quantitative explanation of the following two questions:

(a) Identify the physical damping or stabilizing mechanism(s) that prevent the experimentally observed RHIC π-mode from driving a coherent transverse instability, despite its position outside the incoherent betatron tune spread and the presence of machine impedance. Derive, under stated approximations, the corresponding damping rate or stability criterion as a function of the beam-beam parameter ξ, the synchrotron tune Q_s, the chromaticity, the bunch length, and the relevant impedance.

(b) Determine, under the parameters of the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) (proton-proton head-on collisions at top energy, with its characteristic ξ, Q_s, bunch length, chromaticity, and transverse impedance budget), whether the same mechanism(s) suffice to damp the π-mode, and if not, specify what additional damping mechanism would be required and quantify its necessary strength.

Subsequent literature identifies synchro-betatron coupling, which produces incoherent synchrotron sidebands that overlap with the π-mode and provide Landau damping, as the leading candidate explanation for the absence of π-mode instability at RHIC. Does there exist a closed (compact, without boundary) smooth Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ such that:

1. the sectional curvature $K_g(\sigma) > 0$ for every point $p \in M$ and every 2-plane $\sigma \subset T_pM$, and
2. the geodesic flow $\varphi_t : T^1M \to T^1M$ on the unit tangent bundle is ergodic with respect to the Liouville (Sasaki) measure?

Equivalently, can one find a Riemannian metric of everywhere positive sectional curvature on a closed manifold whose geodesic flow is ergodic?

2. the geodesic flow $\varphi_t : T^1M \to T^1M$ on the unit tangent bundle is ergodic with respect to the Liouville (Sasaki) measure?

Equivalently, can one find a Riemannian metric of everywhere positive sectional curvature on a closed manifold whose geodesic flow is ergodic?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is listed among open problems on geodesic flows (Burns–Matveev problem list). No example of a closed Riemannian manifold with everywhere positive sectional curvature and ergodic geodesic flow is known; even the case of metrics close to the round metric on S² is highlighted as open. Searches as of 2026 reveal no resolution.

Let $M$ be a closed smooth manifold of dimension at least $2$, and for an integer $k \geq 2$ (or $k = \infty$) let $\mathcal{G}^{k}(M)$ denote the space of smooth Riemannian metrics on $M$ equipped with the $C^{k}$-topology. For a Riemannian metric $g$ on $M$, let $h_{\mathrm{top}}(g)$ denote the topological entropy of the geodesic flow of $g$ on the unit tangent bundle of $(M,g)$.

Question: For every integer $k \geq 2$ (and for $k = \infty$), is the set
$$\{\, g \in \mathcal{G}^{k}(M) : h_{\mathrm{top}}(g) > 0 \,\}$$
a $C^{k}$-dense subset of $\mathcal{G}^{k}(M)$?
representations.original:
Let $M$ be a closed smooth manifold of dimension at least $2$, and for an integer $k \geq 2$ (or $k = \infty$) let $\mathcal{G}^{k}(M)$ denote the space of smooth Riemannian metrics on $M$ equipped with the $C^{k}$-topology. For a Riemannian metric $g$ on $M$, let $h_{\mathrm{top}}(g)$ denote the topological entropy of the geodesic flow of $g$ on the unit tangent bundle of $(M,g)$.

Question: For every integer $k \geq 2$ (and for $k = \infty$), is the set
$$\{\, g \in \mathcal{G}^{k}(M) : h_{\mathrm{top}}(g) > 0 \,\}$$
a $C^{k}$-dense subset of $\mathcal{G}^{k}(M)$?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The question is settled in the $C^2$ topology in all dimensions: Contreras (Annals of Math., 2010) showed that on any closed manifold the set of $C^\infty$ metrics whose geodesic flow has positive topological entropy is $C^2$-open and $C^2$-dense. In the $C^\infty$ topology, Knieper–Weiss (2002) established density on the 2-sphere $S^2$ (and $\mathbb{RP}^2$). The general case for $C^k$ with $k \geq 3$, and for $C^\infty$ on arbitrary closed manifolds of dimension $\geq 3$, appears to remain open.

representations.normalized:
Consider a circular hadron collider in which two counter-rotating bunched beams collide head-on at one or more interaction points, and in which each bunch interacts with an electron lens (a co-axial low-energy electron beam acting as a nonlinear lens) intended to compensate the head-on beam-beam tune spread produced by the opposing hadron bunch. Let N denote the bunch intensity (protons per bunch). Weak-strong and strong-strong tracking simulations for representative parameters of the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider and of the Large Hadron Collider show the following qualitative behaviour: there exists a critical bunch intensity N_c such that for N < N_c the electron-lens compensation does not improve, and may even worsen, the beam emittance growth and particle loss caused by the head-on beam-beam interaction, while for N > N_c the compensation reduces these effects. Empirically, this N_c lies above the bunch intensities currently used in operation at RHIC and above the nominal design bunch intensity of the LHC, even though the uncompensated machines already exhibit beam-beam-induced emittance growth and losses at those lower intensities.

Identify and quantitatively characterize the dynamical mechanism that determines the critical bunch intensity N_c above which head-on beam-beam compensation by an electron lens becomes beneficial. Specifically, derive an expression for N_c (or for the corresponding critical beam-beam parameter ξ_c) in terms of the lattice and beam parameters — such as the unperturbed transverse tunes and their working point relative to nearby resonances, the chromaticity, the linear and nonlinear lattice nonlinearities, the rms transverse beam sizes at the hadron and electron interaction points, the electron-lens current profile and length, and the number of head-on collision points — and explain why compensation is ineffective below this threshold despite the presence of beam-beam-driven losses at lower intensities.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent work, in particular the operational demonstration of head-on beam-beam compensation with electron lenses at RHIC (Fischer et al., Phys. Rev. Lett. 115, 264801 (2015)) and the simulation/analysis paper Gu et al., Phys. Rev. Accel. Beams 20, 023501 (2017), as well as weak-strong simulation studies for the LHC, have provided substantial understanding of when electron-lens compensation is beneficial, linking the threshold to the beam-beam-induced tune footprint relative to nearby resonances and to the lattice phase advance between IP and electron lens. However, a clean closed-form criterion for the critical bunch intensity has not been reported; the threshold is generally characterized through case-by-case tracking simulations rather than a universal analytic formula, so the question is best regarded as partially solved.
