For an algebraic structure H (a group or a monoid) and a subset X of H that generates H (as a group or as a monoid, respectively), define the width of H with respect to X to be

  w(H,X) = sup_{h ∈ H} min{ ℓ : h can be expressed as a word of length ℓ in elements of X },

where, in the group case, words are group words (allowing inverses of elements of X) and, in the monoid case, words are monoid words (no inverses, only products of elements of X). Note that w(H,X) ∈ {0,1,2,…} ∪ {∞}.

Say that H has finite width as a group (respectively, as a monoid) if for every subset X ⊆ H that generates H as a group (respectively, as a monoid), the width w(H,X) is finite. (No common finite upper bound on these widths over all generating sets X is required.)

Question: Does there exist a group G that has finite width as a group but does not have finite width as a monoid? Equivalently, does there exist a group G such that, for every generating set X of G as a group, every element of G is a group word of bounded length in X, yet there exists a monoid generating set Y of G for which the lengths of shortest monoid words in Y representing elements of G are unbounded?

representations.normalized:
Setting. Let $\Lambda$ be a finite connected lattice (e.g., a one-dimensional chain with $L$ sites) and consider $N$ interacting fermions on $\Lambda$ described by a Hamiltonian of the form
$$H(t)=\sum_{i,j\in\Lambda} T_{ij}\,c_i^\dagger c_j+\sum_{i\in\Lambda} v_i(t)\,n_i+W,$$
where $T_{ij}$ is a fixed (possibly complex) hopping matrix, $n_i=c_i^\dagger c_i$, $W$ is a fixed two-body interaction (e.g. Hubbard $U\sum_i n_{i\uparrow}n_{i\downarrow}$), and $v(t)=\{v_i(t)\}_{i\in\Lambda}$ is a time-dependent on-site scalar potential. Given an initial state $|\Psi_0\rangle$, the time evolution $i\partial_t|\Psi(t)\rangle=H(t)|\Psi(t)\rangle$ produces site-occupation densities $n_i(t)=\langle\Psi(t)|n_i|\Psi(t)\rangle$.

Definitions. A density trajectory $\{n_i(t)\}$ is called $v_0$-representable (with respect to $|\Psi_0\rangle$) if there exists a real on-site potential $v(t)$ such that the evolution under $H(t)$ starting from $|\Psi_0\rangle$ reproduces $n_i(t)$. Define the partial sums $S_k(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\dot n_i(t)$ (current conservation).

Known facts to be subsumed. (i) For $N=1$ on a one-dimensional lattice, $|S_k(t)|\le 2\sqrt{n_k(t)\,n_{k+1}(t)}$ for all $k$ and $t$ is necessary and sufficient for $v_0$-representability. (ii) For $N>1$ this inequality is only necessary. (iii) For the Hubbard dimer the exact density is $v_0$-representable. (iv) Explicit examples on lattices show that, in general, the map $v\mapsto n$ need not be injective.

Problem. Formulate and prove a rigorous Runge–Gross-type theorem for density-based time-dependent density functional theory on lattices: give necessary and sufficient conditions on the initial state $|\Psi_0\rangle$, the hopping $T_{ij}$, the interaction $W$, and the density trajectory $\{n_i(t)\}$ under which (a) the density trajectory is $v_0$-representable, and (b) the potential $v(t)$ that produces it from $|\Psi_0\rangle$ is unique up to a spatially constant gauge. Equivalently, characterize precisely the class of lattice Hamiltonians, initial states, and densities for which the density-to-potential mapping is well-defined and one-to-one.

Let $G$ be a finite group, and let $A_1, A_2, A_3$ be subsets of $G$ such that the multiplication map
$$A_1 \times A_2 \times A_3 \to G,\qquad (a_1,a_2,a_3)\mapsto a_1 a_2 a_3,$$
is a bijection (so in particular $|A_1|\,|A_2|\,|A_3| = |G|$). Let $\langle A_2\rangle$ denote the subgroup of $G$ generated by $A_2$.

Must $|A_2|$ divide $|\langle A_2\rangle|$?

(It is known that the analogous statement holds for $\langle A_1\rangle$ and for $\langle A_3\rangle$, and that $|A_2|$ divides the order of the smallest subgroup of $G$ that contains $A_2$ and is closed under conjugation by all elements of $A_1$, and similarly with $A_1$ replaced by $A_3$. The question is whether closure under conjugation can be removed for the middle factor.)

representations.normalized:
Work in the category of groups of finite Morley rank (i.e., groups whose first-order theory has finite Morley rank), and let "definable" mean definable in the pure group language with parameters.

Let $S$ be an infinite group of finite Morley rank, and let $M$ be a non-trivial connected group of finite Morley rank. Suppose $M$ acts on $S$ definably and faithfully (so the action $M\times S\to S$ is a definable group action and the kernel of $M\to \mathrm{Aut}(S)$ is trivial). Call this action irreducible if there is no definable subgroup $N$ of $S$ with $1\neq N\neq S$ that is invariant under the action of $M$.

Two definable faithful actions of connected groups $M_1,M_2$ on $S$ are called equivalent if there exists a definable group isomorphism $\varphi: M_1\to M_2$ and a definable group automorphism $\psi$ of $S$ such that $\psi(m\cdot s) = \varphi(m)\cdot \psi(s)$ for all $m\in M_1$, $s\in S$.

Assume in addition that:
(i) $S$ is a simple group, and
(ii) every proper definable subgroup of $S$ is nilpotent.

Prove that if the action of $M$ on $S$ is irreducible, then this action is equivalent to the action of $S$ on itself by inner automorphisms (conjugation).

Consider the 3D homogeneous single-band Hubbard model on a cubic lattice with sites $R$, on-site repulsion $U>0$, hopping $t$, and uniform average density $n$. For each site $R$ let $n_{R\sigma}=c^\dagger_{R\sigma}c_{R\sigma}$ be the number operator for spin $\sigma\in\{\uparrow,\downarrow\}$, and define the local double occupancy
$$d_R=\langle n_{R\uparrow}\,n_{R\downarrow}angle.$$
By construction $0\le d_R\le \min(\langle n_{R\uparrow}angle,\langle n_{R\downarrow}angle)$, so $d_R\ge 0$. In time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT) on this lattice, the density-density response function $\chi(R,R';\omega)$ in a chosen approximation (for example the random-phase approximation (RPA), which uses only the Hartree kernel, or the adiabatic local-density approximation (ALDA), which adds an exchange-correlation kernel $f_{xc}^{	ext{ALDA}}(n)=\partial^2 e_{xc}^{	ext{hom}}(n)/\partial n^2$ taken from the homogeneous reference system) determines, via the fluctuation–dissipation theorem,
$$d_R \;=\; 	frac{1}{4}\langle n_Rangle^2 \;-\;  rac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^\infty d\omega\; \mathrm{Im}\,\chi_{\sigma\sigma}(R,R;\omega) \;+\; (	ext{spin-resolved corrections}),$$
or an equivalent expression giving $d_R$ from the on-site pair correlation function built out of $\chi$.

Problem. Construct an exchange-correlation kernel $f_{xc}(R,R';\omega)$ for the lattice TDDFT linear-response equations, going beyond RPA and ALDA, with the following properties:
(i) it is computable from local/semilocal lattice quantities (or from a controlled non-adiabatic, spatially nonlocal extension thereof);
(ii) when used to compute the density response function $\chi$ of the 3D homogeneous Hubbard model, the resulting on-site double occupancy $d_R$ satisfies $d_R\ge 0$ for all densities $n\in[0,2]$ and all $U/t\ge 0$;
(iii) it correctly captures the short-range correlation behavior of the on-site pair correlation function $g(R,R)$, in particular avoiding the spurious negativity of $d_R$ produced by ALDA (which inherits the short-range failure of the continuum electron-gas ALDA response).

Either exhibit such a kernel and prove that $d_R\ge 0$ holds within the resulting approximation, or prove that no kernel of a specified class (e.g. adiabatic and local in the lattice density) can guarantee $d_R\ge 0$ uniformly in $(n,U/t)$.

representations.normalized:
Consider lattice time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT) applied to the single-band Hubbard model

  H = -t ∑_{⟨i,j⟩,σ} (c†_{iσ} c_{jσ} + h.c.) + U ∑_i n_{i↑} n_{i↓} + ∑_i v_i(τ) n_i,

with site density n_i(τ) and on-site interaction U > 0. Within a Kohn–Sham mapping to a non-interacting lattice system, define the exchange-correlation (XC) potential v_xc[n] and the adiabatic local-density-approximation (ALDA) XC kernel

  f^{ALDA}_{xc}(n) = ∂ v^{hom}_{xc}(n)/∂ n,

where v^{hom}_{xc}(n) is the XC potential of the homogeneous Hubbard model at uniform density n, computed (e.g.) from Bethe-ansatz in 1D or from dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) in higher dimensions.

Two qualitative features of f^{ALDA}_{xc} are observed that have no known counterpart in continuum XC kernels:

(i) Sign change: f^{ALDA}_{xc}(n;U) changes sign as a function of band filling n ∈ (0,2) and interaction strength U.

(ii) Singularity at half filling: for sufficiently large U (specifically U > U_c^{Mott} in dimension d ≥ 2, and for all U > 0 in d = 1), v^{hom}_{xc}(n) has a discontinuity at n = 1 associated with the Mott–Hubbard metal-insulator transition, inducing a Dirac-delta–like singularity in f^{ALDA}_{xc} at n = 1.

Develop a theory of the (in general nonlocal and nonadiabatic) lattice XC kernel f_{xc}[n](i,j;ω) for the Hubbard model that:

(a) reproduces the sign-change behavior of f^{ALDA}_{xc} as a function of (n,U) in the local adiabatic limit,

(b) accounts for the half-filling singularity tied to the discontinuity of v_{xc} at the Mott transition,

(c) shows that these two qualitative features survive (in an appropriate sense to be made precise) the inclusion of nonlocality in (i,j) and frequency dependence in ω, and

(d) describes quantitatively their imprint on the interacting density response function χ(i,j;ω) of the Hubbard model beyond the ALDA.

Provide either an explicit construction of such an f_{xc} (e.g., from DMFT charge susceptibilities) together with a proof/argument that properties (a)–(c) hold and a calculation establishing (d), or else a rigorous demonstration that one of these features is artifactual and disappears when nonlocal/nonadiabatic corrections are included.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

Subsequent work has constructed nonadiabatic XC kernels for the Hubbard model via DMFT charge susceptibilities and studied the Hubbard dimer exactly, confirming strong frequency dependence and features tied to Mott physics. However, no general theory has been established that fully characterizes how the ALDA sign change and the half-filling delta-like singularity propagate into the full nonlocal, nonadiabatic kernel and the density response. The question therefore appears still open as of the latest available literature.

representations.normalized:
Work in the setting of groups of finite Morley rank, i.e., infinite groups whose first‑order theory (in the language of groups, possibly enriched by definable predicates) has finite Morley rank, with all subgroups, homomorphisms, and actions considered are definable.

A group G of finite Morley rank is called connected if it has no proper definable subgroup of finite index. An action of a group H on a group N (both of finite Morley rank) is said to be:
 • definable, if the map H × N → N giving the action is definable;
 • faithful, if only the identity of H acts trivially on N;
 • irreducible, if N is connected and contains no proper non‑trivial definable connected H‑invariant subgroup.

A group G of finite Morley rank is simple if it is infinite and has no proper non‑trivial definable normal subgroup. Recall that every simple group of finite Morley rank acts on itself by conjugation, giving a definable, faithful, irreducible action of G on G.

Prove the following: Let G be a simple group of finite Morley rank that contains no involution (i.e., no element of order 2). Suppose N is a connected group of finite Morley rank, not isomorphic (as a G‑group) to G acting on itself by conjugation, and suppose G acts definably, faithfully, and irreducibly on N. Show that this is impossible; that is, no such action of G on a connected group N other than (G, conjugation) exists.

Recall that a group $K$ is called Hopfian if every surjective homomorphism $K \to K$ is an isomorphism. Given two groups $G$ and $H$, the (standard, restricted) wreath product $G \wr H$ is the semidirect product $\big(\bigoplus_{h \in H} G\big) \rtimes H$, where $H$ acts on the direct sum $\bigoplus_{h \in H} G$ by permuting the coordinates via left multiplication on the index set.

Determine whether the following statement is true: for every pair of finitely generated Hopfian groups $G$ and $H$, the wreath product $G \wr H$ is Hopfian.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question is open. Bradford and Fournier-Facio (Math. Z. 308 (2024), no. 58) showed that the special case where $G$ is abelian (equivalently nilpotent) is equivalent to Kaplansky's stable/direct finiteness conjecture, which itself remains open in general. No proof or counterexample for the full question with arbitrary finitely generated Hopfian $G,H$ is known.

representations.normalized:
For a finite group $G$, define the enhanced power graph $\mathcal{E}(G)$ as the simple graph with vertex set $G$ in which two distinct elements $x, y \in G$ are adjacent if and only if the subgroup $\langle x, y \rangle$ is cyclic. A simple graph is called chordal if it contains no induced cycle on $n$ vertices for any $n \geq 4$.

(a) For each fixed integer $n \geq 4$, determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups $G$ such that $\mathcal{E}(G)$ has no induced cycle on $n$ vertices.

(b) Determine the set of all finite nonabelian simple groups $G$ such that $\mathcal{E}(G)$ is chordal.

representations.normalized:
Let $G$ be a finite group. The power graph $P(G)$ is the simple graph with vertex set $G$ in which two distinct vertices $x$ and $y$ are adjacent if and only if $x \in \langle y \rangle$ or $y \in \langle x \rangle$ (that is, one is a power of the other in $G$).

A simple graph $\Gamma$ is called a cograph if it contains no induced path on four vertices ($P_4$-free). It is called chordal if it contains no induced cycle of length $\ge 4$.

Prove or disprove: for every finite group $G$, if $P(G)$ is a cograph, then $P(G)$ is chordal.
representations.original:
Let $G$ be a finite group. The power graph $P(G)$ is the simple graph with vertex set $G$ in which two distinct vertices $x$ and $y$ are adjacent if and only if $x \in \langle y \rangle$ or $y \in \langle x \rangle$ (that is, one is a power of the other in $G$).

A simple graph $\Gamma$ is called a cograph if it contains no induced path on four vertices ($P_4$-free). It is called chordal if it contains no induced cycle of length $\ge 4$.

Prove or disprove: for every finite group $G$, if $P(G)$ is a cograph, then $P(G)$ is chordal.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The implication is established in several cases: when every element of G has prime power order (Bubboloni–Fumagalli–Praeger, 2025 preprint arXiv:2510.18073), and when G is a nonabelian finite simple group (Cameron–Manna–Mehatari, J. Algebra 591 (2022); Brachter–Kaja, J. Algebraic Combin. 58 (2023)). The general conjecture for arbitrary finite groups appears to remain open.

representations.normalized: Let $G$ be a finite non-abelian simple group, and let $p_1, p_2$ be (not necessarily distinct) prime divisors of $|G|$. Determine whether there always exist a Sylow $p_1$-subgroup $H_1$ and a Sylow $p_2$-subgroup $H_2$ of $G$ such that $G = \langle H_1, H_2 \rangle$.
representations.original: Let $G$ be a finite non-abelian simple group, and let $p_1, p_2$ be (not necessarily distinct) prime divisors of $|G|$. Determine whether there always exist a Sylow $p_1$-subgroup $H_1$ and a Sylow $p_2$-subgroup $H_2$ of $G$ such that $G = \langle H_1, H_2 \rangle$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The conjecture has been confirmed in significant special cases: Breuer and Guralnick (and subsequent work) established that every finite non-abelian simple group $G$ is generated by a Sylow 2-subgroup together with a Sylow $r$-subgroup for any prime $r$ dividing $|G|$, and the statement is known for alternating and sporadic groups. The full statement for arbitrary pairs of (odd) primes $p_1, p_2$ remains a conjecture and is not settled in general.

representations.normalized:
Let $G$ be a non-trivial finite group, and let $p_1, p_2, \dots, p_k$ be the distinct prime divisors of $|G|$. For each $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$, fix a Sylow $p_i$-subgroup $H_i$ of $G$. For $g \in G$, write $H_i^g = g^{-1} H_i g$. Consider, for each $i$, the family of subgroups
$$\mathcal{F}_i = \{\, H_i \cap H_i^g : g \in G \,\},$$
partially ordered by inclusion; call a member of $\mathcal{F}_i$ inclusion-minimal if it does not properly contain any other member of $\mathcal{F}_i$.

Determine whether there always exists a single element $x \in G$ such that, simultaneously for every $i \in \{1,\dots,k\}$, the subgroup $H_i \cap H_i^x$ is inclusion-minimal in $\mathcal{F}_i$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The Lisi–Sabatini conjecture has been verified in several classes: metanilpotent groups of odd order, sufficiently large symmetric and alternating groups, and (in a 2025 preprint using a probabilistic approach) all non-alternating finite simple groups. A complete resolution for arbitrary finite groups does not appear to have been established, so the problem is partially solved.

Let $G$ be a finite simple group acting transitively and faithfully on a set $\Omega$ with $|\Omega| \geq 2$. An element $g \in G$ is called a derangement (with respect to this action) if it has no fixed points on $\Omega$, i.e., $g \cdot \omega \neq \omega$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$. Let $\Delta(G) \subseteq G$ denote the set of all derangements in $G$ for the given action.

Determine whether every element of $G$ can be written as a product of two derangements; equivalently, decide whether
$$G = \Delta(G) \cdot \Delta(G) = \{xy : x,y \in \Delta(G)\}$$

Let $G$ be a finite simple group acting transitively and faithfully on a set $\Omega$ with $|\Omega| \geq 2$. An element $g \in G$ is called a derangement (with respect to this action) if it has no fixed points on $\Omega$, i.e., $g \cdot \omega \neq \omega$ for every $\omega \in \Omega$. Let $\Delta(G) \subseteq G$ denote the set of all derangements in $G$ for the given action.

Determine whether every element of $G$ can be written as a product of two derangements; equivalently, decide whether
$$G = \Delta(G) \cdot \Delta(G) = \{xy : x,y \in \Delta(G)\}$$
holds for every finite simple transitive permutation group $G$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Larsen, Shalev, and Tiep proved that for sufficiently large finite simple transitive permutation groups $G$, one has $G = \Delta(G)^2$, and the result holds for all alternating groups $A_n$ ($n \geq 5$). Subsequent work (e.g., Burness–Fawcett, 2024, arXiv:2409.01043) establishes the property for further classes (such as finite simple primitive groups with soluble point stabilisers) and shows generation by two conjugate derangements, but the full conjecture for all finite simple transitive groups remains open.

Let $N$ be a finite group, and let $\mathrm{Hol}(N) = N \rtimes \mathrm{Aut}(N)$ denote its holomorph, viewed as a permutation group acting on the set $N$ via the regular action of $N$ together with the natural action of $\mathrm{Aut}(N)$. A subgroup $G \le \mathrm{Hol}(N)$ is called regular if it acts regularly on $N$ (transitively and with trivial point stabilisers); equivalently, $|G| = |N|$ and $G$ acts transitively on $N$.

Prove or disprove: if $N$ is a finite soluble group, then every regular subgroup $G$ of $\mathrm{Hol}(N)$ is soluble.

Let G be a totally disconnected locally compact (tdlc) topological group. Following the rational discrete cohomology theory of tdlc groups, define the rational discrete cohomological dimension cd_Q(G) to be the projective dimension of the trivial rational discrete G-module Q in the abelian category of rational discrete G-modules (i.e., Q-vector space G-modules whose stabilizers of every vector are open subgroups). A graph of profinite groups is a graph of groups in the sense of Bass–Serre theory whose vertex and edge groups are profinite groups and whose edge inclusions are continuous open embeddings; its fundamental group carries a natural tdlc topology making vertex groups open and compact.

Question: Must every tdlc group G with cd_Q(G) ≤ 1 be topologically isomorphic to the fundamental group of a graph of profinite groups?

(This is a topological-group analogue of Dunwoody's theorem, which asserts that a discrete group of cohomological dimension at most 1 over a ring R is the fundamental group of a graph of groups with finite vertex stabilizers of orders invertible in R.)

Definitions. Let $G$ be a group with identity element $1$.

(i) $G$ is called a *unique product group* if for every pair of nonempty finite subsets $A, B \subseteq G$, there exists at least one element $x \in G$ that has a unique representation in the form $x = ab$ with $a \in A$ and $b \in B$.

(ii) $G$ is called *locally invariant orderable* if there exists a strict partial order $<$ on $G$ such that for every $g \in G$ and every $h \in G \setminus \{1\}$, at least one of the inequalities $gh > g$ or $gh^{-1} > g$ holds.

Question. Does there exist a group $G$ that is a unique product group but is not locally invariant orderable?

A group-word $w = w(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ is called a multilinear commutator word (or outer commutator word) if it is obtained from the variables $x_1, \dots, x_n$ (each occurring exactly once) by nested commutators; for example, $w = [x_1, x_2]$, $w = [[x_1,x_2],[x_3,x_4]]$, and the lower-central and derived words are of this form. For a group $G$, a $w$-value in $G$ is an element of the form $w(g_1,\dots,g_n)^{\pm 1}$ with $g_i \in G$, and the verbal subgroup $w(G)$ is the subgroup generated by all $w$-values. For a prime $p$, an element has $p'$-order if its order is finite and coprime to $p$; a finite group $H$ is $p$-nilpotent if it has a normal Hall $p'$-subgroup.

Let $G$ be a finite group, let $w$ be a multilinear commutator word, and let $p$ be a prime. Suppose that for every $w$-value $x \in G$ of $p'$-order and every $w$-value $y \in G$ whose order is divisible by $p$, the order $|xy|$ is divisible by $p$. Must the verbal subgroup $w(G)$ be $p$-nilpotent?

Kropholler's hierarchy of discrete groups is defined as follows. Let F denote the class of finite groups. Set H_0 F = F. For an ordinal α > 0, define H_α F to be the class of all groups G that admit a cellular admissible action on a finite-dimensional contractible CW-complex such that every cell stabiliser belongs to ⋃_{β<α} H_β F (an action is admissible if the setwise stabiliser of any cell fixes that cell pointwise). Set HF = ⋃_α H_α F. For a class X of groups and a class Y of groups, write XY for the class of groups G having a normal subgroup N ∈ X with G/N ∈ Y. It is a theorem of Kropholler that HF is closed under finite extensions in the strong sense that (H_α F)F ⊆ H_α F for every ordinal α.

Let $A_5$ denote the alternating group on five letters, acting naturally on the set $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$. For each integer $n\ge 1$, define the $n$-times iterated permutational wreath product
$$W_n \;=\; \underbrace{A_5 \wr A_5 \wr \cdots \wr A_5}_{n\text{ copies}},$$
taken with respect to the natural action, so that $W_n$ acts faithfully on the set of $5^n$ leaves of the rooted $5$-regular tree of depth $n$. The natural projections $W_{n+1}\twoheadrightarrow W_n$ obtained by truncating the tree form an inverse system; let
$$W \;=\; \varprojlim_{n} W_n$$
be the resulting profinite group (the infinite iterated permutational wreath product of $A_5$), endowed with its profinite topology. Recall that a finitely generated group $G$ with finite generating set $S$ has subexponential growth if $\lim_{r\to\infty} |B_S(r)|^{1/r} = 1$, where $B_S(r)$ is the ball of radius $r$ in the word metric.

Question: Does $W$ contain a finitely generated dense subgroup of subexponential growth?

Definitions. An isometric action of a group $G$ on a metric space $(S,d)$ is called acylindrical if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exist constants $R, N > 0$ such that for any two points $x, y \in S$ with $d(x,y) \geq R$, the number of elements $g \in G$ satisfying simultaneously $d(x, gx) \leq \varepsilon$ and $d(y, gy) \leq \varepsilon$ is at most $N$. A group $G$ is called acylindrically hyperbolic if $G$ is not virtually cyclic and $G$ admits an acylindrical isometric action on a (Gromov-)hyperbolic metric space with unbounded orbits.

Question. Let $G$ be a finitely generated acylindrically hyperbolic group. Is the automorphism group $\operatorname{Aut}(G)$ also acylindrically hyperbolic?

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Significant partial results are known: Genevois (2021) proved that the automorphism group of any infinitely-ended finitely generated group is acylindrically hyperbolic; analogous results hold for Aut(F_n) (n≥2), for automorphism groups of one-ended hyperbolic groups, and for relatively hyperbolic groups (with a finite collection of finitely generated proper peripheral subgroups). Let $T$ be a finite 3-group. Does there exist a nontrivial characteristic subgroup $C$ of $T$ with the following property: whenever $G$ is a finite group having $T$ as a Sylow 3-subgroup, and $H = N_G(C)$ denotes the normalizer of $C$ in $G$, one has
$$T \cap G' = T \cap H',$$
where $G'$ and $H'$ denote the derived subgroups of $G$ and $H$, respectively?

Background context: For every prime $p \geq 5$ such a nontrivial characteristic subgroup is known to exist in any finite $p$-group $T$. For $p = 3$ it is known that there exist two nontrivial characteristic subgroups $K_1, K_2$ of $T$ such that, with $H_i = N_G(K_i)$,
$$T \cap G' = (T \cap H_1')(T \cap H_2').$$
The symmetric group $S_4$ shows that the analogous statement can fail for $p = 2$ in some Sylow 2-subgroups. The question asks whether, for $p = 3$, a single characteristic subgroup suffices.

(a) If P contains an abelian subgroup of order p^n, then P contains a normal abelian subgroup of order p^n.

(b) If P contains an elementary abelian subgroup of order p^n (i.e., an abelian subgroup of exponent p), then P contains a normal elementary abelian subgroup of order p^n.

The cases to resolve are:
- p = 5 and n = 6;
- p > 5 and n ∈ {(p+3)/2, (p+5)/2, (p+7)/2}.

(It is known that the answer is "yes" whenever n < (p+2)/2 or n ≤ 5 with p ≠ 2, and "no" whenever n ≥ (p+9)/2 with p ≥ 5; the problem asks to settle the remaining values of n above.)

representations.normalized: Let $L$ be a finite non-abelian simple group, and let $D$ be a conjugacy class of involutions in $L$. Form the complete graph $\Gamma$ with vertex set $D$, and colour its edges by the following equivalence relation: for edges $(a,b)$ and $(c,d)$, declare $(a,b)\sim(c,d)$ if and only if the orders of the products satisfy $|ab|=|cd|$. An automorphism of the edge-coloured graph $\Gamma$ is a permutation $\tau\in\mathrm{Sym}(D)$ such that $(a,b)\sim(a^{\tau},b^{\tau})$ for every edge $(a,b)$; equivalently, $|ab|=|a^{\tau}b^{\tau}|$ for all $a,b\in D$. The group $L$ acts on $D$ by conjugation, and this action extends to an action of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)$ on $D$ by colour-preserving permutations, giving a natural embedding of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)/C_{\mathrm{Aut}(L)}(D)$ into the automorphism group $\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)$ of the coloured graph. Determine whether $\mathrm{Aut}(\Gamma)$ always equals (is contained in) the image of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)$; that is, decide whether for every finite non-abelian simple group $L$ and every conjugacy class $D$ of involutions of $L$, the automorphism group of the coloured complete graph $\Gamma$ described above is a subgroup of $\mathrm{Aut}(L)$.

$$m \cdot m^{\rho} \cdot m^{\rho^2} = 1$$
for every element $m$ of the set
$$M(G) := \{[g,\sigma] : g \in G\} = \{g^{-1} g^{\sigma} : g \in G\}.$$
Assume that:
1. $G$ is finite and soluble;
2. $G$ is a group with triality with respect to $S$ as above;
3. $G = [G,S]$;
4. $G$ is generated by $d$ elements of $M(G)$ together with all of their images under the action of $S$;
5. there is a positive integer $n$ such that $x^n = 1$ for every $x \in M(G)$.

The Fitting height (nilpotent length) $h(G)$ of $G$ is the smallest integer $h$ such that the iterated Fitting series
$$1 = F_0(G) \le F_1(G) \le \cdots \le F_h(G) = G$$
reaches $G$, where $F_{i+1}(G)/F_i(G) = F(G/F_i(G))$ is the Fitting subgroup of $G/F_i(G)$.

Question: Must $h(G)$ be bounded by a function depending only on $d$ and $n$?

For a finite group $X$, let $\ell(X)$ denote its composition length (the number of factors in any composition series of $X$). Let $A$ be a finite nilpotent group acting by automorphisms on a finite soluble group $G$. An $A$-composition series of $G$ is a chain $1 = G_0 \triangleleft G_1 \triangleleft \cdots \triangleleft G_n = G$ of $A$-invariant subgroups of $G$ such that each factor $G_{i+1}/G_i$ admits no proper nontrivial $A$-invariant subgroup; each such factor is regarded as an $A$-module (in the generalized sense). Define $c(G, A)$ to be the number of factors $G_{i+1}/G_i$ in such a series on which $A$ acts trivially. (When $\gcd(|A|, |G|) = 1$, this number coincides with $\ell(C_G(A))$, the composition length of the fixed-point subgroup.) Let $h(G)$ denote the Fitting height (Fitting length) of $G$, i.e. the length of the shortest normal series of $G$ with nilpotent factors.

Prove or disprove: there exist absolute constants $C_1$ and $C_2$ such that for every finite nilpotent group $A$ acting by automorphisms on every finite soluble group $G$,
$$h(G) \le C_1\, \ell(A) + C_2\, c(G, A).$$

representations.normalized:
Let $G$ be a group. For subsets $X, Y \subseteq G$, define their product $XY = \{xy : x \in X,\ y \in Y\}$, and say the product $XY$ is direct if for every $z \in XY$ there exist unique $x \in X$ and $y \in Y$ with $z = xy$ (equivalently, $X^{-1}X \cap YY^{-1} = \{1\}$). For a subset $A \subseteq G$, call a subset $B \subseteq G$ an $A$-complement if $AB$ is direct and $B$ is maximal (with respect to inclusion) among subsets with this property.

Question: Does there exist an infinite group $G$ with the property that for every subset $A \subseteq G$, all maximal $A$-complements $B \subseteq G$ have the same cardinality?

(Equivalently, for an infinite $G$, the condition that $AB$ is direct and $B$ is maximal is equivalent to $A^{-1}A \cap BB^{-1} = \{1\}$ together with $A^{-1}AB = G$, which forces $|G| = |A|\cdot|B|$. Hence the property only needs to be checked for those $A$ with $|A| = |G \setminus A|$.)

For a finite group $G$, let $\chi_1(G)$ denote the multiset of degrees of all irreducible complex characters of $G$, counted with their multiplicities (equivalently, $\chi_1(G)$ records, for each positive integer $d$, the number of irreducible complex characters of $G$ of degree $d$). Recall that a finite group $G$ is called:

- quasisimple if $G$ is perfect (i.e., $G = [G,G]$) and $G/Z(G)$ is non-abelian simple.

Let $H$ be a finite group with $\chi_1(H) = \chi_1(G)$ (equality of multisets of irreducible character degrees).

(a) If $G$ is almost simple, must $H \cong G$?

(b) If $G$ is quasisimple, must $H \cong G$?

Let $G$ be a finite group and $p$ a prime. Denote by $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$ the localization of $\mathbb{Z}$ at the prime ideal $(p)$, and by $\mathbb{F}_p$ the field with $p$ elements. Consider the group rings $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}G$, $\mathbb{Q}G$, and $\mathbb{F}_p G$.

For every simple $\mathbb{Q}G$-module $V$, choose a $G$-invariant $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}$-lattice $L\subseteq V$ (such a lattice exists, and although it is not unique, the resulting class of $\mathbb{F}_p G$-modules is well-defined up to the relations used below). Let $\mathcal{X}$ denote the class of all $\mathbb{F}_p G$-modules of the form $L/pL$ obtained in this way (the "reductions modulo $p$" of simple $\mathbb{Q}G$-modules).

Recall that a ring $R$ is called semiperfect if $R/J(R)$ is semisimple and idempotents lift modulo the Jacobson radical $J(R)$. Let $K_0(\mathbb{F}_p G)$ denote the Grothendieck group of finitely generated $\mathbb{F}_p G$-modules with respect to short exact sequences.

Question: Is it true that $\mathbb{Z}_{(p)}G$ is semiperfect if and only if every projective indecomposable $\mathbb{F}_p G$-module can be expressed as an $\mathbb{N}$-linear combination of classes of modules from $\mathcal{X}$ inside $K_0(\mathbb{F}_p G)$?

It is known that the "only if" direction holds, and that the equivalence holds when $p\nmid |G|$. Determine whether the equivalence holds in general.

Let $\mathrm{Aut}(F[x_1,\dots,x_n])$ denote its group of $F$-algebra automorphisms, and let $\Gamma$ be the principal congruence subgroup consisting of all automorphisms $\varphi$ such that, for every $i\in\{1,\dots,n\}$, $\varphi(x_i) \equiv x_i$ modulo terms of degree $\ge 2$ (i.e.\ $\varphi(x_i)-x_i$ lies in the square of the augmentation ideal $(x_1,\dots,x_n)$). It is known that $\Gamma$ is a residually-$p$ group, so it has a pro-$p$ completion $\widehat{\Gamma}_p$. Recall that a pro-$p$ group $G$ is said to satisfy a pro-$p$ identity if there exists a nontrivial element $w$ in the free pro-$p$ group $F_k$ on some finite number $k$ of generators such that $w$ vanishes under every continuous homomorphism $F_k\to G$.

Question: Does $\Gamma$ satisfy a pro-$p$ identity (equivalently, does its pro-$p$ completion satisfy a pro-$p$ identity)?

In non-commutative (group-based) cryptography, a platform group $G$ is a (typically non-abelian) group used to instantiate cryptographic primitives such as key-exchange protocols (e.g., the Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld protocol or the Ko–Lee/Diffie–Hellman-type conjugacy protocol), digital signatures, and authentication schemes. Such a platform group is required to admit (i) an efficiently computable normal form or a solvable word problem so that elements can be represented and compared efficiently, (ii) an efficient method to sample elements from a distribution that produces hard instances of the underlying algorithmic problem (e.g., the conjugacy search problem, the simultaneous conjugacy search problem, or the decomposition problem), and (iii) no known efficient (probabilistic polynomial-time) algorithm solving the underlying hard problem on a noticeable fraction of instances.

Determine whether, for the purposes of building secure non-commutative cryptographic schemes meeting the above requirements, the platform group $G$ should be taken to be finite or infinite. Specifically, decide which of the following holds:

(a) There exists a family of finite non-abelian groups $\{G_n\}_{n\in\mathbb N}$, with $|G_n|$ growing at most exponentially in a security parameter $n$, on which a chosen group-based hard problem (such as the conjugacy search problem) is provably or empirically intractable, yielding cryptographic schemes with security at least comparable to those built on infinite platform groups; or

(b) Any family of finite non-abelian platform groups admits a subexponential-time attack against the standard group-based hard problems, so that secure non-commutative group-based cryptography essentially requires infinite platform groups (such as braid groups, polycyclic groups, Thompson's group $F$, free metabelian groups, or right-angled Artin groups).

Provide either a construction establishing (a) or a reduction/attack establishing (b).

The question of whether platform groups in non-commutative group-based cryptography should be finite or infinite remains a guiding open design question in the field. Let $p$ be a prime and let $G$ be a finite $p$-soluble group, i.e., a finite group all of whose composition factors are either $p$-groups or $p'$-groups. Recall that the $p$-length $\ell_p(G)$ of $G$ is the number of $p$-factors in a shortest normal series of $G$ whose factors are either $p$-groups or $p'$-groups. Suppose that $P$ is a Sylow $p$-subgroup of $G$ and that $A \trianglelefteq P$ is a normal subgroup of $P$ of exponent dividing $p^{e}$ (so every element of $A$ has order at most $p^{e}$). Let $A^{G} = \langle A^{g} : g \in G\rangle$ denote the normal closure of $A$ in $G$.

Determine whether the $p$-length $\ell_p(A^{G})$ of the normal closure $A^{G}$ is bounded above by a function depending only on $p$ and $e$ (a $(p,e)$-bounded quantity). More strongly, decide whether $\ell_p(A^{G})$ can be bounded above by a function of $e$ alone, independent of $p$ and of $G$.

Let G be a finite soluble group and let φ be an automorphism of G. Denote by |φ| the order of φ, by C_G(φ) = {g ∈ G : φ(g) = g} the fixed-point subgroup of φ in G, and by ⟨φ⟩ the cyclic subgroup generated by φ in Aut(G); the composition length of ⟨φ⟩ is the number of prime factors of |φ| counted with multiplicity. Recall that the Fitting height (nilpotent length) h(H) of a finite soluble group H is the length of the shortest normal series of H all of whose factors are nilpotent.

Decide each of the following.

(a) Does there exist a function f₁ depending only on |φ|, and a function g₁ depending only on |φ| and |C_G(φ)|, such that G always contains a subgroup H with [G : H] ≤ g₁(|φ|, |C_G(φ)|) and h(H) ≤ f₁(|φ|) ?

(b) Does there exist a function f₂ depending only on the composition length c(|φ|) of ⟨φ⟩, and a function g₂ depending only on |φ| and |C_G(φ)|, such that G always contains a subgroup H with [G : H] ≤ g₂(|φ|, |C_G(φ)|) and h(H) ≤ f₂(c(|φ|)) ?

It is known that part (b) (and hence (a)) holds in the special cases when |φ| is a prime power, and when gcd(|G|, |φ|) = 1. The problem is to settle the general case.

representations.normalized:
Let $G$ be a finite soluble group and let $A$ be a finite nilpotent group acting on $G$ by automorphisms. The Fitting height (nilpotent length) $h(G)$ of $G$ is the length of the shortest normal series
$$1 = F_0 \le F_1 \le \cdots \le F_h = G$$
in which each quotient $F_{i+1}/F_i$ is nilpotent. Let $C_G(A) = \{g \in G : g^a = g \text{ for all } a \in A\}$ denote the fixed-point subgroup.

Question: Does there exist a function $f : \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that
$$h(G) \le f(|A|,\,|C_G(A)|)$$
for every finite soluble group $G$ and every finite nilpotent group $A$ acting on $G$ by automorphisms?

(It is known that the answer is affirmative in each of the following cases: when $\gcd(|G|,|A|)=1$; when $A$ is cyclic; and when $C_G(A)=1$. Conversely, for every non-nilpotent finite group $A$ there exist finite soluble groups $G$ of arbitrarily large Fitting height admitting $A$ as a fixed-point-free group of automorphisms, so the nilpotency hypothesis on $A$ is essential.)

The question is a long-standing problem in finite group theory, recorded in the Kourovka Notebook. Affirmative answers are known in the coprime case (Thompson, Kurzweil, Turull, Hartley–Isaacs), the cyclic case, and the fixed-point-free case (Dade), but the general case for arbitrary nilpotent A with nontrivial fixed points and without coprimeness appears still open; recent work continues to address related/partial settings (e.g. Frobenius and Frobenius-like groups of automorphisms) without resolving the general problem.

Definitions. Let G be a finite group.

(a) G is called monomial (or an M-group) if every irreducible complex character of G is induced from a linear (one-dimensional) character of some subgroup of G.

(b) G is called semi-abelian if there exists a chain of subgroups
   1 = G_0 ≤ G_1 ≤ G_2 ≤ ... ≤ G_n = G
such that for each i ∈ {0, 1, ..., n-1}, the group G_{i+1} is isomorphic to a quotient of a semidirect product A_i ⋊ G_i for some abelian group A_i (with some action of G_i on A_i).

Conjecture. Every semi-abelian finite group is monomial.

Prove or disprove this conjecture.

A one-relator group is a group given by a finite presentation of the form G = ⟨ x_1, …, x_n | r ⟩, where r is a single nontrivial cyclically reduced word in the free group F(x_1, …, x_n). A finitely generated group is called (Gromov-)hyperbolic if its Cayley graph (with respect to some, equivalently any, finite generating set) is a δ-hyperbolic metric space for some δ ≥ 0, i.e. every geodesic triangle has each side contained in the δ-neighbourhood of the union of the other two.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, on input a finite presentation ⟨ x_1, …, x_n | r ⟩ of a one-relator group, decides in finite time whether the group it defines is hyperbolic?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

A residue class of $\mathbb{Z}$ is a set of the form $r(m) = \{n \in \mathbb{Z} : n \equiv r \pmod{m}\}$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ and $0 \le r < m$. Given two disjoint residue classes $r_1(m_1)$ and $r_2(m_2)$, the associated class transposition $\tau_{r_1(m_1),\, r_2(m_2)}$ is the involution of $\mathbb{Z}$ that interchanges these two classes via the unique affine bijection $r_1 + km_1 \leftrightarrow r_2 + km_2$ ($k \in \mathbb{Z}$) and fixes every other integer pointwise. Let
$$\mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z}) := \langle \tau_{r_1(m_1),\, r_2(m_2)} : r_1(m_1) \cap r_2(m_2) = \varnothing \rangle$$
be the subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{Z})$ generated by all class transpositions. Each element $g \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ admits a finite description as a residue-class-wise affine permutation, so finite words in class transpositions provide an effective input encoding.

Decide: Is the conjugacy problem in $\mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ algorithmically decidable? That is, does there exist an algorithm that, given two elements $g, h \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ (each presented as a finite product of class transpositions), determines whether there exists $x \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ with $x^{-1} g x = h$?

Let $\mathbb{Z}$ denote the ring of integers. A *residue class* in $\mathbb{Z}$ is a set of the form $r(m) := \{r + km : k \in \mathbb{Z}\}$ for integers $m \geq 1$ and $0 \leq r < m$. Given two disjoint residue classes $r_1(m_1)$ and $r_2(m_2)$, the *class transposition* $\tau_{r_1(m_1),r_2(m_2)}$ is the permutation of $\mathbb{Z}$ that interchanges $r_1 + k m_1$ with $r_2 + k m_2$ for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ and fixes all other integers. Let $\mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ be the subgroup of $\mathrm{Sym}(\mathbb{Z})$ generated by all class transpositions. Every element $g \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ admits a finite description as a word in class transpositions (equivalently, as a residue-class-wise affine bijection of $\mathbb{Z}$ specified by finite data).

A *partition of $\mathbb{Z}$ into residue classes* is a finite partition $\mathbb{Z} = \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{n} r_i(m_i)$ where each block is a residue class; it is *nontrivial* if $n \geq 2$. An element $g \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$ is said to *permute* such a partition if $g$ maps the set of blocks to itself. A *cycle* of $g$ is an orbit of $\langle g \rangle$ on $\mathbb{Z}$; it is *finite* if its length is finite.

Decide whether each of the following decision problems, taking as input a finite description of an element $g \in \mathrm{CT}(\mathbb{Z})$, is algorithmically decidable:

(a) Does $g$ permute some nontrivial partition of $\mathbb{Z}$ into residue classes?

(b) Are all cycles of $g$ on $\mathbb{Z}$ finite?

(c) Does $g$ have no finite cycles on $\mathbb{Z}$?

Let Sym(Z) denote the symmetric group on the set Z of integers. For integers m ≥ 1 and 0 ≤ r < m write r(m) := r + mZ for the residue class of r modulo m. Given disjoint residue classes r1(m1) and r2(m2), the associated class transposition τ_{r1(m1), r2(m2)} ∈ Sym(Z) is the involution that interchanges, for every k ∈ Z, the integers r1 + k m1 and r2 + k m2 (in the natural order-preserving bijection between the two classes) and fixes all other integers.

Let CT(Z) denote the subgroup of Sym(Z) generated by all class transpositions. For any set P of odd primes, define
   CT_P(Z) := ⟨ τ_{r1(m1), r2(m2)} : r1(m1), r2(m2) disjoint, every prime divisor of m1·m2 lies in P ∪ {2} ⟩,
i.e. the subgroup of CT(Z) generated by those class transpositions whose moduli have all odd prime divisors in P.

Question. Let P1 and P2 be two distinct sets of odd primes such that neither is contained in the other (so P1 ⊄ P2 and P2 ⊄ P1). Is the inclusion
   ⟨ CT_{P1}(Z), CT_{P2}(Z) ⟩  ⊊  CT_{P1 ∪ P2}(Z)
necessarily strict? Equivalently, prove or disprove that the subgroup of CT(Z) generated by CT_{P1}(Z) and CT_{P2}(Z) is always a proper subgroup of CT_{P1 ∪ P2}(Z).

Let $K$ be a field and $n\geq 3$. An (elementary) net (or carpet) of order $n$ over $K$ is a collection $\sigma=(\sigma_{ij})_{1\le i\ne j\le n}$ of additive subgroups $\sigma_{ij}\subseteq K$ satisfying the carpet conditions $\sigma_{ir}\sigma_{rj}\subseteq \sigma_{ij}$ for all distinct indices $i,r,j$. A full net additionally specifies additive subgroups $\sigma_{ii}\subseteq K$ on the diagonal with $\sigma_{ij}\sigma_{jj}\subseteq\sigma_{ij}$ and $\sigma_{ii}\sigma_{ij}\subseteq\sigma_{ij}$. The net $\sigma$ is called irreducible if every off-diagonal subgroup $\sigma_{ij}$ is nonzero.

For an elementary net $\sigma$, let $E(\sigma)$ denote the elementary net subgroup, that is, the subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_n(K)$ generated by all elementary transvections $t_{ij}(\alpha)=I+\alpha e_{ij}$ with $\alpha\in\sigma_{ij}$ and $i\ne j$. The net $\sigma$ is said to be closed if $E(\sigma)$ contains no elementary transvections $t_{ij}(\alpha)$ with $\alpha\notin\sigma_{ij}$ (no "new" elementary transvections). The net $\sigma$ is called completable if there exist additive subgroups $\sigma_{ii}\subseteq K$ ($i=1,\dots,n$) such that the resulting full collection $(\sigma_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le n}$ is a (full) net. Every completable elementary net is closed.

It is known that over fields of characteristic $0$ and characteristic $2$ there exist irreducible closed elementary nets of order $n\ge 3$ that are not completable.

Question: Does there exist a field $K$ of odd characteristic and an integer $n\ge 3$ admitting an irreducible closed elementary net $\sigma$ of order $n$ over $K$ that is not completable?

It is known that over fields of characteristic $0$ and characteristic $2$ there exist irreducible closed elementary nets of order $n\ge 3$ that are not completable.

Question: Does there exist a field $K$ of odd characteristic and an integer $n\ge 3$ admitting an irreducible closed elementary net $\sigma$ of order $n$ over $K$ that is not completable?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The problem appears in the 2026 Kourovka Notebook list of new problems on group theory. No published solution was found in web searches; the question is posed as an open problem, with known existence results only in characteristics 0 and 2 (Koibaev, 2011 and 2021).

Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer and let $d \in \mathbb{Z}$ be an integer not divisible by the $n$-th power of any prime, and assume that the polynomial $x^n - d$ is irreducible over $\mathbb{Q}$. Set $\theta = \sqrt[n]{d}$ and let $K = \mathbb{Q}(\theta)$, a radical extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ of degree $n$. The multiplicative group $K^{*}$ acts on $K$ by multiplication, giving a canonical embedding $K^{*} \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(K)$. Identifying $\mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbb{Q}}(K)$ with $G = \mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{Q})$ via the basis $1, \theta, \theta^{2}, \ldots, \theta^{n-1}$, let $T(d) \leq G$ be the image of $K^{*}$ (an unsplit maximal torus of $G$).

A subgroup $H \leq G$ is said to be rich in elementary transvections if for every pair $i \neq j$ the set $\{\alpha \in \mathbb{Q} : I + \alpha e_{ij} \in H\}$ generates the additive group used in defining the associated net. To any such $H$ one associates a net (carpet) of additive subgroups $\sigma = \sigma(H) = (\sigma_{ij})$ of $\mathbb{Q}$, and the net group $G(\sigma) \leq G$ consists of matrices whose $(i,j)$-entry lies in $\sigma_{ij}$ off the diagonal (with appropriate diagonal conditions). Let $E(\sigma) \leq G(\sigma)$ be the subgroup generated by all elementary transvections $I + \alpha e_{ij}$ with $\alpha \in \sigma_{ij}$, $i \neq j$.

Now suppose $H \leq G$ contains $T(d)$ and at least one one-dimensional transformation (a transvection). Then $H$ is rich in elementary transvections and so determines such a net $\sigma = \sigma(H)$ and subgroup $E(\sigma)$.

Question: Is it always true that
$$H \leq N_{G}(E(\sigma))?$$

(The inclusion is known to hold for $n = 2$.)

Definitions. Let G be a finitely generated group with a fixed finite generating set S, and let L_S: G → ℤ_{≥0} denote the corresponding word length (word metric from the identity). An element g ∈ G is called distorted in G if

    lim_{n→∞} L_S(g^n)/n = 0.

This property does not depend on the choice of the finite generating set S. For an arbitrary (not necessarily finitely generated) group H, an element g ∈ H is called distorted in H if there exists a finitely generated subgroup G ≤ H with g ∈ G such that g is distorted in G.

A group H is called left-orderable if there exists a total order ≤ on H that is invariant under left multiplication: for all a, b, c ∈ H, a ≤ b implies ca ≤ cb.

Question. Does there exist a finitely generated left-orderable group H such that every nontrivial element g ∈ H is distorted in H?

Non-commutative (nonabelian) group-based cryptography refers to cryptographic protocols whose security relies on the computational hardness of problems formulated in nonabelian groups, such as the conjugacy search problem, the simultaneous conjugacy search problem, the word problem, the membership problem, the twisted conjugacy search problem, and related problems in groups such as braid groups, polycyclic groups, Thompson's group, matrix groups over finite rings, and finitely presented groups given by generators and relations. Examples of such protocols include the Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld key exchange, the Ko–Lee key exchange, Stickel's protocol, and various commutator/decomposition-based key agreements.

GAP (Groups, Algorithms, Programming) is an open-source computer algebra system designed for computational discrete algebra, with particular emphasis on computational group theory. It provides a high-level programming language, a library of algorithms for finite and finitely presented groups, permutation groups, polycyclic groups, matrix groups, and finite fields, together with extensive data libraries of algebraic objects.

Determine whether GAP can serve as a practical and cryptographically secure implementation platform for nonabelian group-based cryptographic schemes. More precisely:

(a) Identify a class of nonabelian group-based protocols (key exchange, public-key encryption, digital signature, or authentication) whose group-theoretic primitives — including generation of platform groups, sampling of secret elements, normal form computation, multiplication, inversion, and rewriting — can be implemented in GAP with running times suitable for practical use at standard security parameters.

(b) Provide a quantitative analysis showing that such a GAP-based implementation resists known cryptanalytic attacks (length-based attacks, linear-algebra attacks, linear-decomposition attacks, quantum attacks where relevant) while remaining efficient, or alternatively prove that GAP's computational model imposes inherent obstructions (e.g., side-channel leakage, lack of constant-time arithmetic, performance limits in normal-form algorithms) that prevent any such implementation from being simultaneously practical and secure.

The conjugacy class of an element $x \in G$ is the set $\{gxg^{-1} : g \in G\}$; the identity always forms a conjugacy class by itself. A group has "only one nontrivial conjugacy class" if all non-identity elements are pairwise conjugate, i.e., $G \setminus \{1\}$ is a single conjugacy class.

Question: Does there exist a finitely generated left-orderable group $G$ such that all non-identity elements of $G$ are conjugate to one another?

The Wiegold conjecture remains open in general. It is known only in limited cases: Gilman, and later Evans, established it for various families; Avni–Garion used results of Larsen–Pink to obtain transitivity for certain finite simple groups of Lie type in characteristic ≠ 2 with high rank. A 2025 preprint addresses the case of small Ree groups, and Lubotzky's survey discusses the conjecture as still open.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are conventionally divided into two observational classes by means of the duration measure T90 (the time interval over which 5%–95% of the burst's gamma-ray fluence is detected) together with spectral hardness: "long/soft" bursts (T90 ≳ 2 s) and "short/hard" bursts (T90 ≲ 2 s). However, T90 depends on the detector's bandpass, sensitivity, and background, and the long/short observational divide does not faithfully track the underlying progenitor: some long-duration bursts are produced by compact-object mergers and some short-duration bursts arise from massive-star core collapse.

Define two physical progenitor classes:
- Type II GRBs: events produced by the catastrophic collapse of a massive star (typically associated with a broad-lined Type Ic supernova, found in star-forming galaxies);
- Type I GRBs: events produced by the merger of compact objects (no associated supernova, may be found in all galaxy types).

Problem. Devise a multi-parameter classification scheme — using a combination of prompt-emission, afterglow, and host-galaxy observables (e.g., T90, spectral hardness, intrinsic peak energy E_{p,i}, isotropic-equivalent energy E_{iso}, minimum variability timescale, presence/absence of an associated supernova, host-galaxy specific star-formation rate, offset from host, etc.) — that maps any observed GRB to its physical progenitor class (Type I vs. Type II) more reliably than the T90-based criterion, and specify objective decision rules together with quantitative thresholds or a discriminant function realizing this mapping.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Multiple classification schemes beyond T90 have been proposed and are actively being refined. Zhang et al. introduced the Type I/Type II framework based on multiple observables (prompt emission, afterglow, supernova association, host galaxy). More recent works propose discriminants such as the EH and EHD parameters built from E_{p,i}, E_{iso}, and intrinsic T90, the minimum variability timescale (MVT), and machine-learning classifiers. These approaches improve on T90 alone but ambiguous cases remain (e.g., merger-driven long GRBs), so a universally accepted, fully reliable scheme has not yet been established. The problem is therefore best characterized as partially solved and still actively investigated.

representations.normalized:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are brief, intense flashes of gamma-ray radiation observed from cosmological distances. Phenomenologically they are divided into two main observational classes based on duration and spectral hardness: long-soft GRBs (typically with prompt-emission durations T_{90} > 2 s) and short-hard GRBs (typically with T_{90} < 2 s). It is widely conjectured that long-soft GRBs originate from the core collapse of certain rapidly rotating massive stars (the "collapsar" or massive-star channel), supported by a limited number of secure spectroscopic associations between long GRBs and Type Ic broad-lined supernovae, while short-hard GRBs originate from the merger of compact-object binaries (neutron star–neutron star or neutron star–black hole), supported only by indirect evidence such as host-galaxy demographics and offset distributions. However, only a small, observationally biased subset of long GRBs have confirmed supernova counterparts, and certain short-duration events as well as some high-redshift bursts exhibit properties that are difficult to reconcile with a simple compact-binary merger origin.

Problem. Identify the actual astrophysical progenitor systems that produce the main observational classes of gamma-ray bursts. Specifically:
(a) Determine which stellar evolutionary channels (e.g., single rapidly rotating Wolf–Rayet stars, tidally spun-up binary helium stars, chemically homogeneous massive stars, or other configurations) give rise to the massive-star (long-soft) GRB class, and characterize the conditions under which such progenitors yield a successful relativistic jet and an accompanying supernova.
(b) Determine which compact-object channels (e.g., binary neutron star mergers, neutron star–black hole mergers, accretion-induced collapse, magnetar giant flares, or other compact-star configurations) give rise to the compact-star (short-hard) GRB class, and account for short-duration or high-redshift events whose properties are not naturally explained by a binary neutron star merger.
Provide a mapping from progenitor channel to observable signatures (duration distribution, spectral properties, host galaxy demographics, offset distributions, kilonova/supernova counterparts, gravitational-wave signatures) sufficient to discriminate between the proposed channels.

For each positive integer $n$, let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $\{1,2,\dots,n\}$, and define the normalized Hamming distance on $S_n$ by
$$d_n(\sigma,\tau) = \frac{1}{n}\,\bigl|\{x \in \{1,\dots,n\} : \sigma(x) \neq \tau(x)\}\bigr|.$$
Let $G$ be a finitely generated group. A sequence of (set-theoretic) maps $f_n : G \to S_n$ is called an almost-homomorphism if for every $g,h \in G$,
$$d_n\bigl(f_n(g)\,f_n(h),\ f_n(gh)\bigr) \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$
The almost-homomorphism $\{f_n\}$ is said to be close to a homomorphism if there exists a sequence of group homomorphisms $\rho_n : G \to S_n$ such that for every $g \in G$,
$$d_n\bigl(\rho_n(g),\ f_n(g)\bigr) \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n \to \infty.$$
The group $G$ is permutation stable if every almost-homomorphism of $G$ is close to a homomorphism. (Recall that a group is metabelian if its commutator subgroup is abelian.)

Prove or disprove: every finitely generated metabelian group is permutation stable.

The conjecture (attributed to Levit–Lubotzky) is, in general, still open. Significant partial progress is known: Levit and Lubotzky proved permutation stability of permutational wreath products of finitely generated abelian groups, and the lamplighter group has all invariant random subgroups co-sofic (hence is permutation stable). Ishikura (arXiv:2301.07586) proved that all finitely generated free metabelian groups are permutation stable. The general metabelian case has not been resolved.

A gamma-ray burst (GRB) is a transient astrophysical event whose prompt emission requires a "central engine" capable of launching an outflow that is simultaneously (i) extremely luminous (isotropic-equivalent luminosities up to ~10^52–10^54 erg/s), (ii) highly relativistic (bulk Lorentz factors Γ ≳ 100), (iii) baryon-clean (very low rest-mass loading), (iv) collimated into a narrow jet, (v) strongly variable on millisecond timescales, and (vi) in some cases long-lasting (durations of tens to thousands of seconds, with extended emission and plateau phases).

Three theoretical central-engine models are commonly proposed:
1. A stellar-mass black hole surrounded by a hyper-accreting neutrino-cooled or magnetically arrested torus, powering a jet via neutrino annihilation or the Blandford–Znajek mechanism.
2. A newly born, rapidly rotating (millisecond-period), highly magnetized neutron star ("magnetar") with surface magnetic fields B ≳ 10^15 G, powering a jet via magnetic spin-down.
3. A newly born quark star (a compact star composed of deconfined strange quark matter), powering a jet via analogous magnetic or phase-transition-driven mechanisms.

Each of these three engine models has been argued in the literature to be capable of meeting most of the above observational constraints.

Problem: Determine which of these three central-engine types actually powers gamma-ray bursts in nature, and identify a specific observational diagnostic (e.g., a feature of the prompt light curve, spectrum, polarization, afterglow, gravitational-wave signature, or multimessenger signal) that uniquely distinguishes among the black-hole/torus, magnetar, and quark-star engine models.

The identification of the GRB central engine remains an open problem in high-energy astrophysics. Consider a relativistic outflow producing the prompt emission of a gamma-ray burst (GRB). Model the outflow as a relativistic jet carrying both baryonic matter (with possible additional lepton-pair and neutron components) and a large-scale magnetic field. Define the magnetization parameter at the prompt-emission radius as

  sigma = F_Poynting / F_matter,

i.e., the ratio of the Poynting (electromagnetic) energy flux to the matter (kinetic) energy flux through a comoving cross-section of the flow at the radius where the prompt gamma-rays are emitted.

Determine the composition of GRB ejecta at the prompt-emission radius. Specifically:

1. Decide whether the prompt-emission outflow is generically (a) matter-dominated (sigma << 1, a "fireball"), (b) of order equipartition (sigma ~ 1), or (c) magnetically/Poynting-flux dominated (sigma >> 1).

2. Determine the baryon loading, the contribution of electron–positron pairs, and the neutron content of the flow, and how these are related to sigma.

A complete solution would either provide a model-independent diagnostic that fixes sigma at the emission radius from observations, or establish theoretically which regime is realized in long and short GRBs.

Let $S_k$ denote the symmetric group on $\{1,2,\dots,k\}$. For positive integers $n \le m$, $\sigma \in S_n$, and $\tau \in S_m$, define the flexible normalized Hamming distance
$$d^{\mathrm{flex}}_n(\sigma,\tau) \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\Bigl(\,\bigl|\{x\in\{1,\dots,n\} : \sigma(x)\neq \tau(x)\}\bigr| \;+\; (m-n)\Bigr).$$
Let $G$ be a finitely generated group. A sequence $\{f_n\}$ with $f_n \colon G \to S_n$ is called an almost-homomorphism if for every $g,h \in G$,
$$\frac{1}{n}\bigl|\{x \in \{1,\dots,n\} : f_n(gh)(x) \neq f_n(g)f_n(h)(x)\}\bigr| \longrightarrow 0 \quad \text{as } n\to\infty.$$
The almost-homomorphism $\{f_n\}$ is said to be flexibly close to a homomorphism if there exist integers $m_n \ge n$ and group homomorphisms $\rho_n \colon G \to S_{m_n}$ such that $d^{\mathrm{flex}}_n(\rho_n(g), f_n(g)) \to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ for every $g \in G$.

The group $G$ is called flexibly permutation-stable if every almost-homomorphism of $G$ is flexibly close to a homomorphism in this sense.

Question: For each integer $n \ge 2$, is the special linear group $\mathrm{SL}_n(\mathbb{Z})$ flexibly permutation-stable?

The flexible permutation stability of SL_n(Z) (equivalently PSL_n(Z)) is a well-known open problem. Bowen and Burton (2019) showed that flexible stability of PSL_d(Z) for some d ≥ 5 would imply the existence of a non-sofic group, but the question itself remains unresolved. Let $G$ be a countable discrete group with a finite or countable generating set, and let $S_n$ denote the symmetric group on $n$ letters, equipped with the normalized Hamming (permutation) metric $d_n(\sigma,\tau) = \tfrac{1}{n}\,|\{i : \sigma(i) \ne \tau(i)\}|$.

A sequence of maps $\varphi_n : G \to S_{k_n}$ (with $k_n \to \infty$) is called an asymptotic homomorphism in permutations if for every $g,h \in G$,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} d_{k_n}\bigl(\varphi_n(gh),\,\varphi_n(g)\varphi_n(h)\bigr) = 0.$$

The group $G$ is said to be permutation-stable (P-stable) if for every asymptotic homomorphism $\varphi_n : G \to S_{k_n}$ there exists a sequence of genuine homomorphisms $\psi_n : G \to S_{k_n}$ such that $\lim_{n\to\infty} d_{k_n}(\varphi_n(g),\psi_n(g)) = 0$ for every $g \in G$.

The group $G$ is said to be flexibly permutation-stable if for every asymptotic homomorphism $\varphi_n : G \to S_{k_n}$ there exist integers $m_n \ge k_n$ with $(m_n - k_n)/k_n \to 0$, and genuine homomorphisms $\psi_n : G \to S_{m_n}$, such that, identifying $\{1,\dots,k_n\} \subset \{1,\dots,m_n\}$ and viewing each $\varphi_n(g)$ as an element of $S_{m_n}$ fixing the additional points,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} d_{m_n}\bigl(\varphi_n(g),\,\psi_n(g)\bigr) = 0 \quad \text{for every } g \in G.$$

Question: Must every flexibly permutation-stable group be permutation-stable?

The group $G$ is said to be flexibly permutation-stable if for every asymptotic homomorphism $\varphi_n : G \to S_{k_n}$ there exist integers $m_n \ge k_n$ with $(m_n - k_n)/k_n \to 0$, and genuine homomorphisms $\psi_n : G \to S_{m_n}$, such that, identifying $\{1,\dots,k_n\} \subset \{1,\dots,m_n\}$ and viewing each $\varphi_n(g)$ as an element of $S_{m_n}$ fixing the additional points,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty} d_{m_n}\bigl(\varphi_n(g),\,\psi_n(g)\bigr) = 0 \quad \text{for every } g \in G.$$

Question: Must every flexibly permutation-stable group be permutation-stable?

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of whether flexible permutation stability implies (strict) permutation stability is a recognized open problem in the theory of group stability. Recent literature (e.g., works on surface groups being flexibly stable, and on virtually free / free metabelian groups being permutation stable) treats the two notions as a priori distinct, with no known proof that flexible stability implies stability. No published resolution was found.

representations.normalized:
Consider a relativistic outflow ejected by a compact central engine that produces a gamma-ray burst. The outflow expands ultrarelativistically with bulk Lorentz factor Γ ≫ 1 and carries energy in a combination of kinetic (baryonic) and Poynting (magnetic) forms, characterized by the magnetization parameter σ = B'^2/(4π ρ' c^2), where B' and ρ' are the comoving magnetic field strength and rest-mass density. Above the photospheric radius (where the flow becomes optically thin to Thomson scattering), the prompt gamma-ray emission requires that a substantial fraction of the bulk energy be (i) dissipated and (ii) channeled into a nonthermal population of relativistic electrons (and possibly protons) capable of producing the observed keV–MeV spectrum.

Determine the dominant physical mechanism(s) responsible for this dissipation and particle acceleration above the photosphere. Specifically, evaluate among the following candidate mechanisms — internal shocks between shells of differing Lorentz factors in a baryon-dominated flow, external shocks with the circumburst medium, magnetic reconnection in a globally Poynting-flux-dominated outflow (σ ≳ 1), turbulence-driven small-scale reconnection in a magnetized plasma, and direct (ideal-MHD or force-free) electromagnetic acceleration of particles in large-scale fields — which can efficiently convert outflow energy into a power-law distribution of radiating particles, and under what conditions on σ, Γ, the radius of dissipation, the field geometry, and the turbulence/reconnection rate this efficient acceleration is possible. In particular, characterize whether and how diffusive shock acceleration operates in highly magnetized (σ ≳ 0.1) relativistic shocks, and quantify the efficiency of particle acceleration in turbulent reconnection regions in such plasmas.

status_assertions.value: open_status:open

The question of how GRB outflows dissipate energy and accelerate radiating particles above the photosphere remains an active open problem in high-energy astrophysics. Recent reviews and modeling work continue to debate internal shocks, photospheric dissipation, magnetic reconnection (e.g., ICMART models), and turbulent reconnection, with no consensus mechanism. PIC simulations show that diffusive shock acceleration is suppressed in highly magnetized perpendicular shocks, while reconnection-based acceleration in σ ≳ 1 plasmas is a topic of ongoing investigation.

Let $G$ be a finite group and $d$ a positive integer. Assume that $G$ has a family of subgroups $\{H_i\}_{i\in I}$ such that:
(i) each $H_i$ can be generated by $d$ elements, and
(ii) the indices $[G:H_i]$ have no nontrivial common divisor, i.e. $\gcd_{i\in I}[G:H_i]=1$.

The minimal number of generators $d(G)$ of $G$ is known to satisfy $d(G)\le d+2$ for every such $G$, and $d(G)\le d+1$ whenever $G$ is solvable.

Question: Is it true that, for every finite group $G$ as above, $G$ can be generated by $d+1$ elements?

In the standard fireball model of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), the prompt gamma-ray emission is produced by internal dissipation in a relativistic outflow launched by a compact central engine, while the subsequent broadband afterglow is attributed to synchrotron emission from the external forward shock formed when the outflow decelerates in the circumburst medium. Observations reveal, however, two systematic features in the early X-ray afterglow that cannot be reproduced by a purely external-shock model: (i) erratic X-ray flares occurring from tens to thousands of seconds after the trigger, with rise and decay timescales Δt/t ≪ 1 and steep decay indices that violate the high-latitude "curvature" relation expected from external-shock variability; and (ii) X-ray plateaus, sometimes terminated by an unusually steep drop ("internal plateaus") with temporal index α ≲ −3, inconsistent with any simple external-shock evolution.

Provide a physical mechanism for the GRB central engine that simultaneously explains:
1. Why the engine continues to inject energy long (up to 10^4–10^5 s) after the prompt episode ends.
2. The rapid variability and steep rise/decay of late X-ray flares.
3. The duration, luminosity, and abrupt termination of X-ray plateaus.

Candidate mechanisms to be assessed include, but are not limited to: (a) fallback accretion onto a newly formed black hole; (b) spin-down of a millisecond magnetar, possibly followed by collapse to a black hole; (c) fragmentation of a hyperaccreting accretion disk; (d) magnetic barriers and episodic accretion in a magnetically arrested disk; (e) post-merger magnetic reconnection activity in compact-binary remnants; and (f) phase transitions or activity associated with a quark star. Identify which mechanism (or combination) is consistent with the full phenomenology of late-time central-engine emission in both long and short GRBs.

In the standard fireball model of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), a relativistic jet launched by a central engine drives an external blast wave into the circumburst medium, producing a forward shock that heats swept-up ambient material and (during the early deceleration phase) a reverse shock that propagates back into the ejecta. Synchrotron emission from electrons accelerated at these shocks is predicted to give rise to broadband afterglow light curves whose temporal and spectral indices are linked by closure relations depending on the electron energy distribution index p, the circumburst density profile, the cooling regime, and the jet geometry. When the bulk Lorentz factor Γ of a collimated jet of half-opening angle θ_j drops below 1/θ_j, the model predicts an achromatic temporal steepening (a "jet break") observable simultaneously at all wavelengths.

In the Swift era, X-ray and optical afterglow light curves frequently exhibit multiple components — including steep decays, plateaus, flares, and chromatic breaks — that are not naturally accounted for by a single external forward-shock component, suggesting prolonged contributions from the central engine.

Provide a quantitative, observationally testable prescription that does the following:

(a) Specifies, for an arbitrary multi-wavelength GRB afterglow data set, an algorithm to decompose the observed light curve into (i) genuine external forward-shock emission, (ii) external reverse-shock emission, and (iii) emission attributable to long-lasting central-engine activity, using only temporal indices, spectral indices, closure relations, and cross-band timing.

(b) Defines a precise notion of an achromatic ("platinum") jet break — i.e., a simultaneous temporal break at all observed wavelengths consistent with the post-jet-break closure relations — and determines whether such a break exists in the current sample of well-monitored GRB afterglows once central-engine contributions identified by (a) are subtracted.

(c) Identifies clean signatures of the reverse shock (e.g., optical flash, radio flare timing, polarization) that survive after the subtraction in (a) and that allow unambiguous determination of the magnetization parameter and Lorentz factor of the ejecta.

In particular, decide whether, after removal of internal/central-engine components, the remaining afterglow emission of typical Swift-era GRBs is consistent with a single-component external forward + reverse shock model, and whether truly achromatic jet breaks occur.

Subsequent systematic studies (e.g., Wang et al. 2015, ApJS 219, 9; Racusin et al. 2009, ApJ 698, 43) have shown that closure-relation tests and multi-wavelength decompositions can attribute roughly half of Swift GRB afterglows to a simple external forward shock, rising to >90% when long-lasting reverse shocks, structured jets, and arbitrary medium profiles are invoked. Some achromatic breaks (e.g., short GRB 140903A) have been identified, but no universally accepted "platinum" sample of strictly achromatic jet breaks across all bands has emerged. The general decomposition and reverse-shock identification problem remains an active research area without a definitive solution.

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are transient cosmic explosions whose electromagnetic emission is conventionally divided into a short, highly variable "prompt" phase (peaking in the keV–MeV band) and a longer-lasting multiwavelength "afterglow" phase. Observations with the Large Area Telescope (LAT) onboard the Fermi satellite have revealed a high-energy (>100 MeV) component with three characteristic features:

(i) the onset of LAT photons is systematically delayed by up to several seconds with respect to the start of the keV–MeV prompt emission;
(ii) after the prompt phase ends, the >100 MeV (GeV) flux exhibits a long-lived, smoothly decaying tail extending well beyond the prompt duration;
(iii) the spectral relation between the GeV band and the MeV band varies between bursts and within a single burst (sometimes consistent with a single Band-function extrapolation, sometimes requiring an additional hard component).

Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are transient cosmic explosions whose electromagnetic emission is conventionally divided into a short, highly variable "prompt" phase (peaking in the keV–MeV band) and a longer-lasting multiwavelength "afterglow" phase. Observations with the Large Area Telescope (LAT) onboard the Fermi satellite have revealed a high-energy (>100 MeV) component with three characteristic features:

(i) the onset of LAT photons is systematically delayed by up to several seconds with respect to the start of the keV–MeV prompt emission;
(ii) after the prompt phase ends, the >100 MeV (GeV) flux exhibits a long-lived, smoothly decaying tail extending well beyond the prompt duration;
(iii) the spectral relation between the GeV band and the MeV band varies between bursts and within a single burst (sometimes consistent with a single Band-function extrapolation, sometimes requiring an additional hard component).

Provide a physical model of GRB emission above 100 MeV that simultaneously explains (i)–(iii). The model must specify the radiation mechanism(s) (e.g., synchrotron, inverse Compton, hadronic) and the emission site, and in particular must determine, for each of these three features, whether the >100 MeV signal arises from:
(a) internal dissipation within the relativistic outflow (the same region producing the MeV prompt emission),
(b) external-shock afterglow emission produced as the outflow decelerates in the circumburst medium, or
(c) a superposition of two or more such components with different temporal and spectral behavior.

The required answer is a single, predictive framework that accounts for the delayed onset, the extended GeV decay, and the burst-to-burst variation in the GeV/MeV spectral relation.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

Subsequent literature (2019–2025) provides strong evidence that the long-lived >100 MeV decay phase is dominated by external-shock afterglow emission (synchrotron from shock-accelerated electrons, with inverse Compton extending to TeV energies), explaining the delayed onset and long tail. However, the prompt-phase >100 MeV emission, the burst-to-burst variation in the GeV/MeV spectral relation, and the precise role of internal versus external dissipation remain debated; recent work argues for a superposition of internal (prompt) and external (afterglow) components. Thus the problem is partially solved rather than fully resolved.

Long-duration gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) are believed to arise from the collapse of certain massive stars. Let R_GRB(z) denote the comoving rate density of long-duration GRBs as a function of redshift z, and let ψ_*(z) denote the cosmic star-formation rate density. A naive "tracer" hypothesis posits that there exist a redshift-independent constant k > 0 such that R_GRB(z) = k · ψ_*(z) for all z (after correction for instrumental selection effects, beaming, and luminosity function).

Determine whether massive-star (long-duration) GRBs are reliable tracers of the cosmic star-formation history in this sense across all cosmic epochs, particularly at high redshift (z ≳ 3). Specifically:

(a) Decide whether the proportionality R_GRB(z) ∝ ψ_*(z) holds, or whether an additional redshift-dependent factor f(z) (for example arising from a metallicity threshold, an evolving initial mass function, evolving luminosity function, or evolving beaming/jet properties) is required so that R_GRB(z) = k · f(z) · ψ_*(z).

(b) If such a factor f(z) is required, characterize its functional form and identify the dominant physical mechanism (metallicity bias, IMF evolution, luminosity-function evolution, beaming-angle evolution, or a combination) responsible for the deviation.

(c) Assess whether, after correcting for any such bias, GRB-derived measurements of ψ_*(z) at high redshift are consistent with independent determinations from galaxy surveys.

Let Γ be a finite connected simple graph of diameter d, and let d_Γ(·,·) denote the graph distance in Γ. For each i ∈ {1, 2, …, d} define Γ_i to be the graph on the same vertex set as Γ in which two distinct vertices u, w are adjacent if and only if d_Γ(u, w) = i.

Recall that Γ is called distance-regular if for all i ∈ {0,1,…,d} and all vertices u, w with d_Γ(u, w) = i, the numbers
  c_i = |{x : d_Γ(u, x) = i−1, d_Γ(x, w) = 1}|,
  a_i = |{x : d_Γ(u, x) = i, d_Γ(x, w) = 1}|,
  b_i = |{x : d_Γ(u, x) = i+1, d_Γ(x, w) = 1}|
depend only on i (not on the particular pair u, w). A distance-regular graph of diameter d is Q-polynomial (with respect to some ordering E_0, E_1, …, E_d of its primitive idempotents) if there exist scalars such that, in the Bose–Mesner algebra under entrywise multiplication, E_1 ∘ E_j is a linear combination of E_{j−1}, E_j, E_{j+1} for each j, equivalently if the dual eigenvalue sequence makes the dual intersection numbers tridiagonal.

A graph on v vertices is strongly regular with parameters (v, k, λ, μ) if it is k-regular, every two adjacent vertices have exactly λ common neighbours, and every two non-adjacent vertices have exactly μ common neighbours.

Question: Does there exist a Q-polynomial distance-regular graph Γ of diameter 3 such that both Γ_2 and Γ_3 are strongly regular?

holds for every finite group $G$ and every prime $p$.

status_assertions.value: open_status:partially_solved

The conjecture remains open in general. It is known to hold for p = 2 (Malle, Adv. Math. 380 (2021), 107609), and earlier results of Willems established it for p-solvable groups (groups with a p-complement). Tong-Viet has reduced the conjecture to a statement about quasi-simple groups, and partial verifications exist for certain families of quasi-simple groups at odd primes, but no full proof is known.
